events.title: We left our house in a city for a rural cabin. Parts of the monthlong experience were great, but I wouldn't do it again.
events.summary: Leaving city life for a rural cabin meant confronting a lot of my fears. Kate Irwin I spent most of my adult life in cities before moving to a rural cabin for my husband's job. It was hard to adjust, and I had to confront many of my phobias before moving back home. Although I wouldn't choose to live in a cabin again, I'm grateful for what the experience taught me. At the end of the summer, I packed my bags and two cats and got on a plane by myself, leaving our spacious home in Portland, Oregon, for a two-bedroom cabin in the remote woods of upstate New York. I was planning to live there temporarily so I could spend some time with my husband, who had rented the place while he was working on a movie in the area. He had moved to the area a few weeks earlier to start work, and he would stay there until mid-November when the project wrapped. His options for where to stay were limited: a room at a Best Western , or a quaint cottage with a wood-burning stove and brick flooring on a historic acreage with farm animals. If I hadn't planned to come, he might have just chosen the hotel room, but he wanted a pet-friendly option with a little more space. I saw staying in the cabin as a chance to slow down a bit after feeling work-related burnout — but I was nervous, too. The cabin showed me what I took for granted at home The cabin was a far cry from our house in Portland. Kate Irwin Immediately, there were some things I genuinely loved about rural living . One of my favorite parts was the privacy. The cabin sat next to a creek and a grove of trees on a massive acreage at the foot of a mountain. It was part farm, part forest. I rarely saw other people most days, and got plenty of work done. While at the cabin, I started working on the second draft of my novel while planning for my next full-time role. However, it was also tough to adjust to rustic life. For most of my adult life, I'd lived in cities, including Los Angeles, New York, Atlanta, and Portland. Back home in Portland, I'd gotten used to our walkable neighborhood with incredible coffee shops just steps away, plus a slew of local wine bars, restaurants, and other small businesses easily accessible by bike. Although there were a few charming spots in the general area, the surrounding town beyond the acreage was pretty lackluster, and we were living in a grocery-store desert . I was surprised by how little there really was to do, considering we were only about a two-hour drive from New York City. Then there was the cottage itself. After living in a house with a dishwasher and an espresso machine, I had to get used to sputtering hot-water taps and Keurig coffee. Still, none of these inconveniences was the end of the world, especially since I'd only be living here for one month. The biggest challenge, though, was confronting my obsessive-compulsive disorder . Living near so many insects forced me to face my OCD Our property had plenty of animals and insects. Kate Irwin Rustic cabin living meant that there were bugs everywhere , pretty much all the time. Moths, stinkbugs, crane flies the size of my palm, spiders, grasshoppers, and even crickets managed to sneak their way inside. Outside, I'd get swarmed by mosquitoes and gnats. One night, I counted over two dozen sizable bugs that had somehow snuck into our cabin. Sometimes the bugs made me feel trapped because I couldn't fully escape them, no matter where I was. This might be an annoying inconvenience for people used to suburban life or climates with fewer bugs, but for me — someone with OCD — it felt like a test from the universe. Although every person with OCD can and will have completely different fears, obsessions, and compulsions, many of mine center on fears of germs, disease, or contamination. For me, a fear of hurting myself or my pets due to something in the environment — for instance, ticks with Lyme disease — can trigger compulsive handwashing, body-checking, and a general sense of anxiety throughout the day. When these compulsions come into play, I often become less productive, more distracted, and late for everything. The presence of so many bugs, plus corners layered with dust and cobwebs, triggered my fears of contamination and heightened my anxiety. Early on, I was even afraid of walking on the grass outside, since upstate New York has many more reported cases of Lyme disease than in Oregon, my home base. I was also concerned that my spouse, while working on location in the woods or other areas, might bring ticks home on his clothes, transmit them to me, or fall ill from a bite. Being exposed to my fears eventually helped them fade I'm glad I had the chance to confront my fears head-on. Kate Irwin Despite all of this, about a week in, I started to settle into cabin life a bit. My fears were there, but nothing bad happened. The bugs didn't go away, but they didn't get us sick. The cats were happy. At one point, I walked across the grass to go see the goats on the property, and I didn't get any ticks. It might sound silly, but for me, this was a bit of a breakthrough. I love animals, nature, and traveling the world, but the intense, intrusive thoughts that OCD brings can make it difficult to enjoy a new adventure without a constant baseline feeling of anxiety. The best part about living in this rural landscape was being able to see and get close to so many animals. On the property, there were free-range chickens and geese, plus wild turkeys, foxes, deer, and tons of blue jays. And there was this squad of hilarious goats, sheep, and a cow. With time, I was able to enjoy the experience. Spending a month in upstate New York isn't something I'd do again, and after a month at the cottage, I was excited to return to our spacious house and walkable neighborhood. But I'm grateful for the experience that allowed me to try out a new lifestyle, challenge my OCD , and come out stronger. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
events.summary: Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by working multiple full-time public sector jobs Published 21 October 2026, 13:08 BST The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent". Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood. He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021. The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs. He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had other jobs. At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector. In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023. The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity". A succession of Chowdhury's line managers have told the jury that he performed poorly in his roles. Abigail Mounde, who was Chowdhury's line manager at the Department for Business and Trade previously told the court: ''Any basic tasks I asked him to do he either did late or not to the standard I would have expected." Chowdhury was asked whether he accepted the criticism of his performance, including the allegation he failed to deliver work on time. He replied: "I reject them all." The prosecution also alleges Chowdhury used sick notes from his doctor as part of the cover-up. But the prosecution said while he was telling some employers he was sick and unfit to work because of "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" he was not giving sick notes to other employers. The prosecution said this ''underlines the dishonesty involved in the whole affair". His line manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, arranged a video call in May 2023, to support him returning to work after a period of absence. In previous evidence she told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin. She told the court that as the call went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck." Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ told the court: ''This almost laughable incident demonstrates quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit.'' events.title: Foursquare co-founder says equity holders saw no returns from the company’s acquisition
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Last month, advertising company Infillion acquired location-data platform Foursquare, a once popular social network, at an undisclosed value. Now, in a new blog post , Foursquare co-founder and former CEO Dennis Crowley said that investors didn’t see any returns from the sale. Crowley referenced a post by an angel investor , inferred that neither preferred nor common stockholders got any value out of the deal, and said he was disappointed by the outcome. “I was heartbroken by this ending. So many people put so much time and energy and passion and love into building Foursquare – the company, the products, the brand, the culture. If you were part of it (or even close to it), you know exactly what I’m talking about. To our ~1600 former employees over 17 years, I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way that makes it seem like our collective efforts were worth… nothing?,” he said in the post. Crowley said that the company did well after it started focusing on enterprise business and had consecutive years with over $100 million in revenue. In 2019, the company raised capital from a private equity firm and, in 2021, brought in the banker who led the raise as CEO. Crowley blamed the final outcome on that transition, saying that the management of the company wasn’t able to preserve or create new value. Foursquare, which had raised over $411 million in funding according to PitchBook data, eventually shut down its app in 2024 . Several people reacted to Crowley’s post and said that Foursquare was very useful to them in discovering new places in their cities and also gave ideas for new apps . events.title: AI promises productivity, but for managers, it’s mostly a headache for now
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Companies are giving employees AI tools to make them more productive, but the tools appear to be creating new problems for their managers. More than half of senior leaders say they find it harder to evaluate employees’ work after adopting AI, according to a Nielsen survey of 1,700 directors and senior managers across seven countries, commissioned by work-management company Monday.com. The reason is that much of employees’ output now arrives polished in the manager’s inbox, making it hard to tell how much came from the employee and how much from AI. As a result, nearly half of managers say they spend more time reviewing and guiding their teams’ output than they used to. That’s not to say managers are unhappy about AI. Quite the opposite, in fact: 94% of the managers polled said they were excited to improve work using AI, and many are confident they know where to use it to get the most value. Michal Miller Levi, head of market research and customer insights at Monday.com, compared the enthusiasm to the early days of the internet in the 2000s, saying people see a similar kind of “magic” to AI. But the problem, she told TechCrunch, is simply that AI is developing faster than companies can adapt. “AI works very well for [managers] individually, but they also have a different role as managers. They need to drive the organization as well […] Their struggle is [due to] the fact that AI is just moving faster than the organizational processes,” Levi said. Managers are also reconsidering how they judge their teams: 78% of respondents said they have changed how they evaluate employees after adopting AI, placing greater weight on how well staff can create prompts, decide which tasks to delegate to AI, and experiment with new ways of working. But how fairly can employees be judged when managers can’t easily tell how much of their work was produced by AI? And what if the managers themselves are increasingly relying on AI to make those judgments? The survey found that 46% of managers use AI to help inform their decisions, and 39% of leaders are using AI to draft performance reviews. That practice runs the risk of introducing even more bias than usual into the review process, given that LLMs are, at their core, prediction machines, and tend to repeat human patterns found in their training data. Research from the Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research earlier this year found that “in the absence of clear objective standards and when individuals are rated independently,” LLMs tend to rate performance similarly to humans. And a research paper in early 2025 found that AI models can be biased against black male candidates, and “demonstrate significant biases, varying in terms of the directions and magnitudes across different social groups.” When I asked Levi whether using AI to weigh in on people’s performance could introduce outside bias into the process, she said companies have yet to work out how to handle such issues. AI is also changing what a manager’s day looks like. Someone has to decide which tasks to hand over to AI agents, check what they produce, and step in when something goes wrong. The report suggests that this supervision could amount to a new layer of “invisible labor.” The software itself is becoming harder to manage. Fifty-seven percent of managers say their organizations now have more tools in circulation than before, and about 51% said their tools had grown more interdependent and clustered since adopting AI. Only 29% described their AI infrastructure as fully optimized and centralized. Levi said businesses had expected AI to help shrink their software stacks. Instead, they’re dealing with more apps, integrations, and shadow AI usage as employees adopt tools outside their companies’ approved systems. “Managers completed 2025 with the feeling that they will consolidate tools, actually; that they’ll reduce the number of software. But what happened is that the number of tools that they’re using increased,” Levi said. “More than 50% are saying that they’re using more tools now than they did last year, and it’s not stopping […].” This need for control seems to be growing urgent as companies deploy AI agents that can act on their own. The survey found that 58% of managers expect to oversee more AI agents than human employees within the next year, and 46% worry about losing control over those agents’ actions. There’s also quite a bit of fear over being held responsible for decisions made by AI (35% of respondents said so), as LLMs are still largely unpredictable. “They don’t want their agents to be fully autonomous,” Levi said, explaining that managers want people to be involved and consulted by AI when it comes to crucial tasks and decisions.

events.title: Total UK government debt hits £3tn for first time while inflation jumps to highest in nearly a year – business live
events.summary: UK's total government debt hits £3tn for first time The UK’s fiscal position is also not exactly rosy, as the latest public finance figures show. The Treasury ran a higher than expected budget deficit of £24.5bn last month as rising inflation pushed up the interest paid on government debt, increasing pressure on John Healey before his budget next week. Official figures show the government paid £10.9bn in debt interest : the highest September figure since records began, and only the eighth time the monthly number has been above £10bn. Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs. The Office for National Statistics said this had added £4bn to debt interest costs in September alone. Total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time – although as a share of the size of the economy it has dipped to 94%, from 95% a year ago. The £24.5bn monthly deficit on the public finances was up from £17bn in August, and £1.9bn higher than the independent Office for Budget Responsibility had forecast. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing is £97.8bn, the ONS said – £4.4bn lower than last year but still £6bn higher than the OBR expected. The data underlines the impact of the Iran war on the public finances. Healey has been keen to stress his determination to stay within the fiscal rules set out by his predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves . However, he is widely expected to accept a slimmer financial buffer, or “headroom”, against those rules than the £24bn Reeves had built up at the time of her spring forecast . Henning Diederichs , director for public sector at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales , said: The rising cost of borrowing and inflation mean that servicing the debt is a significant concern for the chancellor as he prepares for his first Budget next week. Pressures are mounting to provide additional support for rising energy bills, but the fiscal challenges to balance spending are becoming more acute, particularly as John Healey has less headroom than in the spring forecast. This is why the government needs to clarify the definition of current budget balance in the fiscal stability rule, given it is changing from a current budget surplus at this Budget. events.title: United Airlines set to open its biggest airport lounge in $2.6 billion overhaul at Houston hub
events.summary: United is opening its biggest-ever lounge, part of an overhaul at Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport. The new space in Terminal B can seat 800 people. Lounges overall are getting larger as more customers sign up for airline credit cards and gain elite status, or buy day passes. United Airlines is set to open its biggest airport lounge this week, which it says is the largest in the Americas, as airlines continue to plow money into the facilities for high-spending customers. The 54,000-square-foot lounge is opening Thursday at George Bush Intercontinental Airport's Terminal B in Houston, part of an overhaul of the facility that includes 22 gates for mainline aircraft. The airport, with more than 500 departures a day, is United's main connecting hub for flights to and from Latin America. The new club can seat 800 people and features an outdoor terrace for plane-spotting as well as two full-service bars and buffets. The lounge, part of United's $2.6 billion investment at the airport's Terminal B, shows how airlines are putting more money into larger spaces for premium-travel demand to attract the growing ranks of elite frequent flyers, co-branded credit card holders and customers just willing to spend more to fly. American Airlines earlier this month said it is planning its largest-ever lounge at its Charlotte Douglas International Airport hub in North Carolina. Delta Air Lines has expanded both its popular Delta Sky Clubs and its top-tier Delta One Lounges. Southwest Airlines is building its first-ever network of airport lounges , which are tied to its credit card partner, Chase . Last week, the carrier unveiled mock-ups of the lounges, which it is calling Icon. And JetBlue Airways opened lounges in New York and Boston in the past year. events.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX hitting $1 trillion in revenue in 2028 is 'no longer impossible'
events.summary: SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. JOEL SAGET/AFP via Getty Images Elon Musk says it's "no longer impossible" that SpaceX will generate $1 trillion of revenue in 2028. The SpaceX CEO said in August that his company projected that much revenue for 2030. SpaceX would have to grow its revenue 53-fold in three years to reach Musk's new figure. Elon Musk always shoots for the moon , but he's aiming even higher with his latest suggestion. "As crazy as this sounds, $1T in SpaceX revenue in 2028 is no longer impossible," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO said in a Tuesday post on X. As crazy as this sounds, $1T in SpaceX revenue in 2028 is no longer impossible https://t.co/jF3Wue95nL — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 20, 2026 That's an even more ambitious timeframe than Musk has previously given. He said in August that SpaceX was internally projecting $1 trillion of revenue in 2030, and there was a "non-zero" chance it could reach that amount in 2029. Musk made his latest pronouncement within hours of saying on SpaceX's third-quarter earnings webcast that annual recurring revenue could reach between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027. In a post-earnings note, JPMorgan forecast SpaceX would generate $254 billion of revenue in 2027. If SpaceX were to generate $1 trillion in revenue in 2028, that would represent a 53-fold increase in three years. It earned just under $19 billion in 2025. It shared its historical financials prior to going public this summer. After the bell on Tuesday, SpaceX — the company behind Falcon rockets, Starlink satellites, X, and AI chatbot Grok — posted close to $15 billion in revenue last quarter , up 161% from the same period of 2025. The key driver was its super-intelligence  division, where revenue surged 830%, from around $800 million to $7.6 billion. SpaceX attributed the growth to new cloud services agreements, around $600 million of revenue from its recent Cursor acquisition, and increased Grok adoption by enterprises. To put Musk's $1 trillion revenue figure in context, Amazon and Walmart, the two highest-revenue companies on the planet, both generated a little over $700 billion in net sales last financial year. Musk is floating the possibility that SpaceX could generate more than 40% more revenue than either of them did last year, in about two years' time. It's unclear whether Musk is including Tesla, which generated about $95 billion of revenue last year, in his newest revenue figure. He revealed on Tuesday that Tesla and SpaceX have formed committees to explore a potential merger. Susannah Streeter, Wealth Club's chief investment strategist, told Business Insider by email that a tie-up could "combine expertise in AI, chips, robotics and connectivity." But she added that "bringing two enormous businesses with very different operations and capital demands under one roof would be a hugely complex undertaking." Streeter said that notching $1 trillion in annual revenue in 2028 would be a "very tall order" and require an "extraordinary leap in the scale of the business." "Moving the goalposts from 2030 to 2028 suggests he is increasingly confident that several growth drivers could accelerate at once, but there is a difference between a target that is technically possible and one that is commercially realistic," she added. Neil Wilson, UK investor strategist at Saxo Bank, told BI by email that Musk's latest revenue figure is "pushing it" and "would imply such an enormous pull-forward in demand as to defy credibility." Wilson added that he'd "never say never" about SpaceX hitting $1 trillion of revenue, "but by 2028 I'd say the chance is zero, whatever Elon says!" Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Telehealth Giant Hims Wants to Test Every Dude for Low Testosterone
events.summary: Talk of testosterone deficiency is hard to escape these days, with podcasters and politicians obsessing over how to avoid a “low T” lifestyle. As the hormone’s cultural salience deepens, demand is growing. In a timely move, telehealth giant Hims just launched a testosterone replacement therapy service for cisgender men. The direct-to-consumer juggernaut will offer two types of injectable treatments, as well as an oral pill option that can be sent to patients after they take an at-home capillary blood test. Peter Stahl, a urologist and a senior vice president of men’s health at Hims, wants to “cast as wide a net, and get as many people tested, as possible.” Hims, which started out selling erectile dysfunction medications, has expanded into women’s health and grown from a startup to a publicly traded company serving 2.9 million customers since it launched in 2017. Offering testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, is both a new phase for the health platform and a doubling down on men’s health care. “When we first started, we didn't have the capabilities to take care of a complex condition like testosterone deficiency,” Stahl says. “We've finally grown up.” The company will compete with a wide array of online clinics offering testosterone therapy, many of which have cropped up in the past few years using turnkey telehealth services to launch quickly. Many of these services market the medication as a lifestyle enhancer or anti-aging solution. Stahl sees testosterone deficiency as a medical condition that’s “really underdiagnosed” and “really misunderstood.” Testosterone became a controlled substance following the 1990 Anabolic Steroids Control Act, and for decades, taking it has carried an association with muscle-obsessed gym rats. “That created a lot of stigma,” he says. Older research also showed that testosterone therapy came with cardiovascular risks, though more recent findings suggest those concerns were overestimated. Testosterone levels have become a MAGA fixation. This fall, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth announced a mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for most male troops in the US armed services. Texas Republicans have been hurling the phrase “low T” as a masculinity-questioning insult in a hotly contested Senate midterm race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico. A survey of 2,000 American men this summer commissioned by Hims indicates that they are increasingly willing to talk to one another about testosterone treatment, but the stigma persists around taking medication to address low levels. Because testosterone is a controlled substance, it can’t be dispensed like many other treatments popular with digital clinics. Unlike GLP-1s and estrogen-based hormone replacement therapy , which are now often prescribed by clinicians after patients simply fill out a quick questionnaire , TRT requires "synchronous" care. That means any would-be users have to have a video chat with a clinician before getting a prescription, and for ongoing monitoring. “It's important to remember that testosterone therapy can cause infertility, and you don't give it to someone trying to conceive,” says urologist Mohit Khera, the director of Baylor College of Medicine’s Laboratory for Andrology Research at McNair Medical Institute. Khera sees telehealth TRT services as promising ways to expand access to the medication, “as long as it’s monitored appropriately.” While laboratory testing can show whether testosterone levels are below thresholds set by groups like the American Urological Association to indicate potential issues, diagnoses aren’t made based on bloodwork alone. Instead, clinicians assess labs along with patients’ symptoms and medical history. Common symptoms of hypogonadism (the technical term for the diagnosis) include sexual dysfunction and muscle loss. Stahl calls it a “powerful biomarker” for understanding someone’s health. “Quite frankly, it’s underutilized,” he says, noting that men with low testosterone have a 35 percent increased risk in overall mortality. The test doesn’t require a standard blood draw. Instead, Hims will send patients a Tasso blood collection device, a round single-use wearable that sticks to the upper arm and punctures the skin with microneedles to collect a small sample. (It may sound suspiciously like Theranos , but Tasso devices have a solid track record .) From there, the patient sends the collection off to a lab that will conduct an analysis of a broad selection of 21 different biomarkers to assess health, including triglycerides and thyroid hormones as well as testosterone. Based on the results, a patient might be prescribed a compounded injectable testosterone, a commercially available injectable testosterone, an oral pill—or something else entirely, if their testosterone levels are not low. Stahl sees hormone testing as a way to persuade otherwise-reticent men to go see a doctor.

events.title: How Israel’s war on Lebanon has cost young people with autism and ADHD
events.summary: Experts warn that war takes a heavy toll on neurodivergent people, who often rely on routine. Beirut, Lebanon – After her husband died from COVID-19 in 2020, Lena Kouyoumjian moved back to her parents’ house in Mazraat Yachouh, a village 20 minutes’ drive from Beirut. For Lena, energetic and outgoing, the move was difficult, but she accepted that she needed help to care for her 20-year-old daughter, Vana, who is autistic and non-verbal. Lena first noticed her daughter’s symptoms when she was two years old. Vana is still unable to communicate verbally how she feels, but her mother does her best to understand her. list 1 of 3 Lebanon’s children face physical, psychological trauma amid Israel’s war list 2 of 3 Psychological toll mounts as Lebanese villages erased by Israel’s war list 3 of 3 ‘An act of resistance’: Raja Shehadeh’s diaries find a new home in Scotland Like many autistic individuals – and neurodivergent people in general – Vana needs a supportive and stable environment, alongside a structured routine, to feel well. Lebanon has been engulfed in war since October 2023, with bombings across the country and an economic crisis continuing to impact all Lebanese, particularly neurodivergent people. When Israel escalated its attacks on southern Lebanon in March, as a trainer for children with disabilities, Lena understood that this could impact her autistic daughter. “Any sudden change in routine, loud noises, fear, or uncertainty can increase their anxiety and make them feel unsafe,” Lena told Al Jazeera. “I can see this in my daughter. Since the situation became more difficult, she has become more anxious and sensitive to the changes happening around her.” The symptoms of autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) vary depending on the person and condition, but they frequently include sensory issues and emotional dysregulation. ADHD and autism often occur together, combining to make AuDHD, where traits from both conditions can be seen. People with these neurodevelopmental conditions are often stigmatised by societies that do not fully understand them, including in Lebanon. While the pressures caused by Israel’s war on Lebanon and mass displacement have led to psychological issues for many, neurodivergent people are more vulnerable due to their need for consistent support and routine. “Being a parent of an autistic child isn’t something every parent can handle. A challenge I often face is deciding the amount of time and energy I should allocate to my child,” said Lena. Lebanon’s Autism Awareness Association (AAA) has provided support for both mother and child. Vana has attended classes at AAA, a nonprofit based in Antelias, outside Beirut, for the past six years, which serves as an alternative school for young autistic people. But rising costs in Lebanon during the war have prevented Vana from attending classes regularly. “Even transportation to her centre became very difficult, especially with the increasing financial challenges. At times, it became impossible for her to go, so she had to stay home,” Lena said. Ghada Hayek Makhoul, who co-founded AAA with other parents of autistic children in 2015, said the group has made constant efforts to increase awareness about the condition in Lebanon. “Many people don’t know what autism really is. They don’t know the spectrum; how it can vary from mild to moderate to severe,” Ghada told Al Jazeera. Ghada’s son, Anthony, is a calm 27-year-old autistic, non-verbal man who relies heavily on helpers. Although he is unable to speak, his mother said it is clear when he is distressed, putting his hands over his ears when he is in pain due to sensory discomfort. Autistic people can be more sensitive to noises than neurotypical people. During the war, people in Lebanon have been subjected to a harrowing range of sounds, from Israeli bombs exploding on the ground to the sonic booms of warplanes flying overhead. “So, imagine the drones all the time [for autistic people], the bombs, and the vibration of the bombs … all of this that we were hearing, so of course it affected him a lot,” Ghada said. “My son can’t listen to the TV any more due to the news. He switches it off and removes the remote control. It’s too triggering for him.” Anthony’s mother said he senses tension and anxiety, even if his understanding of what is being said or happening is limited. “[It affects] all the senses, everything. He doesn’t want to go into a pool any more. He used to love the water. And now, he doesn’t want to go into the pool any more,” Ghada said. “I don’t know what changed. Because it’s outside? Because of the sound? I don’t know.” Israel’s war on Lebanon has had a direct economic impact on the AAA and other organisations providing neurodivergent or psychological support. Lebanon’s economic crisis, with inflation potentially reaching 17 percent this year, has also led to a brain drain of professionals who could support neurodivergent people.

events.title: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are dominating the AI stock boom. Here's their edge
events.summary: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan captured nearly 80% of top-five bank equity trading revenues so far this year, generating a combined $52 billion. Growth was driven by "insatiable" hedge fund borrowing for leveraged bets on AI hardware and Asian semiconductor supply chains. The Big Three’s massive balance sheets allow them to absorb possible losses and handle risks that force smaller rivals to cede share. Relaxed rules around leverage helped to unlock bank balance sheets to meet record demand, though bodies including the International Monetary Fund cautioned against rising leverage. Fueled by the global boom in artificial intelligence stocks, relaxed capital rules and greater lending to hedge funds, big Wall Street banks have already had a banner year for equities trading — even with one quarter left to go. The five biggest investment banks have generated about $67 billion in equities revenue through Sept. 30, according to company filings. That is $7 billion more than what the group made during all of 2025, which itself was a record haul. But it's Wall Street's Big Three that have captured the largest slice of what is shaping up to be the industry's most lucrative arena: Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley have made a combined $52 billion in stock trading revenue so far this year, nearly 80% of the total. "When it comes to the AI mega trade, the Big Three consider each other their main competitors, and that's pretty much it," Mike Mayo , Wells Fargo banking analyst, told CNBC. "They've been best positioned to take advantage of this market." Wall Street banks are experiencing an epic run of blockbuster profits as the total value of the stock market balloons and trading activity from institutional and retail investors rises across stocks, ETFs and derivatives. Helping drive this activity are the loans that the banks, through their prime brokerages, are extending to hedge funds so that they can amplify their bets. Prime brokerage — the business of providing hedge funds with margin loans, securities lending and other trading services — has become a key battleground and source of growth. The Big Three's prime brokers are central to the larger equities story because they serve the largest funds across markets and products. Demand for leverage to make bets on AI hardware, hyperscalers and chip suppliers has reached new heights, bank executives said last week. At Goldman Sachs, equities financing activities jumped 96% in the third quarter to a record $3.37 billion. JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley don't break out that figure, but said they saw a similar dynamic. "I like your 'insatiable demand for capital' point. That feels about right," JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the bank's third-quarter conference call, responding to analyst questions about financing demands. "In this moment where AI is such an overwhelming theme ... there is capital being tapped through all kinds of different mechanisms," Barnum said. That demand has helped transform equity desks at the Big Three from cyclical, transactional businesses into more durable, high-margin lending engines, Wall Street executives say. The performance gap between Wall Street's giants and rivals including Bank of America and Citigroup highlights a widening divide in capital markets. "For clients, the value isn't just a price on one trade, it's coverage and continuity," Rachid Alaoui, JPMorgan global head of equities, told CNBC in an interview. "You want a dealer that can give you the full suite across products, and you want that service to travel with you across regions. That matters in stressed markets and periods of volatility." Executing multibillion-dollar bets, like leveraged swaps on volatile AI stocks or sector ETFs, can require an enormous balance sheet. The biggest banks can absorb potential $100 million losses without threatening their quarters, according to trading executives. Smaller or more niche banks can't underwrite single-trade risks of that magnitude, forcing them to decline the business or cede share. U.S. prime brokers have also benefited from the retreat of European banks including Credit Suisse from the equities business, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan . "Prime is one of the ultimate scale businesses," Chan said. "If you have a strong equities franchise, the hedge funds will want to transact with you because you have a bigger pool of trading opportunities with counterparties." While U.S. markets were swept up in software and cloud computing giants this year, trading executives say the fastest-growing frontier for equities was in Asia. Institutional investors poured into South Korea and Taiwan, targeting the "picks and shovels" of the AI supply chain: the memory chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers supporting data center construction, Alaoui said. For the Big Three, with their footprints across Tokyo; Hong Kong; Seoul, South Korea; and Mumbai, India; the Asia trade was a goldmine.

events.title: Heat pump tech is 170 years old. Pascal thinks it’s time for an update.
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When the experimental results came back, they puzzled Adam Slavney and Jinyoung Seo. They had been testing a new class of materials for more efficient refrigerators, air conditioners, and heat pumps , a mission that the cooling appliance industry has been on for eons. The measurements for the materials that the team was testing shouldn’t have been different, but they were. “Why are these things different? What did we change?” Slavney told TechCrunch. “We had an inkling of it within three-ish months, but we didn’t have definitive proof for a year or two.” That proof is now underpinning Slavney’s startup, Pascal , where he’s co-founder and CEO and Seo is co-founder and CTO. The company recently raised $8.5 million in a follow-on to its seed round, co-led by Sazze Partners and LB Investment with participation from KDB Silicon Valley, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. A refrigerator or heat pump using Pascal’s material promises to be around 20% more efficient than existing models, he said. (Both heat pumps and refrigerators use the same basic technology.) The startup has signed a contract with a multinational beverage company for a pilot of the technology. “This whole funding round came together originally because we got a customer contract earlier than we were expecting to,” Slavney said. Pascal is on track to deliver its first prototype early next year, and it hopes to follow that with a batch of more polished refrigerators in 2028. Scientists have been searching for better refrigerants for almost as long as refrigerators have existed. More recently, they’ve been looking for compounds that don’t harm the atmosphere in one way or another. They exist, but they also need to be at least as effective as existing refrigerants. “We’ve been playing whack-a-mole with refrigerants for 35 years, 40 years,” Slavney said. Older gaseous refrigerants like Freon ate a hole in the ozone layer, while newer ones like R-134a are still extremely potent greenhouse gases. “It’s just a never-ending treadmill,” he said. One alternative that has attracted researchers’ attention is a class of materials known as solid-state refrigerants. Because they’re solid, they can’t escape to the atmosphere, eliminating the climate and ozone concerns that haunt modern refrigerants. Solid-state refrigerants promise to make refrigerators and heat pumps more efficient. They work similarly to traditional refrigerants, giving off heat when squeezed and absorb it when that pressure is released. Before his serendipitous discovery, Slavney and his colleagues at Harvard University had been researching the materials. “We wanted to do some high-pressure measurements, and the instrument that we were using required us to use gas. So we used the gas and then we swapped to a different gas and we were like, why are these different?” Slavney said. After numerous additional experiments, the team realized they had discovered another path toward solid-state refrigeration. Rather than squeeze a solid block of material, Pascal’s heat pumps compress a gas — carbon dioxide — into a cartridge that contains a sponge-like material, which Slavney said is proprietary. As the carbon dioxide works its way into the porous material, the gas molecules inside the pores start bouncing off the walls. Those collisions transfer energy to the material, warming it up. A heat exchanger then exhausts some of that heat. Run it in reverse and the material absorbs energy from the heat exchanger and transfers it to the carbon dioxide molecules. In a Pascal refrigerator, two cartridges are running at any given time. One is absorbing heat from the inside of the refrigerator, transferring it to the carbon dioxide, while the other takes the heat from the carbon dioxide and transfers it to the outside air. Eventually, the cartridges become too hot and too cold, so the flow gets reversed. “The material is very robust,” Slavney said. “We’ve cycled it up to 300,000 times. It’s the equivalent of a year or so in operation.” The entire system moves heat more effectively than other solid-state refrigerants, which means that Pascal doesn’t have to operate at high pressures like other solid-state refrigerants might demand. “We’re using conventional systems to do it,” Slavney said. “That mean we believe we can make it cheap, and that means we can make it widespread.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor.

events.title: Jamie Dimon spent years warning about America’s reliance on China. A year in, JPMorgan has put $230 billion behind fixing it
events.summary: Jamie Dimon has warned for years that the U.S. has let itself become dangerously dependent on China. In his 2024 shareholder letter , the JPMorgan Chase CEO argued America had “slept” while China built its economic might. More recently, he has criticized Washington’s sluggish defense procurement and warned about the country’s reliance on China for the critical minerals powering American weapons and technology. Now his bank has a number to show for it. JPMorgan said on Monday it has financed or facilitated $230 billion into sectors it considers essential for economic and national security—including critical minerals, defense, and frontier technology—a year into its 10-year, $1.5 trillion Security and Resiliency Initiative . The bank also said it committed $5 billion of its own capital investing into defense-related startups like Hadrian and Castelion —halfway through its initial $10 billion allocation.  “Strong economies and national security don’t happen by accident,” Dimon said in the press release. “They require investment in critical infrastructure, manufacturing, energy, defense and innovation, as well as policies that encourage growth.” Critical minerals are where the bank’s bets are easiest to see. China dominates the processing of many of these materials. JPMorgan has taken a stake in an Idaho mine holding the only identified U.S. antimony reserve, helped arrange financing for a $7.4 billion Korea Zinc processing plant in Tennessee, and hired a critical minerals chief. The bank’s own researchers flagged critical minerals as a potential next battleground between the U.S. and China back in 2024. This reflects a growing overlap between Wall Street financing and Washington’s national security priorities. JPMorgan is helping to finance the companies and infrastructure behind the U.S.’s effort to break its dependence on China and rebuild its manufacturing. For the bank, this is a big commercial opportunity.  Jeff Barrington, managing director of sell-side mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Windsor Drake, told Fortune JPMorgan is investing into areas “that now have a federal tailwind behind them” rather than necessarily acting from patriotism. “The bank is following the capital that the state is effectively guiding,” Barrington said. The Pentagon plans to spend $5 billion over fiscal year 2026 and 2027 to shore up critical minerals supply chains, including $3.6 billion to address shortages of antimony, gallium, germanium, aluminum, and other strategic materials used in military equipment. The Trump administration said it has signed or approved $40 billion in critical minerals deals since January 2025.  JPMorgan’s role in critical minerals The bank has invested $75 million for a 2.7% stake in Perpetua Resources, which is developing a mine in Idaho expected to hold the U.S.’s only identified reserve for antimony, a mineral used in ammunition. JPMorgan is also helping to arrange financing for Korea Zinc’s $7.4 billion critical minerals processing project in Clarksville, Tennessee, which includes $1.4 billion in planned Pentagon equity and debt financing and $210 million in Commerce Department funding, according to Korea Zinc’s letter to shareholders . The facility will produce zinc, germanium, and gallium among other minerals when it starts commercially operating in 2029 .  The bank has also worked alongside the Pentagon on MP Materials , helping arrange $1 billion in financing for the company to expand U.S. production of rare earth magnets used in fighter jets. The deal accompanied an investment that made the Defense Department the company’s largest shareholder. And JPMorgan’s moves extend beyond American mines as Washington looks to Latin America to get critical minerals outside of China, which essentially controls the world’s supply . In August, the bank issued a conditional commitment to provide up to $500 million in loans to a U.S. government-backed entity created to purchase rare earth minerals from Brazilian producer Serra Verde, which USA Rare Earth announced plans to acquire.  JP Morgan also hired a critical minerals chief, Andrew Frame, who “will lead SRI’s efforts to strengthen domestic and allied critical minerals supply chains,” according to a JPMorgan spokesperson.  Beyond minerals  JPMorgan’s direct investments are also reaching companies building weapons and military equipment. Todd Combs, Berkshire Hathaway’s former stock-picker, helped JPMorgan allocate the $5 billion equity sum to 10 firms, Bloomberg reported . The full list hasn’t been disclosed, but among the companies are startups Hadrian and Castelion. The bank led a nearly $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories for precision weapons, and an $800 million round for Castelion, which builds hypersonic missiles. It also advised deals between the Pentagon and defense contractors. In January, JPMorgan advised aerospace company L3Harris on a $1 billion Pentagon investment in its missile business, which makes parts used in Tomahawk and Patriot missiles. The Pentagon completed the investment in April, taking a financial stake in the business, which L3Harris plans to take public, according to its SEC filing . The money will help expand missile production and modernize factories. Looking ahead into SRI’s second year, JPMorgan said it plans to invest into more companies “that can expand critical capacity” and help make more strategic projects financeable.  “Success will be measured not only by capital mobilization, but also by stronger industrial capacity, more reliable supply chains and a deeper pipeline of companies able to scale when demand rises or disruption occurs,” JPMorgan said.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt broke down how he sees AI agents changing C-suite jobs
events.summary: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt said AI could make companies flatter by taking over some planning and coordination work. Bloomberg/Getty Images AI is changing how executives oversee their companies, Eric Schmidt said on the "In Good Company" podcast. Google's former CEO described several ways execs he knows use AI agents to manage staff. He described one company that uses AI assistants to ensure that staff are following its core values. Eric Schmidt thinks the CEO of the future will have an AI assistant that can see across the entire company. For employees whose job is to keep a sprawling business coordinated, that could be bad news. In an episode of the "In Good Company" podcast, the former Google chief executive described assistants that check whether company activity aligns with a leader's values, follow up on projects, and help identify ways to increase profits. He argued that the technology could make businesses faster and flatter, with fewer people needed to plan, relay information, and move numbers around. Schmidt sees little time for companies to adjust. He said competition in AI is fiercer than the PC-versus-Mac or Android-versus-iPhone battles: a model can take roughly six months to build, another two to test, and then be overtaken within five months of release. "Time compresses every cycle," he said. He also rejected the idea that AI is a bubble, pointing to Anthropic's rapid revenue growth . Schmidt said the company had grown faster than a record set during his time at Google , calling it "real money with real customers." The changes he envisions are already visible in smaller experiments, he said. Schmidt gave the example of two founders he knows who ask an AI assistant every Friday to flag anything happening at their company that conflicts with their values. Another executive created an AI version of himself that checks on an employee's progress, gives him instructions, and responds when he needs help, Schmidt said. That exchange sounded potentially abusive and worried him, he added, though he also saw how it sped up the executive's decisions. Schmidt said his days as CEO were consumed by meetings, 12 hours a day, five days a week, as he listened to people explain projects and decisions. He thinks AI platforms can eliminate much of that "coordination tax": the effort of gathering updates, passing them upward, and keeping teams aligned. For a company with 10,000 employees, Schmidt guessed AI could leave "a couple of thousand people who you don’t need." He cited a friend whose fast-growing company cut 20% of its staff, including the "glue people" who handled planning and coordination. The friend later told Schmidt he had received death threats over the cuts. Schmidt said companies would still need people who build products, make sales, speak with regulators, and lead teams. His advice to workers whose roles were disappearing was that executives should transition them "legally and humanely." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Japan’s trade deficit hits record $17.8 billion as Iran war sends oil import prices soaring
events.summary: Japan’s trade deficit reached 2.81 trillion yen ($17.8 billion) for the first fiscal half, according to government data released Wednesday, as the war in Iran sent oil import prices soaring. The Finance Ministry’s preliminary data showed that Japan’s exports for the April-September period grew 18.4% from the same period the previous year to 63.5 trillion yen, while imports soared to 66.3 trillion yen, up 20.4% year-over-year. Both were record highs for Japan. The soaring price of oil affects a wide range of sectors, including plastic goods and shipping costs. Resource-poor Japan imports virtually all its oil and has relied on access to the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East for its oil shipments. That’s now basically blocked, and Japan has had to pay more to get shipments from other routes. Brent crude, the international standard, has soared from $70 a barrel in February to around $110 a barrel. Analysts say prices are unlikely to ease soon. For the month of September, Japan’s trade deficit totaled 536.6 billion yen, marking the fifth month of deficits, down from 1.1 trillion yen in August. Japan’s September imports grew 18.9% from the previous year, while exports rose 16.7%. One sore point is the weakening yen, which drives up the cost of imports. The U.S. dollar is lately trading at 150-yen levels. The central bank, which kept borrowing costs at below or near zero for years to help keep a shaky economy going, has been gradually raising interest rates, in part to prop up the yen. Last month, the Bank of Japan raised the benchmark interest rate to 1.25% from 1.0%, a 31-year high. Its monetary policy board meets again next week. The bank has an inflation target of about 2%. The Japanese government has repeatedly stressed it’s working closely with the Bank of Japan. The government of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is promising a tax cut on food to 1% from 8% to help lower-income families cope with soaring prices. That bill is now being debated in Parliament. ___ Yuri Kageyama is on Threads: https://www.threads.com/@yurikageyama This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict?
events.summary: The European states say their support for Riyadh is ‘defensive’, but analysts warn Houthi reaction may complicate that. France and the United Kingdom have both moved to deploy military assets to Saudi Arabia, deepening their defence ties with the kingdom as its conflict with the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), in Yemen escalates. Paris last week said it had begun sending assets to Saudi Arabia as part of a previously announced agreement, after President Emmanuel Macron committed to deploying troops and air defence systems to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis . list 1 of 2 Egyptian parliament delays vote on military support for Saudi Arabia list 2 of 2 UK to deploy Typhoon jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks The UK , for its part, on Tuesday announced plans to deploy fighter jets to help shield Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks. Both countries stressed that their support would be defensive. Analysts say the European moves serve several geopolitical purposes: protecting Saudi oil exports that are important to European energy markets, shoring up their strategic alliance in the Gulf amid US reluctance to offer direct military assistance to Saudi Arabia, and strengthening deterrence against future Houthi attacks. But the deployments also carry significant risks, many analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states more directly into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict. “If insufficiently deterred, the Houthis may decide that the moment is ripe to test the resolve and resilience of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture, and attempt to draw Saudi Arabia’s allies even further into the Yemen-Saudi confrontation,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East Security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera. The British and French military support measures come as Saudi Arabia faces a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign against it , including targeting energy and transport infrastructure. Houthi attacks targeting Saudi airports in Riyadh and Abha this month have killed 19 people and injured more than 300 others, according to the Saudi-led coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki. Addressing the UK’s stepped-up military support for Saudi Arabia, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia “absolutely despicable”, specifically condemning the group’s targeting of Riyadh airport. The UK Ministry of Defence said it would deploy Typhoon fighter jets to fly “defensive counter air missions” in Saudi Arabia, send UK military advisers to work with Saudi staff officers and provide an A400M transport aircraft to help move defence material within the kingdom. French support for Saudi Arabia would include soldiers, radars and defence systems, Macron has said, without detailing the scale of the support. Urban Coningham, a research fellow at RUSI, noted differences in the British and French roles, with the French mainly limited to protecting Saudi export infrastructure. The British, by contrast, will conduct “defensive patrols where they would shoot down incoming missiles or drones” in Saudi Arabia, as well as provide air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi bombers and jets heading into Yemeni airspace, he said. Camille Lons, policy fellow and deputy head of the Paris office at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France is limited in what it can provide to Saudi Arabia, particularly given the demands on European defences amid the war in Ukraine. Still, Paris sees its assistance as a way to “show support [for Saudi Arabia] in times of crisis, and a way to deepen the defence partnership”, Lons told Al Jazeera. Saudi Arabia will welcome the European deployments, as it has struggled to translate some of its security partnerships into high-level military support. In September, US President Donald Trump rejected multiple Saudi requests to participate in strikes on the Houthis, agreeing only to provide intelligence and targeting support, the news agency Reuters cited informed sources saying. Turkiye and Pakistan have committed to “collective deterrence measures”, including potential troop deployments, under the newly signed Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia, but the agreement has yet to be ratified in Turkiye . Egypt’s parliament has also postponed a vote that would authorise its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia. Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at King’s College War Studies Department, called the UK and French deployments “militarily valuable and politically significant”, saying they could help shield the kingdom’s sprawling territory from persistent Houthi air attacks while giving Riyadh more room to focus its own assets on offensive operations. “The British Typhoons can reinforce Saudi air defences and, crucially, free up Saudi Eurofighters for offensive operations,” Obaid told Al Jazeera.

events.title: I thought loneliness came from having too few friends. For me, it came from having too many.
events.summary: Focusing on a smaller circle of friends made me feel less lonely. Carrie Berk Despite having a lot of friends in college , I felt like I was surrounded by strangers. After a careful analysis, I discovered meaningful connections fulfilled me more than casual ones. I stopped spreading myself too thin and have since focused my time on a smaller circle of friends. My 21st birthday party was packed with a dozen faces I half-knew. They all smiled as I blew out the candles and made a wish, yet I felt as if I were surrounded by strangers. As I looked out into the crowd, I realized that most of my friendships were surface-level, rather than genuine connections. We talked about upcoming school assignments, trending TV shows, and our favorite restaurants , but I wanted more. What was supposed to be a celebration turned into a rude awakening: Did these people even know me at all? I've always been someone with many hobbies, which meant making friends across all walks of life. Although I'm lucky to have so many people in my corner, there came a point where it felt like I was collecting friendships like tokens rather than forming meaningful relationships. The realization set in: I had tons of friends, but somehow, I was lonely. I needed to learn how to distinguish casual friendships from meaningful ones I realized friendships with a strong emotional connection were the most fulfilling. Carrie Berk Even years after graduating from college, I couldn't shake the feeling that I'd been collecting the wrong type of friendships. I realized many of my relationships had been rooted in transactions or shared activities, which may explain why I was still feeling lonely. Upon reflection, I noticed that the most genuine friendships I had involved some emotional depth and connection. I only have two of these in my life — one who lives close by, and another who is across the country. Regardless of where they are, the empathy goes both ways — I share in their joys and sit with them through their struggles, and they do the same for me. We're not just shoulders for each other to cry on, but supportive pillars who help each other walk through life. These were the friendships that fulfilled me most, and I needed to make more room in my life for them. I used to be scared of sharing my feelings with friends, but I realized that it was the only way to strengthen my relationships. Carrie Berk In order to do this, I needed to figure out what was holding me back. I came to the conclusion that, when it comes to friends, I'd kept many people at a distance, afraid that opening up would make me seem like "too much" or leave me hurt again. I'd also been spreading myself too thin, trying to maintain too many relationships instead of investing in the ones that mattered most. For example, I felt like I rushed through dinners to mentally check a box that I was keeping up the relationship. Not only was that a waste of time, but it led to major emotional burnout . Now, I focus on a handful of friends with whom I can build a deeper bond. Even though I only have time to see a select few people, I make sure the few hours we spend together are packed with thoughtful, not superficial, conversations. Recently, I spent some time with a work colleague outside the office, and we discussed how fitness helped us during difficult points in our lives. We connected on something beyond our jobs, and for the first time in a long time, I felt less lonely. Once I stopped chasing a bigger circle and was more vulnerable, I felt less alone Investing more time and energy into my close friendships has been so rewarding. Carrie Berk At first, it was difficult to let go of my larger circle. There's nothing wrong with casual friendships , but they couldn't give me the depth I was craving. Instead, the friends I need are the ones who will hold me up at my worst and cheer me on at my best without expecting anything in return — and I never think twice about doing the same for them. These connections take more time and care to develop, but are well worth the wait. Once I started watering the friendships I truly valued, I noticed our moments together aren't rushed, and our connection is stronger now because of the care we put into each conversation. This year, I'm thinking about having a birthday dinner with two or three close friends rather than a larger celebration. Ironically, when I began filtering superficial relationships out of my life, I felt less lonely — and that's all I could have ever wished for. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ‘From Greece to France, give money to education’: European protesters make clear it’s not immigration that has them on the march
events.summary: Thousands of students and teachers marched through the streets of the Greek capital of Athens Wednesday, calling for affordable student housing and more state investment in education, as protests that have swept Europe spread further. Similar protests were being held in several cities in Greece, including Thessaloniki in the north and the western port city of Patras. The rising cost of living, including increased fuel costs, and anger over the state of schools and lack of affordable housing for students have been fueling protests across Europe , with violence breaking out particularly at demonstrations in France, as well as in Italy and Albania. “From Greece to France, give money to education,” one banner read in the Athens protest. Others held up cardboard signs in French reading: “To study or to survive.” Engineering student Panagiotis Moschonas, 20, criticized the conservative government for not taking any measures to help students cope with the high cost of living. “It says that it is allegedly helping students, with a rent subsidy of 120 euros ($135) per month. That isn’t even enough for half a rent, and it’s also given at the end of the year.” Riot police closely shadowed the march, while officers conducted spot checks and bag searches on people heading toward the protest. Demonstrations in Greece often turn violent , and stores and cafes along the route rolled down steel shutters to guard against their windows being smashed. Teachers declared a strike for Wednesday, although some schools were open. “Today we are striking because this situation can’t continue for our families, with the high costs, with us struggling to make it to the end of the month, with the situation in schools which is deteriorating exponentially year after year,” said teacher Ioannis Rompas. events.title: UK Treasury chief vows to give families ‘some breathing space’ as inflation runs hot, highest in a year
events.summary: Inflation in the U.K. rose to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to ratchet up fuel prices, official figures showed Wednesday, cementing market expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month. The Office for National Statistics said consumer prices rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August. That’s the highest reading since October last year, and above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month. The increase takes inflation further above the Bank of England’s target rate of 2%. Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump. Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August. Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz , which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies. Treasury chief John Healey said his budget statement next week will aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from the upward march in the cost of living. Whatever measures he comes up with to keep a lid on rising prices, economists expect the Bank of England to increase interest rates at its next meeting on Nov. 5. Last month, rate-setters held the bank’s main rate at 3.75% but gave a big hint that they were ready to hike soon. “With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise,” said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW. Most economists expect an increase in the bank’s main rate to 4%. Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank , have raised rates recently. Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: More output isn’t better business: Workday’s CFO Zane Rowe on how finance chiefs should really measure AI
events.summary: Good morning. For Workday CFO Zane Rowe, the promise of AI isn’t just about automating tasks. It’s about giving employees the freedom to rethink how they work, uncover new insights, and add more value to the business. Rowe recently reviewed a list of 10 AI agents being developed by his tax team to improve how employees work. Not every agent will make the cut. But the projects offer a glimpse into how the enterprise software company is exploring agentic AI internally, he told me. Workday’s finance transformation team is part of that strategy. The group works with the company’s research and development and business technology teams to test its own products and explore other technologies. It also engages with customers to exchange feedback and learn how finance organizations are adopting AI, he said. Workday puts AI agents to work across finance Rowe sees two major opportunities: improving business insights and redesigning processes from end to end. On the first front, Workday is expanding Decision Intelligence beyond Adaptive across its portfolio to HR and finance. The tool helps finance teams understand what’s driving business performance, test different scenarios, and assess the potential impact on the company, he said.  For example, finance teams can model what would happen if they hired more or fewer people in certain parts of the world or in particular business areas, then forecast the impact on the company, Rowe said. “It’s a whole way of identifying how we think about planning; it’s not just forecasting,” he said. At its annual Rising event last week, Workday also announced new “autopilot agents” designed to automate routine workflows across accounting, payroll, and hiring; an expanded “Trusted Agent Platform” for building and deploying custom AI agents; and a new partnership with Anthropic to connect their platforms and agentic experiences. The announcements come as Workday, a Fortune 500 company, enters a new chapter under co-founder Aneel Bhusri, who reclaimed the CEO role in February and began what the company calls its “refounding” chapter. “Great companies are not built on one generation of technology. They pass the test of time,” Bhusri told Fortune ’s Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell on the latest episode of the Fortune 500 Titans podcast . Why AI’s value goes beyond efficiency As CFOs become key strategic partners to CEOs in shaping AI strategy, I asked Rowe how he measures the success of AI investments. “I always hear people talk about ROI, and I think it’s so much more than that,” he said. Rowe described an outcome-based approach to measuring AI’s impact. ROI remains important, but success is ultimately defined by better work, stronger decisions, greater organizational capacity, and improved customer value. For example, AI might enable a finance team to generate twice as many reports, but that alone doesn’t necessarily make the business better, he explained. A more meaningful measure is whether the team can use AI to uncover insights, anticipate problems, advise business leaders, and improve decisions. The shift he describes moves people away from simply producing information and toward using it to drive the business forward. “CFOs are leaning in on: How do we make sure the teams are motivated and engaged?” he said. “It’s not just about finding efficiencies. It’s about people actually doing the work that they thought they were going to do when they signed up to join a company.” Sheryl   Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: From one house to villages: Israeli settlers have Palestinians surrounded
events.summary: A family in the South Hebron Hills has spent more than two weeks cut off by settlers camped outside. Israeli siege tactics are spreading across hamlets and villages in the occupied West Bank. Yousef Shanaran, 52, built a well beside his house, which he can no longer reach. Since October 5, Israeli settlers have besieged his family home in Wadi Rakhim around the clock, a once-quiet corner of the South Hebron Hills among limestone rocks and thorny brush. They are unable to go outside on their own, even to fetch a little water from the well. It took five days for the army to coordinate the family’s access to the well. After running out of water three days earlier, the Israeli army on Tuesday allowed them to retrieve some from the well. list 1 of 3 The night watch: Palestinians protecting their homes from settler pogroms list 2 of 3 How Israel’s 2026 election works list 3 of 3 Palestine weekly: Israeli settlers attack journalist and diplomats “Food, there’s none,” Shanaran, who built the sturdy two-storey house in 2016 on land between the Palestinian town of as-Samu and the village of Susiya, planting about 70 grapevines and 30 to 40 olive trees, told Al Jazeera by phone. “My well, full of water; I built it and lost money on it,” he said. “They keep me from it because they want to get me out of my house.” More than half a year ago, settlers pitched a tent 300 metres (about 1,000 feet) from the Shanaran residence, restricting the family’s movement and exposing them to attacks and intimidation. On October 5, the tent was moved just 30 metres from their home. That day, about 50 settlers attacked the family with sticks and pepper spray. This marked the beginning of the full siege on Shanaran’s home. A siege the army ‘doesn’t recognise’ Nasser Nawajeh, a longtime B’Tselem field researcher who now heads the Susiya village council in Masafer Yatta, has tried to deliver supplies to the Shanaran family during the siege, but most attempts have failed. “Once I tried to bring aid to the people, and right away there was an attack from the settlers,” he told Al Jazeera. “I mean they’re there 24 hours to attack.” Nothing can move in or out of Shanaran’s home without the army’s permission. “This is a displacement policy,” he said. “If they want to take the kids out to school, we have to wait for the army to take them. If you want to bring in food or water, we have to do coordination.” Since October 15, he has kept asking the army for coordination to deliver supplies to the family — and given excuses each day: “‘The army’s busy, can’t come, there aren’t any forces’ — they tell us ‘tomorrow and tomorrow’,” he said. There are now two armies to contend with, Nawajeh said: the settlers’ regional units, the Kitat Konenut, meaning rapid response squads in Hebrew; and the regular army, which “comes, demolishes [the settlers’ tent] and leaves”. When the soldiers leave, the settlers simply pitch up their tent again. Shanaran said the soldiers stationed outside his house do nothing. “They stand and sit, eating and drinking, relaxed, at the door of the house,” he said. Nawajeh said the soldiers’ presence essentially amounts to a green light for the siege to continue. “Sometimes the soldiers don’t even stop the settlers coming close; they hit people and sit with the soldiers at the door,” he said. As the house is in Area B, an area technically under joint Israeli-Palestinian control, the army could arrest all the settlers as there is a closure order against them. “But there’s no enforcement of these laws,” he added. The soldiers posted outside the family home see their ostensible job as shielding the family from a beating, not ending the blockade. “In practice, the Palestinians are living in a prison inside. The siege is basically a prison,” he added. Shanaran said his family, trapped in their home, is living a life worse than prison. “Prison ends. Here, you’re sitting in your own house, and they’ve locked you up in it — and you’re afraid,” he said. ‘If they drive out the first house, they drive out the second’ The Shanaran home is the closest Palestinian one to the outposts encroaching on it, Nawajeh said. Settlers see no difference between Area A, intended to be administered by Palestinians, Area B under mixed Israeli-Palestinian authority, and Area C, which is fully under Israeli military and civil control. “They start with the house on the edge, in the corner. If they drive out the first house, they drive out the second,” he added. This tactic is now being applied in Masafer Yatta, an area south of the occupied West Bank which has come under repeated Israeli settler and military attacks. Following similar sieges further north in Jalud, where the Tubasi family was forced from their home in July and attacked in September when they tried to return under a court order, and in Qusra, where settlers besieged three homes , one owned by an American citizen, before the army set up barracks beside the besieged homes.
