events.title: A protester and a robot duck hiccup: 2 moments from Jensen Huang's keynote didn't go to plan
events.summary: Jensen Huang interacted with Microduck robots onstage. Sean Gallup/Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Berlin keynote was interrupted by Greenpeace protesters onstage. Huang was making the case for Europe to build an AI economy with factories and agents. His finale featured a wobbly Microduck robot demo and an AI-generated Eurovision-style video. Even for a seasoned keynote pro like Jensen Huang, there's always the risk that things don't go fully to plan. The Nvidia CEO opened the company's Berlin conference on Wednesday to make the case that Europe should build its own AI economy — complete with AI factories, autonomous agents, and robots. But the pitch was interrupted about 20 minutes into the keynote by protesters holding a Greenpeace banner reading, "Nvidia, clean your dirty business!" One protester shouted: "Clean up your act! What about the technology that was found in Russian drones? Those were Nvidia chips . What are you doing about that? What are you doing about the environmental destruction?" Greenpeace protesters held a banner, reading "Nvidia, clean up your dirty business!" John MACDOUGALL / AFP via Getty Images The protester appeared to be referring to an August statement from Ukraine's Defence Intelligence, which said it had identified an Nvidia Jetson Orin computer module in a Russian S-71 Monochrome cruise missile. The agency did not allege that Nvidia knowingly supplied the component to Russia . Greenpeace said in a press release that it's calling on Nvidia to extend its 100% renewable energy target across its wider supply chain and to conduct audits to ensure its technology doesn't end up in military equipment. Nvidia did not immediately respond to Business Insider's request for comments. As security escorted the protester away, Huang said, "Give her a chance," and that "everybody has a chance to say something." He then told the applauding crowd: "All important issues … but let me get through my keynote." Huang, after joking that he had to "torture" the audience with "some education" before "the entertainment," then pressed on with Nvidia's pitch for Europe's AI future. He unveiled DSX POD, a modular system for AI factories, and promoted OpenShell, a platform designed to help companies run autonomous AI agents securely. 'Pay attention!' The entertainment came near the end of the keynote, when Huang brought four small robots, known as Microducks, from French startup Pollen Robotics onstage. The demo was charming, but not entirely obedient. When Huang told the robots to "take a nap," one kept walking before eventually falling alongside the others. Later, only two appeared to perform a somersault when he asked them to. The cute robots didn't always listen to Huang's instructions. Bloomberg/Getty Images Another robot lingered farther away from the group and tripped before getting back up. "Pay attention! Stay focused. Come here, come here. Stay focused," Huang told it. It eventually approached and sat down, drawing laughter from the audience. Huang then closed the event with an AI-generated video of robots singing in a Eurovision-style contest. The demo came a day after Huang told German Chancellor Friedrich Merz that Europe could not regulate its way to technological leadership . "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," Huang told Merz. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets
events.summary: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets. With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone. The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor ( Oat ) , issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%. The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks. Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living. Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics , sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges. No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024 . The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending. France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action. International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies. “The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”

events.title: Starlink is getting dragged into Russia's hybrid war against the West
events.summary: Starlink is being drawn into Russia's shadow war against the West. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto Elon Musk's Starlink service is being drawn into Russia's campaign of hybrid operations in Europe. There have been several attacks against Starlink infrastructure across Europe in recent weeks. SpaceX's lucrative connectivity business has become a military and political target. Elon Musk and SpaceX have gotten caught up in very public battles over Starlink's role in the war in Ukraine, but they're also being drawn into another, less visible conflict: Russia's shadowy campaign of hybrid operations against the West. The past few weeks have seen attacks and attempted sabotage against Starlink infrastructure across Europe. Western officials are blaming Russia for at least some of the incidents, and Ukrainian intelligence has warned that Moscow could ramp up these efforts. Kęstutis Budrys, Lithuania's foreign minister, said on Sunday that a sabotage attempt targeting Starlink infrastructure near Vilnius was thwarted the previous night. He said that the aim was to "undermine a capability critical" to Ukrainian defense and civilian communications. Budrys characterized the incident as "a direct consequence of Russia's war" and later described the act as an element of Russian hybrid operations against Europe — sabotage, attacks, drone incursions, and other actions that Western officials have attributed to Moscow in recent years. The Kremlin has repeatedly denied involvement. Starlink infrastructure is a growing target. The civilian satellite internet service and its military-grade variant are used by NATO and Ukraine for battlefield communications and operations . Last week, Poland blamed Russian intelligence services for a sabotage incident in September — two Turkish citizens were arrested in connection with a fire at a Starlink satellite station near Warsaw. Donald Tusk, the country's prime minister, called the attack "another act of hybrid warfare." There was also a recent attack on Starlink antennas near Bulgaria's capital, according to media reports. Ukraine's GUR military intelligence warned on October 2 that Russia could target Starlink infrastructure in Europe as part of its campaign. Starlink's civilian and military-grade services are used by NATO and Ukraine for battlefield communications and operations. Stringer/REUTERS Speaking Monday, after the most recent incident involving Starlink, Lithuania's Budrys said that "we are seeing coordinated efforts to target critical infrastructure linked to support for Ukraine, logistics chains and other important facilities." "These are not isolated crimes," he added. "They are part of Russia's broader hybrid campaign against Europe, aimed at intimidating allies, undermining support for Ukraine, and testing our resilience." Neither Russia's defense ministry nor its embassies in Poland or Lithuania responded to requests for comment from Business Insider about these allegations. Lithuania's defense ministry said in a statement that the thwarted attack is not the first time it has seen an attempt to set fire to companies providing support to Ukraine . The ministry added that "attempts to damage Starlink equipment have recently occurred in other countries as well." Attempted sabotage of Starlink infrastructure is not a recent development, though. British authorities, for instance, determined that Russian intelligence was behind a March 2024 arson attack targeting a London warehouse storing Starlink equipment bound for Ukraine. "Neither space nor our societies are sanctuaries," US Army Col. Martin O'Donnell, a spokesperson for Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe, told Business Insider. "Fortunately, NATO has strategies for countering threats to both, and for defending the alliance." NATO leadership and European Union officials have said the hybrid campaign won't derail support for Ukraine. "As the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness," Christian Wigand, the EU's lead foreign affairs and security policy spokesperson, told Business Insider. "Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine," he said. "This will not happen." A satellite image from April shows the area of a Starlink station in Poland. Pleiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/via REUTERS SpaceX in the crosshairs Although the sabotage attempts in Poland and Lithuania targeted Starlink equipment at sites run by third parties, not by SpaceX directly, the incidents are a sign of how the company and Starlink are becoming increasingly entangled in the war between Ukraine and Russia and Moscow's hybrid operations against the West. That entanglement is turning SpaceX's lucrative connectivity business into a military and political target. Starlink accounted for over 60% of SpaceX's revenue last year and has been the funding engine for the company's cash-burning artificial intelligence and rocket ventures. In SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call this week, the company reported that government and enterprise revenues were up 91% year over year, and executives told investors they expect this revenue stream to eventually exceed income from selling Starlink terminals to consumers. As SpaceX contends with Starlink infrastructure becoming a target of hybrid Russian warfare, the company and its leadership are also facing controversies from the war in Ukraine that put that business at risk. Earlier this month, Ukraine's access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, was limited without warning , complicating operations. Ukrainian defense ministry sources told Business Insider that Starshield was restricted at speeds above 100 miles per hour, disrupting the Starlink-equipped drones that have become a crucial part of Ukraine's war machine, with some Ukrainian and foreign officials initially blaming SpaceX and Musk. Musk redirected concerns in a social media post, saying that Starshield is operated by the US government and that the president and the Pentagon are responsible for such decisions. A senior US official told Business Insider last week that President Donald Trump did not order the Starshield restrictions. Musk has denied that SpaceX imposed the speed restrictions on Ukraine. REUTERS/Evan Vucci/File Photo Multiple media outlets have since reported that Musk ordered the disruption. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. This incident has sparked calls from European officials for the EU to divest from Starlink in favor of local alternatives not controlled by Musk or the US. Christophe Grudler, a member of the European Parliament, wrote to EU leaders urging them to accelerate development of IRIS2, a European rival to Starlink that is set to begin satellite deployments in 2029, while other lawmakers also called on Europe to reduce its reliance on US tech . events.title: Mortgage rates drop for the first time in 2 months, but demand still falls further
events.summary: The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances decreased last week to 7.41% from 7.50% Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell a steeper 7% for the week and were 18% lower from the year before. Refinance demand dropped 2% or the week and 59% year over year. Mortgage demand took another leg lower, despite a brief respite from rising interest rates. Total mortgage application volume fell 5.3% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, dropped last week to 7.41% from 7.50%, with points falling to 0.75 from 0.83 including the origination fee for loans with a 20% down payment. "Mortgage rates decreased for the first time in over two months," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "However, lower rates were not enough to boost application activity, as both purchase and refinance applications continued to decline." Applications to refinance a home loan, which are most sensitive to weekly moves, fell just 2% week to week, a smaller drop than some previous weeks when rates were moving higher. Refinance demand was still 59% lower than the same week one year ago. With rates now over a full percentage point higher than they were a year ago, there is a very small pool of borrowers who can benefit from a refinance. Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home declined a steeper 7% for the week and were 18% lower from the year before. Buyers are reacting less to the weekly move in rates but more to the overall higher level. A report from the National Association of Realtors on Tuesday showed a sharp drop in September pending home sales. These are measured by signed contracts, so it showed the real-time impact of rising rates during the month. Rates remained at that higher level in October. Get Property Play directly to your inbox CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. For those buyers in the market, a continued high share are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs, which offer lower rates but are considered riskier because they will eventually reset to whatever the market rate is at the end of their term. "The ARM share held steady at 10.5 percent, as ARM rates remained almost a full percentage point lower than the 30-year fixed rate, giving qualified borrowers a lower rate option to purchase a home," Kan added. Mortgage rates haven't done much to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. Last week was a particularly volatile week for rates, due to multiple monthly inflation reports. This week the moves have seemed to follow oil prices. "But we'd caution against placing too much emphasis on the oil price correlation," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "It's been highly unreliable for more than a month." Correction: The National Association of Realtors on Tuesday reported September pending home sales. An earlier version misstated the day.

events.title: "I am giving you money!" Nvidia's CEO wants every country to build its own AI
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is crisscrossing Europe with a multibillion-dollar checkbook and a grand ambition: Make his company the indispensable backbone of the global AI economy. Why it matters: As fears of an AI bubble rattle Wall Street, Huang is working to spread the boom beyond the U.S. and China — courting governments, bankrolling startups and cultivating massive new markets for Nvidia's chips. The big picture: The godfather of AI is trying to single-handedly build a new market for Nvidia chips, betting that governments and institutions around the world will want their own, highly customized data centers running open models. If it works, it could shore up demand for Nvidia chips just as another big group of customers — neoclouds — appear financially shaky. Driving the news: Part showman, part salesman, Huang has spent the past week preaching the gospel of AI across Europe ahead of a keynote Wednesday at Nvidia's flagship conference in Berlin. In France, Huang announced investments in four startups and joked, whisky glass in hand , that he's "the biggest VC in Europe." President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to Paris, while France's economy minister compared the AI revolution to the Gold Rush. In Britain, Huang channeled Oprah Winfrey while announcing stakes in five startups. "I am giving you money! And I am giving you money! And I am giving you money!" he shouted from the stage of a converted London church. In Sweden, Huang unveiled a supercomputer backed by the country's industrial elite, likening Nvidia's technology to a "time machine" capable of compressing years of scientific research into days. In Germany, Huang challenged Chancellor Friedrich Merz to loosen Europe's regulatory instincts. "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," he warned Monday. "Give Germany a chance. Give this industry a chance." Zoom in: At the heart of Huang's global strategy is "sovereign AI" — the idea that every nation should build and control its own AI infrastructure, data and models, rather than depend on U.S. or Chinese tech giants. In addition to roughly $10 billion in investments in Europe, Nvidia is helping build national AI ecosystems across Saudi Arabia, South Korea, India, Malaysia and Africa. For Huang, the prize is a vast new class of customers, including entire countries that see AI infrastructure as an economic and national security imperative. Between the lines: Huang's global offensive comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry, with Wall Street increasingly questioning whether the technology's enormous promise can justify its astronomical costs. Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave and other "neocloud" providers have plunged, fueling fears that the companies borrowing billions to buy Nvidia's chips may struggle to pay their debts. Investors are also scrutinizing a circular flow of money in which Nvidia helps finance the very companies buying its products, raising questions about how much demand is self-sustaining. What to watch: Huang has emerged as the AI industry's chief cheerleader during periods of market turmoil, countering predictions of a bubble with assurances that demand is still accelerating. His Berlin keynote offers another chance to calm investors by arguing that the next wave of AI spending will come from governments treating the technology as a national necessity, not a speculative bet. The bottom line: Countries racing to secure their independence in the AI age may find themselves more reliant than ever on one American company.

events.summary: Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026. Reform: more than writing rulesIn this sector, we’re just past peak rule making. The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.But we’re not done yet.We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.It takes a strategic approach. One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions.And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.We’ve introduced targeted support.And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.We’re already seeing real progress.Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.But it’s well worth it.

events.title: Pakistani authorities arrest man accused in $126m US postage fraud
events.summary: Faheem Akram has been charged with several offences including conspiracy to defraud the United States. Pakistani authorities have arrested a man accused of masterminding an online counterfeit operation that United States prosecutors say resulted in more than $125m of losses to the US Postal Service. Faheem Akram, 33, was arrested on Tuesday after an expansive search operation and raids across Pakistan, a senior official at the Pakistani National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency told reporters. list 1 of 3 Dozens of South Koreans freed from Cambodia scam centres now home, arrested list 2 of 3 US drops fraud charges after billionaire Adani pledges $10bn investment list 3 of 3 The $3.7bn man: Inside one of US’s biggest Medicare frauds Akram was indicted last month by a federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida, and is accused of operating a fraudulent website where he sold more than 5.1 million counterfeit stamps in the US. The stamps, which cost about $2 each, allowed customers to ship their packages at a lower price than official postal rates, causing significant losses to the Postal Service, according to the US Attorney’s office. The estimate of more than $124m however, represents the losses to the Postal Service and not the proceeds from the website, officials said. Pakistani investigators discovered that Akram has been operating the website since August 2023 and used 16 bank accounts, including his own and several family members’, for the operation. Akram has been charged with several offences, including conspiracy to defraud the US and the making and selling of fake postage stamps, as well as four counts of wire fraud, according to the US Postal Service. He could face 20 years in prison on each count of wire fraud, as well as five years in prison for conspiracy. Akram is currently in custody in Pakistan, but it is unclear whether he will face trial in the country or be extradited to the US.

events.title: E-scooter hospitalisations more than tripled since 2019
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts E-scooter and e-bike hospitalisations on the rise in Australia, report finds Topic: Transport Accidents and Incidents The report found boys aged between 12 and 15 had the largest increase in hospitalisations due to e-scooter falls. ( ABC News: Marcus Stinson ) A report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) has found e-scooter hospitalisations have more than tripled since 2019. There were 4,089 hospitalisations involving e-scooter in the 2024-25 compared to 1,291 in 2019-20. Two-thirds of those hospitalised in 2024-25 were male with largest increase in young boys aged between 12 and 15. Teenage boys riding e-scooters drove a sharp rise in hospitalisations over the last five years, according to a report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW). The number of boys aged 12 to 15 hospitalised following e-scooter falls saw a 15-fold increase between 2019/20 and 2024/25. Boys in that cohort were four times more likely than girls to end up in hospital because of an e-scooter fall. It also found hospitalisation rates increased for e-bike riders, but these data were harder to capture because of how these injuries were classified. The report found e-scooter-related deaths increased over the last decade from seven in 2014/15 to 20 in 2024/25; however, the proportion of deaths was stable. New codes introduced in July this year will help better differentiate between e-mobility devices such as e-scooters and e-bikes, the report said. AIHW spokesperson Jacqueline Rek said the improved data will help better understand the risks surrounding e-mobility devices. "Meaning these findings should not be interpreted as precise counts of injuries involving e-scooters or e-bikes alone," Ms Rek said. E-bikes and e-scooters are now mainstream, with almost 1 million privately owned by Queenslanders, according to University of Queensland research. When Barnaby Joyce was deputy prime minister and transport minister in 2021, his assistant minister Kevin Hogan made a quiet, but hugely significant change to the Road Vehicle Standards Act. Richard J Buning, who worked on the research, said improving safety was crucial given the growth. "Every single year over the last five years, the growth in e-mobility device purchases has risen by 30 per cent," he said. Dr Buning said unsafe devices such as over-powered e-bikes were among his chief concerns. Last year, the federal government introduced stronger e-bike import standards similar to those in the European Union (EU), limiting access to unsafe devices. "It's these unsafe, uncompliant, illegal devices that are creating much of the problems of people riding really fast on high-powered devices," Dr Buning said. "But the safe, compliant devices, they don't provide more power than just a normal typical average fit person can provide." Dr Buning highlighted Queensland as one jurisdiction in the country leading e-mobility device regulation. People riding e-bikes in the state must be 16 or older and hold a valid driver's licence, including a learner licence. Children aged between 12 and 17 (where 16- and 17-year-olds do not hold a driver's licence) will only be able to ride an e-bike or e-scooter with parental supervision. New laws for e-mobility devices in effect from today: what you need to know Laws for e-bike and e-scooter riders come into effect from July 1: we've unpacked the changes for you Dr Buning disagreed with licensing e-bikes but praised the state's e-bike assurance scheme, which followed EU regulations. It will mean from March 2027, all e-bikes in the state must have a compliance label to ride in public. "So stopping those things from being sold and making sure that the public knows if they buy one of these devices that are uncompliant, they cannot legally ride it on the road," he said. Dr Buning also suggested more targeted initiatives to better educate those who are riding unsafely, which was mostly younger people. "Because the vast majority of people that use e-bikes are actually much older, 70 per cent of e-mobility device users are over the age of 40. "That highly visible behaviour may be obscuring public perception of an overall quite inclusive and sustainable transport mode.

events.title: House prices across capitals post steepest quarterly decline ever: Domain
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts House values drop in all capital cities for first time in 15 years, Domain says Topic: Construction and Real Estate Industry Australia's most valuable homes are falling the most in value. ( ABC News: Charlie Mclean ) House prices have fallen across every capital city for the first time in 15 years, Domain reports. Data shows Australia's most expensive homes have recorded the biggest drops this year, while lower-value homes have remained largely stable. Experts say increasing interest rates and lower confidence in the market are driving the downturn. House prices have fallen 4.7 per cent, the steepest quarterly drop on record, according to new data from Domain. Prices dropped in every capital city in the September quarter, the first time in 15 years and only the second time on record. The real estate platform's data showed the sharpest decline was in Perth, where prices dropped 7.4 per cent. Combined capital city house prices fell to $1,226,566. Domain said markets that started the year in very different positions "are now moving in the same direction". Houses and units dropped in price for a second consecutive month. ( ABC News: Steve Keen ) Australia's biggest property markets of Sydney and Melbourne recorded their largest quarterly house price drop in four years, falling 4.7 per cent and 3.3 per cent respectively. Unit prices also dropped by 3.5 per cent, the second consecutive quarter of both property types declining. It marked a clear shift in the housing cycle, according to Nicola Powell, Domain's chief residential economist. Nicola Powell says conditions have shifted to be more favourable for buyers. ( Supplied ) "What began as weakness concentrated in some cities has broadened considerably," Dr Powell said. "The balance of power has shifted towards buyers. "Homes are taking longer to sell, there is greater scope to negotiate, and sellers are having to be more realistic about price expectations." The cumulative impact of the rate rises, lower affordability and cost of living pressure has reduced demand, according to Gerard Burg of data firm Cotality. Gerard Burg says the fall in prices has been driven by lower demand. ( ABC News: Darryl Torpy ) Australia's most valuable homes falling the most While all major markets across the country have joined the downturn, prices have not been dropping equally within cities. Australia's most valuable homes are dropping the most, while lower value homes were relatively stable in three months to September, according to property data firm Cotality. In Sydney, the most valuable quartile of homes dropped more than twice as much as the least valuable quartile. Nationwide, lower value homes have experienced much slower drop in prices, Cotality said. Prices grew in Darwin's lowest value quartile. Cameron Kusher says fewer buyers and higher interest rates are pushing down the prices of more expensive properties. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) The heavier downturn in the more expensive properties is a result of fewer buyers and higher borrowing costs, according to property economist Cameron Kusher. "They've typically seen larger increases in values over recent years and when you see that market slowdown, there's overall fewer buyers for those properties," he said. However, he said the ultra-top end of the market had remained largely stable. Mr Burg agreed, saying the lower-priced homes remained affordable to a higher number of buyers. Prices were falling before federal budget The federal budget was a factor, but not the only factor, in house price falls, according to Mr Kusher. House prices peaked last year, and had already begun to drop before the changes to investment taxes in May's federal budget, both Mr Kusher and Mr Burg noted. While the changes to the budget have been a factor, house prices were decreasing before the budget. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Mr Burg said prices were already falling in many capital cities, and the three consecutive interest rate hikes had dampened confidence in the market. The real estate industry says new laws targeting agents underquoting a house price are well-intentioned but poorly designed. Auction activity, a common gauge of market confidence, has roughly halved compared to last year, with a total of 1,423 auctions across capital cities last week, according to Cotality. "Confidence has really evaporated. Affordability is very stretched and borrowing capacity is reduced dramatically," Mr Kusher said. He said home ownership rates had not moved much since the May budget changes, as a result of lower buyer confidence and stretched affordability.

events.title: As a former Disney employee, fall is the best time to visit the parks. Here are 9 of my favorite things to do there.
events.summary: Fall is the best time to visit Disney World, in my opinion. Kayleigh Price I worked in several locations across Disney World, and fall is my favorite time to visit the parks. I love dressing up for the Halloween events at Magic Kingdom and seeing the characters in costumes. There are some great food opportunities in the fall, like the Food and Wine Festival at Epcot.  If you're planning a trip to Disney, I suggest you look at the fall. After years of working at Disney World and visiting during every season, fall is still my absolute favorite time of year to be in the parks. It's usually less crowded since schools are back in session, and the Florida weather cools slightly from the oppressive summer heat.  This is during Florida's hurricane season, which typically runs from June through the end of November, so I recommend packing a rain poncho and checking weather alerts before you travel. Otherwise, here's my list of some of the best things to do , see, and eat at Disney World in the fall.  I love strolling down Main Street right after the fall decorations go up. David Roark/Walt Disney World There is nothing like walking down Magic Kingdom's Main Street USA in the fall. It's lined with pumpkins, seasonal drapes, scarecrows in funny outfits, and Mickey-shaped jack-o'-lantern wreaths.  I like to grab a seasonal coffee at the Main Street Bakery (Starbucks) and spend time soaking it all in.  The decorations make it feel so cozy and allow for some really cute photos. I make sure to have a little photo shoot in this area every year.  Although they cost extra, events like Mickey's Not-So-Scary Halloween Party are worth it. There are a bunch of rare characters at the party. Kayleigh Price I think Mickey's Not-So-Scary Halloween Party  is the best special event at Disney World all year. It runs from the end of August through October 31, and it requires a special park ticket, which is usually a little more expensive. However, during this event, guests get the opportunity to trick-or-treat all around Magic Kingdom and feel like a kid again.  There are also special entertainment offerings unique to the event, such as the "Boo to You" Parade, the "Hocus Pocus" stage show, and exclusive character meet-and-greets.  "Boo to You" is my favorite. It features all the classic characters, including Mickey and friends, the Hundred Acre Woods gang, most of the princesses and their princes, Pixar stars, Haunted Mansion maids and butlers, and a wide range of villains.  For adults, this is also the only time of year to go all out with costumes in the parks. Adults can dress up for the Halloween party. Kayleigh Price Typically, only children under 14 are allowed to wear full costumes at Disney World. But when special events like Mickey's Not-So-Scary Halloween Party are running, adults can go all out (as long as they're still following park guidelines). This is such a fun way to celebrate Halloween, especially because you can see all of the unique costumes that everyone comes up with.  If you're not into wearing a full costume to the parks, you can also Disneybound by using your regular clothes to match the color scheme or aesthetic of your favorite character in a more subtle way. Park employees and other guests will usually pick up on your outfits, too, which makes for some fun interactions with fellow fans.  I love Disneybounding different characters all year, but it's especially fun when the park is decorated for Halloween.  This is probably the best time of year to see characters in unique outfits. Some character get to wear Halloween costumes during the party. Kayleigh Price Seeing characters is always a huge highlight of any Disney trip, but it's extra special in the fall when you can see their Halloween outfits. It's the cutest thing to see Mickey dressed as a vampire or Winnie the Pooh dressed as a bumblebee.  You never know what your favorite character will dress up as, and it's exciting to see them in something other than their typical outfit.  I also love seeing all of the Magic Kingdom park employees in their festive Halloween uniforms. Hollywood and Vine gets a total makeover for Halloween. There were several hot dishes available at lunch. Jenna Clark Hollywood and Vine in Hollywood Studios serves a buffet-style meal with character meet-and-greets. But in the fall, it typically transforms into a Halloween-themed dining experience.  All of the classic Disney characters — Mickey, Minnie, Goofy, and Donald — are dressed up in their Halloween costumes. They also have Halloween-inspired desserts and festive decor throughout the restaurant.  Haunted Mansion always gets me in the Halloween spirit. The ride gets a spooky makeover during Halloween. Kayleigh Price Out of all of the rides at Disney World , Haunted Mansion truly embodies the Halloween season. If you're anything like me and like to be spooked — but are also a huge wimp when it comes to anything scary — this is the perfect ride for you. It has such a good mix of scare and fun.  Taking a ride always gets me into the Halloween spirit. You must pop over to Epcot for the International Food and Wine Festival. Steven Diaz/Disney Fall isn't complete unless I go to Food and Wine at Epcot , which usually runs from August to November. It's my favorite festival that Epcot offers throughout the year because it's full of amazing foods and drinks inspired by cuisines from around the world. The stands and offerings always rotate, but one of my favorites was Appleseed Orchard in the Canada Pavilion. It had an assortment of different beers and ciders along with sweet treats like a frozen apple-pie drink and apple-crumble tarts.  Garden Grill reminds me of a Thanksgiving feast. The Garden Grill always provides a memorable experience. Kari Becker One of my favorite things about the fall season is all of the amazing food, and the Garden Grill buffet reminds me of a Thanksgiving meal with turkey, mashed potatoes, stuffing, a harvest salad, and a berry shortcake. This restaurant, located in Epcot's The Land pavilion, is another character dining experience featuring an all-you-can-eat, family-style meal . The seasonal, Halloween-themed treats are absolutely worth getting, too. There are some fun seasonal treats at the parks. Kayleigh Price Speaking of food, there are a lot of great seasonal Halloween-themed treats to be found throughout Disney World at the resorts, parks, and Disney Springs throughout autumn. Although these tend to rotate, one of my favorites is the candy-corn milkshake at Auntie Gravity's Galactic Goodies in Tomorrowland. It's candy-corn flavored and topped with a big Mickey-shaped marshmallow. Whenever it's available, I'm sure to order one. events.title: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
events.summary: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another editor from the project has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

events.title: OpenAI expands ChatGPT Ads to 26 new countries as diversification push accelerates
events.summary: OpenAI announced it is expanding ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, bringing the total to 89 nations around the globe. The company's free users and Go subscribers in countries including Argentina, Peru, Nigeria, South Africa and Ukraine will start to see ads within ChatGPT. OpenAI's ad business hit $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate in August. OpenAI on Wednesday announced it will roll out ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, its latest push to build out its nascent advertising unit. The artificial intelligence company has been touting its 8-month-old ads product as a new pillar of its business, which also includes enterprise contracts, consumer subscriptions and usage-based application programming interfaces, or APIs. Digital ads have long been a major revenue stream for other big tech companies, including Google and Meta . OpenAI said its free users and Go subscribers in countries including Argentina, Peru, Nigeria, South Africa and Ukraine will start to see ads in ChatGPT. The ads are separate from ChatGPT's response to prompts, don't influence its answers and are clearly labeled, the company said. "Our goal is to make ads useful to people as they pursue their goals and make decisions — and effective for the businesses that advertise with us," OpenAI said in a release. SpaceX earnings live updates: Here's why analysts are bullish ahead of the report Salesforce announces $5.66 billion deal for Braze, sending BRZE stock soaring 50% Anthropic in talks with neocloud Nscale over second multibillion-dollar deal, source tells CNBC Apple adds U.S. titanium supplier for iPhone Duo as supply stays tight OpenAI's ad business hit $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate in August, up from $100 million in March, as CNBC previously reported. The company said Wednesday that more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on the platform. Wednesday's announced expansion brings ChatGPT Ads to a total of 89 countries worldwide, OpenAI said. The company began testing ads in the U.S. in February, a decision that was ridiculed by chief rival Anthropic . Anthropic made OpenAI's ads push the focus of its first Super Bowl campaign and pledged to keep its competing chatbot, Claude, ad free. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are gearing up for what are widely expected to be blockbuster initial public offerings , though they have not publicly disclosed when they plan to debut. OpenAI executives have signaled that they are eyeing a 2027 listing , while Anthropic's leaders have been actively meeting with prospective investors in recent weeks. OpenAI said it plans to continue developing additional ChatGPT Ads formats, measurement capabilities and buying options during its next phase of growth. The company is also looking at new ways for businesses to natively interact with ChatGPT consumers. "As more people turn to ChatGPT to explore needs, evaluate options, and make decisions, we see an opportunity to help them discover products and services — and to help businesses of every size grow and thrive," OpenAI said. events.title: Mach9 raises $34M after pivoting to AI CAD software
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When Alex Baikovitz co-founded Mach9 Robotics in 2021, his goal was to build a better, faster, and cheaper way for civil engineers to do visual inspections. The company aimed to cut through red tape and modernize the slow, outdated processes that bog down construction in the United States. Within a few years, Mach9 Robotics had built that hardware, but the effort led Baikovitz to a realization: hardware wasn’t the bottleneck. “We saw how tedious it was for civil engineering organizations to take data from these amazing laser scanners and image data capture systems and turn that into a usable survey,” he told TechCrunch in an interview, referring to a detailed map of a site that engineers use for design work. “The real pain was in their workflows,” he said, and “how to turn all the endless amounts of data that they’re able to collect into . . .information that people can use to make the best design and asset management decisions across the board.” So Baikovitz dropped “Robotics” from the company’s name and pivoted to developing AI-powered computer-aided design (CAD) software instead. The bet paid off, as Mach9 has racked up nearly 100 customers for the private beta of its software, and they’ve used it on more than 2,500 projects to date. That momentum helped Mach9 unlock new funding. On Wednesday, the startup announced a $34 million Series A funding round co-led by First Round Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners. Also throwing in were Prudence, an early-stage, New York-based firm that focuses on investing in AI software use cases for construction and real estate, and Quiet Capital, a VC firm already on the cap table. Mach9 is one of a number of startups racing to modernize the planning-to-building pipeline for construction and infrastructure. In August, a startup called CivilGrid raised $26 million to grow what it calls the “Google Maps for the underground.” Meanwhile, Blueprints AI , which uses AI to produce code-compliant, permit-ready architectural blueprints in just a few minutes, was among the top 200 companies in the Startup Battlefield competition at last week’s TechCrunch Disrupt. Baikovitz said Mach9 is focused on disrupting CAD software because it’s one of the slowest and most labor-intensive pieces of that overall pipeline. “It takes months to be able to deliver a project, and about a week per mile for someone to do manually in the legacy incumbent software that’s built by the Autodesk and Bentley Systems of the world,” he said. Mach9 says its software automates a lot of that work, making the process 10 times faster and dramatically reducing costs. This allows customers doing surveying and civil engineering work to “expand their own capacity and take on more types of work, bigger projects, and expand the reach of how reality-capture data can influence major infrastructure decisions,” Baikovitz said. Baikovitz said Mach9 developed and trained its own in-house AI models to reach the centimeter-accurate level that construction and infrastructure work requires. “That’s not something that a lot of off-the-shelf models are able to do or deliver at in any capacity,” he said. “A big part of what our development process has looked like since 2024 has been, how do we build the industry leading models that can turn imagery or these multimodal image and laser scan data sets into survey grade like geometry, like tracing out the curbs, the pavement striping, all of this exactly how our customers want it to be at the accuracies that the industry demands.” Mach9’s AI CAD system takes the survey data and creates a first draft of a plan, which engineers can then refine. The startup is “giving them all of the tools to draw, remove, adjust vertices, assess the quality of the AI-generated model, so that they can put effectively their name behind the deliverable that they’re producing, because there is a lot of liability in this particular industry, and it requires licensed professionals that know what they’re looking at,” Baikovitz said. As for the funding, Baikovitz said his startup will split it between improving the product, hiring industry experts, and scaling “all parts of our organization to keep up with where the market is taking us.” In retrospect, Baikovitz said he’s thankful that he initially went down the hardware path. It gave his startup something to pitch to potential customers, and it was largely those customers who told him they didn’t need better devices to capture data. “I’m not interested in getting this cheaper, lower-cost hardware,” he remembers one VP telling him. But better software could “improve our efficiency in delivering these big statewide transportation mapping initiatives,” he said. He added that such projects help make states that Mach9 has worked with, like Texas, “much more like safe [and] effective.

events.title: Keppel, SGX and Thakral CEOs win SIAS outstanding CEO award
events.summary: (From left) Thakral Corporation CEO Inderbethal “Bethal” Singh Thakral, Keppel CEO Mr Loh Chin Hua, and SGX Group CEO Loh Boon Chye. SINGAPORE – Three chief executive officers won the Investors’ Choice Outstanding CEO Award given out by the Securities Investors Association (Singapore), or Sias , on Oct 21. They were recognised for excellence in corporate governance, sustainability, transparency and shareholder communications. The three CEOs tell The Straits Times how they increased the shareholder value of their companies and the top traits a CEO should have. Keppel CEO: Bring shareholders and staff along on the transformation journey Keppel CEO Loh Chin Hua faced a challenge about a decade ago, when the company was trying to transform from a conglomerate with distinctly separate businesses to an asset-light global asset manager and operator. His goal: to communicate the multi-year transformation journey clearly to shareholders to ensure they were on board. Loh recalled that at the time, there was very little synergy among the various businesses, which were listed separately and run vertically. “The market wasn’t according us the valuation that we thought we should have,” he said. Keppel privatised some listed entities and changed its business model from building projects to owning and operating specialised assets. This has significantly reduced its balance sheet and enabled Keppel to return capital to shareholders while growing its assets under management. Loh said: “We set milestones because this multi-year transformation can be quite daunting for the market to absorb. It is important that we communicate to the market what are the milestones along the way, so that they can follow and track how we are progressing on our transformation.” He added that “communication is key” for a listed company. “In the old days, you might say, ‘Well, we are Keppel. Trust us. We know what we are doing.’ I think nowadays, even if the market does trust us, they also want to see tangible results,” Loh said. He noted that the transformation was a fundamental rework of the business structure and its processes, not “just a narrative”. Keppel has also set and met its goals around aspects like monetisation of non-core assets and growth of funds under management. Loh also emphasised the importance of ensuring that staff were invested in the transformation. Keppel uses engagement surveys to check that staff understand where it is headed, especially as it moves towards integrating AI to become an “AI native” firm. Loh said: “I wouldn’t say that we started off by thinking about share performance. “You start off by developing a strategy that will strengthen the company and allow it to be better valued, better appreciated by the market. Bring your board, your management, and your people along this journey, and the rest takes care of itself.” When asked about the traits a good CEO should have, Loh said Keppel’s core values about being agile, having a “can-do” spirit, and trust are vital. Being able to galvanise people is essential, he said. “Most importantly, they feel that they are part of this journey... not because you ask them to, but because they actually feel it, they can see it, and they support it.” SGX CEO: Growing the local investing ecosystem and unlocking value Growing the Singapore Exchange (SGX) as a business and developing the local ecosystem around it has been the focus of group CEO Loh Boon Chye in recent years. The progress so far has been gratifying, he said, with initiatives such as Value Unlock introduced to help companies strengthen their investor relations and close valuation gaps, and the push to revitalise the local equities market. “In the last two years in particular, it was very gratifying to see the whole ecosystem coming together to work on our stock market. SGX in many ways can’t do it alone,” he said. “Importantly, this is not a one-time effort. This is just the start. Indeed, there’s been good momentum, but we need to sustain it to make this durable and sustainable.” He added that SGX has also been working to broaden its offerings of investment tools in a macro environment that is more fragmented, and that offerings go beyond access into just one market or asset class. “It is now really about portfolio risk management, and our focus to broaden that is not just a one-year effort,” Loh said. Some of his plans include growing the foreign exchange (FX) business and commodities business, with SGX’s expansion of its gold segment. But besides growth, the market also needs to ensure transparency and good governance, which is done through clear communication with shareholders. “What we’re talking about is more than disclosure – it’s about firms being able to explain the business model, dynamics, strategy, and then how the company can fit into the environment they’re operating in, allocating capital as efficiently as they can,” he said.

events.title: Companies involved in illegal activities that cause haze may face financial ramifications: Chee Hong Tat
events.summary: Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat warned on Oct 21 that listed companies involved in illegal activities that cause transboundary haze may face legal and financial ramifications. Chee Hong Tat warned that listed companies involved in illegal haze-causing activities may face legal and financial penalties, which can also hurt shareholders. SIAS urged investors to avoid firms with poor environmental records, while MAS will help by developing IPO guides to improve investor education and decision-making. Chee said Singapore’s listing market is seeing renewed interest, with 10 new listings by end-August raising about S$1.4 billion, as awards recognised governance, sustainability and transparency. SINGAPORE – The rece nt haze crisis has put the spotlight on corporate governance and accountability, with National Development Minister Chee Hong Tat warning that listed companies involved in illegal activities that cause transboundary haze may face legal and financial ramifications. “These consequences, these penalties, do not just affect the company’s directors and management. They also affect the value and interests of shareholders,” he said at the SIAS Investors’ Choice Awards on Oct 21. “Hence, it is very legitimate for SIAS (Securities Investors Association, Singapore) to complement the actions of regulators, SGX and banks to speak out on behalf of investors and to seek answers from the companies concerned.” Chee also said good corporate governance means conducting business responsibly and within the law. “The Government takes this very seriously. Where companies are found to have contravened our laws based on the facts and evidence, we will take the necessary enforcement actions against the errant firms and individuals.” he said. Speaking at the event, SIAS founder, president and chief executive David Gerald said all investors should “think carefully about where they put their money”, urging them to “absolutely avoid companies with poor environmental records”. This applies especially to those linked to the haze, he said, noting that the massive destruction of forests and green spaces causes harm to public health. “Investors who fund such companies, even indirectly, share some responsibility for these outcomes.” He said SIAS will continue to raise awareness among investors about environmental, social and governance risks, and encourage them to check a company’s sustainability practices before investing. “By choosing responsible companies, retail investors can protect their own returns while supporting a cleaner, healthier region,” he said. Chee, who is also deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), also announced that MAS will support SIAS in enhancing investor education through the development of initial public offering (IPO) guides. These guides will distil key information from public offer documents when a company wants to list and help investors identify the issues that are most relevant to them, while highlighting matters that they should consider. Chee said: “They will not recommend whether an IPO is a good or bad investment. They will complement, not replace, investors’ own assessment of the risks and the research available to them. The objective is to help investors ask the right questions and make more informed decisions.” The Singapore Exchange (SGX) saw 10 new listings in 2026 by the end of August, which raised about $1.4 billion. Chee Hong Tat, National Development Minister and deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said MAS will support SIAS in enhancing investor education through the development of initial public offering guides. Chee noted that there has been renewed interest from a broader range of companies considering Singapore as a listing venue, from real estate investment trusts and real assets to firms in growth sectors such as technology, digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing. He said: “The external global environment has become more challenging, but Singapore’s fundamentals remain sound. We know markets will go through cycles – what matters is that we stay focused on rebuilding broader and deeper capabilities over the long term.” He added that turning near-term momentum into lasting investor confidence requires well-governed companies that earn trust, well-informed investors, and strong bridges between the companies and investors. “As more companies consider Singapore as a listing venue, our IPO ecosystem must inspire confidence among both issuers and investors,” Chee said. This is where the IPO guides and increased research coverage of listed companies come in. MAS has supported SIAS over the years by collaborating in investor education, promoting good corporate governance and raising awareness of investment scams, and this partnership is set to deepen as the market evolves, he added.

events.title: My kids don't spend their days in classrooms. They spend them exploring the woods.
events.summary: Caitlin Conway is a mom of two in Colorado. Courtesy of Caitlin Conway Caitlin Conway is a mom of two who lives in Colorado. She sends her two kids, ages 8 and 5, to a forest school and homeschools them. She says the impact on them physically and emotionally is unparalleled. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Caitlin Conway . It has been edited for length and clarity. Years ago, when my oldest was an infant, my husband and I had seen a documentary about outdoor schooling in Nordic countries . It really resonated with us, but it also felt intense because we're not used to seeing that kind of setup here. It was cool, but also terrifying — kids were using knives in the woods. Then I found a forest school in Colorado, where we live. We started forest school when my oldest was 4.5 We started my son on the coldest day of the year, in February, and I was nervous. We sent him out, and when he came home, he didn't say anything about the weather. He never even mentioned that it was cold; he was immediately engrossed. It was his primary source of education until two years ago, through first grade. They age out of a full-day program around then, so we now homeschool and leverage a homeschool enrichment program for him because we were not ready to leave the program. My youngest attends forest school three days a week and is also homeschooled the other days. The school goes from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. every day as long as it's 15 degrees Fahrenheit or warmer. Sometimes they have a shelter; sometimes they don't. They learn how to keep their bodies warm. The primary focus is on social and emotional development . It gives kids opportunities to test their capabilities, both physically and emotionally. The guides are there to keep them safe, but they're not there to solve a kid's every problem. They learn to negotiate conflicts with each other and can get help when they need it. When at home, we also prioritize being outside We don't follow a strict homeschooling curriculum . Our main focus is on exposure. We homeschool so they can continue to stay outside and strengthen their bodies and minds. We've also found a group of people through forest school that we call our homeschool co-op. It's two other families, and we all help facilitate "adventure days" outside. I'm not sitting at a kitchen table with them all day. We do an art program, and both kids also take piano lessons and swim. We also do our own work around reading, writing, and math. I never expected to be homeschooling my kids, but they love it I don't have an educational background. I come from early-stage start-ups and am currently a real estate agent. But I continue to double down on this method because I see an incredible impact on my kids' ability to adapt to different situations. They can sit still at a restaurant, but they can also jump off a cliff into a river. They know that bravery has a great payoff. The hardest part is other people's opinions. We've had to defend what we're doing, something I'm sure every homeschool parent has had to do. An instant reaction to me sharing that my kids are in the woods all day is, "But how are they learning if they're not in the real world?" That can be frustrating, but I think it's important to make sure people know there are other options for early childhood development. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: France’s Macron says protesters won’t be allowed to ‘cause chaos’
events.summary: French president criticises comments by ‘foreign leaders’ trying to exploit disorder for their own political agenda. French President Emmanuel Macron has said people who plan to “cause chaos” during protests against the high cost of living will not be allowed to do so. Speaking to the press in Doha, where he met Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Macron said he would meet with French intelligence services before protests planned for Saturday. list 1 of 3 ‘I am still traumatised’: French police accused of brutalising minors list 2 of 3 ‘It’s hard for us’: Paris small businesses bear brunt of protest violence list 3 of 3 Europe is in trouble, and it is blaming Muslims He maintained that there has not been any “visible ‌foreign interference in the events ‌that took place”, but warned that “there had been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath.” More than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday to demand better conditions in schools and denounce high living costs. At least 2,500 people were arrested after riots broke out in certain areas, with shops looted. Macron insisted he would “adopt all the measures necessary” to restore what he described as “calm, security and order”. The French president also criticised “unacceptable and even stupid comments by many, including foreign leaders”. Macron said the leaders were weighing in on protests in France to rally their political supporters. His comments appeared to be related to United States President Donald Trump, who claimed the protests were about immigration. Macron’s criticism also appeared to relate to claims made by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who said France had been engulfed by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Neither Trump nor Netanyahu provided any evidence to support their claims. On Wednesday, France’s Yellow Vest movement filed plans for a large protest in Paris this weekend, following a second consecutive night of curfews that passed without major incidents. Macron said it was not currently necessary to enforce a state of emergency, but Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has pledged to increase security at future protests. Lecornu said there would be a “massive deployment” of police, backed by the military.

events.title: Oil prices little changed as traders assess Middle East developments
events.summary: Oil prices were little changed on Wednesday as escalating supply risks in the Middle East keep investors on edge. Attacks on tanker near the Hormuz Strait and on Saudi Arabian facilities by Iran-backed Houthis have Oil prices were little changed Wednesday as worries over Middle East supply disruptions keep the market on edge, with attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy facilities denting sentiment. Brent crude futures lost 17 cents to $108.62 a barrel as of 8:47 a.m. ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 8 cents to $97.90 a barrel. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that naval mines had prevented three tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz using routes Tehran deemed unauthorized. "Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," IRGC said in a statement published on their official Sepah News website . Adding to regional worries, Yemen's Houthi militants claimed responsibility on Monday for strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Riyadh and Abha. The escalating tensions have also sent global oil shipping costs soaring, adding another layer of pressure to energy markets. The global average crude freight rate has surged above $20 per barrel, compared with just $3 a year earlier, according to a Goldman Sachs report published Tuesday. While rates have eased slightly in recent days, they remain roughly seven times higher than a year ago. Goldman estimated that war-risk premiums associated with crossing the Strait of Hormuz accounted for about $7 of the $20 year-on-year increase in average crude freight rates, while ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf contributed another $4. The investment bank warned that elevated shipping costs could widen price differences between crude grades, squeeze refiners' profit margins and ultimately push up refined fuel prices. "High freight costs have weighed particularly heavily on Asian refineries' net margins, threatening their refined product output, which could then raise global refined product prices," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote.
