events.title: Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work
events.summary: President Donald Trump's offer to pay out $5,000 checks if Republicans win belongs to a long political tradition of cash for votes. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win. President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “ DOGE dividend ” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues , and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans. But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view . For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races . I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote. Why vote buying rarely works The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia. By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants . Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s. But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes. If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence. Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent . As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “ Against the Machine .” The importance of competition There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops. First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights. This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “ Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos .” In Mexico’s 2018 election, the PAN party, whose flags are pictured here, ran into opposition in Nuevo Laredo due to its vote-buying attempts. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets : Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision. Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret. It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment. Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it. Bringing it home Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely. Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate . There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism. The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.” At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vot

events.title: The permitting bill enters a critical stretch
events.summary: Data: Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy; Table: Ben Geman/Axios The push to pass a sweeping permitting bill is gaining powerful allies and encountering fresh resistance as Congress prepares for a post-midterms showdown. Why it matters: It's the most important energy bill in a long time. Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But some environmentalists say it badly weakens crucial protections in the name of speeding reviews. Driving the news: A new, interactive analysis out on Wednesday projects potentially huge time savings if the bill becomes law. Transmission projects could see the biggest acceleration, per Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh, a researcher with Columbia's energy think tank. He based it on historical data about a large number of specific projects, then estimated how much quicker they would have proceeded under the bill. Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy doesn't have an institutional position on the bill. But founding director Jason Bordoff, a prominent voice in energy policy circles, is urging environmentalists not to oppose it. State of play: A who's who of economic and national security officials spanning six presidents (including Trump) are linking arms behind the bill in a new letter to Capitol Hill leaders. What's next: The effort goes beyond signatures for some of the former officials, according to letter organizer Arnab Datta of the Institute for Progress, a nonpartisan think tank. "Some folks are engaging beyond the letter itself with stakeholders across the board, and some have made themselves available for members briefings or conversations," he tells me via email. Catch up quick: The letter from 19 officials includes Biden-era Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and Trump 1.0 Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, among five people who held the job. The list also features Trump 1.0 Secretary of State and CIA boss Mike Pompeo, and Leon Panetta, who had top Obama-era defense and CIA gigs, to name just two others. Friction point: The last 24 hours has also brought new signs of simmering opposition to the bill, or at least parts of it, adding to existing concerns among tribal leaders and some green groups. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) posted on X that it would be "tone deaf if Congress makes it easier to build data centers." That drew pushback from backers who emphasized provisions to ensure data center companies cover grid costs. What we're watching: The Edison Electric Institute, a powerful group of for-profit utilities, still hasn't weighed in. But David Pomerantz, who's with the progressive Energy & Policy Institute obtained an Oklahoma Gas & Electric document criticizing the transmission provisions. The bottom line: The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bipartisan permitting bill immediately after lawmakers return from recess. events.title: eBay to lay off 9% of workforce in push to simplify operations, internal memo shows
events.summary: EBay has set itself apart from rivals by pushing into authenticated luxury goods, collectibles and refurbished products, which draw enthusiasts willing to pay more for valuable items. eBay will cut about 9% of its staff to simplify operations and move money to faster-growing areas, CEO Jamie Iannone said in a memo reviewed by Reuters. eBay is focusing on authenticated luxury goods, collectibles and refurbished products, which have helped its shares rise nearly 40% in 2026, far above the S&P 500. The company also gained from its US$1.4 billion Depop deal and rejected Ryan Cohen’s US$56 billion bid as “neither credible nor attractive”. EBay will lay off about 9% of its workforce as the online marketplace looks to simplify operations and shift resources to its fastest-growing areas, its chief executive officer Jamie Iannone told staff in a memo that was reviewed by Reuters. A spokesperson for eBay confirmed the layoffs to Reuters on Oct 21. The company also let go about 6% of its workforce, or 800 employees, in February as part of efforts to streamline operations. That has helped its shares rise nearly 40% in 2026, outperforming the benchmark S&P 500’s around 12% gain. “Our strategy is working,” Iannone said in the memo, adding that “continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest”. He said affected staff would be informed in the coming days. The company has this year also benefited from its US$1.4 billion (S$1.79 billion) deal for ​fashion resale platform Depop, which expanded its reach among younger consumers ​and strengthened its position in the growing re-commerce market. That helped eBay forecast third-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates when it last posted results, in August. The company is slated to report latest earnings next week. Those efforts have also caught the eye of GameStop chief executive officer Ryan Cohen, who made an unsolicited US$56 billion bid for the much larger eBay in May. EBay had rejected the offer , saying that it was “neither credible nor attractive”. REUTERS

events.title: Australians also don’t like data centers: NextDC shares fall 42% after community opposition stalls a grid upgrade
events.summary: NextDC, an Australian data center operator, is the latest such company to get hit by a growing investor selloff of AI stocks. Shares in the Brisbane-based company fell by 41.7% on Wednesday after it sharply cut its annual revenue and earnings forecast, blaming community opposition and delays to grid upgrades. NextDC now expects to generate between 475 million and 500 million Australian dollars ($333 million to $350 million), down from a previous forecast of 615 million to 640 million Australian dollars. It also cut its forecast for earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) to between 245 million Australian dollars and 265 million Australian dollars ($172 million to $186 million) In an exchange filing to the Australian Securities Exchange, NextDC blamed setbacks to its M3 Melbourne data center. Jemena, an electricity provider that supplies power to M3, suspended part of its improvement works last month; it does not expect to restart them before February 2027. “Jemena has suspended parts of the network works required for the next increase in grid supply to M3 Melbourne,” Craig Scroggie, NextDC’s CEO, said in the stock filing. “Jemena has attributed the suspension to community and stakeholder opposition to the works and to the absence of local council consent pending further consultation.” NextDC also cut its capital expenditure by 750 million Australian dollars ($527 million), and put land aquisitions and new development projects “on hold for the foreseeable future.” Australian data centers—much like their counterparts in the U.S.—are sparking protests among local communities. Residents are worried about how data centers will affect power and water supplies, as well as worsening noise pollution. Not just NextDC NextDC’s share plunge caps a rough few weeks for data center and AI infrastructure companies. On Oct. 9, Firmus—another Australian data center operator— abruptly canceled its Australian IPO, which was set to be one of the largest debuts in the country’s history. The company instead said it would raise funds through private markets. Investors were reportedly concerned about the company’s debt and the lack of a track record on data center construction. AirTrunk, a Blackstone-owned data center operator, decided on Oct. 13 to postpone a Singapore listing for its real estate investment trust, according to media reports . Also last week, bonds from U.S.-based neocloud CoreWeave plunged to below 80 cents on the dollar, a level that typically signals a company under financial strain . Tesla CEO Elon Musk took notice, posting “ yikes ” on his social media platform X. Then, on Oct. 20, shares of South Korean cloud provider Elice Group plunged by 32% on their first day of trading. (Shares recovered on Wednesday, rising by 30%, the daily limit.) More dominoes may be about to fall. Singapore-based DayOne Data Centers is considering delaying or cutting the size of its upcoming U.S. IPO, Bloomberg reported Wednesday, citing unnamed sources. (DayOne didn’t immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment; it declined comment to Bloomberg.) This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Nvidia announces plug and play Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck
events.summary: Nvidia's new DSX Pod AI Factory packages seven Vera Rubin AI racks in a shipping container designed to be transported by truck. All the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory. Nvidia did not disclose a price; analysts estimate a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million. Nvidia announced Wednesday a new product that will put seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container, the company's latest effort to move up the stack and offer complete systems for artificial intelligence computing. The DSX Pod AI Factory is roughly the size of a standard shipping container and weighs about 28,000 kilograms (nearly 62,000 pounds), Nvidia said. It's designed to be shipped on a truck on normal roads and all the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory, the company said. "The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it's placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing," Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale computing at Nvidia, said on a call with reporters this week. The DSX Pod AI factory will reduce the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days, according to the company. Nvidia said the pod is intended for customers worldwide and could help address deployment challenges faced by European customers. Nvidia did not announce a price for the system, but analysts say a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million. The DSX Pod is a reference design that will ship from Nvidia's manufacturing partners. Nvidia said it was working with manufacturers including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron. Nvidia expects deliveries to start in early 2027. Nvidia, once a chip company, now offers networking, storage and other data center needs to its customers. Its AI systems have evolved from single graphics processing unit chips to servers with four or eight GPUs, then to entire racks and now to the DSX Pod, a containerized building block with several racks already integrated. "What we offer into one gigawatt went from about $18 billion or so per gigawatt, to $20-something billion per gigawatt, to now $40-plus billion per gigawatt," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said recently on a podcast. Gigawatts refer to the size of data center infrastructure by how much power is used. "My sense is that's going to keep going up." events.title: Ghana eyes mineral export ban to boost domestic processing
events.summary: Ghana plans to ban exports of raw mineral ores by 2030 to boost domestic processing, its president said, reinforcing a broader push by Africa’s resource-rich countries to capture more value from their minerals. “Investors must understand the processing obligations associated with access to our resources,” President John Dramani Mahama said at a mining conference in Accra. The country is Africa’s largest gold producer and also mines manganese, bauxite, and diamonds. The global race for minerals used in clean energy and advanced technologies has intensified competition between China, the US, and Europe for African supplies. Ghana’s proposed restrictions would put it alongside countries such as DR Congo, which restricts exports of copper and cobalt concentrates. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Euro nears 3-month low against Singdollar amid political unrest in Europe, may weaken further
events.summary: The euro has declined 4.8% against the Singapore dollar in 2026. The euro is near a three-month low against the Singdollar, as unrest in France, Portugal and Italy adds to worries over Europe’s growth, inflation and public finances. Analysts said Europe’s weaker growth and political risk may keep pressuring the euro, with some seeing $1.42 and even $1.40 if $1.43 breaks. The Singdollar stays supported by Singapore’s policy and AAA rating, while experts say safe-haven demand may also lift Singapore bonds and other stable Asian currencies. SINGAPORE – Political unrest in parts of Europe over the rising cost of living and pressure on public services has weighed on the euro, with the currency hovering near a three-month low against the Singapore dollar on Oct 21. The euro gained 6.76% against the Singdollar in 2025, but has declined 4.8% so far in 2026. The Singdollar was trading at 1.43 to the euro on Oct 21. Analysts said continued political uncertainty could put further pressure on the euro against the Singdollar, although its direction will also depend on interest rate expectations and broader economic conditions. Mark Matthews, head of research for Asia at Julius Baer, said much of the euro’s weakness against the Singdollar can be attributed to differences in economic growth, with Europe’s economy expanding by around 1% compared with Singapore’s growth of about 5%. “The rioting in France is just the cherry on top,” he said. He added that the unrest also highlights deeper fiscal and economic challenges, as the French government tries to bring its budget under control amid public dissatisfaction over school funding, financial assistance to Ukraine and higher living costs. Protests in France began in September over inadequate school facilities and teacher shortages, before widening to include concerns over rising living costs and declining public services. Thousands also gathered in Portugal to demand action on rising housing costs and other living expenses, while protests in Italy over the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services turned violent, with demonstrators clashing with police in Milan and several other northern cities. Eugene Koh, sales trader at CMC Markets Singapore, expects further weakness in the euro against the Singdollar in the near term. “A sustained break below $1.43 could bring $1.42 into focus, followed by $1.40,” he said. Koh said the euro is facing pressure from rising energy costs, weaker growth prospects, and political and fiscal uncertainty across Europe. European gas prices have risen above €80 per megawatt-hour, while inflation in countries using the euro climbed to 3.8% in September. “This creates a difficult trade-off for the European Central Bank (ECB): Higher rates may help contain inflation but could further weigh on economic activity,” said Koh. In contrast, the Singdollar continues to benefit from the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) policy of allowing the currency to appreciate. Although MAS kept its monetary policy unchanged in October, its existing stance continues to support the Singdollar and help contain imported inflation, said Koh. “Still, a sustained decline in energy prices, easing political tensions or a more hawkish ECB could trigger a rebound in the euro,” he noted. OCBC foreign exchange strategist Christopher Wong said the euro could face further pressure against the Singdollar in the near term if the political uncertainty in France persists. But he cautioned against assuming that the euro would continue to weaken following its recent decline. OCBC forecasts the euro to trade at $1.43 against the Singdollar in the first quarter of 2027, suggesting some stabilisation, although a further deterioration in European sentiment could put additional pressure on the currency. Kelvin Tay, chief investment officer for Asia at Pictet Wealth Management, said France, in particular, faces significant challenges in stabilising its public debt, with the interest rate on its debt projected to exceed nominal economic growth by 2029. He noted that much of the country’s public spending, including pensions, healthcare and defence, would be difficult to cut, while its already high tax burden leaves limited room to raise additional revenue. But France’s fiscal troubles are unlikely to have a significant direct impact on Asia, although concerns over its rising borrowing costs could spread to other government bond markets if investors become increasingly wary of sovereign debt risks. “In this situation, the Chinese yuan and Singdollar would likely be the most stable currencies in Asia due to strong government fundamentals such as high foreign exchange reserves and large current account surpluses,” said Tay. “Singapore Government bonds could also benefit from safe-haven demand amid heightened global uncertainty,” he added.

events.title: Tokenized stock trading takes off overseas as Goldman, other U.S. companies object
events.summary: Trading activity around blockchain-based versions of traditional financial assets including stocks is growing. Tokenized volume on Robinhood Chain surged to $11.31 billion in September, up from $526 million in July. Major U.S. companies such as Goldman Sachs, Microsoft and McDonald's are objecting to having tokenized versions of their shares traded. Trading in so-called tokenized stocks is gaining momentum in international markets, even as major U.S. companies are pushing back against efforts to introduce them domestically. Trading activity around blockchain-based versions of traditional financial assets including equities is growing, according to the latest quarterly staking report by Bitwise Asset Management, published Tuesday. On Robinhood Chain, the brokerage firm's newly launched network for users and AI agents to trade various assets onchain, tokenized stocks volume surged from $526 million in July to $2.21 billion in August, then rocketed to $11.31 billion in September. In the same quarter, non-crypto markets made up 36.5% of Hyperliquid's perpetuals volume, up from 32.7% in the previous quarter. Also, tokenized equities were the fastest-growing category on Solana. Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs , Microsoft , Qualcomm , Caterpillar , McDonald's , Western Digital and Alphabet have objected to having tokenized versions of their shares traded on the OKXICE platform, the tokenized securities venue jointly launched the crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange. OKXICE disclosed the company objections in a public notice Monday, adding them to a group of earlier objectors including CoreWeave , UnitedHealth , Broadcom , Applied Digital , AppLovin and Cerebras . The contrast highlights a growing debate and challenge for the crypto industry: how to convince companies that tokenized trading of their stock is worth embracing. Tokenization – the process of issuing digital representations of publicly traded securities, real world assets or any other form of value on a blockchain network – has become a major topic of interest in the market given the potential for blockchain technology to improve accessibility and liquidity across financial assets. It's also raising questions about what rights tokens should provide for holders. The debate centers on whether investors should receive the same economic and shareholder rights as they would with traditional shares, particularly voting rights. The issue first came into focus in September after a public fight between the CEOs of Robinhood and AMC over Robinhood's stock-token model. Trading of tokenized equities is currently concentrated overseas, where tokenized products are more widely available. Crypto industry watchers are monitoring whether adoption picks up in the U.S., however, after the SEC last month put out an innovation exemption creating a temporary pathway for tokenized stocks in the U.S. – which requires that companies be able to object to having their shares represented as tokens. "The divergence comes down to what's actually being traded. Offshore, most of this activity is price exposure through onchain perps and wrapped tokens that never needed a company's permission, while the U.S. framework is trying to put real shares onchain, and that gives issuers a say," said Mirza Uddin, chief operating officer of Injective. "Right now companies like Goldman and Microsoft see all of the risk and none of the upside – a token they don't control trading 24/7 with unclear voting rights," he added. "Until the industry shows issuers what they gain – a global shareholder base and a market that never closes – the growth will keep happening abroad while the U.S. debates permission slips." ClearStreet analyst Owen Lau said companies may not yet realize the full benefits of tokenization and that he expects some will eventually embrace it. "Some companies will say yes or will not object to this because of the benefits … the expanded investor base, 24/7 [access], increased distribution channel. Some of the beaten down stocks with low trading volume could be good candidates," he said. Additionally, companies would also benefit from greater visibility, direct dividend payments and cost savings, Lau explained. For investors, tokenized assets can also act as collateral for decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms, offering them more flexibility and control. "This is a very natural response. The model was designed to give companies the right to determine whether they want to opt in or opt out. We always anticipated that, because this is such a dramatic and revolutionary change, many companies would want to wait and see how it goes rather than be the first to participate," Andrew Cuomo, co-chairman of OKXICE, said in a statement. "The SEC model is designed to accommodate both approaches," he added. "There are limits on how many companies can participate and on the volume that can be traded ...

events.title: UK inflation rise to highest in almost a year as Iran war drives fuel prices higher
events.summary: Inflation in the U.K. has risen to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to drive up fuel prices LONDON -- Inflation in the U.K. rose to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to ratchet up fuel prices, official figures showed Wednesday, cementing market expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month. The Office for National Statistics said consumer prices rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August. That's the highest reading since October last year, and above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month. The increase takes inflation further above the Bank of England's target rate of 2%. Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump. Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August. Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz , which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies. Treasury chief John Healey said his budget statement next week will aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from the upward march in the cost of living. Last month, rate-setters held the bank's main rate at 3.75% but gave a big hint that they were ready to hike soon. “With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW. Most economists expect an increase in the bank's main rate to 4%. Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank , have raised rates recently. Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. events.title: Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
events.summary: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners Miatta Fahnbulleh is leaning towards rejecting the giant Rosebank oilfield, the Guardian understands, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. Officials say the energy secretary is minded to refuse approval for the field, which would be one of the biggest in the North Sea. Fahnbulleh approved the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, prompting protests from some in the green movement. But she told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it. “One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.” Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet taken a final decision on Rosebank, but a ruling is expected later this year. The field would emit about seven times the carbon of Jackdaw and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given most of the oil would be exported. On a visit to Aberdeen, Fahnbulleh said she had been satisfied that Jackdaw, which is due to begin producing gas within weeks and will add an estimated 36m tonnes of carbon emissions, would not violate the UK’s climate commitments. “As we make the transition, we are going to need gas,” she said on a visit to Aberdeen to announce the decision. “At a point when we have got conflict in the Middle East that is triggering an energy crisis, energy security is vital, and homegrown energy is key.” She admitted, however, it would not help achieve the government’s main energy target of bringing down bills, saying: “This is not about bills.” The UN Environment Programme has recommended that global carbon emissions be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through a new energy wealth fund. The fund will be given £2bn in the budget, she said, some of which will be reallocated from other parts of her department’s budget. “When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes. However, she could not say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the new fund, or how much that might generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said. While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfield project have sought approval for existing licences. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. The Jackdaw field will start supplying gas to homes and businesses from the end of the month, the government said after approving the scheme. Asked how confident he was that the Rosebank field would be approved, Neil McCulloch, the chief executive of Adura, one of the companies behind the plans, told the Press Association: “We’re very confident now.” He said: “We’ve seen a decision made that there is a process that can result in a decision, but it’s a matter for the secretary of state and her team to examine the two fields separately. But we believe we’ve done as good a job in arguing our case with Rosebank as we did with Jackdaw. “Obviously, the economic benefits of Rosebank are different. It’s a bigger field. It will last longer than Jackdaw, and so I’m sure she’ll take that into account when she makes her decision in terms of the jobs and economic impact for the UK.” The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland , where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted. But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party. A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G, seen by the Guardian, found that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gave the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling.

events.title: Apple iPhone Duo hands-on: Your productivity will hinge on this
events.summary: Apple , this had better be good; you made us wait more than seven years for this to unfold. At long last, the company has introduced the iPhone Duo , its first entry into the foldable device category, and first major hardware release under new boss John Ternus. And, on a personal note, I've never seen my peers this hyped for a device. The National gave the device a spin and ran through its features. Here are our initial thoughts. The lowdown The passport-sized iPhone Duo, when folded, gives you a 13.7cm (5.4-inch) display. Open it up and that digital real estate stretches to 19.3cm (7.6 inches). And it's now Apple's thinnest smartphone, at only 5.2mm when open. The power and camera control buttons remain in their usual slots on the right while it's closed or open in landscape mode. But from here, things get shaken up quite a bit. The volume buttons are now on top, and switching to portrait mode while unfolded brings them to the left for more familiar control. Meanwhile, the USB-C charging port, while still at the bottom when folded, switches to the left side when unfolded, which is a little odd as we're used to that on the right. But there are two notable omissions: there is no Action Button, which is customisable and (probably) most commonly used as the silent toggle No Face ID Face ID – repeat, no Face ID. Instead, a Touch ID, nestled on the power button, makes its return. Skipping the Action Button and Face ID will need some getting used to, particularly the latter, but Apple says key stuff like transactions and verifying your identity will still be seamless – you'll just need your fingers instead of your eyes. Also, battery percentage and carrier details won't be readily visible on the homescreens. Instead, you have to swipe down from the top-right, like the iPhone X. The latest, smaller version of Dynamic Island is also present, but now it now appears on the top right. As for the crease, it is virtually invisible. Apple hasn't released a figure for fold-unfold durability, though the Duo has ceramic shield protection for scratchproofing and is rated IP68 for dust and waterproofing. There are four cameras – the main 48MP Dual Fusion system, the 12MP Centre Stage camera on the cover and the under-display camera on the inner display. You can choose from two colours, night sky and star white, with the former our winner. (It would've been better if there was a defining option like lavender or our all-time favourite, cosmic orange.) By now we know that the Duo's prices in the UAE range from Dh8,499 to Dh13,599, and there are extended shipping times due to overwhelming demand. First steps The iPhone Duo has a clean feel: opening and closing feels reliable, and the sturdy hinge ensures it will stay in place without any wobble or movement. Multitasking is a key feature that allows you to do more with fewer swipes and taps. For example, you can have your email on one side and photos on the other, and you can just drag an image as an attachment. Let the Duo sit L-shaped and you'll be able to do some easy stuff. If you're in the camera app or a streaming service like Netflix, controls will be on screen below for easier navigation. The camera also has a new feature that automatically takes pictures without having to control it; trigger the function, let the main cameras face you and it will track subjects and take pictures from time to time, which you will know when the torch briefly lights up. It also acts as a good teleprompter, which creators and on-camera people will find useful. Apple says apps have been and are being optimised to work with the Duo, and a sign that an app has been updated is when you see controls on the right side. It's also optimised for popular apps such as WhatsApp, Instagram and Slack, to make work, play and creation easier. While we don't have the full list, updates for popular apps are expected to be rolled out on Friday, when the device finally becomes available in stores. While we haven't fully tested it, Apple guarantees battery life on a par with the iPhone 18 Pro, meaning it should, according to our own tests , make it through more than a day and a half. There are two batteries in the Duo, although according to Apple, they work as one, discharge as one and do all things together. The Duo is compatible with the USB-C version of the Apple Pencil. At this point, it is unclear if and when other models of the company's stylus will follow the same path. Initial verdict We're still not sure how much of the iPhone Duo's bigger display we'll be using, considering it has specific purposes and the front screen is big enough to perform most of our tasks. We're foreseeing we'll be using the front display for work and communication, and the bigger one for entertainment and gaming. If the overwhelming orders are any indication, Apple's iPhone Duo is poised to do well. The device feels refined, but its biggest draw may be its seamless integration into Apple's ecosystem. That's a compelling selling point for those who usually find foldables cumbersome or complicated, if they're willing to splash the cash.

events.title: ‘They try to break us’: Pro-Palestine activists in Czech custody
events.summary: As a group is accused of an attack on a weapons factory, activists allege a growing crackdown on the solidarity movement. Prague, Czech Republic – Youssef Moursi, a 25-year-old Egyptian university student and activist in Prague, has spent the last six months in pre-trial detention, accused of an arson attack in March against a Czech weapons factory with alleged ties to Israel. Moursi is one of 11 people being charged with “terrorism” for the attack and could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted. The case has echoes of legal battles in the United Kingdom , where Palestine Action activists have been sentenced under terrorism laws, and Germany , where five people accused of targeting a site linked to Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest weapons maker, are on trial. Moursi, a humanities student at Charles University, said in a statement to Al Jazeera that “a group of armed and masked policemen smashed down [my] front door”, two days after the alleged attack, in which he denies any involvement. He spent the first three months of his detention in solitary confinement, according to his lawyer. Today, he is allowed one hour outside his cell and 20 minutes on the phone a day, with visits from friends and family every two weeks. “[There] is the psychological front being waged against us, where [the police] deliberately try to break us by putting some of us in solitary confinement for months, denying us visits, blocking correspondence, or spreading fear,” Moursi said. “Putting people in custody and prolonging it time and time again without direct evidence, mainly based on a mix of inclinations, activism, racism, and an attempted blurring of freedom of speech, is unacceptable.” Moursi and his lawyer, Pavel Cizinsky, believe he has been targeted because of his involvement in pro-Palestine activism in Prague. Cizinsky said part of the evidence police have against Moursi is that on the day after the fire, he posted advice for pro-Palestinian activists on social media, should they be approached by officers. Cizinsky called this “ridiculous.” “If you put into Google what to do when interviewed by the police, the first advice is wait for your lawyer. But if you say it as a pro-Palestinian activist, if you write it to your friends, then it’s reason against you that you are guilty,” Cizinsky said. At the beginning of the investigation, Cizinsky said he faced pressure from the authorities not to take the case. As a result, he was not present during the initial interrogation and house raid on Moursi’s flat. “It is clear that there is extraordinary attention to this investigation by the police, and really great resources dedicated to this case,” Cizinsky said. “But the fact that he is already five months in prison is surely a breach of law.” Under Czech law, individuals held in pre-trial detention who have not been convicted must have their detention reviewed by a court every three months. Moursi’s detention has so far been reviewed twice, with the court deciding each time that he must stay in prison. His detention will be reviewed again in early December, and the trial is expected to start within a year. The fire broke out in the early hours of March 20 at LPP Holding, a Czech weapons factory in Pardubice, about 120km (75 miles) east of Prague. No one was injured but police said the building was destroyed, with damage estimates reaching hundreds of millions of crowns, or at least four million euros. A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group called The Earthquake Faction claimed responsibility and posted videos of the fire, saying it targeted LPP Holding for its cooperation with Elbit Systems, an Israeli weapons company. In 2023, LPP Holding and Elbit Systems announced a partnership to build drones in the Czech Republic. But on the day of the fire, an LPP Holding spokesperson told Czech media the collaboration never happened. In the weeks following the attack, police launched a manhunt and arrested several foreign nationals including Ukrainian, Czech, Slovak, Polish and American citizens. Of the 10 other individuals accused, three are under house arrest in Poland and seven remain behind bars in the Czech Republic. Over the past two years, Elbit Systems has become a primary target for pro-Palestine activists across Europe. In June, a UK court convicted four imprisoned Palestine Action members of criminal damage with a “terrorist connection” after a raid on an Elbit Systems factory in Filton, near Bristol. In September last year, police in Poland arrested protesters at an arms fair for throwing red liquid over an Elbit Systems stand. This week, an elderly man in Germany was arrested after protesting against the Israeli weapons giant. In Prague, the atmosphere for pro-Palestinian activists has grown increasingly tense. A collective called Prague 4 Palestine Youth stopped organising demonstrations and charity events after police investigations into dozens of its members in the months following the arson attack.

events.title: Carriers reroute Riyadh flights to airport four hours' drive away
events.summary: Saudi airlines are turning to Al Qassim, about a four-hour drive from Riyadh, as an alternative to the capital while its airport remains closed following a deadly Houthi attack almost two weeks ago. The kingdom’s main flag carrier, Saudia, is offering tickets to Riyadh via Al Qassim, with a bus connection to the Saudi capital. Riyadh Air, Public Investment Fund’s startup airline, is also giving passengers booked on flights to Riyadh the option to fly to Al Qassim. Riyadh airport is now open to traffic with prior permission, but passenger flights have yet to resume and most airlines have canceled services until anywhere from next week to next year. Local airlines have moved planes parked at Riyadh airport to other locations while the airport remains a Houthi target, suggesting that travel to the capital is not expected to resume soon. — Matthew Martin

events.title: SpaceX and Tesla mega-merger under discussion
events.summary: The News Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX and Tesla, have begun exploring a merger that would create a $3.5 trillion corporate giant spanning key sectors of cutting-edge technology. Musk argued that combining the companies would allow them to deepen cooperation on chip design, robotics, software, and other technologies ; both firms’ share prices rose following the announcement. Liz’s view The outlines of MegaMusk Inc. are starting to emerge, where special committees of SpaceX and Tesla directors will now have to bless the merger. Combining the two would bring the tech and infrastructure parts of Musk’s empire together (the Wall Street pitch) and a hyperconcentrated bet on the billionaire’s inventions, politics, and personality (the actual pitch). Musk already rolled up X, xAI, and SpaceX, whose June IPO paved the way for the Tesla deal. Many of Musk’s projects already bleed into each other — the new Roadster has SpaceX thrusters — and Musk’s employees often work interchangeably across his companies, so there’s some business and governance sense in formalizing what’s already happening. But it’s clear Musk is again using Tesla’s shareholders — and its massive retail investor base — to fund his other exploits, just as he did in 2016 when Tesla bailed out his cash-strapped solar company, SolarCity, and, more recently, when he reallocated Tesla talent and GPUs to xAI. While Musk says he’ll recuse himself from the decision, his companies’ boards don’t have a history of pushing back. Tesla Chair Robyn Denholm told Semafor last year she was skeptical of Tesla investing in xAI; four months later, it invested $2 billion . And a combo would further strengthen Musk’s control over Tesla: Super-voting shares give him roughly 84% of the vote at SpaceX, compared to 20% at Tesla, where every share has equal voting weight. Notable The SpaceX-Tesla tie-up has its own strong logic, one early SpaceX investor told Bloomberg: “Combined, it would be the only company owning the full physical-AI stack … No competitor has an analog .”

events.title: Mecca draws Indonesian sovereign wealth fund investment
events.summary: Opening up real estate ownership in Mecca and Medina to foreign investors could help deliver a boost to investment into Saudi Arabia, after Indonesia’s sovereign fund Danantara completed a 2 billion riyal ($533 million) deal to purchase a hotel and development plots. That agreement is the first time a foreign state has acquired property in Mecca, one of the holiest sites in Islam, and opens the door for further sales to Muslim-majority states, Faisal Shaker, chief executive of Thakher Development, owner of the development sold to Danantara, told Semafor. The company is the master developer behind Thakher Mecca , less than a mile from the Grand Mosque in the city. Sales of another Mecca development called Mathabah will also be launched next year, Shaker said. As part of its plan for sales to foreign investors next year “transactions we aspire to close will not be less than the deal we just announced,” Shaker said. “We are in discussion with multiple stakeholders and different parties from different parts of the world.” Investment into the two cities is “driven by faith and not by cycles,” Shaker said. Saudi Arabia opened Mecca and Medina real estate to Muslims abroad and selected foreign institutions in January. Saudis are still the majority buyers, but Gulf investors are also pouring money into the two cities, Shaker said. Danantara is also considering investing in Medina , Asharq Bloomberg reported. A key part of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s strategy to grow non-oil income is more than doubling religious visitors to the kingdom to 50 million by 2030 from about 20 million last year.

events.title: OpenAI to bring AI models to Google's cloud, in further expansion beyond Microsoft
events.summary: OpenAI said its models will be available for developers through Google's cloud after years of competition between the two companies. The ChatGPT maker will now have its models on the three major U.S. clouds. Amazon started hosting OpenAI models in April after exclusivity ended with Microsoft. OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies. For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers. That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers. Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models . Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks. "Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post. Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively. All three report quarterly results next week. Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model. OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering. Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when the AI lab said it was using Google's cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface. events.title: Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Iran’s nuclear enrichment has emerged as a major point of contention amid diplomatic push to end the war. The renewed diplomatic push to end the United States-Israel war on Iran is facing headwinds as Tehran’s nuclear programme, which the two countries invoked to launch the war in February, has once again emerged as one of the biggest stumbling blocks in reaching a ceasefire. Nearly eight months into the war, which has caused a global energy crisis, a deal to ensure a permanent ceasefire remains elusive. Moreover, the war has since spilled into a regional conflict, with Yemen emerging as its latest theatre. The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz – a global oil chokepoint – was the focus of the June Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran. The MoU had also stated that Iran “shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons”, but a comprehensive deal, including the nuclear issue, could not be thrashed out within the stipulated 60-day period. Analysts said that differing interpretations of the agreement clauses caused the MoU to fall apart. Now the nuclear issue has once again emerged as the central point of contention, with Tehran insisting that uranium enrichment is a right guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). US President Donald Trump, on the other hand, has called for “zero uranium enrichment”. His ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on Sunday reiterated his pledge to topple the Iranian government, which he said is key to preventing it from developing nuclear weapons. Earlier this week, US Vice President JD Vance appeared to offer concessions on the nuclear doctrine to reach a deal. While Qatar and Pakistan are engaged in mediation efforts, how will they get the sides to agree on the nuclear enrichment issue? Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, who is also a key negotiator in the conflict, is currently in Tehran, where he met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday. In the meeting, Rezaei said “even a particle of enriched uranium will not exit Iran at all,” according to comments carried by Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency, describing the material as a major national asset that would remain in the country for domestic use. His response came amid media reports that the US wants Iran to transfer part of its enriched uranium out of the country. Trump has previously called for the removal of the enriched uranium stockpile from Iran. Rezaei also said negotiations with the US would not begin until Washington fulfils trust-building measures, including meeting the latest conditions Iran has set. Iran wants the US to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets as part of its latest terms to end the war. In return, Iran has promised to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Another Iranian lawmaker, Alaeddin Boroujerdi, also a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, reiterated that Iran is not seeking the production of nuclear weapons. “Iran’s enrichment activities are unrelated to the US, and Washington should focus on fulfilling its own obligations regarding nuclear arms reduction,” he said. Addressing a Republican Party campaign rally earlier this week, Trump claimed that the US bombing had destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities and that he would not allow Tehran to rebuild them. “They cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told his supporters at a rally at Northern Kentucky University. Vice President Vance said earlier this week that the US has “in some ways decisively won” the war on Iran and has destroyed the country’s nuclear programme. He told a town hall hosted by CBS News that the US was now focused on ensuring that Iran makes a “long-term” and “verifiable commitment” not to rebuild its nuclear programme. “Not over the administration of Donald Trump … but five years from now, could the Iranians rebuild that nuclear arsenal? Could they try to rebuild that enrichment capacity?” he asked. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said this week that a decision to end the war finally rests with Trump. “The US will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to have a nuclear weapon. As long as President Trump is in office, they will not have a nuclear weapon,” he reiterated. Last month, Vance told the Reuters news agency in an interview that Tehran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the war. “If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said. “I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity,” he added.

events.title: Hungarian police arrest Orbán-era central bank governor on suspicion of fraud and abuse
events.summary: Hungarian police have taken former Central Bank governor György Matolcsy into custody BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungarian police arrested the country's former Central Bank governor on Wednesday, a significant step in the new government’s pursuit of suspected financial abuses during the rein of Viktor Orbán , whose government has been accused of widespread corruption. Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote in a post on Facebook that the former governor, György Matolcsy, who had also served as finance minister, was in custody, without providing further details. Since taking office earlier this year, Magyar’s government has prioritized investigating suspected financial abuses committed by Orbán-era officials. The arrest followed a statement from Hungary's Central Prosecutor's Office earlier in the day, saying it was “carrying out coordinated investigative actions" in several locations in connection with a Central Bank-related investigation into criminal misappropriation of funds. It did not mention Matolcsy by name but said more details about the case would come later. Matolcsy led Hungary’s central bank from 2013 to 2025, after serving as Orbán’s minister of economy from 2010 to 2013. He was long one of Orbán’s closest economic allies, and has denied any wrongdoing. Matolcsy's lawyer, Pál Bátki, told Hungarian news outlet Telex that the former governor was detained on suspicion of economic fraud that caused significant financial damage and using a forged private document. Christina Applegate says learning she doesn't have MS is ‘very unnerving’ Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Much of Matolcsy's tenure as head of the central bank was mired in accusations of corruption related to the bank's establishment of foundations that it endowed with hundreds of billions of forints — equivalent to hundreds of millions of dollars — in public funds. A criminal complaint was filed last month on suspicion of embezzlement, negligence, fraud, and abuse of office while Matolcsy was governor. The complaint came after the central bank audited past real estate investments that it found to have been purchased for inflated prices, causing significant financial damage to the bank. It was unclear whether Matolcsy's detention was related to the real estate purchases or the endowments to the bank's foundations. In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Magyar said it was clear that “certain members of the previous government as well as oligarchs, businessmen and family members connected to them committed serious crimes, typically corruption crimes, both with national funding and EU funding.” His administration in July launched the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, which holds investigative and prosecutorial powers to pursue cases of misused public funds. events.title: The robot revolution faces these three big challenges
events.summary: J Studios/Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Daft Punk only had it half right. Robots don't just rock ; they also draw a ton of investment. The French musicians who famously donned robot helmets retired five years ago, but Silicon Valley's obsession with robotics is reaching a fever pitch. Robotics and physical AI companies raised $33.4 billion globally in the first half of 2026. It's a stunning rise for a sector that didn't even hit $5 billion in funding in all of 2020. Rya Jetha, our resident robotics expert , wrote about why Silicon Valley is betting billions on a robot revolution . It's the first installment in Robonomics, our new series examining the rise of robots and their impact on business, jobs, and everyday life. The size of the market that robotics can address is a big draw. The need for physical labor is so vast — from construction sites to at-home butlers — the possibilities are almost endless. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, a huge proponent of physical AI, valued the industry at … $50 trillion. Just because the opportunity is there doesn't mean it'll be easy to realize. Here are some of the biggest pain points standing in the way of the robotics revolution: Not an easy hand-off: When talking about robots, the discussion typically starts and ends with human hands. It turns out our paws are pretty special, and quite difficult to recreate. Granted, not every company wants to replicate the human hand. But a lot of tasks require the dexterity we have. Figuring out how to build those capabilities into robots hasn't been easy. Hardware is hard: Building robots has gotten considerably cheaper than years ago thanks to advancements in computing and hardware. It's still a much more expensive endeavor than most software work, though. It's one thing to rewrite some code. It's another to build an entirely new prototype. Those problems get magnified as you try to scale up physical production. The smallest mistake becomes a bigger problem if it gets too far down your supply chain . Just ask Elon Musk about it . Human pushback: Companies often pitch AI tools as a way to enhance, not eliminate, human workers. Whether that's the reality is up for debate. Building robots to perform the same physical labor as humans leaves less room for interpretation. Some still don't see it as a zero-sum game. Edward Mehr, the CEO of robotics startup Machina Labs, previously told me his new factory had the same number of human workers as one at a robot-free facility. If robots do start replacing humans, they'll have to navigate another nuance specific to the blue-collar world: unions. AI has benefited some blue-collar workers, including those involved in building AI data centers. That construction has been a boon for tradespeople, with some national labor unions even siding with developers . They'll be a lot less friendly if robots mean replacing their members, though. events.title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Introducing: the Impossible issue We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue . We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood , build cities on the moon , and attain cognitive immortality . We investigate AI’s ability to say no , a bionic eye that can restore sight , and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years . This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride. Subscribe now to read the full print issue . Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month. The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation. Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration . —Tereza Pultarova How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time. The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead. Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster . —James Temple MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head. Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced. MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. events.title: Current price of oil as of October 21, 2026
events.summary: At 8 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $110.74 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s a decrease of $2.11 since yesterday morning and roughly $49 more than at this time last year. oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $112.85 -1.86% Price of oil 1 month ago $104.61 +5.85% Price of oil 1 year ago $61.75 +79.33% Will oil prices go up? Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges. Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted. It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. When you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as weaker demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with rising global demand, but soon crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before, bringing prices to under $20 per barrel. In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: How Trump made EVs more expensive and harder to find just as he went to war on Iran Databricks sets sights on Abu Dhabi as Middle East growth takes off The way we consume energy is changing Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: Microsoft empowers more than 330,000 Volkswagen Group employees with Copilot
events.summary: October 21, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft empowers more than 330,000 Volkswagen Group employees with Copilot Microsoft Copilot brings secure, AI-powered assistance into employees’ daily workflows and business processes Microsoft Source | 2 minutes REDMOND, Wash. — Oct. 21, 2026 — Microsoft Corp. on Wednesday announced that Volkswagen Group has now equipped more than 330,000 employees across the company with Microsoft Copilot, helping its workforce increase productivity, accelerate decisions and improve knowledge-based processes across the organization. “The real value of AI comes from making it available at scale in everyday work,” said Sophie Vassarotti, Head of Group Data and AI, Volkswagen Group. “With Copilot, we are bringing secure and trusted AI support to our employees, helping them work more efficiently and make better-informed decisions.” Volkswagen Group’s broad-scale deployment of Copilot is the latest step in the Group’s deliberate, phased approach to AI adoption. The organization’s phased rollout began with providing employees with broad access to AI-powered chat via Copilot Chat, for which Volkswagen saw upwards of 300,000 monthly active users on the platform. Today, employees are leveraging Copilot with Work IQ for more advanced productivity scenarios, embedding AI even more deeply into the most business processes — spanning from engineering to production, procurement and sales. In addition, more than 26,000 agents have been active across the Group over the past month alone, scaling AI-driven productivity gains. “By bringing Microsoft Copilot to more than 330,000 employees, Volkswagen Group is putting AI directly into the flow of work — helping people boost productivity, accelerate decisions and focus on higher-value tasks,” said Agnes Heftberger, Chair of the Management Board of Microsoft Germany. “Volkswagen shows how companies can evolve AI from a personal productivity tool into a foundation for future AI innovation.” In addition, Microsoft and Volkswagen Group intend to expand their collaboration and further scale the Intelligent Data Foundation, the Group’s unified data ecosystem, on Microsoft Fabric, to make trusted data easier to find, understand and use across the entire company. events.title: AI is getting better at hacking power and water systems, new research shows
events.summary: The world's most advanced AI models are suddenly capable of blueprinting cyberttacks on critical services like power grids and water systems with alarming success rates, according to new research . Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are running out of time. Top-tier frontier models are dangerously adept at mapping out attacks, new research from cybersecurity company Frenos shows, and it's only a matter of time before freely available AI models make such hacks easier to execute. "It's a clock that is moving faster than we've ever seen," Steve Swick, former top security executive at American Electric Power, told reporters during a briefing. Driving the news: Researchers at Frenos tested 10 AI models on their ability to plan attacks against industrial systems, such as the software that monitors water treatment processes. Three out of 10 models tested successfully constructed attack plans in roughly 90% of attempts. Performance varied widely: Three models the researchers considered to be at the frontier of capabilities succeeded in just 17.9% to 31.9% of attempts. The strongest foreign open-weight model succeeded 36.2% of the time, while the strongest U.S. open-weight model succeeded just 5.2%. Frenos did not disclose the names of the models tested. Zoom in : The research included nearly 17,000 tests, including 2,520 attempts to construct complete attack plans. The models received information about potential targets and tasked with piecing together the steps needed to achieve specific objectives. The big picture: Critical services like water systems and manufacturing plants have long been targets for nation-state adversaries and cybercriminals. Many operators face staffing and budget constraints. Testing and upgrading their systems can also risk disruptions to essential services that they can't afford. Unlike traditional corporate networks, industrial systems can be sensitive to unexpected traffic and commands. Even an unsuccessful attack attempt could disrupt essential operations. Threat level: Once attackers gain access to an industrial network, AI could help them quietly map out systems and identify weaknesses without the same time constraints facing human hackers, Frenos co-founder and CTO Harry Thomas said. "AI doesn't have the problem with patience," Thomas said. "It doesn't need to eat. It doesn't need to sleep, and it doesn't need to use the restroom." Paul Shaver, head of operational technology at cybersecurity firm Armadin, added that AI agents can already conduct reconnaissance and analyze large volumes of data without necessarily triggering security alerts. The intrigue : Thomas said the researchers used a relatively simple setup to guide the models through their tasks. More sophisticated tools that provide additional context and feedback could improve their performance. "A more capable harness could have given these AI models more of an edge," he said. What to watch : Several initiatives — including from the White House , frontier AI companies , and cybersecurity organizations — have cropped up in recent weeks to help lower the costs and provide resources for critical infrastructure organizations.
