events.title: OpenAI brings its frontier models to rival Google Cloud
events.summary: OpenAI is bringing its AI models and Codex coding tools to Google Cloud , expanding its reach to customers of all three major U.S. cloud providers — including companies that are also among its fiercest AI rivals. Why it matters: The move underscores a growing recognition that winning the enterprise AI race isn't just about building the smartest models. It's also about making those models available wherever businesses already run their software and store their data. For OpenAI, the agreement offers another way to reach corporate customers without requiring them to establish a separate relationship with the ChatGPT-maker. For Google, it means selling a competitor's AI models alongside its own Gemini offerings, potentially capturing business that might otherwise go to rival cloud providers. Driving the news: Under the agreement announced Wednesday, Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI's frontier models through Google's "Model Garden and Marketplace," including by using existing cloud spending commitments. The deal also brings OpenAI models to Google's Antigravity development environment and Gemini Agent. General availability is planned in the coming weeks. The big picture: The agreement follows OpenAI's expansion onto Amazon Web Services earlier this year, after changes to its Microsoft partnership opened the door to broader cloud distribution. AWS CEO Matt Garman said at the time that customers had long wanted to run OpenAI models where their existing applications and data already resided. Amazon has since expanded the OpenAI models and services available through its Bedrock platform, although neither company has publicly quantified the additional business generated by the arrangement. What they're saying: Mike Leone, VP and analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said the deal is significant for both companies, particularly because many Google Cloud customers want access to OpenAI models without moving their data. "For Google, I read the deal as confidence, because Gemini now has to win those customers with OpenAI sitting right next to it," Leone told Axios. But he doesn't see Google as necessarily hurting Gemini, since customers will still pay Google for its cloud platform, data services and security regardless of which AI models they choose. Yes, but: Distribution is only part of the equation. OpenAI still has to persuade enterprises to choose its models over those from Google, Anthropic and other competitors, many of which are available through the same cloud platforms. That could make the cloud providers' existing enterprise relationships and infrastructure as important as the models they offer. "Once every cloud has the top models, I think the competitive advantage goes to whoever does the best job with a company's data, governance, and costs," Leone said.

events.title: Visa's CMO is giving the brand a new look and betting that less is more
events.summary: Visa CMO Frank Cooper III is freshening up the company's look. Jason Mendez/Getty Images for The Whitaker Peace & Development Initiative Visa is rolling out a new "V" to pop on mobile screens as people move to contactless payments. It's the company's first refresh of this size since 2021. Other brands have increasingly leaned on symbols and pared-down names for better mobile visibility. Visa is betting that less is more when it comes to how it shows up to customers. Starting Wednesday, the letter "V" will replace "Visa" in the center of its credit cards and on its digital properties, the company exclusively told Business Insider. Visa's move signals that after 50 years of using the name, it feels it has enough brand recognition to be represented by a single letter. The change is also meant to pop more on small screens as people conduct more of their lives on their mobile devices. In addition to the "V," Visa is introducing a new font, called Visa Sans, lopping off the serif in the first letter of "Visa." "V" will now stand in for "Visa." Visa The changes were developed by Visa's in-house creative studio and Base Design. It's Visa's first significant refresh since 2021, when it introduced a blue, white, and yellow flag-like brand symbol and a new font. With the new "V," that brand symbol will go away. "There was an opportunity for us to modernize that and make it feel fresh, particularly for the next generation of consumers," Frank Cooper III , CMO of Visa, told CMO Insider. "We think it marries well with the evolution of the brand overall." Cooper said the process took about a year. "We do not have an awareness issue. We have deep trust. Playing around with the brand positioning is no light matter," he said. Other big brands have increasingly leaned on symbols and pared-down names for better visibility on smaller screens. Mastercard dropped its name from its logo in 2019. Google introduced a sans-serif logo and a new, four-color "G" icon in 2015. Dan Nicholas, design director at creative studio Super Okay, said the move to a singular V aligns with a mobile-first approach that tech and media brands like Verizon and The New York Times have taken, in which they adopt a single letter as an icon. He said the move simplifies Visa's appearance but could undermine brand recognition. "What remains to be seen in the rollout is how Visa manages this new equity," he said. "If thoughtfully and strategically executed and invested in over the next few years, we can see it becoming a strong way for the brand to express itself." Visa sees its visual changes as a companion to an effort to associate itself with culture and aspiration. It enlisted celebrities like Pharrell Williams for its " Power of Small Steps " campaign and has a partnership with the FIFA World Cup that extends through 2030. This year's World Cup campaign promoted its contactless payment option to emphasize that Visa's long-running slogan, "everywhere you want to be," was more than just a physical destination. "We see that phrase now as representing both a physical destination and a personal aspiration," Cooper said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Azoma wants to help brands win the AI shopping race. See the pitch deck that helped it raise $11.2 million.
events.summary: Azoma, cofounded by Timur Luguev and Max Sinclair, just raised $11.2 million in Series A funding. Azoma Azoma helps brands get their products discovered by AI shopping agents. Its platform measures brands' AI visibility among specific shoppers and offers tips to improve. Azoma just raised $11.2 million in a round led by Puma Growth Partners. As people begin to delegate online purchases to AI assistants and agents, the startup Azoma wants to ensure its consumer-goods clients make the shopping list. Azoma works with brands to help their products be discovered by AI shopping agents and platforms, including OpenAI's ChatGPT , Google's Gemini , Alexa for Shopping , and Walmart's Sparky . The company exclusively told CMO Insider on Wednesday that it had raised an $11.2 million Series A funding round, led by Puma Growth Partners. Founded in 2022, Azoma initially focused on helping brands show up prominently in AI search and chatbots, operating in the fast-growing field of generative engine optimization , or GEO. Then, over the past year, at least a dozen new AI shopping assistants from retailers rolled out, alongside the launch of personal AI assistants like Meta's Muse , OpenAI's Dots , and Instinct, which can also make purchases on a user's behalf. In December, Morgan Stanley estimated that AI-powered shopping assistants could account for up to $385 billion in US e-commerce sales by 2030. "The space has evolved rapidly from customers just really caring about answer engines to caring about the other types as well," Azoma CEO Max Sinclair told CMO Insider. Azoma's customers include Unilever, L'Oréal, Reckitt, and Mars. It offers them a service it calls agentic commerce optimization, a technique that helps make their products more discoverable by large language models and more likely to be recommended by them. Azoma suggests actions the clients can take to improve their visibility, from honing their marketplace listings to optimizing their content on YouTube and Reddit. It also uses " digital twin " technology to simulate different consumer demographics, so brands can see how their products are presented to the specific shoppers they want to target. Sinclair said Azoma differs from other GEO companies because it's laser-focused on the commerce space and working with brands who sell physical goods. "Many of our customers have tried these generic GEO platforms and found that they don't understand commerce at all," Sinclair said. "They don't understand the integrations, they don't understand the workflows, they don't understand the existing tech stack, they don't understand how the teams work, how they're operated, how they're motivated." Sinclair said Azoma plans to invest the fresh funds in ensuring its technology can track across all the latest agents, from Meta's Muse to TikTok's new Shopping Assistant. The company charges a fee per brand, geography, and shopping agent. Sinclair estimated the company's head count would grow to around 80 to 100 people next year, up from 40 currently, as it ramps up hiring in areas including sales, customer success, AI research, software development, and operations. Azoma also plans to integrate data from the Tesco-owned retail analytics company Dunnhumby to help brands determine whether increasing their share of voice on a platform like ChatGPT translates into a sales lift at brick-and-mortar retailers. Dunnhumby Ventures also participated in the round, alongside Twinpath, Mars IAF, Rank Ventures, and Ignite Ventures. Check out the pitch deck Azoma used to secure its $11.2 million Series A investment, shared exclusively with CMO Insider. Some of the slides have been omitted or redacted. Azoma's tech helps brands drive revenue through AI shopping agents. Azoma The 'about us' slide provides company details. Azoma Azoma has offices in London and Toronto and has previously received investment from eBay Ventures and Dunnhumby Ventures. Its clients include Unilever, Reckitt, and Heinz. Azoma The presentation features testimonials from clients at Dentsu, Perfect Ted, L'Oréal, and Mars. Azoma Azoma tees up the business opportunity. Azoma Consumers are using AI to discover brands and products. events.title: Influencers have a baby boomer problem
events.summary: Baby boomers, like this baby right here, often find influencers … annoying. Debrocke/ClassicStock/Getty Images A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . Influencer marketing to baby boomers hits different — and not in the way brands intended. Research from Morning Consult , conducted exclusively for Business Insider, reveals a stark generational divide in attitudes toward influencers. Boomers — people born between 1946 and 1964 — are distrustful of influencers, skeptical of their recommendations, and more likely to find their content "annoying." In the survey of roughly 2,000 US adults conducted in September, 31% of boomers said they trust influencer recommendations at least somewhat, compared with 62% of Gen Z and 64% of millennials. Two in five (40%) boomers surveyed said they trust influencers less than they did a few years ago. Sure, plenty of adults become set in their ways and harder to persuade as they age. But advertising pros said there's another factor that could help explain boomers' wariness of influencer marketing : brands themselves continue to overlook the older generation. "Brands are terrified of taking any dollars away from speaking to young people," said Jennifer Meehan, an EVP at the communications agency Edelman. That fear also extends into the creators they look to partner with. Florian Dost, a marketing professor at Brandenburg University of Technology in Germany, interviewed influencer agencies and talent managers as part of a recent study . Some of the managers his team interviewed found that older influencers often drove higher campaign conversion rates, but brands rejected them. "Agencies may know that," Dost said. "They certainly sometimes try to put it forth because they also see the numbers. But clients don't want to hear." Boomers' distaste for influencers presents a challenge for CMOs. The generation is a considerable consumer force, accounting for 42% of spending among affluent US households , according to Visa research from last year. With US marketers forecast to spend $40 billion on creator economy partnerships and ads this year, per Business Insider sister company EMARKETER, brands risk leaving a lucrative audience on the sidelines. Getting boomers to click Stewart Reynolds, 56, a Canadian comedy creator who posts under the name Brittlestar, said that older consumers rarely see themselves reflected in influencer marketing, which tends to favor young, attractive influencers. Reynolds, a Gen Xer, said 45% of his audience is over 45 years old. And while he has landed plenty of brand deals with the likes of Yorkshire Tea, Yoplait, and Dairy Farmers of Ontario, he jokingly admits he's jealous of the opportunities that his son, Gregor Reynolds, another successful comedy creator, receives. "He's getting brand deals and campaigns that I wouldn't get because I'm not young and fit," Reynolds said. Stewart Reynolds, 56, a Canadian comedy creator who posts under the name "Brittlestar." Terry Manzo It's not just the brands, though. Marketing insiders said some of the disconnect could be explained by influencers failing to create content that's relatable to an older audience. About a quarter (26%) of boomers surveyed by Morning Consult said influencer content made them feel annoyed — the highest proportion of any generation. Only 5% of boomers said it made them feel happy, versus 28% of Gen Z, 30% of millennials, and 13% of Gen X. Other generations said influencer content was most likely to leave them feeling "entertained," while boomers' top choice was "annoyed." A separate study published earlier this year by Edelman, which surveyed more than 17,000 respondents worldwide, found that just 24% of boomers said they followed a content creator, compared with 86% of Gen Z, 77% of millennials, and 51% of Gen X. The age of the influencers older generations see on their screens isn't the only factor at play. "It's less about finding someone who's the same age and more about finding someone they can see something of themselves in," said Lucy Kruszynski, global head of brand at influencer marketing agency Buttermilk. Shared interests and experiences can be more powerful than demographic similarities, she said. As boomers enter retirement, many have more time to rediscover hobbies and passions that took a backseat during their working lives. Brands could tap into those interests by partnering with creators who share their enthusiasm for pursuits like music, art, or home improvement. Some of the most successful boomer creators have scored deals that lean into these passion points. The boomer weightlifting influencer Marlene "Granny Guns" Flowers has more than 4.5 million followers across her social platforms and has collaborated with brands such as YoungLA and Ryse Supps. Barbara Costello, who is in her 70s and known as " Brunch with Babs ," has more than 9 million followers and has scored partnerships with brands that range from the furniture brand Birch Lane to Nellie's Eggs and Walmart. Brands may also have to exercise patience when trying to convert older consumers. The Morning Consult survey found that 43% of boomers said they had never purchased a product based on an influencer's recommendation. For brands accustomed to measuring influencer marketing success in clicks and immediate sales, that could require a rethink. Kruszynski said some boomers follow creators for months, sometimes up to a year, before feeling comfortable purchasing something they've recommended. "Even though there is absolutely a level of annoyance and a lack of trust, I don't think that baby boomers are immune to influencer marketing," Kruszynski said. "Brands need to think about how creators can build credibility through consistent content over time." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Singapore court gives green light for bridal services firm Korea Artiz Studio to wind up
events.summary: The winding-up application filed by CF Consultancy was granted on Oct 9, the judiciary confirmed to The Straits Times on Oct 21. SINGAPORE – The Supreme Court has given the green light for wedding photography studio Korea Artiz Studio to be wound up. The winding-up application filed by CF Consultancy was granted on Oct 9 after the studio’s representative failed to appear for its winding-up hearing that day, the judiciary confirmed to The Straits Times on Oct 21. CF Consultancy nominated three individuals from Avery Corporate Advisory as the proposed liquidators, according to a Gazette notice published on Sept 28. Korea Artiz Studio was also a no-show at its hearing on possible Central Provident Fund Act charges on Sept 30. The court’s hearing list had stated that the studio faces offences under the CPF Act, which typically means that the employer has failed to pay its employees’ monthly CPF contributions on time. Founded in Busan, South Korea, in 2008, Korea Artiz Studio describes itself as a Korean luxury bridal photography brand with studios worldwide. It had abruptly ceased operations on Aug 14 after failing to pay staff salaries, with its premises repossessed by Carlton Hotel. A Telegram group chat formed by affected customers has 393 members as at Oct 21. In the group chat seen by The Straits Times, one member had previously lamented in September that they had filed a case under the Small Claims Tribunal, but no one from the studio showed up for the hearing. Others shared that they got their money back after filing credit card chargeback claims with their banks.

events.title: Aid groups told to account for $700M of Ebola funding
events.summary: The News Global aid groups, including the UN, are facing demands to inform the Congolese government of the whereabouts of more than $700 million that was donated to deal with the Ebola outbreak that has killed more than 4,600 people in the country. Last week, Jean Kaseya, who heads Africa CDC, the continental body coordinating the response to the spread of the virus, said that Kinshasa had only been told about what had happened to $220 million of the $962 million donated. In a pointed statement, Africa CDC said it “strongly deplores the lack of cooperation from organizations,” accusing them of not respecting Congolese sovereignty and threatening to withdraw their permission to work in the country if they fail to comply. Julien Harneis, the UN’s senior Ebola coordinator, told Semafor that Africa CDC itself has established a joint system with the World Health Organization (WHO) to track disbursements reported by donors. But, he said, the government’s request for recipients to report what they had received and spent was new and was taking time to implement, adding that 43 organizations had already submitted the information. WHO spokesperson Tarik Jasarevic said the UN body supported “clear and transparent processes for tracking financing … including the government establishing a mechanism to account for funds delivered by partners” — a message repeated by other UN bodies. Despite the demands for greater transparency, aid agencies say they still need more money. Jasarevic told Semafor that WHO’s $115 million budget for Ebola was 80% funded, while Fleur Vernat, UNICEF’s partnerships manager in DR Congo, said her agency’s response faced a 65% funding gap. Know More DR Congo is recording fewer daily Ebola cases and deaths than a month ago, but the outbreak is spreading to new provinces in the country, Harneis told Semafor. Nigeria has recorded a case of a woman who had travelled from Uganda, the authorities said and Kenya has now confirmed nine infections. The Ebola response has drawn funding from several countries, with the US as the largest donor. DR Congo’s health minister, Roger Kamba, had already accused aid organizations in August of withholding information about their spending. “You cannot tell people that $800 million has been given to Congo when we cannot find out how much you have spent,” he told reporters at a government briefing. “They demand traceability and compliance from us as local actors, but they do not do it themselves. It is a double standard,” De-Joseph Kakisingi, who heads a network of Congolese aid organizations, told Semafor. But he acknowledged that DR Congo lacked a law specifying what aid organizations must report to the government about the money they receive and spend. This latest Ebola outbreak is the second deadliest in history after the 2014-16 epidemic which killed more than 11,300 people, mostly in West Africa. There is no known vaccine for this species of the virus, known as Bundibugyo, but Ervebo, effective against another species, is being tested. So far 9,000 frontline workers have been vaccinated. Notable Ebola healthcare workers in DR Congo went on strike in August , citing unpaid wages since the outbreak had begun in mid-May.

events.title: Survey: Energy executives upbeat about Gulf opportunities despite war
events.summary: The News Middle East energy executives are more optimistic about their industry’s future than their peers elsewhere, a testament to their ability to keep oil flowing despite the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, according to research commissioned by the organizers of ADIPEC, the Abu Dhabi energy conference. Global demand for energy from all sources is forecast to rise over the next decade, driven by electrification and AI adoption. The International Energy Agency estimates energy investment at a record $3.4 trillion this year: $2.2 trillion in clean energy and grids, and $1.2 trillion in oil, gas, and coal. Almost two-thirds of the more than 1,800 decision-makers surveyed expect the pace of capital deployment to increase by more than a fifth over the next five years. The upbeat assessment isn’t surprising from producers who can get their product out of the Gulf amid higher prices from the US-Iran war. Most respondents said the energy system passed its biggest “stress test in 50 years” and proved more resilient than expected, thanks to quick adjustments to shocks, continued supply to customers, and the diversification of sources and routes before the conflict. But a third of executives from consuming countries in Asia — the most vulnerable to the disruptions — said the global energy system proved less resilient than expected. Know More ADIPEC, the world’s biggest energy exhibition , organized by dmg events, comes at a moment of unprecedented upheaval for a region that supplies a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas. The disruption has pushed dozens of countries to rethink their energy security priorities. While many governments may pursue domestic self-reliance to avert future shocks, those in the industry are betting on a connected system, ranking renewables, source diversification, and infrastructure protection as bigger priorities than self-sufficiency. The survey showed broad consensus on artificial intelligence, both as a driver of future demand and as a way to unlock efficiencies from the wellhead to distribution. Just 3% of respondents expect electricity demand from AI to be lower than forecast; a majority see the technology as becoming more influential than innovations in renewable energy over the next decade. AI applications in oil production have moved beyond the pilot phase: One executive said in the report that software “distributes the power on the drilling rig in the exact amount required and stores the unused energy for later use. It reduces the total power consumption of the rig by 25 to 30%.” Notable The Hormuz closure is the biggest energy security crisis the world has faced, according to IEA chief Fatih Birol, who expects it to reshape investment much as the 1970s oil shocks did . Asia is rethinking its reliance on Gulf energy. The region is shifting “from just-in-time supply chains to just-in-case supply chains,” one analyst told Fortune .

events.title: Washington won’t say what it wants on AGOA, says South Africa ambassador
events.summary: South Africa’s ambassador to the US says Washington has repeatedly rejected Pretoria’s trade offers without explaining what it wants instead. His complaint comes a day after President Cyril Ramaphosa told South Africans to brace for losing duty-free access under the African Growth and Opportunity Act. “It’s not helpful when we hear the answer is, ‘that’s not good enough,’” Roelf Meyer told Semafor. “It would have been more helpful if we could hear, ‘what is not good enough?’” The US Congress extended AGOA to 2028 last month, but the White House reviews country eligibility every year. Removing South Africa from Jan. 1 would require notice to Congress and Pretoria 60 days ahead, so a decision is expected by early November. That scenario has become a distinct possibility after nearly two years of a worsening relationship between Washington and Africa’s largest economy. Meyer, who took up the post this year after more than a year without a South African ambassador in Washington, describes relations with the Trump administration as a “stalemate.” “I’m not satisfied about where we find ourselves,” he said. The deeper rift, he suggested, is ideological. Meyer said he read the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 early and saw a “deviation” from the Republican Party he knew in the 1980s. Asked why Pretoria’s rebuttals of white genocide claims aren’t landing, he said either Washington hasn’t heard him clearly, or there is “a fundamental ideological difference.” Meyer helped lead the apartheid government’s side opposite Ramaphosa in the talks that ended white minority rule. He says those negotiations worked because both sides were prepared to talk. “That is my experience, the difference here,” he said. “It’s hard to find a basis for real dialogue.” Yet he also signaled flexibility on the policy irritant most cited in Washington. Black EconomicEmpowerment rules in mining and telecoms “still leave room for further adjustments,” he said, adding that discussions are underway with companies looking to invest. The opening of the new office follows a series of openings by the company globally, including in Tokyo and Hong Kong, the company said in a statement on Wednesday. “The new presence builds on Advent’s long-standing relationships across the Middle East, giving Advent a local base from which to deepen its engagement with investors and support the firm’s existing portfolio companies and explore potential investment opportunities,” the company said. Set up in 1984, the company has made 460 investments in 45 countries. It has 18 offices globally, including in Abu Dhabi. The announcement comes as a growing number of global financial institutions launch their operations at ADGM, despite uncertainty arising from the Iran war. Earlier this month, New Mountain Capital, an alternative investment firm based in New York, said it was opening an office in ADGM to strengthen its presence in the Middle East, while Capital Group, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, has secured a licence from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Abu Dhabi's ADGM to operate as a regulated investment manager. The Paris-listed Eurazeo, a European asset manager with €40 billion ($45.2 billion) in assets under management, has also opened an office in the ADGM amid its expansion plans in the region. Other high-profile companies that the UAE capital has attracted in recent months include private credit lender Blue Owl Capital, the tech-focused US company Vista Equity Partners, the world’s largest listed hedge fund Man Group, Barings, Bain Capital, Cantor and the Swiss derivative investment company Adapt Investment Managers. “Advent’s decision to establish an office in ADGM reflects the strength of Abu Dhabi’s proposition as a leading destination for global investment firms,” Arvind Ramamurthy, chief market development officer at ADGM, said. Assets under management at ADGM grew 54 per cent annually in the first six months of 2026, with 49,027 professionals now based at Al Maryah Island and Al Reem Island, an increase of 34 per cent on the same period last year. Collectively, asset managers that established operations in ADGM in the first half of the year oversee more than $2.1 trillion in global assets under management.

events.title: Trump’s remarkable mess on electric vehicles: How he made them more expensive and harder to find just as he went to war on Iran
events.summary: Within three months of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, 2026, the average price of gasoline for American drivers climbed from US$2.94 to $4.35 a gallon . If there was ever a moment for Americans to switch to electric vehicles, this was it. From March to May 2026, in fact, sales of hybrid electric vehicles were 18% higher than over the same months in 2025. But sales of fully electric vehicles were 16% lower from March to May 2026 compared with the same months in 2025. Some observers took that as evidence that high gas prices alone wouldn’t push Americans toward fully electric cars , but that conclusion misses half the story. I study car buyers and their preferences , and there is an important distinction between what consumers want and what they can actually buy. Sales reveal what cars people actually bought, but not necessarily what they actually wanted. When the supply of some kinds of cars can’t keep up with demand, prices rise, and that’s exactly what happened for electric vehicles in 2026. While there were plenty of hybrids available to meet that demand, the same was not true for EVs. Hybrid production had been growing for years, led by Toyota , which sells about half of the hybrids bought in the United States . As a result, even as sales surged, hybrid inventories on dealer lots were 19% higher in March 2026 than they had been a year earlier. However, EV production had been in retreat since the tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed in July 2025 ended federal tax credits for EVs. Buyers had been able to get up to $7,500 for new EVs and $4,000 for used ones, but that ended after Sept. 30, 2025. Automakers responded by cutting back their EV production. General Motors laid off more than 3,400 workers at its EV and battery plants and shifted its Tennessee plant to make batteries for energy storage , not cars. Ford wrote off $19.5 billion from its EV business , ended production of the all-electric F-150 Lightning and converted a Tennessee EV plant to build gas-powered trucks. Buyers, for their part, rushed to beat the tax credit deadline, pushing EVs to 11.3% of new vehicle sales in September 2025. But by November 2025, after the tax credits ended, their share dropped to 4.3% . As 2026 progressed and gas prices began to rise, so did EV demand. New EV inventories declined, shrinking from about 130 days of supply in the first quarter of 2026 to 78 days by August – just two days above the supply level of gas-burning cars. Discounts on new EV models shrank too. My analysis of online listings from marketcheck.com shows the median new EV was listed 9.8% below sticker price in February. By April, the median discount was 6.6%, and 4.7% in June. That’s a sign that dealers saw rising demand, not inventory to clear. A run on used electric vehicles Before the war, prices for used electric vehicles were still drifting down in the wake of the expired used EV federal tax credit. After the war began, they climbed 13% through late June 2026 . For a typical used electric vehicle, that’s about $3,500 more. Other data sources point in the same direction. Recurrent, a company that reports on batteries and used EVs , found that the price of a used 2023 Chevrolet Bolt rose almost 20% from January to June 2026. And inventories of used electric vehicles dropped too, with only 31 days of supply in May , 23% below the year before. High prices and uncertain access to charging stations are real stumbling blocks for people who are thinking about buying an EV . But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them. Rather, the sales stalled because there weren’t enough EVs available to buy – and there were plenty of hybrids as an alternative. The distinction matters because automakers have treated a change in the policy landscape as a change in consumer demand, leading to shortages with real costs. The average new car now sells for about $50,000 and the average new electric vehicle for about $55,000, according to Kelley Blue Book , a company that tracks car prices. The current situation leaves drivers exposed to the volatility of oil prices with fewer alternatives. The U.S. is the world’s largest oil producer , yet a war in the Persian Gulf raised gas prices significantly in just three months. Oil trades on a global market, so American drivers pay global prices . Seven months into the war, the pressure on drivers is still going full throttle . Oil was still above $100 a barrel in mid-October, and diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22. Electric vehicle sales haven’t caught up. Argonne’s data show 86,000 of them sold in August, fewer than the 101,000 sold in May, while hybrid sales stayed above 216,000 a month all summer. A look ahead Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector. The fuel economy rule released Sept. 28, 2026 , loosens efficiency requirements for gas-powered vehicles and in 2028 ends a system that let automakers that beat the standards – mostly EV makers – earn credits for exceeding them and sell those to automakers that fell short. That means automakers will have fewer regulatory incentives to produce EVs going forward. Regulators say buyers will save $1,289 on the purchase price of a new gas-powered vehicle from reduced engineering and manufacturing costs to make less efficient engines. But the same analysis estimates drivers will spend about $1,600 more on gas over the life of the car, and that’s using fuel price forecasts well below today’s prices. Economists say the administration’s math does not properly account for those fuel costs. events.title: Is Anthropic the IPO market’s last hope for 2026? The clock is ticking
events.summary: Morgan Chittum here. More bad news in the IPO market this week. On Monday, Chinese manufacturer Kepuni Holdings withdrew plans for a Nasdaq listing that had been expected to raise $15 million. A day later, Gravitics Holdings slashed its deal size by a whopping 60% ahead of the space-system developer’s $50 million IPO.  Meanwhile, South Korea’s Elice Group plunged 32% on its first day of trading due to jitters about AI-related stocks. According to Dealogic data, it was the country’s worst-ever debut for a company that raised more than $100 million. Sure, these are small deals in the grand scheme of 2026. SpaceX had a record-breaking $75 billion public offering in June. But they add to a string of recent disappointments. (Let’s not forget when Oura, the smart-ring maker behind one of the season’s most anticipated IPOs, shelved plans just hours before pricing shares in September.) The problem, according to Jay Ritter, director of the University of Florida’s IPO Initiative, has come down to valuations. “Some of those companies have pulled their IPOs, rather than accepting a less optimistic valuation than they had hoped to get,” Ritter, known as “Mr. IPO,” told me. “You’re just asking too much. It’s not that you’ve got a bad business model. It’s a question of price.” So, what’s it going to take to reignite the IPO market in 2026? After all, the first six months of the year were great in terms of deal proceeds at roughly $137 billion , partly thanks to SpaceX. Matt Kennedy, a senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, told me that a fruitful public debut from Anthropic could do the trick.  “There’s no question, a successful Anthropic IPO would be a huge win for the rest of the market,” Kennedy said, pointing to the deal’s potentially landmark size. A long-time Anthropic investor, who asked not to be named, told Fortune ’s Shawn Tully that he expects shares to be priced at roughly $1.8 trillion . Although it’s below the Claude creator’s $2 trillion target, the investor predicts a post-IPO trading value of up to $2.4 trillion. That tops SpaceX’s $2.1 trillion market cap at the end of its first trading day. Kennedy added, “When investors make money with IPOs, they begin to put that money back into work on future deals.” But Anthropic’s IPO is still up in the air. The company hasn’t said when it will file, and it does face a number of risk factors. On Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal reported a new draft prospectus where the AI giant disclosed an $80.7 billion net loss for the first six months of the year. There was still breakneck revenue growth for Anthropic. The company garnered revenue of roughly $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, much higher than $1.1 billion during the year-ago period. Another wrinkle: Time is of the essence. The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg both previously reported that Anthropic is preparing for a potential November IPO. With that timeline in mind, Renaissance Capital’s Kennedy says a filing could come out as soon as Friday.  But any delay would leave less room for a 2026 debut—and for other companies to follow suit—before the end of the year. With midterm elections and the holiday season approaching, more prospective issuers could opt to wait until early 2027. That would push back a potential rebound in deals but not necessarily derail it. After all, Kennedy said the benefits of a successful Anthropic listing could extend well into next year.  “With such a large deal, I think this has legs,” he said. “It can help 2027 activity.” See you tomorrow, Morgan Chittum X: @morgan_chittum Email: morgan.chittum@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . events.title: Whoop sees Abu Dhabi as springboard for shift to predictive health, says chief executive
events.summary: Whoop is pushing deeper into the Gulf's longevity economy. The Boston-based human performance company this week announced a clinical research partnership with Abu Dhabi's Department of Health. The deal builds on a $75 million anchor investment from Mubadala Investment Company and a broader buildout that has made the GCC one of Whoop's fastest-growing markets . “This region has become one of the most important regions for Whoop,” its founder and chief executive Will Ahmed tells On the Record with Hadley Gamble . “We're growing extraordinarily fast here in the GCC. We're up about 15 times in the last three years. Our membership base here has grown over 85 per cent just in the past year.” The company has separately put GCC year-on-year growth at more than 75 per cent. Speaking on stage at the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit , Mr Ahmed said the Department of Health agreement would fund “powerful clinical research to drive health outcomes” around prevention, sleep, cardiovascular health and ageing. The announcement is the latest layer in a multiyear capital and operational push by Abu Dhabi entities into Whoop, which produces wearable health trackers. On May 7, Whoop and Mubadala said they had formed a strategic partnership “to advance proactive health, performance science and preventative healthcare innovation in the UAE”, anchored by the $75 million investment. That investment was made as part of Whoop's $575 million Series G, which valued the company at $10.1 billion. The round was led by Collaborative Fund and, according to the company, included Mubadala and Abu Dhabi-based 2PointZero Group. Under terms disclosed by both sides, Whoop would establish a dedicated office in Abu Dhabi , expand its Advanced Labs blood-testing product, introduce full Arabic localisation across its platform – launched this month with a GCC-wide campaign – and launch the Whoop-Mubadala Health Research Initiative, a longitudinal research programme aimed at strengthening the UAE's health value chain from diagnostics and genomics to prevention and behavioural optimisation. Mr Ahmed has cast the UAE capital as a proving ground for a shift from reactive to predictive care. “The power of continuous health monitoring is that it can really understand signals in your body that you may not be able to feel,” he says. “We believe those insights can actually drive health outcomes, which is to say it can make you lower your weight, it can make you decrease your blood pressure.” He says the company's thesis since its launch 14 years ago – to validate continuous monitoring with elite athletes and then move into the mainstream – is now playing out in the Gulf. He acknowledges the timing, closing a large Gulf investment shortly after the Iran war began, reflects a long-term commitment. “The timing of some of that partnership was complicated with the wars in this region. But to me, it was obvious to show up because I'd been showing up for the last decade,” he says. For Abu Dhabi, the Whoop partnership is one piece of a broader longevity infrastructure play. An EY survey cited by Abu Dhabi officials found only 43 per cent of respondents follow a structured fitness plan, even as 61 per cent had used a wearable in the past year and 87 per cent reported a positive experience using AI for health decisions – a gap officials believe wearables plus clinical integration can close. Whoop, which has now raised about $1 billion in total capital, said the Gulf expansion would be paired with retail distribution, sponsorships with the UAE Team Emirates-XRG cyclists and Al Nassr football team, and, through Whoop Qatar, its first performance research and developement lab outside Boston, later in 2026. “There are many countries in the world that are excited about wearable technology,” Mr Ahmed says. “When you can remove bureaucracy and you can say, look, no, we want health care not to be reactive but actually proactive, then a lot of things fall in suit.”

events.title: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
events.summary: Fresh data points from September showed the housing market continues to deteriorate just as the Federal Reserve is considering raising interest rates again. Building permits, new starts and pending sales all were considerably worse than Wall Street forecasts. Under some circumstances, Fed officials would use easier policy to spur demand. However, the central bank is currently battling inflation, which it could prioritize over a flagging housing picture. The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist. Housing data deteriorated further in September , according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates. Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage. "The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze." The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%. Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday. Privately owned housing starts fell 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data. Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023. "Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates." The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily . Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices. Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years. Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs. But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009. Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing. However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months." Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall. The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels. Walker attributed the middling levels as a product of the "lock-in" effect in which it's too expensive for current homeowners to move and take on higher borrowing costs while deteriorating affordability weighs on new construction.

events.title: Rather than giving in to RTO, I took the leap and built my own business. It's better for my family and me.
events.summary: The author left her job after an RTO mandate and started her own business. Courtesy of Rose Ann Mullet While pregnant with my second child, an RTO mandate was issued at work. Going into the office five days a week wasn't going to work for me, or for my family. I decided to take the leap and build my own business instead. I never imagined myself starting a business, but after a return-to-office mandate that wasn't going to work for my family, I had to rethink what should come next in my career. I spent a lot of time networking on LinkedIn, and after some encouragement, I started asking myself, "Why not?" I worked in marketing as a content writer, and I've always been ambitious. I was a top performer at my company, receiving glowing reviews and setting a record for campaign performance. However, there was always a constant pull between time at the office and time with my family. Being required to show up to the office five days a week simply wouldn't work for me The office was about an hour from my house, which was fine for two to three days a week, especially with the flexibility to work remotely for additional days as necessary. When they instituted the expectation for a full five days in office with no flexibility at the beginning of the year, I knew it wasn't going to work. I was expecting my second child, and my 5-year-old had a weekly appointment and some commitments I didn't want to miss. Showing up to my kid's events often meant working from home an extra day or leaving the office early, and even though I was crushing performance metrics, those absences made me feel like I wasn't doing enough at work, especially as my department began focusing on new goals. Worse, as departmental pressure increased, my boss made a few comments that left me wondering whether he felt I wasn't sufficiently dedicated to the new direction and my role, adding a layer of fear about my job when I was trying to be present with my family . Then, there were the moments I felt like I wasn't doing enough as a mom. I apologized on more than one occasion for a school closure or my kid getting sick, and I found myself checking messages while he napped in my arms. It was uncomfortable to acknowledge the guilt I felt across all aspects of my life. The tug-of-war had become a constant since becoming a mom, and I kept thinking there had to be a way to be true to my high-achieving nature while still being the kind of loving, involved parent I aspired to be. After a series of coffee chats with other "mompreneurs" and marketing colleagues, I realized building a business , like motherhood, isn't about having it all figured out. I could chase entrepreneurship like I once chased accolades. I've always been a writer. Communication and storytelling have been the constants in my career across industries and roles. I'd helped friends and family with marketing for their law firms while still working full-time; I'd worked in education , both in the classroom and in marketing. I realized my experience would translate to the kind of business I wanted to build: brand development, content strategy, and ghostwriting in higher education and law. I spent most of my third trimester balancing business planning and baby preparation. I took the leap and started my own business My LinkedIn community encouraged me to take the leap and supported me again as I began shifting my personal brand to support the business after my son was born. I signed my first client before he arrived, and had two referrals come in during my first couple of months in business. By the time both my children started school and day care earlier this year, I'd built something that would support the life I wanted without requiring an apology. My first client was recommended in AI overviews after only 30 days. I was a guest on a podcast about AI visibility called Found In AI and invited on a few others focused on motherhood and ambition. I build my own schedule . I work between pickup and dropoff, and I don't feel the need to check my phone while volunteering or at school events. I relish the details I get when my oldest hops in the car: the games at recess or the math facts that fascinated him in class. I build Magna Tiles cities and go for "treasure hunts" around the neighborhood without guilt or explanation. Sure, there are days when I'm logging back in after bedtime, but instead of putting in those hours to chase titles or prove something, I'm simply putting the work where it fits for me or pursuing something I'm genuinely excited about for one of my clients. I spent a lot of my career frantically trying to prove that motherhood didn't lessen my capability, while simultaneously feeling guilty for every ask that mattered: the Halloween school parade or my child's sick days. I was afraid of losing respect at my job and afraid of missing out on my kids' childhood. Now, I recognize that fear was holding me back from building a life that feels much more fulfilled. I've let go of the competition between the roles of "Mom" and "Career Woman." Three ghostwriting clients alone equal my monthly salary from corporate, which was the goal, and anything after that is a bonus. The control of my time is priceless; I'll never have to ask permission to be fully present with my children. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Malaysian palm oil drops over 1% on profit-taking
events.summary: The benchmark palm oil contract for January delivery on the Bursa Malaysia Derivatives Exchange lost RM49. Malaysian palm oil futures fell 1.02% to RM4,768 a tonne on Oct 21, as traders took profits near the top of the trading range. Reuters analyst Wang Tao said prices may fall back to RM4,706-RM4,736 after failing to break resistance at RM4,834. Malaysia’s Oct 1-20 palm oil exports rose 58.5%-78.4% month on month, while higher oil prices could support palm oil demand for biodiesel. JAKARTA – Malaysian palm oil futures fell more than 1% on Oct 21 , with profit-taking near the top of the trading range outweighing gains in rival vegetable oils on the Dalian Commodity Exchange. The benchmark palm oil contract for January delivery on the Bursa Malaysia Derivatives Exchange lost RM49 (S$15), or 1.02%, to RM4,768 a metric ton at the close. “Prices retreated on profit-taking as they hovered near the upper end of the trading range,” a Kuala Lumpur-based trader said. Reuters technical analyst Wang Tao earlier said palm oil may retrace into a range of RM4,706 to RM4,736 per metric ton, following its failure to break resistance at RM4,834. Dalian’s most-active soyoil contract rose 0.26%, while its palm oil contract climbed 1.31%. Soyoil prices on the Chicago Board of Trade were down 0.12%. Palm oil tracks rival edible oils, as it competes for a share of the global vegetable oils market. Cargo surveyors estimated that Malaysian palm oil products exports for Oct 1-20 rose between 58.5% and 78.4% from a month earlier. Oil prices rose by more than US$1 on Oct 21 as attacks on Gulf shipping and no signs of diplomatic progress to end the Iran war fuelled supply disruption fears, with the Brent benchmark hovering near 5-month highs, while falling US crude and product inventories also lent support to the market. Stronger crude oil futures make palm a more attractive option for biodiesel feedstock. REUTERS

events.title: Bereaved civil service families could face ‘unjust’ tax bills due to pension scheme delays
events.summary: MPs say ‘chaos’ at Capita-run scheme could mean some claims miss tax-free time limit on lump sum payments Bereaved families could face “unconscionable” tax bills because of “chaos” in the civil service pension scheme, the government has been warned. Some lump sum pension payments to families are only tax-free if made within two years of a scheme being told of the member’s death. MPs are now voicing fears that severe delays in the administration of the civil service pension scheme, which is run by the outsourcing company Capita , could push some families over that threshold. They would then be hit with a tax bill calculated at the recipient’s personal rate. The families of more than 1,600 deceased civil servants have been waiting for more than 100 days for their “death in benefit” claim to be processed, according to the latest figures . Some of those have reported struggling to pay bills because of the delay. The Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Commons public accounts committee (PAC), said: “The chaos currently engulfing the civil service pensions scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim.” He added: “It is unconscionable that the families of loyal and dedicated civil servants, who are continuing to suffer through this serious government failing, could potentially face such an unjust financial penalty.” The Cabinet Office, which is responsible for the pension scheme, said it was unable to prevent HM Revenue and Customs from taxing delayed claims, and that affected members would have to claw back the money by taking their case to the Pensions Ombudsman. The ombudsman estimates an 18-month wait to resolve cases because of the volume of complaints from those affected. The PAC has called for a change in legislation to prevent relatives paying the price for administrative delays. The government has already been accused of letting down civil servants and their families by repeatedly outsourcing the 1.7-million-member pension scheme to private companies that failed to deliver. The PAC last year urged ministers to take the scheme in-house after a previous contractor, MyCSP, was blamed for plummeting service levels. However, the £239m contract passed to Capita last December, despite concerns voiced by some that the company was inadequately prepared. The Cabinet Office said it was confident that Capita would offer an improved service. It has since acknowledged that service levels were “unacceptable”. MyCSP and Capita were contacted for a comment. In February, a dedicated email address was set up for unions to escalate cases of severe hardship caused by the delays. The cases referred included claimants at risk of suicide or of losing their homes. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Clare Norris has been waiting 11 months for the death benefit and pension payments she is due after her husband died last November. “I was petrified – I am 52 and early death was not part of our financial plan,” she said. “Losing your partner is one of the most difficult experiences anyone can go through. The lack of clarity, communication and basic administrative handling from Civil Service Pensions has made it considerably worse.” Capita said her case would be progressed under a new process. “It remains a high priority and the member can expect to hear on next steps as soon as possible.” Under HMRC rules, in cases in which someone dies under the age of 75, tax-free lump sum payments must be made within two years, otherwise they will be taxed at the recipient’s marginal rate of tax. The Cabinet Office said it was committed to ensuring scheme members were not left out of pocket. “We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure individuals do not experience delays,” said a spokesperson. “If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses.”

events.title: Witkoff asks Putin to resume direct peace talks, Russia releases U.S. detainee
events.summary: White House envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow the resumption of trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. in order to reach an end to the war. Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after President Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. Driving the news: Witkoff presented Putin with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine during a meeting in St. Petersburg. Before the meeting, Russia released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, 74, who had spent more than four years in captivity after being seized by Russian troops in eastern Ukraine in April 2022. Putin announced his release at the top of the meeting with Witkoff. "He is at Pulkovo Airport," Putin told Witkoff in front of the cameras. "Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release," Trump wrote on Truth Social. State of play: Witkoff arrived in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo , Norway, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the U.K., Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO. Zelensky said Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — a format Russia has so far rejected. The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war. What he is saying: "I believe the talks [in Oslo] were productive, and I would like to say that there is progress, and I will update you on this. I hope that we have truly laid the groundwork for a successful end to hostilities in this Ukrainian-Russian conflict," Witkoff told Putin. Witkoff asked Putin to "consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, where we could discuss the next steps toward achieving a settlement." Witkoff said the talks could include representatives of technical groups of specialists who could discuss these issues in detail. "We have brought several documents outlining approaches to achieving a peaceful settlement in the Ukrainian-Russian conflict. I would ask you, Mr. President, to review these documents a little later," Witkoff said. The intrigue : Putin also told Witkoff he wants to discuss possible Russian mediation between the U.S. and Iran. "You know that we have a special, trusting relationship with Iran, with our partners in Iran, our friends, built over decades, and if there's anything we can do to resolve this crisis, we'll be happy to do so. You're also well aware of our proposals in this area," Putin said. What's next: Putin told Witkoff he wants to discuss a possible meeting with Trump in China in mid-November.

events.title: House committee says Webull messages point to China access to U.S. customer data
events.summary: The House Select Committee on China says internal Webull messages from 2021 indicate that an employee believed to be in China had access to information about a U.S. customer account. Webull, which is an online investing platform, has said sensitive U.S. customer data is restricted to U.S.-based employees An Oct. 7 report by the select committee found that Webull is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to American finance. Internal messages between employees of online investing platform Webull suggest a company employee in China had access to information about a U.S. customer, despite the company having said it bars such sharing, according to an analysis of the messages by the House Select Committee on China . The analysis comes nearly two weeks after CNBC first detailed the bipartisan select committee's report that concluded that Webull, which counts 28 million users, is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to American finance. Webull shares slid more than 19% on the heels of that Oct. 7 report. At the time of the report, Webull told CNBC in a statement that "U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S." But the newly released internal messages by the House Select Committee on China, which CNBC exclusively obtained, raise questions about whether that has always been the case. The committee has focused on threats posed by China and protecting U.S. industry from Chinese competition. One message thread suggests a Webull employee was in China during a discussion about a U.S. customer account. The thread also indicates the account was previously approved by a China Webull team member and an American counterpart. The messages, dating to 2021, were sent on Microsoft Teams between Brendan Fuller, a manager at Webull's U.S. brokerage, and an employee named Zhenghan Wang, whose nickname is "Rock." The select committee says Wang was likely in China at the time. In one message, Fuller messaged Wang about concerns involving a particular trading account. "We saw these problems ... and approve account," Fuller wrote. CIP is an acronym for Customer Identification Program, a U.S. regulatory requirement that financial institutions verify the identities of individuals and entities opening accounts. Wang asked Fuller: "Who approve the account?" Fuller responded: "One China team member and one US team." Wang then asked: "I want to know in what situation (CIP), can we approve the account open?" Fuller responded: "I think we just approve them all no matter what ..." "And then we pay for vendors. And create report and work," Fuller added. Wang then replied that "CIP=" followed by Mandarin Chinese characters forming a common phrase that translates as "Exists in name only," or "Useless." A spokesperson for the select committee, in a statement to CNBC, said, "All the evidence in these text messages points to Zhenghan Wang, a Webull employee, being located in China with access to U.S. customer data at the time he worked for the company." An analysis by the committee concluded that Wang was in China at the time of the exchange because the messages' time stamps indicated that Wang was working daytime hours in Beijing, and because he set his software to translate the messages into simplified Chinese. A Webull spokesperson did not directly respond to CNBC's questions about Wang's access to U.S. customer data in 2021 and whether that disproved the company's assertion that its U.S. data does not go to China. The Webull spokesperson said, "Protecting customer data is central to Webull's operations." "Webull's U.S. customer data is stored only in the U.S. on AWS servers in Virginia and Oregon, with access to sensitive data restricted to U.S.-based employees," the spokesperson said. "U.S. broker-dealer operations are directed exclusively by U.S.-based personnel, and no individuals based outside the U.S. have ever exercised operational or decision-making authority over Webull's U.S. broker-dealer business." The company spokesperson also criticized the select committee's release of the messages. "The Teams messages now being referenced date back to a 2021 routine FINRA matter, which was concluded," the spokesperson said. FINRA, or the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, is the self-regulatory organization for member broker-dealers. events.title: The AI 'vibe directing' startup OpenArt has hired a former Salesforce marketer to turn it into a household name
events.summary: Scott Larson is joining OpenArt AI as its VP of brand marketing. He first experimented with the platform to create a short film starring a stick of butter about to meet an unfortunate end. OpenArt/LinkedIn, Scott Larson A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing industry newsletter . Salesforce and Meta marketing alum Scott Larson says OpenArt AI' s conversational text-to-video generator is the tool he wished he'd had earlier in his career. The platform helps whizz up short videos, arty images, and music by typing in a few prompts. OpenArt this week tapped Larson as the company's vice president of brand marketing, the company exclusively told CMO Insider. He joins in a period of rapid growth for the company, which said it's on track to pass $250 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2026. It's increased its head count to 80 employees over the past year, up from 20, and grown to 8 million monthly users, the company said. Larson told CMO Insider he's on a mission to make OpenArt "as close to a household name as a creative AI can be." He said the biggest challenge will be to wrap all of OpenArt's different use cases into a single "North Star" story. It recently launched a new product called Director that lets users describe an idea, visual style, and narrative arc, which it then turns into videos up to 5 minutes long. It promoted the launch with a cinema and billboard campaign that it hoped would spark a "vibe directing" craze among the creative community. Others use its platform to create social posts, AI voiceovers, or lyric videos. It also offers an AI model leaderboard to help its users benchmark different AI video and image models. Larson previously worked at advertising agencies on large consumer brands such as Nike, Levi's, and Gatorade. He later became global executive creative director at Meta, then known as Facebook. Larson went on to be an SVP at Salesforce, where he helped shape the branding behind its annual Dreamforce conference and launched ad campaigns starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson. Larson first experimented with OpenArt two months ago, creating a very short film with three cuts. Called "Life is Short," it shows a man made out of a stick of butter walking alongside a swimming pool. The butter man looks up at the scorching sun above before the video cuts to an old-school title card saying "The End." "Had I had this tool starting back when I was a little creative junkie up until today, I'd be making everything all the time," Larson said. Earlier this year, OpenArt plucked another exec from Big Tech, hiring former Google executive Raj Gajwani as its chief business officer. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Stratford International on track to get cross-Channel trains in budget boost
events.summary: Sadiq Khan says upgrade would unlock station’s true potential and allow it to live up to its name Stratford International train station in east London will receive funding in next week’s budget, according to reports, putting it on track to live up to its name and become a hub for cross-Channel services. London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has been making a case to ministers for funding to upgrade the station to allow it to start running international rail services. Until now only domestic routes running to and from central London and Kent have stopped at the station, although Eurostar services pass through on the way to and from St Pancras. Khan said: “We’ve been working closely with the government to make Stratford International truly ‘international’ for the first time – opening up new opportunities for jobs, investment and tourism, while connecting one of the UK’s fastest-growing economic centres directly to Europe. “It’s time to unlock the full potential of this station and help write the next chapter in Stratford’s remarkable success story.” Khan recently argued that growth in international rail travel and environmental concerns meant it would be better to improve Stratford International than expand Heathrow airport by building a third runway. Stratford International would require a significant upgrade from its current two platforms to allow it to welcome international services, including adding a border post and security checks as well as a check-in zone, waiting area and facilities for passengers. The work opening up the station and the mothballed international section of the station, including platforms and a waiting area, would cost an estimated £20m , according to the Standard. It reported Khan’s plan was for one in three trains to and from France to stop at the station, while it could also become a hub for rail services from the continent to the Midlands and the north of England. The station, located close to the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, opened in late 2009 and was originally designed and built with the intention of handling Eurostar trains, but this was not fully developed. The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly planning to greenlight the mayor’s proposal to create a business rate retention zone, according to the Financial Times, to help fund the station’s redevelopment. Such zones allow local authorities to keep all of the businesses rates growth collected in their area – rather than half of the rates collected, as is standard – to fund local regeneration directly. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In recent months, Virgin and other rail companies have been in talks with City Hall about operating future international rail services from Stratford. Virgin is planning to launch rail services from London to the continent in 2030, bringing direct competition to Eurostar on the cross-Channel route for the first time since the opening of the tunnel. The operator has been granted access by the rail regulator to the track and to Eurostar’s nearby Temple Mills depot . A spokesperson for the Virgin Group said the operator was “looking forward to exploring additional stops, including Stratford International”. They added that the company had been “actively engaging with stakeholders to explore future expansion” beyond its initial launch plans. Gemini Trains, chaired by the Labour peer Tony Berkeley, is hoping to run trains to France, Belgium and Germany and has said it wanted to use Stratford as its London hub. However, it has not yet been granted depot and track access.
