events.title: Solid-state batteries
events.summary: The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has its drawbacks, not least that the batteries have a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer, creating power packs that charge faster, last longer, cram more energy into smaller spaces, and (crucially) run cooler. A new generation of companies aim to bring such batteries to market, and if their bets pan out, the tech could substantially ease the shift away from fossil fuels.  The sticking points Solid-state batteries have been “just a few years away” for more than a decade now. In laboratories, the technology works. But there have been challenges. In designs that pair the solid electrolyte with a lithium-metal anode (the side of the battery that releases electrons into an electrical circuit), needlelike filaments called dendrites tend to grow during charging, and they eventually push through the electrolyte and short the cell. Solid electrolytes are supposed to physically block the formation of dendrites, but many of them crack as the treelike projections break through like roots in a concrete foundation.  Then there’s the problem of manufacturing at scale. Mass production requires large quantities of defect-free sheets of ceramic-like material to make the electrolytes as well as dry rooms for assembly, since those electrolytes have a tendency to react with water. Would-be manufacturers quote a range of potential prices for solid-state batteries, but most expect them to fall in line with lithium-ion packs sometime in the mid-2030s.  The progress Nascent as the technology is, solid-state batteries have already seen high-­profile missteps . But one of America’s most advanced solid-state-battery companies says it’s closing in on being able to bring its product to market. The Bill Gates–backed QuantumScape launched in Silicon Valley in 2010 and built its battery around a class of ceramic materials that it says is compatible with lithium—meaning no dendrite formation. “We spent, then, like 10 years learning how to process it to satisfy all of the other requirements,” says Tim Holme, QuantumScape’s cofounder and chief technology officer. In 2025, the startup announced a proprietary, large-scale manufacturing method for quickly producing and heat-treating the ceramic electrolytes used in its batteries. “Nobody has ever done this in the field of ceramics before,” Holme claims. For 10,000 years, producing ceramics has involved slowly cooking the starting materials in an oven over the course of days. “We figured out a way to shorten that down to several minutes,” he says.  Plenty of other companies are pushing the tech forward as well. Toyota, the world’s biggest automaker, launched a research program on solid-state batteries way back in 2010. It’s now partnering with the global energy and petroleum company Idemitsu Kosan on a pilot plant, promising cars that can travel up to 745 miles after charging 10 minutes or less—a huge leap, if it works out. In China, CATL, the giant behind roughly 40% of the global battery market, is aggressively pursuing solid-state batteries too, pumping nearly $2.6 billion into a research program in 2024 alone. Mercedes, meanwhile, equipped one of its EQS sedans with solid-state batteries last fall; after driving nonstop for 750 miles, the car still had some range to spare.  Will the tech gain traction? Investing in vehicle batteries makes sense given the size of the potential market. But any little uptick in cost typically gets passed on to buyers, so the first solid-state EV batteries will inevitably be more expensive.  Grid storage buyers, who are working to meet the increasing demands posed by data centers, may also hesitate to purchase new technologies that still haven’t come down the cost curve. Then again, the promise of energy storage that lasts longer than lithium-­ion’s typical eight hours could make them easier to persuade.  Some companies are taking a page from a playbook employed by outfits pursuing fusion: Focus on near-term markets with better margins to help fund development and bring down costs. Solid-state firms including California-based Solid Energies and Arizona-headquartered Sion Power are looking at selling batteries to the aviation industry or the military. “Those are sectors that are less sensitive to cost, and they typically require lower volumes as well,” says Evelina Stoikou, head analyst for battery technologies and supply chains at the consultancy BloombergNEF. “It’s a good way to prove your concept, then go through and fund the pilot plant where you can make that and eventually scale up.” Progress meter ………… 7 The technology works, the capital is there, and demand is not far behind. But as with anything in manufacturing, unknown unknowns remain.

events.title: Eliminating traffic deaths
events.summary: Every year, traffic crashes kill more than one million people , and they’re the leading cause of death for children and young adults. In the US, 100 people a day lose their lives this way, in many cases not on highways but on rural and local streets. “Traffic deaths are a leading cause of preventable death, yet we treat it like it’s inevitable,” says Leah Shahum, founder and director of the Vision Zero Network, a nonprofit focused on making streets less deadly.  The sticking points The causes of a crash can be muddy. Drivers make mistakes like speeding or getting distracted, but infrastructure fails them too: Perhaps they were on a road built for speed and not safety, in a screen-filled vehicle, or at an intersection where pedestrians, cyclists, and other cars aren’t visible.  Cheap and proven traffic-calming opportunities abound—from using planters to tighten intersections to lowering speed limits —but government logjams and red tape can be speed bumps. “There’s so many moving parts,” says Laura Sandt of the University of North Carolina Highway Safety Research Center. “On the flip side, it shows that we have so many opportunities for injury prevention.”  The progress The total number of traffic deaths has increased over the last century. And though the US rate has dipped from a peak of 30.8 deaths per 100,000 people in the 1930s, the past decade has seen a concerning jump in deadly pedestrian incidents . At the same time, communities are waking up to the essential role of traffic safety policy, Shahum says.  One success story is Hoboken, New Jersey, which hasn’t had a traffic fatality since 2017 . This is due to a combination of efforts like boosting investment in public transit, promoting walkability by extending curbs, and using cameras to identify crash-prone intersections in need of a redesign. But even there, obstacles remain. If an intersection hasn’t been proved to be deadly, for example, it can be an uphill battle to argue for removing parking spaces to widen curbs. “You’re kind of selling insurance through these improvements, and that’s not always easy,” says Greg Francese, the city’s acting director of transportation and parking. There’s also no silver bullet that will work everywhere. Situated directly across the river from New York City, Hoboken is a highly transit-oriented city of less than 60,000 people. Success there might not translate to traffic-death hot spots like Memphis or Dallas . But it’s not impossible. Take Edmonton, Alberta, a sprawling, car-centric Canadian city of around one million people: Between 2015 and 2020, it cut traffic fatalities by 63% and serious injuries by 40% by adjusting speed limits and improving signals at crosswalks.  Progress meter ………… 6 We know how to tweak intersections and adjust traffic signals. Getting the funding and will to roll out those changes is the big red light.

events.title: Fewer say US federal government improves their lives, poll finds
events.summary: The share of Americans who believe the federal government is effective at improving their lives has dropped significantly since last year, a warning sign for Republicans struggling to assuage voters’ cost of living concerns and keep control of Washington. Forty-three percent of US adults say the federal government is effective at bettering people’s lives, down from 51% in 2025, according to a new Bentley University-Gallup survey . In comparison, 58% say state and local governments improve their lives, while 56% say the same of businesses and 77% of charitable and advocacy groups. At the same time, more than nine in 10 Americans say the federal government has the power to make a positive impact on society — suggesting many believe the current administration is not making use of that power. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Youth-led AI safety group demands protections for young users
events.summary: Design It For Us, a youth-led group that advocates for guardrails on Big Tech companies, is releasing an ambitious 2027 AI policy platform, shared first with Semafor. Its top goals : Prevent catastrophic risk, allow states to pass their own laws, protect against digital fakes, and focus on design that helps and protects people. The platform is based on feedback from 700+ members across 40 states, co-founder Zamaan Qureshi said. He added that Anthropic’s recently leaked bill falls short and said the group is calling on Congress to pass a bill by the end of 2027, “because it’s our future on the line.” The group says it’s shaped several must-haves by taking lessons from Washington’s failure to regulate social media. Among them: The government should be able to block the deployment of dangerous models; large AI companies should be required to have independent testing and meet minimum standards for capabilities; companies should be liable for their projects injuring people; and states should have leeway to regulate AI. “The decisions about AI today will define the world we inherit,” the group’s policy platform states. “We cannot afford to be excluded. Those who build and regulate AI systems must be accountable to the generation that will live with these consequences the longest.” Design It For Us has played an active role in debates on Capitol Hill over kids’ online safety bills, often influencing lawmakers to draft stronger legislation — but one of its key legislative goals, the Kids Online Safety Act, has yet to pass Congress. However, if Democrats focus on AI safety after winning control of one or both chambers of Congress next month, the group’s work on AI issues leaves it well-positioned.

events.title: How a MAGA youth movement is training ‘10,000 Stephen Millers’
events.summary: The Scene The cozy Capitol Hill restaurant — andfavorite MAGA clubhouse — Butterworth’s is closed on Friday mornings, so Nick Solheim let me in through a side door. American Moment, the group he cofounded in 2021, was leading a training upstairs for a group of earnest young right-wing political staffers, 17 men and one woman. When I poked my head into the room, they were listening to one of the heterodox economists orbiting the Trump White House explain what is wrong with traditional notions of free trade. These young conservatives are the vanguard of a new class in Washington that you encounter at the junior levels of federal agencies and congressional offices. It left me wondering: Where did all these very nice, very young, and very MAGA kids ?When I worked as a reporter in Washington during the George W. Bush and Obama administrations, the ambitious young conservatives were involved in Republican politics at Penn or writing for the conservative student newspaper at Dartmouth. They would go on to become the so-called neocons — many of whom still occupy positions of power in conservative Washington, though their politics have shifted to better match President Donald Trump’s. The members of this new generation are more likely to have grown up outside a city like Columbus, Ohio, and to have gone to state school or Christian college. Solheim, a compact, blond 29-year-old who is American Moment’s CEO, boasts he’s never admitted an Ivy League alumnus to his organization. In their jobs in the Trump administration and Republican congressional offices, American Moment’s fellows do a lot of answering the phones, and they always politely take a message and call back — sometimes with an outrageous Trumpian statement or hardline defense of ICE arrests to pass on. “I came of age politically when it was really important to have sharp elbows, and I just don’t see that in these young conservatives,” said Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts, who calls American Moment “one of the most important organizations in the conservative movement today.” Solheim started American Moment with Jake Mercier and Saurabh Sharma, the latter of whom left the organization for a senior role in Trump’s presidential personnel office. The group, which had a $2 million budget in 2024, hasn’t sought or gotten much publicity: Sharma said on American Moment’s podcast in 2023 that if he had his preference, “this would be a completely dark-arts project, almost like a glacier. You’d see a tiny 10% poking out over top, and the rest of it would happen without any attention whatsoever.” By then, he said, they’d trained about 1,500 young conservatives; that number, Solheim said, is now several thousand. (Earlier this month, Solheim would only let me in for a brief, off-the-record peek at the training.) Their goal has been to bring the Trump generation of young people to Washington. That has partly meant broadening the pipeline beyond those with elite credentials. The program has clear ideological tests: Applicants should oppose immigration, free trade, and foreign adventures. “Our goal is to create 10,000 Stephen Millers,” Solheim said on the podcast last September. He told me the hardline Trump aide is a model not only for his effectiveness, but also “because his career trajectory perfectly tracks what we’re attempting to achieve with our young people. From junior Senate staffer to assistant to the president, and everything in between.” Much of their training is practical: The group takes in 15-30 paid fellows each semester in its most intensive, paid program, and teaches them to tuck in their shirts, shower daily, and network relentlessly. The training includes mock networking happy hours and credit cards with $100 to take people out to coffee. (Solheim himself favors Butterworth’s Vesper martini.) The project is well-regarded inside the Trump administration, including by Vice President JD Vance, who was an adviser to American Moment in its early days. Vance’s former national security adviser, Andy Baker, is joining the group as a senior adviser. “When people hire a fellow from American Moment, they know they are getting someone who has had ideological and intellectual formation with whom the principal may agree,” said Rachel Bovard, the vice president of programs at the Conservative Partnership Institute and a member of the group’s board. “And they know the standards of how you should behave.” American Moment’s critics on the left and the right accuse the group of flying too close to the racism and nihilism of the online right. The group’s podcast guests have included Jeremy Carl, a Trump administration official whose confirmation faltered because his views on anti-white racism were seen as too extreme. In the spirit of Vance’s relationship with Tucker Carlson, Solheim and his allies avoid criticizing allies to the right. But in the taxonomy of the young American right, there are degrees of difference. People involved in American Moment insist they screen for extremist tweets, telling their fellows to stay off the internet and avoid edgelord politics. “You haven’t seen the Paul Ingrassia types come through American Moment,” said one Trump administration official, referring to a colleague who noted his own “Nazi streak” in leaked text messages. White supremacist Nick Fuentes, meanwhile, groups American Moment on his enemies list with “neocons” and “Zionists.” He once delivered an extended racist rant directed at Sharma and the group. “If you are at all adjacent to Nick Fuentes or anything he says, you are not getting in,” Bovard said. Instead, the group recognizes that “especially for young men, there’s this toxic stew of nihilism and Andrew Tate out there that can be attractive if you have nothing else. Some of the American Moment project is taking young men like that and giving them purpose.” American Moment’s biggest challenge right now is identical to the one vexing Republican voters at the polls next month: Even if they find ICE’s sweeps inspiring, they feel betrayed by the Iran war. “A lot of the younger staff are pretty demoralized by the war,” notes one administration official. He and a former Trump administration official both told me they’d been counseling junior staff to play the long game. “Those guys are showing up to work every day and carrying out a policy they disagree with,” the former Trump administration official said. “That’s the essence of government work.” Ben’s view There’s a daydream among Democrats and Republicans who dislike Trump that the party will return to something like “normal.” That may in some sense be true: The American Moment crowd has little in common with the political appointees at the higher levels of the administration, a motley crew often chosen for social ties and financial connections that’s currently reeling through a series of lurid scandals . events.title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
events.summary: Elon Musk is chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday. While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move. "The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained." With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history. SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business. That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia. US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown . Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions. Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google. The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year. Why does Elon Musk want to merge Tesla and SpaceX? Published 7 hours ago Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger. He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of both Tesla and SpaceX. Even commenting on the possibility of combining the two companies, Musk compared it to "tap dancing through a minefield". A merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, he added. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve a combination, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve". While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics. SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its market debut in June. Elon Musk and Donald Trump have denied limiting Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starshield network SpaceX, as a whole is not profitable, despite revenue jumping to $27bn from $13.7bn over the first nine months of the year. Over that same period it lost $1.1bn although it did report a $4.4bn profit for the most recent three months. Following Musk's comments, SpaceX's share price rose 8% in after-hours trading. Shares in Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose by 2% Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X , the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned. The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together. Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence and software. events.title: What is happening to UK prices?
events.summary: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, the highest rate in nearly a year and above the Bank of England's 2% target. The rise was slightly higher than economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices. Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months. Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%. How is the UK's inflation rate measured and what does it mean for UK interest rates? The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026 , while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed. The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation. The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) , external , and the latest figure is published every month. The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%. Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises. But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy. For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals. Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment. Although CPI inflation of 3.5% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. That was the highest rate for 40 years. While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly. The higher figure for September was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 29.8% compared to September last year. Food price inflation remained at 1.3%. But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran. How do energy prices affect UK inflation? Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine. Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026. But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario. When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July . As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the 4% increase in household energy bills from 1 October when the latest Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher. As part of his pledge to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living, Prime Minister Andy Burnham scrapped VAT on household electricity bills in October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation. Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs. Core CPI was 2.8% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to August. Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 October What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 28 September What does an Andy Burnham-led government mean for your money? Published 22 July What is happening to UK interest rates and will they fall again? The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023. In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario. At its September meeting , Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise. Are wages keeping up with inflation? The Bank also looks closely at what is happening to wages and unemployment.

events.title: GIC, Temasek rebut allegations of pressuring MSCI to downgrade Indonesia
events.summary: This was not the first time MSCI has warned that it would downgrade Indonesia. It previously warned in January that it could downgrade the country from emerging to frontier market. GIC and Temasek denied claims they pressured MSCI to downgrade Indonesia. GIC said it invests based on “company- and asset-level fundamentals”, while Temasek said the claims are “patently untrue”. MSCI is reviewing whether to reclassify Indonesia from an emerging market to standalone status. It says its decisions use “transparent and rules-based methodologies” and will decide by June 30, 2027. The warning has shaken Indonesian stocks, with the Jakarta Composite Index falling more than 14% before recovering 5%. IDX is tightening rules on concentrated share ownership to avoid exclusion from MSCI benchmarks. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC and investment company Temasek have rejected allegations that they or their staff pressured index provider MSCI to consider downgrading Indonesia’s stock market classification. This follows accusations on Oct 20 by former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi that the two investors coerced MSCI to consider downgrading Indonesia. The former minister claimed that a downgrade could trigger market panic and create opportunities to acquire Indonesian equities at lower prices. A GIC spokesperson told The Straits Times: “Our investment decisions are not driven by index classifications or top-down views of a market, and instead by company- and asset-level fundamentals. “We have been invested in Indonesia for over 30 years across asset classes and will continue to invest where we find good, bottom-up, risk-adjusted opportunities.” Fock Wai Hoong, head of Asia-Pacific excluding China and India at Temasek Global Investments, said the allegations have “no basis and are patently untrue”. “No one from Temasek – neither the institution nor the individuals working for the institution – has ever reached out to MSCI in order to influence any decisions they have ever made around any exchange across the region. “Maybe I’ll leave it at that,” he said. Fock was responding to the media during the launch of the e-Conomy SEA 2026 report at Google’s office in Mapletree Business City on Oct 21. Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) president director Jeffrey Hendrik defended the independence of MSCI on Oct 20 following the allegations. “We have always believed, and continue to believe, that global index providers are independent,” he told reporters at the IDX building in Jakarta. MSCI, meanwhile, told ST that its index decisions follow transparent and rules-based methodologies. It is accepting market feedback until April 30, 2027, and will announce its decision by June 30. “MSCI will continue to monitor developments in the Indonesian market and engage with market participants and authorities,” it said, adding that it does not disclose investor feedback during an open consultation period. The controversy comes after a record two-day market sell-off following MSCI’s warning on Oct 15 of the possible removal of Indonesia from its global indexes. Among its concerns were shareholding opacity, insider trading and regulatory enforcement. Every year, MSCI reviews all global markets and determines whether they should be classified as developed, emerging, frontier or standalone, based on economic development, market size, liquidity and accessibility. The index provider has launched a consultation on whether to reclassify Indonesia from an emerging market to standalone status, a move which can be a big blow for the country as its stocks would be excluded from indexes used by investors. Any reclassification could have significant implications for Indonesian equities, including investment flows from funds that track MSCI indexes , which are widely used as benchmarks for tracking different global markets. The index provider’s move indicates that the concerns extend beyond market size or liquidity and relate to more fundamental issues involving the integrity and credibility of trading mechanisms, said Eastspring Investments, an asset management business of Prudential. Other standalone markets include Argentina, Lebanon and Zimbabwe. The Jakarta Composite Index fell more than 14% from Oct 16 to 19 following MSCI’s warning. However, the index recovered 5% on Oct 20, after IDX said the night before that it would expel companies with highly concentrated share ownership from its flagship index in its latest attempt to avoid ejection from MSCI’s global emerging markets benchmark. The announcement followed a virtual meeting between the exchange and MSCI officials. Such companies, which make up almost a fifth of the index’s combined market value, include Dian Swastatika Sentosa and Barito Renewables Energy – two of the biggest companies in the index by market value. The exchange did not say when the expulsions would take effect.

events.title: Europe Wants Data Centers. Its Climate Goals Are Getting in the Way
events.summary: Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan : By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe —and boost its faltering economy. However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy. As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations. “We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED. In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back . Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “ data center prevention act .” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility. Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate. The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment. Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.” In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act. Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says. When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.” Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change. The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten. But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns.

events.title: US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors
events.summary: Can Iran's rail network offset expanding US sanctions? As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade. The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran , this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult. On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast. Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) . The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey. Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it. Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives. The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year. Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices? Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan. The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies. Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days. In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days. For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz . But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences. A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability. It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days. The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran. Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay. Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries. Rail works best for critical inputs Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade. "A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW. Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport. That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line. US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran? Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges. For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit. Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging. If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived. "Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said.

events.title: What’s brewing behind South Korea’s Mega Coffee deal rush?
events.summary: Mega MGC Coffee, South Korea’s largest coffee chain with 4,500 outlets, now harbours an appetite for a larger share of the retail landscape. Mega Coffee is using its strong cash flow and franchise network to chase bigger retail deals, moving beyond coffee into supermarkets and drinks. It lost the Homeplus Express bid to Harim Group, but is now shortlisted for Haitai HTB, a deal worth about 300 billion won, with enough cash likely available. Mega is also growing fast at home and abroad, while possible bids for Burger King and Tim Hortons remain uncertain because of weak fit and different business models. SEOUL – In South Korea’s food and beverage deal market these days, the most persistent bidder sells cheap coffee . Mega MGC Coffee, the country’s largest coffee chain with 4,500 bright-yellow storefronts, no longer seems content merely selling Americanos. It now harbours an appetite for a larger share of the retail landscape. “With a nationwide franchise logistics network and strong cash generation, Mega Coffee has emerged as a key strategic investor in F&B deals,” one industry official said. The hunt began in the spring with Homeplus Express, the supermarket unit carved out of embattled retailer Homeplus. MGC Global, Mega Coffee’s operator, made it to the main bidding round, but Harim Group, the parent of NS Shopping, ultimately won the deal in May. The coffee chain’s goal, industry officials say, was to become an everyday retail platform by adding supermarket retail to its cafes and to the food supply business of Boratr, a Kosdaq-listed sister company. MGC Global Chairman Kim Dae-young founded Boratr in 2000, built his fortune on it and used it to buy Mega Coffee in 2021. Homeplus Express’ stores, logistics and familiar name would have let Boratr sell its meals and fresh food directly to consumers, and its global sourcing network could have filled the shelves with imported goods. The chain might also have carried Mega-branded ready-to-drink beverages and private-label food. Undeterred, MGC Global has since turned its attention to Haitai HTB, the beverage unit LG Household & Health Care is selling, though it is keeping separate its Coca-Cola bottler. MGC Global and private equity firm Godo Partners have made the shortlist for a deal LG H&H hopes will fetch about 300 billion won (S$289.5 million), with a main bid looming but no date yet disclosed. Should it prevail, MGC Global is expected to draw on Haitai’s plants and logistics network to produce cup coffee and bottled drinks. Funding is unlikely to be the obstacle. Parent company Wooyoon, which holds 82.3% of MGC Global, had 195.1 billion won in cash and short-term financial instruments at the end of 2025. Boratr held another 150 billion won in cash and liquid financial assets in the first half. Together, the two Kim-controlled firms can tap at least 350 billion won, and analysts say acquisition financing could stretch that far enough for a sizeable deal. Meanwhile, Mega pursues growth with equal vigour. It opened its 4,500th outlet in October and has expanded abroad with stores in Mongolia and Cambodia. Japan is under review, and a US store is reportedly on the way. MGC Global’s revenue jumped 30.4% on-year to 646.9 billion won in 2025, with operating profit of 111.4 billion won. MGC Global has also lately surfaced as a potential suitor for BKR, the South Korean operator of Burger King and Tim Hortons, after sale advisers Deutsche Bank Securities and Lazard Korea floated the business to the coffee chain, according to investment banking sources. Affinity Equity Partners, which owns BKR, is even mulling a carve-out of Tim Hortons, which would spare Mega a clash with its core business, the sources added. For now, synergy between Mega and Burger King remains an open question, except for the likely prospect of Mega coffee at the burger chain. Sceptics argue that coffee shops and burger chains differ in operations and customer demand, and that most Burger King Korea stores are company-run, unlike Mega’s franchise model. “The Haitai HTB outcome, and the money it requires, will decide whether Mega joins the Burger King race,” another industry observer noted. events.title: Data centre gas plant could be mothballed after two years, court told
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Court hears gas power plant for Moss Vale data centre could be mothballed An artist's impression of one of three data centres planned for the Moss Vale site. ( Supplied: Cloud Carrier ) Nakar Property is appealing in court to build a $23 million gas power plant and battery storage system in the Southern Highlands. Its lawyers say the gas plant will be eventually replaced with cheaper energy supplied via the grid. Cross-examination of expert witnesses will continue for the hearing's third day on Thursday. A gas-fired power station proposed for the NSW Southern Highlands could be mothballed once the grid can meet the energy demands of an onsite data centre, a court has heard. The NSW Land and Environment Court is considering an appeal by developers Nakar Property, after Wingecarribee Shire Council refused its development application for a 16-megawatt power station and battery energy storage system in Moss Vale. The station is one of three planned to power a data centre campus on site proposed by Sydney company Cloud Carrier. Barrister James Smith, acting for Nakar Property, told the court the power plant was needed to provide constant power for customers using the centre. "[Cloud Carrier's] investment in computers is circa a $1 billion; the fundamental requirement is firm supply," Mr Smith said. "It's akin to enrolling your child in school without any teachers; Cloud Carrier can't sell any product unless there is firm supply." The proposed gas-fired power plant would be used to run Cloud Carrier's data centre campus. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) The second day of hearings before Commissioner Nicola Targett came after the court travelled to Moss Vale to inspect the site of the $23 million project on Tuesday. In his opening submissions, Mr Smith said developers would stop using gas power as soon as a reliable supply of energy from the grid could be secured. "The cost savings per year via connecting to the grid is approximately $14 million per year," he said. "There is clear financial incentive to use the grid when that power becomes available. The issue is there is not sufficient supply." Referencing expert reports, Mr Smith said the power plant was projected to emit less greenhouse emissions than if it were powered by the grid until approximately 2029. Addressing Commissioner Targett, barrister Michael Staunton, for Wingecarribee Shire Council, said that power supplied by the grid had been touted as a "panacea" to the project, but not investigated thoroughly. "All of that work and investigation should have been done, and you'll find when you get to the documents, it hasn't been," Mr Staunton said. After an adjournment, Wingecarribee Shire Council tendered draft conditions of consent in the middle of the hearing. These included a new requirement that canopy trees be planted across approximately 40 per cent of the development site. Expert air-quality, electrical and engineering consultants appeared as witnesses for cross-examination about reports they had prepared for the project. Mr Staunton argued during cross-examination that the project would not have the secure power needed to fill the full capacity of servers in the proposed data centre for two years, when an upgrade of a nearby power substation operated by Endeavour Energy would be completed. "You've got no firm supply for two years," Mr Staunton said. "That time could be spent negotiating with Endeavour Energy while you wait for the permanent connection." The matter will return to court on Thursday for a third day of hearings.

events.title: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations
events.summary: U.K. inflation jumped to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% the previous month. Economists polled by Reuters had been forecasting an annual inflation rate of 3.4%. Markets are pricing in two rate hikes from the Bank of England by the end of the year. U.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels. September's print marked a continuation of the U.K.'s upward trend for inflation, which came in at 3.1% in August and 2.9% in July. The September reading was the highest annual inflation figure in almost a year. The U.K.'s Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that the motor fuel inflation rate had hit its highest level since August 2022, when fuel costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Britain is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks, such as the U.S.-Iran war and the subsequent struggle to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz. U.K. motor fuel prices surged 29.8% in the year to September, ONS data showed on Wednesday. The British pound was flat against both the euro and the U.S. dollar following the data release, and yields on U.K. government bonds were also little changed. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said in a note Wednesday morning that recent growth in headline inflation had "undone the progress we saw in the spring." "Bank of England policymakers will be looking beyond the headline figure," he said. "Services inflation, in particular, has accelerated in recent months which will create concern that we are starting to see second round inflationary effects beyond energy prices. While we face a different set of challenges compared to 2021, the prolonged conflict is weighing on the U.K. economy and making the case for a rate hike stronger." Markets are pricing in a 98% chance that the Bank of England raises its key interest rate by 25 basis points to 4% next month, according to LSEG data, with the majority of traders also pricing in a further hike of the same size at the central bank's final meeting of the year in December. Wednesday's expected rise in inflation also complicates the fiscal picture for the U.K. government and its finance minister. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is set to unveil his first fiscal shakeup next week during the U.K.'s hotly anticipated Autumn Budget. He is tasked with sticking to the previous government's so-called fiscal rules, which aim to rein in public debt while delivering on promises to soften the blow of surging consumer costs. But separate data published Wednesday showed the U.K.'s national debt was estimated to have exceeded £3 trillion ($4 trillion) in September for the first time. The cost of servicing those debts has risen drastically over the past year, and the British economy is struggling to grow . Healey said in a statement following Wednesday's data release that he would be "maintaining our fiscal discipline" in the budget next week, while working to "drive for growth [and give] businesses and families some breathing space." Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said in a note Wednesday morning that rising inflation is turning the Autumn Budget into "a perilous high-wire act for the Chancellor." He said surging prices were "increasing pressure for cost-of-living support while pushing up government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options." "With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," he said. "Policymakers will also be looking to the Chancellor to avoid adding fuel to the inflation fire by delivering a credible, fiscally disciplined Budget."

events.title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
events.summary: OpenAI has disclosed two internal coding incidents in which agents weakened the company’s misalignment monitoring safeguards. Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months. OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so. An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks. "In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post. Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech. The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks. OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.

events.title: Singapore to update restructuring and insolvency framework to better serve economy, businesses
events.summary: Law Minister Edwin Tong speaking at the Singapore Insolvency Conference on Oct 21. The IRDA will be amended to make judicial management a clear rescue process. Applicants must show how it can save a business and why it is better than liquidation. Cross-class cramdown rules will be made easier to use. Voting thresholds will be refined, and shareholders may be bound in some cases, with safeguards to protect fairness. Singapore will adopt two more UNCITRAL model laws on group insolvency and insolvency-related judgments. This will improve cross-border cooperation and support its role as a restructuring hub. SINGAPORE – Forty years after judicial management was introduced in Singapore, the process has not always fulfilled its purpose of rescuing beleaguered but viable businesses and preserving their value. “Too often, it has become a precursor to liquidation, adding time and costs without necessarily achieving meaningful rehabilitation,” said Minister for Law Edwin Tong on Oct 21. “This is unacceptable,” he added, giving the keynote address at the Singapore Insolvency Conference organised by the Insolvency Practitioners Association of Singapore. His ministry will amend the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018 (IRDA) to make it clear that judicial management is a rehabilitative process, with the first reading of the Bill in Parliament slated for later in 2026 or early 2027. In May, the Ministry of Law broadly accepted reform recommendations made in 2025 by the Committee to Enhance Singapore’s Corporate Restructuring and Insolvency Regime, after a public consultation. Tong stressed that premature liquidation can destroy value and that financial distress does not necessarily mean a business is no longer viable. “The company may well have a very sound underlying business and good assets, but an unsustainable debt burden or temporary liquidity difficulties. And in such a situation, premature liquidation or prolonged administration can destroy them,” said Tong, who is also Second Minister for Home Affairs. “In a mature economy like Singapore’s, business cycles, ups and downs will be inevitable. They will be recurring, and industries will go through periods of growth and decline. We need a stronger restructuring framework to allow businesses to recover and to absorb the shocks of that ebb and flow.” Under judicial management, control of a financially distressed company is temporarily placed under an independent, court-appointed judicial manager with the aim of keeping the company afloat, or to work out a debt restructuring plan. The company is protected against lawsuits by creditors during this period. The business typically shifts to liquidation and winding up if the creditors reject the proposed rescue plan by the judicial manager. As part of the amendments to the IRDA, applicants for judicial management must be able to explain how the process is expected to rehabilitate the company or its business, and the tangible benefits compared with winding up the company. A company, its directors or a creditor can apply to the court for a judicial management order. Should judicial management fail to rehabilitate the company and it proceeds to liquidation, the circumstances leading to this must be explained. The judicial manager will also typically not be allowed to transition into the company’s liquidator role. “Not every rescue will succeed, even when there were good prospects at the outset for a successful restructuring,” Tong said. “But it is really about making sure that the judicial management is pursued for the right reasons, with clear objectives and, importantly, in this case, accountability for the outcomes that are sought.” The second recommendation is to make cross-class cramdown to be more accessible and user-friendly. Cross-class cramdown allows the court to approve a restructuring plan even if there are dissenting classes of voting creditors. Such plans are typically structured to ensure a better overall outcome for stakeholders compared with other alternatives. In a cross-class cramdown in Singapore , a restructuring plan must be approved by at least one group of creditors who would be worse off or whose rights would be affected by the plan and who would receive some payment if the company were wound up. At least a majority in number and 75% in value of the creditors across the classes must vote to support the plan. At the conference, Tong noted that the cross-class cramdown mechanism has seen limited use since its introduction in 2017. In its report, the committee noted that the “overall numerosity and value cramdown conditions jointly constitute a high threshold, which deters the putting together of a plan that involves a cross-class cramdown”. Tong said voting thresholds will be refined under the reform, and cross-class cramdowns will be extended to shareholders in appropriate circumstances.

events.title: Polymarket removes contract allowing wagers on fate of Cornell students accused of sexual assault
events.summary: Polymarket has removed a contract from its prediction market platform that allowed users to wager on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime Polymarket has removed a contract from its prediction market platform that allowed users to wager on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime. The market was made available on Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. It had more than $450,000 in volume before it was taken off Polymarket's international platform. The company's U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to “activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law.” “Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time,” a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. “This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market.” Front Office Sports was the first to report on the contract. Some outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with Polymarket, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several celebrities. Messages were left by the AP on Tuesday with representatives for James, Jeter, Manning and Bird. Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. Messages were left by the AP seeking comment from each organization. A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, said the director had no comment. Messages also were left with representatives for actors Craig Robinson, John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario — who were also part of the commercial with James. A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren’t involved. An online petition launched by UltraViolet, a women-led national advocacy organization, singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company. A message was left seeking comment from a representative for Ratajkowski, who also appears in the celebrity-filled commercial with James. Prediction markets provide an opportunity to trade on the result of future events. Sports account for a major portion of the volume generated by the array of typically yes-or-no question, depending on the platform. When a U.S. Army sergeant was indicted earlier this year over bets on the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, he was trading on Polymarket’s international platform. The Associated Press reported in April that 50 brand new accounts on Polymarket’s international platform placed substantial bets on a U.S.-Iran ceasefire in the hours, even minutes, before President Donald Trump announced a ceasefire on social media, raising concerns of insider trading. Polymarket had an active market on its international platform on Tuesday that allowed customers to trade on whether Cornell president Michael Kotlikoff will be out by Oct. 31. events.title: AI's spending boom faces a 'gut check': Who can actually make money?
events.summary: Elice's bruising IPO debut and next-day recovery highlights growing investor scrutiny over whether AI infrastructure spending can deliver sustainable profits. Rising borrowing costs are exposing debt-heavy neocloud providers to financing risks. Analysts expect a widening divide between AI companies generating sustainable returns and those reliant on external financing. The artificial intelligence boom may be entering a more unforgiving phase, as investors increasingly question whether the billions poured into data centers will translate into sustainable profits. A bruising stock market debut by South Korean AI infrastructure provider Elice has become the latest warning sign that investors may be more closely scrutinizing ambitious expansion plans and paths to profitability. "This is a gut check moment in the tech trade," said Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives. "Investors are trying to better discern between the winners and losers and if there are any weak links in the tech AI food chain." "Patience is wearing thin and scrutiny will be elevated especially for those taking on a major debt load like some of the neoclouds," he added. The weak debut underscores a broader shift in sentiment toward the AI trade, where rising borrowing costs and concerns over debt-fueled expansion may force investors to distinguish between companies generating cash from the boom and those spending heavily in anticipation of future demand. "The AI trade has moved from a phase where the size of the capex announcement was itself viewed positively to one where investors are asking who can actually earn an adequate return on that capital," said Billy Leung of Global X ETFs. "The market is distinguishing between companies that need capital to survive the build-out and companies that are being paid as the build-out continues." The most vulnerable companies are neocloud providers expanding faster than their ability to generate cash, particularly those heavily dependent on external financing, according to Leung. CoreWeave, one of the largest neocloud providers, is "the poster child of this whole thing," according to John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks Investment Research. "This is broad market stress, not just speculation," he said, pointing to widening credit spreads. Companies borrowing heavily to build computing capacity could face a squeeze if financing costs rise faster than revenue, particularly where construction expenses and depreciation mount before facilities reach full utilization. The shift is particularly significant for Asia, where technology markets are heavily exposed to the semiconductor and memory-chip industries that have powered the global AI investment frenzy. "U.S. semiconductor and AI plays are overbuilt. And in South Korea, even more overbuilt," Blank said. South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics have been among the biggest beneficiaries of soaring demand for advanced memory chips, but their shares have come under pressure as investors reassess the sustainability of AI spending. "Asia is simply much more directly geared to the hardware and memory side of the AI trade, so when investors question AI capex and financing, Korea and other North Asian technology markets feel it disproportionately," Leung said. He added that rising earnings estimates across South Korea and Taiwan suggest the recent selloff reflects deteriorating sentiment and shrinking valuations rather than a sudden collapse in demand. The change reflects a growing divide between companies with the financial firepower to sustain aggressive AI investments and those relying heavily on borrowing to fund expansion. HSBC Chief Executive Officer Georges Elhedery warned that investors and lenders must become more discerning about which data-center projects deserve financing. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements," he said. "You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."

SINGAPORE – Restaurant chain Lao Huo Tang’s parent company, Soup Empire Holdings, has been given four weeks to pay its remaining Central Provident Fund (CPF) arrears. A State Court heard that the company has paid off about $5,300 so far and has about $18,900 in outstanding CPF contributions for May, June and July. During an Oct 21 hearing, the company was given a four-week adjournment until the next hearing on Nov 11 to clear its CPF arrears. Soup Empire operates a portfolio of restaurant brands, including Eng’s Wantan Noodle and Kenny Rogers. This comes after two other companies linked to the Lao Huo Tang restaurant chain cleared their CPF arrears, with charges against them disposed of after the matters were compounded, a court heard on Oct 6.

events.title: UK approves long-awaited Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
events.summary: Britain on Wednesday approved the Jackdaw North Sea ​gasfield , ending years ​of legal and political wrangling that had ⁠pitted the Labour government's climate commitments against its push ⁠to bolster energy security. Energy Minister Miatta ​Fahnbulleh said the project will start to supply gas to British homes and businesses from as ⁠early as the end of this month. At the same time, she said a new Energy Wealth Fund would be established by the government with a £2 billion downpayment to reinvest oil and ⁠gas revenue into the climate transition. Ms Fahnbulleh said Jackdaw was expected to increase ​domestic gas ⁠production by about 6 per cent at ‌its peak and support the country's gas supply over its lifespan of up to ​11 years, boosting energy security and protecting hundreds of jobs. “At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” said Prime Minister Andy Burnham. “Even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.” Adura, the joint venture between energy giants Shell and Norway's Equinor that operates the project, has said Jackdaw will produce gas equivalent to up to 40,000 barrels of oil a day at peak output. Environmental groups could mount a fresh legal challenge to the approval. The issue ​has become a rallying point for climate activists, who say approving new fossil fuel projects undermines Labour's green pledges and ignores warnings from a summer of record-breaking heat across Europe. The fate of Jackdaw had been in ​limbo for years and has forced Mr Burnham to take sides in a battle over the future of the North Sea while risking alienating voters. The relatively small gas project has become a symbol of a bitter political fight over Britain’s energy transition. Approving Jackdaw risked a backlash from some on the left of the Labour Party and the Greens. Rejecting drilling in the field would have fuelled criticism from Reform UK, the Conservatives and the oil industry that climate policies are costing Britain jobs and investment. The previous Conservative government approved the project ‌in 2022, but climate activists challenged ⁠the decision in court alongside approval for ​the Rosebank oil and gasfield. A 2025 ruling barred operators from ​extracting oil ‌or gas until they received fresh government consent that takes into account emissions from the burning ⁠of the fields' hydrocarbons. The decision has taken on added significance for Mr Burnham since ⁠he took office in July. In its 2024 general election manifesto, the Labour Party pledged to block new drilling in the North Sea, but officials say decisions on Jackdaw and Rosebank – the largest undeveloped oil and gas reservoir in British waters – fall outside that commitment because they involve licences approved years ago under the previous government. “Jackdaw has been made into this big issue because it’s become a symbol of the wider North Sea debate,” said Jess Ralston, head of energy at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, an independent non-profit. “But even if the government approves it and Rosebank, the North Sea debate isn’t going to get any less flammable.” Even once drilling gets under way, few believe the UK could ever compete again with major oil and gas regions. Its stretch of the North Sea is 90 per cent depleted for commercial resources, according to consultant Wood Mackenzie. The international companies that pioneered drilling there 60 years ago have retreated.

events.title: Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Fiber alignment is the main bottleneck to optical engine testing, which would be alleviated significantly by multi-site probe cards. Optical connectors must be optimized for the best optical properties yet be mechanically robust to withstand assembly and use. Simultaneous loopback on both optical and electrical sides could simplify testing. Experts At The Table : The industry is forging a path from single-site to multi-site testing while system architectures and connector types continue to evolve. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at Teradyne ; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at Advantest America ; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of ASE Group ; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at Keysight Technologies . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one, click here . Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal. SE: Is it true that you can only test one die at a time today? Armstrong: I would hope some insertions will go away over time, but right now there are more things being added than being subtracted. It’s a hard one. In terms of testing one die, that depends on the die. If an 8 kW GPU is your main ASIC, and you have multiple connectors around multiple sides of the part from a tester resource standpoint, and the amount of power a tester can deliver and take out of the part, it’s pretty challenging to get beyond one die. But if you look down the NPO-versus-CPO path, NPO is typically a single connector device. You’re going to have to be able to go to multi-site to scale that to high volume. Insertions two and three are the fertile ground for multi-site. Those are longer more complex test insertions. PIC wafer testing tends to be single-site today. From my experience, there is some hope on the horizon to bring it up a little bit higher with some capabilities in the probe card area, notably from Technoprobe. Griffin: I agree with Dave. Most production solutions today are single-site, and when you talk about the optical engine, the main bottleneck is fiber alignment. Many companies are working on multi-site solutions, and I hope they succeed and take off because that only helps the whole industry ramp faster. But we’ve got a little bit longer to go there. SE: For these alignment ports, can you repeatedly test at that site? Griffin: Ideally, you’re able to repeatedly test almost infinitely because you should never be contacting the device with the optical probe or the fiber array unit (FAU). When you’re bringing up a new test solution, you do sometimes crash FAUs on first systems. In reality, the bigger concern is contamination on the FAU, so cleaning is needed. On the connector side, at the module level or for optical engines with receptacles attached, the optical connector lifecycle is where we need more effort, because the device-side connector is designed to be attached once and, hopefully, never disconnected. And every new connector generation changes both the connector recipe and the automation recipe. Leventhal: In a sense, this is nothing new. For instance, with BGAs, if you socket at the device too many times, then you start worrying about damaging the balls on the BGA. It’s a similar problem and the industry will gravitate toward connector designs that are more robust. Matt made a really important point about how your test side connector needs to be some sort of a hardened connector that doesn’t wear out easily after 20 to 50 insertions. It needs to last for tens of thousands or 100,000 insertions. So you’ve got to go to a hardened metal, and then you’ve got a hardened metal going against the receptacle on the device, which is not going to be that hardened metal. If you’re not careful, you could damage that connector sooner than the spec lifetime. So as the industry evolves to the winning connector designs, robustness on the device side is going to be a really important part of that. SE: What are the challenges with making simultaneous electrical and optical connections? Armstrong: It’s just a question of time. Yamaguchi: Beyond DC and optical probing, the harder part of simultaneous electrical and optical connection is characterizing electro-optic devices in RF. Modulator and photodetector performance is ultimately validated through S-parameters, so you need optical and high-frequency RF contact at the same time. Probe cards can only fit a limited number of RF lines, and their bandwidth is also limited, while today’s devices are characterized beyond 200 GHz. At wafer and die insertions, simultaneous connection is really an RF probing challenge. Leventhal: Warpage is going to create additional challenges on top of just trying to solve the problem in an ideal case. You need to be able to align in multiple axes. And the BGA has a crazy amount of pins that you have to make reliable contact with, so that problem is getting more challenging. Adding to that is being able to do the right level of alignment, either coming from the top or coming from the side. It’s significantly challenging. I agree with Dave, it’s a question of time in multiple senses. Each insertion takes time, although there are ways of minimizing that by integrating certain operations together. But also, it’s going to take time for all of this to mature to the point that it’s going to be easier to test at scale. Griffin: At its core, there’s an optical and an electrical interface to the device at every insertion, and sometimes those interfaces are on the top side of the device, sometimes the bottom side, and sometimes both. And then when you talk about module level, they’re on two to four sides of the package across some number of optical engines. So if you look at optical alignment on its own, it’s not that big of a challenge. But when you start combining it with all the different, I’ll say, flavors of architecture that we’re seeing, and trying to design a scalable test system that can handle as many of those flavors as possible for your customers, that’s really where some of the fun challenges are. Armstrong: I also chair the IPSR test roadmap for photonics, and in our latest report we highlight a test methodology for AC testing. AC testing, bit error rate testing, will be one of the bigger time sinks. If we had good DFT, we could just do loopback on the optical side and loopback on the electrical side at the same time. And technically, there’s no reason you couldn’t combine those two tests. But today, most people are saying, “Okay, I’ll do loopback on one side or the other side, and a bit error rate test of some nature on the other side, so that becomes a very expensive setup that doubles the effective test time.
