events.title: Accelerating Manufacturing-Aware Simulations For Photonic Integrated Circuits With FTCO And Digital Twins
events.summary: Photonic integrated circuit (PIC) performance is increasingly bounded by fabrication realities such as sidewall angle, critical-dimension bias, thickness variation, and line-edge roughness, which idealized, as-drawn FDTD simulations fail to capture. Here, we show a Fab Technology Co-Optimization (FTCO) workflow that connects GDS layout import, three-dimensional process simulation, GPU-accelerated FDTD, design of experiments (DOE), with AI-based surrogate modeling. We show that when manufacturing variations are included in the modeling that the simulation results align well with experimentally reported results. A directional-coupler DOE with 25 unique combinations of 4 different process variations requiring a 65-million-cell 3D FDTD model and completes in under 10 hours on a single NVIDIA A100-equipped workstation is showcased. The generated digital twin provides intuitive and real-time access to the process-to-performance relationship for non-simulation experts: A game-changer in the industry. Read more here . Achieving the requisite target yield as early as possible during silicon ramp is a lead indicator of product success. Delays in reaching yield entitlement can impact time-to-market, increase manufacturing costs, and reduce overall product competitiveness—particularly at advanced nodes where complexity and cost continue to rise. As a result, incorporating a solution that can rapidly identify and resolve systematic yield limiters has become essential to enabling efficient ramp to high-volume production. Such a solution requires analytics-driven volume diagnostic and failure analysis capabilities to reverse engineer test failures captured on automatic test equipment (ATE). These capabilities identify the precise failing location within the chip, rank failure candidates based on yield impact, and provide the highest-priority candidates to the failure analysis lab for final root-cause confirmation. Corrective action can then be performed on either the design or the silicon process to correct and improve the yield of your chip and ultimately enable you to go to high volume production and into the market ahead of the competition. events.title: UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change
events.summary: Humanity is losing more ground in its fight against climate change WASHINGTON -- Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says. If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday's update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That's about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year's projections by the same science team. “This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas. “In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report. The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries' climate fighting plans. He wasn't part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound. The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year's projection. Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact . The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees. The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.” Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen. “The report's message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn't part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.” Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century. events.title: What a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would mean
events.summary: Elon Musk believes a merger between Tesla and SpaceX is a good idea, he said on Tuesday, publicly backing an idea that would create ​one ​of the most valuable companies in the ​world, worth about $3.5 trillion. While electric-vehicle maker Tesla and rocket company ⁠SpaceX were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as ⁠Mr Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing , satellite communications and computing infrastructure, ​including data centres on Earth and potentially in orbit. Here's what a potential merger could mean: Why merge the companies? A merger would create a ⁠single company at the centre of Mr Musk's long-term vision: an integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications, and transportation on Earth and beyond. “I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained ⁠from co-operating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation (of orbital data centres), connectivity,” Mr Musk said on Tuesday. Bringing ​the companies ⁠together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Mr Musk's projects ‌already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy capital, engineering ​talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity. Mr Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence. What does it mean for investors? Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses. A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about $3.5 trillion, combining leadership positions in cars, robotics, satellite communications, launch services, energy storage and AI infrastructure. Supporters would likely argue that the combined company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly interdependent. Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another. Where could SpaceX and Tesla work together? Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future ​data-centre projects. Mr Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing ‌the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and ⁠Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Mr Musk ​hopes it can start volume production by late 2028. Tesla's expertise in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship production, ​while SpaceX technologies ‌have already appeared in Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster. A merged company could also co-ordinate efforts to secure strategic ⁠supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialised metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite ⁠hardware. What are the key risks? The biggest challenges may be geopolitics and regulation. SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and Nasa. Tesla, meanwhile, remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing. The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors ​would need to be persuaded that combining two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow. Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres, mobile communications and orbital infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place them under one roof.

events.title: Plans for commercial helium production on Yorke Peninsula
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Commercial helium production planned for the Yorke Peninsula Neil McDonald (left) during a proof-of-concept exercise with extracted helium. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) Gold Hydrogen has announced plans for commercial helium production at its Yorke Peninsula site. It will be the first time helium is produced in Australia since 2023. The plant is expected to be up and running within 18 months. Australia's only commercial helium production is expected to begin on the Yorke Peninsula within 18 months, aiming to address a global shortage of the rare and vital gas. Three months after it first extracted the gas at its Ramsay 1 site just outside Port Vincent, Gold Hydrogen has announced plans to turn the project commercial. It would be the first helium production in Australia in three years. While additional testing and approvals are required before a commercial plant can begin, managing director Neil McDonald said he was feeling positive. "Based on the robust numbers, not of just having the world's best helium purities ever reported, but all our geology and all the economics, we're very confident." The drilling process involves an almost 900-metre-deep hole in the ground. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) As part of commercialisation, a modular helium plant "the size of two tennis courts" will be constructed on the company's 75,000-square-kilometre Yorke Peninsula tenement, creating additional jobs. "As we progress with working out the feasibility ... we'll be able to then isolate what type of specialty jobs and ongoing normal jobs would be available," Mr McDonald said. "But it will be reasonably significant for the size of York Peninsula." Helium has not been produced in Australia since Santos's Darwin LNG plant exhausted its supply in 2023 , and at the time there was little concern about supply constraints. But a global shortage has developed after about a third of the world's helium supply was taken out by Iranian missile strikes on Qatar's Ras Laffan gas plant in March. Mr McDonald said he believed there was enough helium at the Yorke Peninsula site for "tens of years" of domestic and international supply. Gold Hydrogen's Ramsay 1 site, just outside Port Vincent, has produced helium gas. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) There is an estimated 41 billion cubic feet (BCF) of the gas in total at just one of the company's seven permits. "To give that context, the world consumes approximately 5BCF of helium per year," Mr McDonald said. Mr McDonald said local and international markets were interested. "Our initial plan is to scale up and make sure that we can supply initially the domestic market and get as much supply into the domestic market as we can," he said. "But like all commodities ... quite often Australia produces a lot more than they can ever consume." events.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
events.summary: Published 21 October 2026, 05:13 BST Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together . Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed. With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever. Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together. "In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group. The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said. Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects. Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations. The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers. Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year. Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car? But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions. Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors. He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said. But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added. "There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said. SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%. Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine. In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said. Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models . Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus. Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3 Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said. "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added. The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights. The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January. The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year. The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider. A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said. "The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said. However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said. The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month. "I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said. The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

events.title: Samsung, SK Hynix upgrading China plants to make more advanced chips: Sources
events.summary: Both companies are now required to seek US licences annually if they want to install US-made equipment such as etching machines in China. Samsung and SK Hynix are upgrading China plants to make more advanced NAND chips. They want to meet AI demand and compete with China’s YMTC, but US export controls make the work difficult. Samsung’s Xian site may switch to 286-layer V9 NAND, with output targets of 5,000 wafers a month in December 2026 and 40,000 by December 2027. Samsung says the plan follows US rules and does not add capacity. SK Hynix aims to make 240-layer-plus NAND at Dalian and may seek approval for 300-plus-layer research. YMTC has grown fast, reaching 38.5% of China’s NAND market in the second quarter, while Samsung and SK Hynix have lost share. SEOUL/BEIJING/NEW YORK – Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are upgrading their China factories to produce more advanced memory chips, four people familiar with the plans said, aiming to fend off competition from a fast-growing Chinese rival and meet huge AI demand. How much to invest in their Chinese operations has become a tricky question for the South Korean semiconductor giants ever since the US began imposing export controls on some chip-making equipment in 2022 amid an effort to slow China’s technological progress. The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security also said in 2025 it did not intend to grant licences to upgrade technology and expand capacity at the foreign chipmakers’ factories in China. The regulatory headaches have limited their ability to refit their factories and contributed to loss of market share to Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). Executives at the South Korean chipmakers have publicly warned that geopolitical tensions are undermining their Chinese operations. Samsung and SK Hynix confirmed in statements to Reuters that upgrades were underway and were being done in close consultation with Washington, but did not disclose details of production plans that are being reported here for the first time. Reuters could not, however, determine to what extent US authorities have granted export licences for equipment that Samsung and SK Hynix need for their planned upgrades. According to the sources, the two companies are working to manufacture flash NAND memory chips with more than 200 layers at their Chinese plants, which would bring them in line with what is being produced in South Korea. NAND, a type of memory chip that retains data without power, is widely used in smartphones, PCs and solid-state drives for AI data centres. More layers per chip means more storage density and lower costs. Samsung sets signs on 286-layer chips Samsung’s plant in Xian in north-western China, which accounts for about 40% of the company’s global NAND output, currently makes chips that have about 200 layers, according to two of the people. As part of a project known internally as “Monami” – from the French for “my friend” – Samsung is converting the facility to make 286-layer V9 NAND chips, aiming for monthly output of 5,000 wafers in December 2026 and then a jump to 40,000 wafers by December 2027, one of the people said. Samsung said its upgrade was in compliance with US export regulations, adding: “The upgrade is aimed at meeting growing demand from global customers, including those in the US. The company is not expanding production capacity or constructing new manufacturing facilities.” SK Hynix is looking to switch to producing NAND products with 240 layers or more at its Dalian facilities in north-eastern China, three people familiar with the matter said. It currently makes products with 192 layers there, one person said. SK Hynix acquired the Dalian site when it bought Intel’s NAND operations in 2021 and it remains the sole NAND chip manufacturing site for that business, which is now named Solidigm and is preparing for a US initial public offering. One of the sources said the company is authorised to make chips with up to 240 layers at Dalian and may seek permission from Washington to conduct research and development on 300-plus-layer chips there that would help it lay the groundwork for potential production in the US. The company is in discussions with the Trump administration over plans to build a new NAND factory in the United States. The US government’s Bureau of Industry and Security did not directly address Reuters questions on the status of approvals for the South Korean chipmakers. It referred Reuters to its 2025 statement that the bureau intended to grant licence applications for them to operate their existing factories in China, but not expand capacity or upgrade technology. As Samsung and SK Hynix have wrestled with the question of how much to invest in their Chinese plants, YMTC has made great strides. It commanded 38.5% of China’s NAND market in the second quarter, up from 28% for all of 2025 and overtaking Samsung, according to research firm Omdia.

events.title: Singapore sets aside $45m to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI solutions
events.summary: Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang speaks at the Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific event on Oct 21. Singapore has set aside more than $45 million over three years to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI. The Catalytic AI Solutions initiative will offer ready-to-deploy tools for design, scheduling and predictive maintenance. Enterprise Singapore will co-fund adoption of AI solutions for eligible SMEs, and is working to extend the initiative to the logistics and wholesale trade sectors. SINGAPORE – More than $45 million has been set aside over the next three years to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the advanced manufacturing industry deploy artificial intelligence solutions. This is one of the initiatives under Singapore’s national AI strategy that were announced by Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang on Oct 21. Gan said the Catalytic AI Solutions initiative will make the technology more accessible to SMEs, and support them in overcoming common barriers when adopting AI. “We want AI to be accessible not just to large manufacturers, but also to our SMEs,” she said at the Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific (ITAP) event at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre. “Through this initiative, manufacturers can access ready-to-deploy AI solutions to improve productivity, optimise efficiency and strengthen their competitiveness,” she added. Under the initiative, Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) will work with trade associations and chambers and qualified vendors to offer a suite of solutions to SMEs, with some firms having already confirmed their interest. The solutions will enable tasks such as the optimisation of product and component design, and the enhancement of production scheduling and predictive maintenance. EnterpriseSG’s assistant managing director for manufacturing Wong Zeng Yi said: “AI is creating new possibilities for manufacturers to improve productivity, quality and responsiveness, while opening new revenue opportunities through faster innovation. “We want to help more manufacturers embed AI into their core operations, so they can realise these gains at scale.” Eligible SMEs will have their adoption of AI solutions co-funded by EnterpriseSG, which plans to extend the initiative to the logistics and wholesale trade sectors. Another initiative announced at ITAP was a manufacturing jobs portal developed by the Singapore Manufacturing Federation. Gan encouraged prospective employers and job seekers to sign up for the Manufacturing and Talent Connection Hub, which is expected to be operational later in 2026 . The manufacturing industry accounts for around 20% of Singapore’s gross domestic product, and employs about 12% of its workforce. Industrial transformation has never been more important, Gan said, as manufacturers are operating in a more complex environment, with tight labour markets, intensifying competition for investments, and supply chains that are being reshaped by geopolitics. Companies must also become more sustainable while remaining competitive, she added. Gan said: “Advanced technologies such as robotics, digital twins and AI can help our manufacturers raise productivity, strengthen competitiveness, and bring about skilled roles for our workforce. “If we move decisively, Singapore can strengthen our position as a critical global node for advanced manufacturing, where companies develop new technologies and engineering capabilities, deploy them at scale, and contribute to global manufacturing.” A set of national AI missions, namely in advanced manufacturing, connectivity, finance and healthcare, was announced by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong earlier at Budget 2026. This came alongside the creation of a National AI Council, chaired by PM Wong, to help Singapore harness AI as a strategic advantage. The advanced manufacturing mission aims to reimagine the industry to grow its output and productivity. This involves advancing product and process innovation, anchoring best-in-class factories in Singapore, and building a base of industrial AI companies that develop AI solutions locally and export them to the rest of the world. Gan said the AI Centre of Excellence for Manufacturing, jointly established by A*STAR and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry in September 2024 , has been an important enabler of this mission. Companies including drinks producer Coca-Cola and tech manufacturer Philips had signed on to collaborate with the centre at its launch. In all, Gan said the centre has collaborated with 30 manufacturers in sectors including aerospace, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and energy, ranging from local firm Sunningdale Tech to the multinational Rockwell Automation. It has also completed 23 projects that deployed AI solutions to companies.

events.title: How might Andy Burnham tackle Thames Water debacle?
events.summary: A look at some of the options after PM is urged to consider radical alternatives to deal with stricken company Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company. Here are some ideas the prime minister is being urged to consider. Burnham must introduce emergency legislation immediately to protect the supply of water for the public, said Richard Murphy, tax accountant and the brains behind Corbynomics. A new state-owned company, with a management team in waiting and all the necessary steps ready to take over the existing company’s systems, has to be put in place now. “A prime minister who cannot deliver water to maybe a quarter of the UK’s population would not be someone to be trusted with anything else. Andy Burnham has no choice but to address this matter, now,” said Murphy. The 1971 nationalisation of the Rolls-Royce aeronautical engineering company, to protect the national interest after it collapsed into receivership, could be used as a blue print. A similar national emergency exists now to protect the supply of water, Murphy said. Murphy said that, in essence, Thames Water was financially insolvent, with real doubt about whether it could survive into 2027. It was failing in its regulatory obligations, including to maintain clean water supplies and keep rivers and beaches clean. Emergency legislation should ensure that the nationalisation is of the assets and undertakings of Thames Water, and not of the company itself. All financial liabilities of Thames Water would be left for the old company to settle. The government should not acquire them. The new company needed to be structured within days, said Murphy. “There is no time to wait.” Public control – probably via the courts Burnham must be prepared to go to court to take Thames Water back into public control, said Ewen McGaughey, professor of law at University College London. Moody’s has estimated a one-off cost of £14.5bn in 2019 to bring water into public ownership. But privatisation, said McGaughey, would cost up to £22bn extra for bill payers from 2025 to 2030, or £176 a household a year, in returns on capital to shareholders and banks, as set by Ofwat’s price review. McGaughey believes that this year public ownership of failed water companies will cost closer to £0, using the special administration procedure within the 1991 Water Industry Act. The higher the repair bills, the less that creditors or shareholders deserve under UK law, international law and our investment treaties, he said. He advises Burnham to prepare to go to court – creditors will probably sue – but they have no reasonable prospect of success. McGaughey says privatised water and the regulators have failed so badly that England pays among the highest bills in Europe, while nearly every river is illegally polluted, taps run dry and a trillion litres of water is leaked each year. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The government should bring our accounting practice up to international and European standards, by separating public corporation borrowing from the national debt, so that the borrowing of a publicly owned company does not contribute to national debt. Continuing the theme of using the special administrative powers of the 1991 legislation, Cat Hobbs of We Own It wants Thames Water’s licence taken away immediately. Hobbs has written to the government and water regulator, Ofwat, calling for bill rises to be blocked and for Thames Water to be brought into public hands. “It is absurd that Thames Water is now asking its creditors for a further £2.4bn to stay afloat – this saga has dragged out since July 2024 when the company was first in breach of its licence conditions,” said Hobbs. Under the 1991 act, companies can have their licences removed if they are insolvent or if they fail to fulfil their statutory duties to provide water, protect the environment and properly manage wastewater. Hobbs told Burnham his government should be using this power and facing down threats from the water industry and the prospect of a legal challenge from special administration under the 1991 act. Public ownership of water would deliver savings of £3bn to £5bn a year over time from cheaper financing costs – no shareholder dividends, less expensive debt. Taking water into public ownership would reduce the cost of living burden as well as freeing up money for infrastructure. The government should make it possible for new publicly owned water companies to borrow to invest on their own account – rather than adding to the national debt – as is standard practice elsewhere in Europe. Hobbs pointed out that when Network Rail’s debt of £31bn was transferred to the public sector, bond yields fell from 3% a year to 2.2% a year.

events.title: ‘I can charge my car for £6’: could new rules cut costs for EV drivers?
events.summary: Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lottery W hen Alison Williams bought her electric Volkswagen ID.3 two years ago, she thought she was making the right choice for the environment, having already upgraded her end-of-terrace London home with insulation and solar panels. However, charging the car has proved more costly than she hoped, as she is not able to install the cross-pavement gully – a narrow electric vehicle cable channel embedded in the pavement – that she would need to charge at home. That will remain the case despite a change in the law. From Wednesday, drivers in England who do not have off-street parking will no longer need to get planning permission to put in a pavement gully outside their home. The gullies sit flush within the pavement and allow an EV charging cable to reach a parked vehicle without creating a trip hazard. By charging in front of their house via an energy supply in their home, rather than using a public charger, drivers can slash the cost by up to 90% . But some of the 9.3 million households without off-street parking will be left frustrated as more than 20 local authorities will still not allow the installation of gullies after the law changes. Williams’s council is Ealing, which does not allow them for cost and safety reasons. She charges her car at a public charger, at much greater cost than if she could do it at home. “It’s really frustrating,” Williams says. “When we decided to buy an electric car … the reason we wanted to buy one was for the environmental impact. “You either have to have enough money to have a house with a driveway, or you have to be able to afford the additional cost of charging at a public charger.” Motorists are not allowed to string EV charging cables across the pavement from their home to the road, but many councils allow cross-pavement charging if you use a gully. To use one, a charging cable is run from the home through the gully and then plugged into the car. This previously meant getting planning permission from the local authority. Removing that step will save drivers between £300 and £500. However, anyone who lives in a conservation area will still have to apply. Caroline Pidgeon, a Liberal Democrat peer, campaigned for the change in the law. She says one in three households in England do not have a driveway. Approval for the gullies has taken up to 15 months in some areas, she says. “Simpler rules will make it easier for people to switch to an electric car,” she adds. The government has given £25m in funding to councils in England for pavement gullies for people with on-street parking, but the money is being distributed in different ways, depending on the local authority. How much you pay for installation varies widely around the country. If you want to apply for a gully to be installed, you should check with your council to see whether it allows them and, if it does, it should direct you on how to apply. Kerbo Charge, a company that installs gullies, operates a postcode checker you can use to see whether you can get one in your area and sign up for an alert if that changes. Ben Whitaker of Kerbo Charge says the average fee for the work is about £1,200 (including VAT) without a grant. “Some [councils] are using it [the funding] to provide half-price channels to early adopters, others are making it totally free while funds last – but, after that, residents will have to pay full price,” he says. “For example, Surrey is £499 for the channel and installation, South Gloucestershire is £250,” he adds. “Sadly, there is quite a variety of approaches and prices.” To illustrate the difference in prices between local authorities, Redbridge council in London says the grant will cover up to £1,200 of installation costs. But applicants must pay £815 in fees and for a bond, as well as any additional installation costs. On top of the cost of installing the gullies, some councils charge an additional annual fee for maintenance. For example, Redbridge charges an “ongoing annual licence fee” of £185. Enfield, also in London, charges £107 a year . Shayne Rees of Gul-e, a company that has installed 400 gullies, says it takes between one and two hours to put the unit in place. “It’s a really heavy-duty steel channel that can take a truck driving over it, and once we put it in the ground, that will be there for decades and decades without any maintenance,” he adds. It emerged in May that more than 20 local authorities appear to be holding out against having the gullies installed, among them Kent, Leicester and Worcestershire. Most of the holdouts are in London, including Waltham Forest and Hackney. The reasons given often concern safety and maintenance, and because of issues over who will be liable if there is an injury.

events.title: Childcare chain collapses amid wave of closures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Childcare chain's collapse into administration highlights private credit risks A former national children's commissioner says a lot of private providers are divesting childcare centres or pulling out of the sector altogether. Childcare chain Shared Beginnings has hit financial strife, becoming the latest early education provider to run into trouble amid a wave of closures in the sector. The childcare service, owned by private lender Finexia Financial Group, operates centres in Queensland, Victoria and the ACT. Finexia wrote to staff, informing them the centres had been operating "at a loss". The collapse highlights the risks of the private credit sector, with Finexia taking on ownership of the centres in the 2025 financial year after the previous owner, Genius Education, defaulted on substantial loans owed to Finexia. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has recently said it was closely scrutinising private lending , which has typically been a much more lightly regulated sector than the banking industry, and was concerned "the first significant cracks" were appearing. The impact on childcare places and jobs at Shared Beginnings remains unclear as the administrators continue to operate the centres. The firm said the decision came after exhausting all other options. Neil Sheather says all options to save Shared Beginnings have been exhausted. ( Supplied: Linkedin ) Finexia managing director Neil Sheather said placing Shared Beginnings into administration was not taken lightly, but was necessary. "Ultimately, the administrators are in control of Shared Beginnings." In a letter to staff, Mr Sheather said the administration would affect all seven of its centres, including Sinnamon Park and Kenmore in Queensland, Reservoir, Mont Albert and Beaumaris in Victoria, and Bonython and Conder in the ACT. All Shared Beginnings centres remain open under the control of administrators. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) In a separate letter to parents, Mr Sheather assured families that all centres remained open, and care would continue as normal. Bill Karageozis and Nick Keramos of DVT McLeods have been appointed administrators to find suitable buyers. Minister for Early Childhood Education Jessica Walsh said she acknowledged the news from Shared Beginnings would "cause disruption and uncertainty for families and educators". "Since coming to government, we've seen 1,200 new centres, 52,000 more educators and 57,000 more children in early learning." A September report by the Early Learning and Care Council Australia has found the rate of early childhood education and care (ECEC) service closures has continued to increase. The report said 152 long daycare services had closed since 2024, with a further 276 services (both long day care and preschool/kindergarten) identified as at risk of closing in the next 12 months. Anne Hollonds AO says the childcare sector is undergoing a significant adjustment. ( Supplied: Australian Human Rights Commission ) Former national children's commissioner Anne Hollonds AO said the childcare sector was undergoing a significant adjustment, driven by increased regulatory costs and a number of prominent crises. For-profit centres dominate the long daycare sector. Most of the growth in recent years has been in private for-profit providers, with a recent report from the Mitchell Institute finding they made up 74 per cent of long daycare places. Ms Hollonds said the sector would be better if it were shared 50-50 between non-profit and for-profit organisations. "We really need to focus on the safety and well-being of children as the priority," she said, adding that she had no problem with for-profit providers as long as their operation was up to scratch. A recent report finds for-profit centres drive substantial instability in the long day care sector. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) The Mitchell Institute also found substantial instability or "churn" in the long daycare sector was driven by for-profit centres. "Since 2013, about one-third [32 per cent] of long day care services open in 2025 had changed approved provider," the report said. "The rate is higher in for-profit centres where 40 per cent have changed provider, compared to 11 per cent of all other centres." Have you been impacted by the closure of childcare centres or private lending? We would like to hear from you! Contact our journalist confidentially on li.yiying@abc.net.au or li.yiying@proton.me .

events.title: Fortescue senior executive sacked after sexual harassment probe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Executive at Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals sacked after sexual harassment, bullying probe A senior Fortescue executive has been sacked for alleged ( Supplied: Fortescue Metals Group ) A senior executive at Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals Group has been sacked following an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment and bullying at the iron ore miner. The executive, who was not named by Fortescue in its short statement about the matter, "breached Fortescue’s policies, as well as our values", it said. Fortescue had engaged law firm MinterEllison to examine a series of allegations about the employee's conduct. "Sexual harassment, bullying, and other behaviour that makes people feel unsafe has no place at Fortescue," the company said. Mining magnate Dr Andrew Forrest is the founder of Fortescue. ( ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates ) It said it would provide "ongoing support" to those who took part in the investigation. In August, Reuters reported Fortescue had allowed the executive to continue working at the firm while the MinterEllison investigation was underway. The company's energy chief Gus Pichot said at the time the company was "quite confident we are following the proper process" in allowing it. It comes after a group of female Fortescue employees launched a class action in the Federal Court against the company in June, alleging rape, sexual assault and stalking at remote FMG mine sites in WA's Pilbara. The allegations included drink spiking, promotions offered in exchange for sexual favours and a widespread culture of sexual harassment and denigration. Andrew 'Twiggy' Forrest warns Fortescue staff after sexual harassment class action In an email sent to all staff, Mr Forrest said: "Anyone who thinks this behaviour has a place at Fortescue is in the wrong company." The sacking comes despite a 2023 deal with WorkSafe WA in which Fortescue agreed to spend $1.4 million on addressing inappropriate workplace behaviour after allegedly failing to supply documents about dozens of sexual harassment allegations to the work safety regulator. FMG is not the first mining company to face claims of unsafe work practices and a toxic culture. Hundreds of women have come forward in the two years since BHP and Rio Tinto were taken to federal court over similar allegations . A 2022 report into the sexual harassment of women in the mining industry by a parliamentary committee found nearly three quarters of women in mining had experienced sexual harassment at work in the past five years, and that it was generally accepted in workplaces. The scathing report found mining companies failed to recognise the problem or act on it, and while the government accepted its recommendations, not all have been enacted. Some of these included changes to equal opportunities laws, which the WA government yesterday announced it would introduce , four years on from the landmark report.

( Supplied: Bass Coast Shire Council ) Bass Coast Shire Council has rejected a bid by McDonald's to open a restaurant on Phillip Island. The application drew an angry response from members of the Phillip Island community. McDonald's can appeal the decision to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. An application by McDonald's to build a restaurant in the Victorian tourist hotspot of Phillip Island has been rejected after councillors voted to refuse it a planning permit. The fast-food giant lodged its application earlier this year with the Bass Coast Shire Council to build a new restaurant in Cowes , which has a population of 6,593. But councillors unanimously voted to reject the application, saying it was inconsistent with the local planning scheme. The public gallery was full at Bass Coast Shire Council's meeting. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Island ward councillor Tim O'Brien said the proposal failed the community "on so many levels". "Where is the community benefit?" Mr O'Brien said. "This will be muscling its way into a part of a market it had no part in building." The plan to build a McDonald's on Phillip Island has angered some community members. ( Supplied: Say No To McDonald's Cowes group ) Councillor Mat Morgan, who is a Greens candidate at the upcoming Victorian election, said the application "should obviously be rejected" because of inappropriate residential development. "There are a thousand ethical and moral reasons to throw this in the bin," he said. The proposal raised the ire of thousands of residents , with more than 5,800 people signing a petition rejecting the proposal, citing traffic concerns and the threat to small businesses in town. The no vote came after a recommendation by council officers to grant McDonald's a planning permit, which they found "acceptable" after assessing it against the planning scheme. Councillor Jan Thompson told the meeting that the decision would likely be overturned on appeal to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT), but voted to reject the application anyway. The council received 1,543 objections and 32 submissions relating to the McDonald's application. The proposed site is home to a petrol station and a vacant plot of land. Cowes is the main township on Phillip Island. ( Supplied: Bass Coast Shire Council ) Cowes resident and business owner, Trevor Ware, said the community's concerns were heard by the council in rejecting the proposal. "We didn't need this, and I think the community has done very well to fight it," he said. Trevor Ware says the community has been heard. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "There's still a big track ahead and [McDonald's] are going to push very hard. We just can't let it just ride through. "The way it's been approached and the area that they put it in so close to the school, everything was just so wrong." Island residents celebrate after Bass Coast Shire council's rejection of the planning permit. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Cowes resident Megan Ryan said the decision made her emotional. "If McDonald's haven't got the message, we don't want them here," she said. "My dad lives at Melaleuca [aged care] right next door to here. He's lived here, he's served here, and the last thing I want my dad to hear in the middle of the night is, 'Do you want fries with that?' because there's a 24-hour McDonald's sitting right there." A spokesperson for McDonald's Australia expressed disappointment with the Bass Coast Shire decision. "The proposed restaurant represents a significant investment into Phillip Island and will mean more than 100 new local jobs, as well as more support for local community groups in the area. "We remain committed to working collaboratively with Council, being a good neighbour and making a positive contribution to the Cowes and broader Phillip Island community." events.title: World must cut emissions by 18% in four years ‘to find our way back’, UN says
events.summary: Action needed to avoid disastrous overshoot of climate targets, according to organisation’s environment body The world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. Although the “window has closed” on holding temperature rises to 1.5C , in line with scientific advice, limiting the “overshoot” of that target is still possible, according to the UN Environment Programme (Unep). But countries are failing to translate their long-term targets on reducing emissions into short-term actions, a report on the “emissions gap” between climate goals and policies has found. Global carbon output appears to have stalled: the emission levels in 2025 were broadly similar to those of the previous year. But Unep analysts were wary of calling it a peak or plateau, given the vast uncertainties of geopolitics and an increased reliance on fossil fuels, despite strong growth in renewable energy . Cutting greenhouse gases by 18% by 2030, and by 45% by 2035, would yield a good chance of limiting temperature rises to 1.7C above preindustrial levels. This would still allow events such as the record heatwaves of the last few months to become frequent and common, but could help prevent them from getting drastically worse. Governments were warned for years that time was running out, said Inger Andersen, the executive director of Unep. “[We used to say] there’s still an opportunity if we make this herculean effort [to stay within the 1.5C limit],” she said. “It’s now clear the herculean effort was not made. We procrastinated, and now we are saying this window has closed.” Nevertheless, she urged countries to keep the 1.5C goal – the centrepiece of the Paris climate agreement. “We can make the overshoot as brief and as short as possible. It’s not time to throw in the towel and give up. This is about how to find our way back, as shortly and quickly as possible.” Under Donald Trump, the US – the world’s second biggest emitter, after China – has withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement and is threatening to reverse its longstanding trend of falling greenhouse gas emissions. Bill Hare, the chief executive of the Climate Analytics thinktank, said: “All governments have a job to do, but in particular it is time for major fossil fuel producers such as the US and Saudi Arabia, which produce 20-25% of fossil fuels globally, to stop playing politics and face the scientific reality. Right now they are looking at the fire, denying it exists and pouring more petrol on it, while their own citizens increasingly face searing heat, wildfires and other impacts.” Other countries appear to have been affected by US intransigence – pledges made last year on greenhouse gases were noticeably weak, according to UNEP analysis. At the Cop30 climate summit in Brazil last November , governments were supposed to make fresh commitments under the Paris agreement to cut emissions. But the commitments made were nowhere near strong enough. Even if all of those updated pledges were fulfilled, temperatures would still rise to 2.6C above preindustrial levels, according to Unep’s projections, endangering life across swathes of the globe. Policy has also not kept up with pledges: on current policies around the world, temperatures would rise to 2.8C. Every five years of greenhouse gas emissions at current levels pushes up forecasts of global heating by 0.1C. Scientists also fear that the greater the margin by which we exceed 1.5C, the greater the likelihood of triggering tipping points in the climate system . Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, said: “The tragedy is that we have the solutions within our grasp. Solar and wind power are growing far faster than anyone expected, yet governments are still failing to move away from fossil fuels quickly enough. The technology is racing ahead while political leadership is dragging its feet.” The shortfall in countries’ commitments is supposed to be corrected under a Paris agreement mechanism called the “global stocktake”, an assessment of emissions targets next scheduled for 2028. But that has also been thrown into doubt: this week, the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change failed to set a timetable to publish its latest report before the global stocktake, which would prevent governments from assessing their progress against the latest science. Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and one of the world’s leading climate scientists, said rows over the timing of IPCC reports must not be allowed to stall government action. “If all current national commitments are implemented, global emissions are projected to reach approximately 50 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually by 2035, when they should be below 35 gigatonnes. The science is already clear.

Proposals for six new data centres were revealed in Tasmanian parliament last month, though the government did not disclose the names of the proponents. Mr Hendriks confirmed the proposal referred to by Mr Bayley was project B — a 200–300 megawatt data centre in the feasibility stage in the north-west. Mr Bayley questioned the appropriateness of locals finding out about the proposal from a "Sydney consultancy firm". Mr Hendricks said the office only had a "very limited amount of information" about the project. He took a question on notice about identifying the proponent to the committee. Government says no final site confirmed Mr Bayley asked Minister for Business, Resources and Industry Felix Ellis if agricultural land should be used for AI data centres. The Greens said north-west residents have been told about a potential AI data centre development for Nook, which is near Sheffield (pictured). AI data centre company Firmus Technologies has previously said it was not behind any of the six confidential new proposals. Firmus has three data centre projects underway in Tasmania — one under construction in Launceston, another approved for construction at Long Reach in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone, and another waiting for approval at Wesley Vale, in the state's north-west. events.title: Veggie Thursdays and vegan surprises! How Ghent became a plant-based paradise
events.summary: In 2014, 13% of the population of this Belgian city described themselves as flexitarian. This year, 83% did. Here is how everyone was convinced to eat their greens – and love them S ixty bowls of slime-green soup sit waiting for the children to arrive. Pupils rush in from their morning lessons, grab the bowls by the handles and start slurping. No complaints, no refusals. (OK, maybe a few “bleurgh” faces.) Chicory soup dispatched, they get stuck into the main course: falafel, Mediterranean vegetable tagine and couscous. Some ask for seconds; most grab a piece of fruit for dessert and run out to play. This is a typical Thursday lunchtime in BS De Stadspoort primary school in Ghent, Belgium. Similar meat-free menus are being eaten in other schools and nurseries across the city, plus community centres, care homes and assisted living facilities, not to mention many work canteens and restaurants. Thursday in Ghent is officially “Veggie Day” , with residents encouraged to eschew any meat or fish. So how did a city get its children – and everyone else – to eat their greens? It didn’t happen overnight. “The success story of Ghent is one where we had an amazing grassroots movement, with people asking for more climate action. But the magic happened when politicians actually listened and implemented policy to introduce the Thursday Veggie Day in 2009,” says Vanessa Debruyne, the head of communications for the nonprofit organisation ProVeg Belgium , who is showing me around town. “It got the ball rolling, companies and restaurants joined, the population got used to it, and more entrepreneurs made the move to plant-based. We’ve been unstoppable ever since! Ghent is the best town in Belgium for plant-based food.” Veggie day was just the start, agrees Hafsa El-Bazioui, the Green deputy mayor of Ghent, who has cycled over to join us (the city centre has been largely car-free since 2017). “A few years ago, we changed to prioritise plant-based protein,” she says. In 2021, the Flemish government launched the Green Deal Protein Shift – a commitment to switch the ratio of animal to plant proteins consumed from 60:40 to 40:60 by 2030. Ghent has already reached the target. As well as vegetarian Thursdays and vegetarian options every day, school caterers have turned traditional meat dishes such as burgers, sausages and meatballs into hybrids, cutting out at least half the beef or pork and replacing them with, say, lentils. Stews might combine meat with chickpeas or beans. An incredible amount of effort is put in to making each dish taste good: they are screened by a “taste panel” made up of dietitians, chefs, childcare professionals and people with sensitivities to flavour, bitterness, texture and mouthfeel. Recipes are constantly modified and improved after feedback from children, parents and school staff. As a result, children get to eat the food they know and like, but the dishes are healthier and better for the planet – Ghent has reduced the carbon footprint of its school meals by 38% since 2018. Although she is a vegan herself, El-Bazioui believes reducing meat consumption across the board is the most effective and achievable policy, rather than trying to convince people to cut it out altogether. “When you approach a lot of people, the impact is more than if you focus on a small group of vegans,” she says. “That’s my philosophy in food, in politics, in life.” This stealth approach is echoed all over the city. I pop in to the Viernulvier art centre , AKA De Vooruit, for a chat with Tom De Vleesschauwer, its kitchen coordinator – De Vooruit is as popular for its large art deco cafe as for its programme of theatre, dance, film and music. “A few years ago, we made oat milk the default: if you don’t ask for cow’s milk, you get oat,” says De Vleesschauwer. “About 90% of customers now have oat milk. If we had a sign saying you can choose, it would only be 10-20%.” There have been other changes in De Vooruit’s cafe, too. The soup is now always vegan; the dish of the day is vegetarian; the staff and performers are served a daily “ Ottolenghi -style vegetarian buffet” instead of cheese and charcuterie. And, as in the school canteens, the few meat dishes on the menu – today just spaghetti bolognese and meatballs in tomato sauce – have been hybridised. “We cut down the meat by 70% and increased the carrots, cutting them to the same size – 30% still gives the flavour and the idea of meat, and carrots give sweetness,” says De Vleesschauwer. “People say plant-based is niche, but we have a very wide audience.” There are plenty of fully vegan businesses in the city, too, such as Madam Bakster , where I drink coffee with homemade hazelnut milk and devour rich, chewy chocolate-chip cookies fresh from the oven. Laura Verhulst, the founder, sees her cafe as more, not less, inclusive. “I wanted to make desserts that everyone could enjoy: vegan, allergen-free, non-refined sugar,” she says.

events.title: Last drinks for Boag's as final Tasmanian beers roll off production line
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Final Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers come off production line as brewer exits home state Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry The last Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers were packaged up in the Launceston factory today. Parent company Lion announced the closure of the 145-year-old brewery in June, with the brand now to be fully produced on the mainland. Decommissioning the brewery is expected to take a year, with the Tasmanian government interested in buying the large CBD site. The last Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers were bottled in Launceston this morning, marking an end to 145 years of local production. In the past century and a half, Boag's has cemented itself as a state icon and often run ads about being brewed with clean Tasmanian water. The final bottles exited the assembly line this afternoon, ahead of the brewery shutting its doors for the final time on November 6, taking with it 42 local jobs. Boag's will cease their Tasmanian operations in Launceston in November after 145 years of local operation. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) While the bottle production finished today, the final brewing day was in September. Brewer Adrian Hinds, who has been a Boag's employee for 22 years, said it was an emotional day. "To be honest, I'm holding it together; it's quite emotional," he said. "Today was the last drop of Boag's put into containers; tanks are empty, everything's on a carton or pallet ready to go out to the public. "Everyone was on the packaging line watching the bottles go through the labeller; it just shows what it means to the staff here. Brewer Adrian Hinds has been a Boag's employee for over two decades. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) Mr Hinds said for the last mashing, "everyone came up, got a sample of grain, put it in the mash tuns, so everyone had that final little touch on the last brew of draught that we did". "After everyone left the brew house and I was in there by myself, I just sat there for a while and just listened to all the sounds, the pumps going and then sugar going in and then smelling the hops going in. "To be here for the last fill, it's sad. I didn't think it would ever happen; it's a shame it's happening, but you can't control it. The Boag's Brewery site sits on the banks of the North Esk river in central Launceston. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) Tasmania to start importing Boag's from mainland Boag's has existed in Launceston longer than electricity. Originally called the Esk Brewery, Scottish migrant James Boag and his son James Boag II began the operation in 1881. Bottling machines in the brewery's early years. ( Supplied: State Library and Archives Tasmania ) In 2008, Lion Australia, owned by Japanese beer giant Kirin, snapped up the brand for $325 million. But in June, Lion announced an end to local brewing operations in Launceston , citing inflation and long-term declines in beer sales. Brewing of the Boag's brand will continue on the mainland in New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Most of Boag's brewing had already been moved interstate the previous year, leaving the Launceston operation running at one-fifth of its capacity. The Boag's brand will continue to live on, being brewed in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland. Tasmania will now become an importer of its beverage icon. Boag's tour guide Phil Crowden has been taking visitors from around the world into the Boag's Brewery's inner sanctum for 17 years. He said the skills of the local brewers were "unparalleled", but he had faith the mainland-brewed Boag's would still hit the spot for rusted-on fans. James Boag beers can be found in every northern Tasmanian pub, bar and bottleshop. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) "The technology's got so good at the moment," he said. "I mean, breweries are making beers for other breweries around the world, and you can actually emulate the water from any particular place in the world." An online petition was launched in a bid to try and stop the closure of the brewery. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Tasmanian water has long been lauded as the essential ingredient in Boag's, something the brand has heavily promoted in its advertising. Mr Crowden said the exact mineral count of Tasmanian water would be replicated at the other breweries to get as close to the taste as possible. A spokesperson for Lion said the company were considering whether the equipment from the Launceston site may be deployed to its other sites. Decommissioning of the brewing equipment will begin after the November closure date and is estimated to take an additional 12 months. Boag's is easily the bestseller at Launceston mainstay The Gunners Arms.

events.title: Singapore’s DayOne said to weigh options for US IPO after data centre rout
events.summary: DayOne was initially considering raising as much as US$5 billion from the listing as soon as the fourth quarter. DayOne Data Centers is weighing a delay or smaller US IPO after a data centre market rout, with plans still under review and no final decision made. The Singapore-based firm may cut fundraising to US$2.5 billion-US$3 billion, down from an earlier target of up to US$5 billion and a US$20 billion valuation. Investor caution is rising across data centre and AI-linked listings, after failed or delayed IPOs at Firmus Grid, AirTrunk and others, while DayOne keeps talking to investors. DayOne Data Centers is weighing options for its US initial public offering , including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases, according to people familiar with the matter. While Singapore-based DayOne has been waiting for the right window to launch the IPO, it has also been considering the possibility of pushing back the share sale until the market recovers, the people said. Other options include going ahead with a smaller listing that may raise US$2.5 billion (S$3.2 billion) to US$3 billion, roughly half of what it had originally aimed for, the people said. DayOne, whose backers include Coatue and Hillhouse, is continuing to engage with potential investors and still wants to move forward as soon as the market allows, the people said. The company was initially considering raising as much as US$5 billion from the listing as soon as the fourth quarter, people familiar with the matter said previously. It had been eyeing a valuation of about US$20 billion, the people have said. Deliberations are ongoing and DayOne has not made any final decisions, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. The company could still opt to move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks, according to the people. While data centres have drawn global investor demand amid a boom in sectors related to artificial intelligence, a more negative sentiment has started to have ripple effects on IPOs. DayOne has been raising billions of dollars in private funding rounds as it seeks capital to build out its pipeline. Australian data centre company Firmus Grid pulled its roughly US$5 billion IPO when investors balked at the valuation it sought, while AirTrunk, which also operates data centres, delayed a planned real estate investment trust IPO in Singapore to 2027. South Korean digital infrastructure company Elice plunged 32% in its Seoul trading debut on Oct 20. Coreweave’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, and Nscale is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, Bloomberg News reported. On Oct 21, shares of Australian data center operator Nextdc plummeted after it cut earnings guidance. Some investors are hoping that the recent market volatility will pass after the US midterm elections on Nov 3. They are also looking ahead to the performance of Anthropic PBC’s upcoming listing as an important gauge of sentiment toward the AI sector. DayOne filed for a US IPO earlier in October. The offering is being led by Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Bank of America and Citigroup IFR reported on Oct 19 that DayOne was gathering more investor feedback before launching the share sale. DayOne is running or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia , Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong, Japan, Finland and Spain. Other backers include GDS Holdings, the SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

events.title: An AI slowdown could be exactly what businesses need
events.summary: The artificial intelligence industry has spent years feathering the accelerator of frontier model development in a fierce contest to dominate the technology . Now, it is considering something that until recently seemed almost unthinkable: slamming on the brakes. The prospects of the frontier labs are closely linked to the fortunes of the US stock market, and they buttress vast spending on infrastructure. But for businesses still working out how to harness AI’s illusive productivity gains, a slowdown is not a bad thing. It will give them time to close the yawning gap between AI’s accelerating capabilities and their productive use of them. Still, calls to pace the frontier grow louder. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei made the case in an essay in which he said capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to understand, align and control them. His proposal was to deliberately slow the improvement enough to give safety research and independent evaluation time to catch up. Is it practical? There remains considerable disagreement over whether this is practical, desirable or possible. But that’s beside the point for businesses, since most of them are nowhere close to exhausting the AI capabilities they already possess. According to the Stanford 2026 AI Index, 88 per cent of organisations surveyed reported using AI in at least one business function last year. But breadth of adoption is not the same thing as depth. The research shows that the use of AI agents remained in the single digits across almost every business function. Relatively few have fundamentally redesigned how work gets done around it. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis found that generative AI accounted for only 5.7 per cent of total working hours by August last year. This tells us that companies already have powerful AI, and are simply failing to make the most of it. They don’t need another massive leap in model capability to claim the productivity gains that are already on the table. A METR randomised study found that experienced open-source developers working on highly familiar repositories actually took 19 per cent longer when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools. The reason is that the bottleneck is increasingly organisational. Companies have to connect models to proprietary data. They have to integrate AI into existing systems. And they need to redesign workflows rather than simply insert a chatbot into them. They also need appropriate governance, security and human oversight, while employees have to learn how to delegate effectively to AI. Managers, meanwhile, need to rethink roles, performance measures and decision rights. Those changes happen at a comparatively glacial pace when compared with the speed at which AI labs have been pushing the frontier. More capabilities OpenAI's enterprise research finds that the heaviest AI adopters use substantially more capabilities across more tasks than the median employee. These intensive users report much larger productivity benefits. Seventy-five per cent of surveyed workers also reported being able to perform tasks using AI that they previously could not do. So the AI productivity frontier inside most companies sits far behind the technological one. This is not unusual. General-purpose technologies typically arrive before organisations learn how to exploit them. Electricity existed before factories were redesigned around distributed electric motors, and computers came along long before companies reorganised processes around digital information. AI is likely to follow the same pattern, which only strengthens the case for hitting the brakes. That will not stall the AI economy , which is so crucial to public equity markets, because it will give companies the badly needed time to extract value from the marvellous capabilities already at their fingertips. That means moving beyond experimentation towards workflow redesign. Moving from individual productivity tools towards end-to-end processes. Connecting AI to enterprise data and systems. Using agents where they genuinely add value. Building governance that allows experimentation without unacceptable risk. And, perhaps most importantly, developing the organisational capabilities required to use AI well. Executives should continue watching the frontier, of course. Better models will create new opportunities, and a substantial slowdown is far from guaranteed. But they should not confuse a slower technological frontier with a slower business opportunity. Even if frontier development paused dramatically tomorrow, companies would still have an enormous backlog of economically valuable opportunities across customer service, software development, finance , procurement, marketing and many other functions. So just because the frontier slows, it doesn’t mean the business opportunity does. The AI race, at least for enterprise users, needs to shift from simply building better AI to building better businesses around it.
