events.title: Ahead of massive IPOs, AI companies are sketching plans to share their wealth
events.summary: As they steam toward massive public offerings on Wall Street, the companies at the forefront of artificial intelligence have begun sketching plans to share their wealth with the public NEW YORK -- As they steam toward massive public offerings on Wall Street, the companies at the forefront of artificial intelligence have begun sketching plans to share their wealth with the public — a commitment they say is imperative to address disruptions the technology could bring to the workforce and people’s livelihoods. Executives at Anthropic and OpenAI have long argued the technology's arrival will bring many benefits for everyday people , and they've promised that will include a share of the profits. The companies are outlining a range of proposals for distributing AI fortunes, but so far they have not resolved key questions over how they would work, how transparent they will be, and who will determine beneficiaries. On Sunday, Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity within the company, pending approval from stockholders. The stake could increase “as the company grows” in the future. The maker of AI assistant Claude said the fund “might explore” larger donations to traditional nonprofits or potentially distribute money to “specific populations.” The San Francisco-based company shared little information about the types of organizations supported by the fund and the issues they will address. One area it will not support, Anthropic said, is lobbying and political giving. Phil Buchanan, the president of The Center for Effective Philanthropy, said he welcomed Anthropic’s commitment — especially at a time when he said some billionaires are “diminishing the importance of philanthropy.” But he cautioned that Anthropic should avoid the “arrogance” of previous technology barons who assumed their professional expertise would translate to philanthropic wisdom. Buchanan recommended the fund support highly effective, existing nonprofits but said it is “hard to talk about any of this because it’s all so abstract.” “I guess I’m hopeful,” Buchanan said, “but I’m not going to get too excited until I see some evidence of what’s actually happening.” Anthropic, which was valued at close to $1 trillion earlier this year , is preparing for an initial public offering as soon as next month that is shaping up as one of the biggest ever. Once a company is public, donations might be made through the selling of future shares, or potentially turning to cash dividends in the future, explained Jay R. Ritter, director of The IPO Initiative at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business. The specifics on how charitable donations will be made through Anthropic’s fund are not clear yet. Regardless, Ritter said the announcement now is helpful for potential investors to “know what they’re buying.” Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study the economic effects of AI more broadly. Combined with Sunday’s announcement, Anthropic said roughly 20% of its shares will be dedicated to the “public good,” plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company’s valuation reaches certain milestones. In announcing the benefit fund, Anthropic offered labor market impacts as one example of its philanthropic focus. “AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic said in a blog post Sunday. It added the fund will have the “versatility” to pursue “bolder approaches” that might be necessary to offset that. The company said it would share more details about the fund's structure and governance in the coming months. In a May interview with The Associated Press, Anthropic president Daniela Amodei said she expected the company’s success would generally lead to more philanthropic support for disease research and “ensuring that everyone around the world gets to share in the prosperity that we hope AI creates.” The companies' pledges have met with skepticism from some critics. “Anthropic is playing games here,” Gary Marcus, a longtime AI expert and professor emeritus at New York University, wrote on social media Sunday. “Trying to curry public favor while still holding control and resisting disclosure is annoying.” Christina Applegate says learning she doesn't have MS is ‘very unnerving’ Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Anthropic and OpenAI are each structured as a public benefit corporation , a designation that requires the companies to pursue not just profit but a social good. OpenAI Foundation, the nonprofit that controls OpenAI, promised to build out its grantmaking capacity earlier this year with a $1 billion commitment. Separately, OpenAI in April proposed the creation of a “Public Wealth Fund” with a stake in “AI-driven economic growth” across companies more broadly.

events.title: Microsoft opens a hands-on STEM and AI hub for students at its Grange Castle data center campus
events.summary: Microsoft opens €1m Dream Space hub at its data centre campus in Grange Castle to bring STEM and AI skills to young people in surrounding communities Microsoft Vice Chair and President, Brad Smith, today joined students, teachers and community representatives from Dublin and Kildare at the company’s data centre campus in Grange Castle to officially open its new €1m Dream Space hub. Dream Space @ the Data Centre marks the next step in Microsoft’s mission to create lasting benefits for people living near its current and proposed data centre operations. More than 5,000 students from schools in Dublin and Kildare are expected to participate in learning sessions at the hub over the next 12 months. Providing a wide range of tailored STEM and AI experiences for primary and post-primary students, Dream Space @ the Data Centre will also help to build awareness of the wide-ranging career opportunities that exist in the digital infrastructure sector. Through the new hub, Microsoft is delivering on its Data Centre Community Pledge to be a responsible and supportive neighbour to communities that host its data centres. Since 2018, Microsoft has invested over €6.5 million in Irish communities close to its current and future data centre operations, supporting programmes that advance community prosperity, sustainability and wellbeing and directly benefiting more than 135,000 people. Dream Space was first introduced at Microsoft’s Leopardstown campus, One Microsoft Place, in 2018. Since then, more than 550,000 students have taken part in its STEM and AI education sessions, developing the skills and confidence to become the next generation of digital leaders. Building on Dream Space’s strong foundations in coding, robotics and AI, the new hub at the data centre features a new curriculum that introduces learners to the specific technology and skills needed to support the digital infrastructure sector. These will range from electrical engineering and physical computing to cloud operations. Supported by a mini data centre lab and many other hands-on learning experiences, the facility will bring to life the technology, skills and careers powering the digital world for learners. Microsoft has invested €1m in the development of the new hub. This comes from a €4m investment fund that was set aside by the company in March last year to help ‘Skill Up Ireland’ for the era of AI. An integrated approach to STEM skills development across Dream Space @ the Data Centre and Microsoft Ireland’s other skilling and education initiatives, such as the Collinstown Data Centre Academy, will help to build awareness of pathways into further education, apprenticeships and careers in the data centre and broader technology sector. Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President, Microsoft, said: “We have been part of Ireland for more than 40 years and see it as Microsoft’s home in Europe. As our presence continues to grow, so too has our commitment to creating lasting benefits for the Irish people. Since 2018, we’ve invested over €6.5 million in local data centre communities, benefitting more than 135,000 people. Microsoft ‘s Dream Space is the next step in that journey, giving thousands of young people the chance to experience and understand the technology behind the digital services they use every day, and envision a future career for themselves in Ireland’s digital economy.” Lavinia Morris, General Manager, Microsoft’s EMEA Data Centre Operations said: “Today is an exciting milestone for Microsoft as we officially open Dream Space @ the Data Centre. This new hub builds on Dream Space’s strong foundations in STEM, AI and digital skilling, while bringing students closer to the real-world skills, careers and opportunities shaping Ireland’s growing digital infrastructure sector. “Over the next year, more than 5,000 students and teachers from communities near our data centre will enjoy the hub. Through hands-on experiences in areas such as physical computing, electrical engineering and cloud operations, learners will gain practical skills and direct exposure to the technologies that power the digital world. The new hub will deepen our connection to the local community, helping young people develop vital STEM skills for the future and gain a better understanding of the exciting possibilities that exist in the sector.” To learn more, visit the Microsoft Dream Space website: https://DreamSpace.ie

events.title: Ex-Nvidia-turned-VC Amulya Vishwanath: ‘Physical AI is in its LEGO era’
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity. She is the founder and managing partner of Techable Ventures, a VC firm focused on physical AI, which she started after spending nearly seven years as a product marketer at Nvidia. Before that, she held the same role at a company that was later bought by Intel and was a digital signal processing engineer at Interconnect Systems, which was later bought by the electronics manufacturer Molex. She stopped by Equity to talk about the future of physical AI — one of the industry’s latest buzzwords. “A lot of companies and experts have been talking about the ChatGPT moment for robotics,” she said, adding that right now the industry was more in a “LEGO era.” “There are a lot of foundational software and building blocks for robotics that are being rethought right now as we speak, and it’s super important in order for innovation to scale,” she continued. Right now, people are building the basics — the robotic hands or the actuators — that can one day come together and build that big-ticket-item, like a bunch of LEGOs coming together. There’s general- and special-purpose robots being built right now, too, and eventually, as people continue building them, they will get better and more advanced. “We’ve done this during the internet era,” she said. “We’ve done this long, long time ago with the Industrial Revolution. I think it’s just a matter of time before things fall into place.” “Talent is also going to be very critical,” she continued, adding elsewhere in the convo that talent is still a key definer of the U.S. market. This is one of the “moats” of her firm, she said, helping connect founders to top talent so they can stay competitive right now, as so much talent is going to big companies like Anthropic and Nvidia. She pointed out that she’s built up a strong network to help founders from her years of working in this space. “This just makes it a lot easier for me to be the strength or the first call for founders,” she said. events.title: Plants can speak using electricity, so this startup built an AI model to decipher their language
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant. A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source. “I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.” Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers. The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant. To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said. “That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said. Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said. The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry. Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said. “This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Homebuilder sentiment is at a 14-year low
events.summary: The AI boom is sucking up all the capital. The Federal Reserve is raising rates to try to cool inflation. And one sector is bearing the brunt of the pain from both: housing . The big picture: The situation is lose-lose for both homebuilders and homebuyers. Builders are facing more expensive capital and bidding for scarce construction-related resources. Would-be buyers are being quoted some of the highest mortgage rates of this century. New September housing starts data out Tuesday morning puts an exclamation point on what has been a slow-moving disaster for a sector that plays an outsized role in the economic cycle and in Americans' basic living standards. By the numbers: The number of housing units started by builders fell 5.2% last month, the Census Bureau said , to 1.22 million. It's down 7.4% year over year and near post-pandemic lows. Starts of single-family homes fell 4.6% to their lowest level since March 2023. Pending home sales fell 7.3% last month, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday morning, to the lowest since the data was tracked going back to 2001. Homebuilder sentiment fell this month to its lowest level since 2012, the National Association of Home Builders said Monday. State of play: The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was 7.4% earlier this month, Freddie Mac said in its most recent weekly reading. The rate was briefly higher than that in 2023, but has not been consistently above that level since the fall of 2000. That has kept homebuyers on the sidelines — while a parallel rise in borrowing costs for developers has made it harder for new projects to pencil out. In effect, the bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and the U.S. government has to squeeze something, and that something has been the housing sector. Residential investment has subtracted from overall GDP for five of the last six quarters. Zoom out: Housing affordability is the crux of Americans' broader dissatisfaction with economic conditions, and all signs point to it getting worse, not better. For all the bipartisan emphasis on increasing housing supply — most prominently in the passage of a law to encourage more building earlier this year — conditions are weighted against a building boom. Housing developers are competing with data center builders for labor and materials like copper, concrete and HVAC equipment. Of note: Restrictionist immigration policy has also crimped the supply of construction workers . "Nationwide, more than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas during the past month, causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work," said NAHB chairman Bill Owens, an Ohio homebuilder, in the sentiment release . Between the lines: An unfortunate side effect of relying on Fed interest rate policy for macroeconomic stabilization is that interest-sensitive sectors, particularly housing, take it on the chin when the economy shows signs of overheating. It's particularly problematic now, when persistent undersupply of housing is a defining economic challenge of our age. The bottom line: The current alignment of interest rates, housing supply and construction costs isn't making anybody happy. Builders can't afford to build, buyers can't afford to buy, and even the people sitting pretty with pre-2022 mortgages can't afford to move.

events.title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
events.summary: Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry. Staff based in Leeds and Dublin, as well as workers for its UK and Ireland business at Flutter's Portugal and Romania sites, will be most affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed. The government announced taxes rises on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last year. Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market". "We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter Entertainment said on Tuesday. Flutter, which also owns Sky Bet and Betfair, employs 28,500 people across the world, including 9,000 in the UK and Ireland. As well as its Leeds and Dublin offices, the BBC understands the cuts could also affect staff based in London and Sunderland, as well as Malta and Gibraltar. Harrington, who is chief executive of the betting giant's UK and Ireland business, said: "As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future." A government spokesperson said the job cuts were a "commercial decision for Flutter, not the UK government". "However, we understand this will be a difficult time for the workers," they added. Flutter delisted from the London Stock Exchange in August in a blow to the UK, with its shares now solely traded in New York. In its most recent results, the company reported a $299m (£224m) pre-tax loss for the three months to June for its entire business worldwide, compared to a $205m profit in the same period last year. Sales rose 3% to $4.3bn. However, revenues in the UK and Ireland rose by 4% over the period, due to strong growth in online gambling games. Some online gambling tax rises announced in last year's Budget took effect in April. This included remote gaming duty, which is paid on online casino betting, rising from 21% to 40%. General betting duty, paid on the profits made from various forms of sports betting, was kept at 15% in betting shops, but is set to rise from 15% to 25% online in April next year. Betting firms had warned that cost increases would lead to job losses and betting shop closures, but MPs dismissed the warnings as "scaremongering". During the summer, Ladbrokes owner Entain announced job cuts, with news agency Reuters reporting 500 roles were being removed. Punters' winnings from gambling are not taxed in the UK, nor is VAT charged on bets. Flutter said its restructuring plan would cost between $80m and $90m. The company has claimed in previous financial results that the impact of UK tax rises would hit its underlying profit by $320m this year and $540m in 2027, before any savings or restructure to mitigate the impact. events.title: Dh1m gets you in the queue for Tesla's new Roadster in the UAE
events.summary: Tesla has opened the ordering process for its next-generation Roadster in the UAE – but the “flying” version is not yet available. The Roadster, unveiled by Tesla chief executive Elon Musk at a demonstration in Texas last week, comes in three models: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. UAE customers can reserve the Performance with an initial refundable payment of Dh20,000 ($4,847), followed by another Dh190,000 within 10 days. The more powerful Thrust requires the same initial payment, followed by Dh1 million within 10 days. The car's built-in thrusters are purely for acceleration, not flight. The Rocket model – which is fitted with SpaceX -made thrusters – demonstrated its ability to “fly” last week. It can be bought through invitation only and remains unavailable in the UAE. It has yet to be revealed how Tesla will determine who can get hold of this top-end version. Tesla has made clear payments are deposits, as the final prices have yet to be decided. The Texas-based company plans to start production of the next-generation vehicles in 2028. Tesla has said availability of the Rocket is subject to domestic laws and regulations, and that configuration will not be offered in all regions. What does UAE law say? The “flying” capabilities of the Rocket Roadster have raised questions about the legality of such vehicles on roads, whether it would be classified as an aircraft and what approvals would be required. Flying raises a separate set of legal questions. UAE law states that aircraft operating in the Emirates must meet registration, licensing and airworthiness requirements. Hefty fines await those who breach these laws. However, the UAE is already developing regulations and infrastructure for flying taxis. In July, the General Civil Aviation Authority certified Dubai 's first purpose-built commercial vertiport for electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. The UAE has separate laws governing road vehicles and aircraft but there is no publicly established approval framework specifically addressing a vehicle such as the Rocket Roadster. Federal regulations in the Emirates stipulate all vehicles must be registered and licensed, meet approved technical and safety standards and undergo inspection as part of the registration process. They require approval for substantial changes to the body, chassis or engine power, although this concerns modifications and does not necessarily apply to factory-built vehicles. The authority has also published operating procedures for such aircraft at Abu Dhabi's Al Bateen Executive Airport. But these frameworks do not automatically establish whether a vehicle designed for both roads and flight, such as the Rocket, would be permitted to operate. The Roadster would still need to meet UAE road regulations – and the Rocket version is expected to require particular aviation approval.

events.title: France riots become Republican midterm boogeyman
events.summary: As the French right-wing National Rally is seizing on fiery protests in the country for its pre-election pitch, so are President Trump and his Republican allies in the U.S. The big picture: The Trump administration has used the unrest, which began over education grievances , to bolster its messaging on immigration and the threat of "communists," a group Trump has repeatedly claimed is threatening American civilization. Driving the news: "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical 'Dumocrats' want to do to America," Trump said before a Kansas rally crowd Monday. He claimed France was being "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity" and "the Western civilization itself." Speaking earlier to reporters, the president claimed, without evidence, that the situation in France was about "immigration, not schools." He's repeatedly blamed immigration for the protests. The White House referred Axios to the president's Truth Social post echoing that rhetoric. Catch up quick: Localized demonstrations by high school students that began in Paris last month have broadened into a massive nationwide movement over poor school conditions and costs of living, sparking thousands of arrests and clashes between police and protesters, Axios' Bec Falconer reports. The civil unrest gave way to rioting and looting, leading French President Emmanuel Macron to condemn "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals," per the AP . Some 550,000 people demonstrated in France Saturday, per the interior ministry, though Reuters reported that a key union estimated 800,000. On the sidelines, "thugs" chose "violence," per a translation of the interior ministry's statement , which added that some 500 police officers and firefighters were injured. The forceful police response to student demonstrators has also been scrutinized , sparking dozens of probes into officer conduct. Zoom out: Other U.S. Republicans have followed Trump in evoking the protests, which have spread to other countries , to rally voters and condemn immigration . Vice President Vance wrote on X, " Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," sharing a video of a historic town hall reportedly set ablaze by masked protesters, per AFP. "This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country," Vance contended. Yes, but: Macron, per a translation of his nationwide address over the weekend protests, said the hundreds of thousands of demonstrators had " legitimate demands" and should not be conflated with violent rioters. He said those concerns included the cost of living and fuel price spikes triggered by the war in Iran. The bottom line: The spiraling violence has created global shock that Trump is harnessing as a boogeyman ahead of an uphill midterm battle. events.title: Apple unveils the 2026 Designers of Tomorrow
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Text of this article October 20, 2026 UPDATE Apple unveils the 2026 Designers of Tomorrow Curated by Rodman Primack, the exhibition celebrates next-generation designers and how they integrated Apple products into their creative processes Apple’s Designers of Tomorrow showcase, in collaboration with Design Miami, returns for a second year to spotlight the best in emerging talent, this time focusing on the theme of presence. Exploring what still holds the public’s attention amid the hurried pace of the modern world, designers Salem S. Charabi, Isabel Rower, Yoonjeong Lee, and Parafernalia (Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla) crafted original works that invite reflection and aim to shift perspectives, engage the senses, and kindle curiosity. “The theme was born from an honest recognition of just how busy our lives have become,” says Rodman Primack, the program’s curator and former longtime creative director of Design Miami. “In answering it, our designers demonstrate the power of objects to shape our physical environments and transform the human experiences that are possible within them.” This year’s participants were handpicked by a jury of global design voices — including Alexandra Cunningham Cameron, Fabien Cappello, Jennifer Dunlop Fletcher, Minjae Kim, Hun Chung Lee, Marion Mailaender, Nifemi Marcus-Bello, Jennifer Roberts, and Apple’s Molly Anderson — for their storytelling, material innovation, and craft. Their work also highlights Apple’s dynamic role in the creative process, empowering designers at every level to capture, refine, and share their ideas with the world. “Apple products continue to emerge as a through line so many extraordinary designers share, spanning disciplines, cultures, and processes,” explains Primack. “It’s a testament to how seamlessly these products and tools can integrate into any workflow.” Ahead of the exhibition, which opens today at Hôtel de Maisons in Paris, the featured designers discussed their final pieces and the tools they used to bring them to life. Salem S. Charabi Egyptian Danish architect Salem S. Charabi blends old-world practices and the latest digital tools to create timeless pieces, and his Designers of Tomorrow project, The Emergence of Light , is no exception. “Light is something we’re all instinctively drawn to, dating back to our earliest fires,” Charabi notes. “A lantern felt like the perfect encapsulation of this idea — a reflection of our capacity to light up the world.” Charabi constructed the lantern’s veil from banana paper, applying Japanese methods to Egyptian palms. A delicate skeleton of meticulously stacked date palm fronds provides a satisfying contrast to the limestone base, which carries the traces of its own formation in its grooves. “Each strand is an octagon in profile — just 3 millimeters wide, split by hand, and carefully drilled,” Charabi explains. “The ends are then sharpened with a chisel to interlock.” Both the lamp and the audience’s attention are suspended by the same tension. The resulting piece feels at once deeply natural and finely engineered. “For this project, every component had to be mapped out in detail,” Charabi says. “I sketched and did all the 3D modeling on my MacBook Pro. It was a complex process getting everything to fit just right — from the carving of the stone and the paper molds, down to the delicate base.” Isabel Rower By blending familiar forms with the unexpected, Brooklyn-based designer Isabel Rower cultivates presence and transforms everyday objects into active sensory experiences. “The surface functions as a site for curiosity for me,” explains Rower. “People don’t always know what my pieces are made of, even as they’re touching them. It’s captivating when something that isn’t readily understood takes the form of a familiar object, like a table or teapot. It generates a kind of friction that brings you into immediate awareness of the objects we use every day.” This intrigue is captured by her piece Padded Chair 1860 , whose dramatic proportions draw on 18th- and 19th-century papier-mâché furniture and objets d’art. Its high-gloss finish stands in sharp contrast to the beaded fringe lining the seat. “The ceramic beads make a sound when brushed, drawing attention to both the material and its form, turning the unconscious act of sitting down into a mindful encounter,” Rower says. Apple is a fixture throughout her creative process. “I use iPhone to capture quick thoughts and document my process, AirPods Pro to listen to music, and MacBook Pro to build my personal visual archive,” says Rower. “I’ll also use Keynote to juxtapose ideas and explore the relationship between images and text.” Yoonjeong Lee For Seoul-based designer Yoonjeong Lee, presence begins with quiet discovery. Through material transformation, she repositions overlooked background objects as central subjects. Her piece New Form showcases a trio of worn-down pencils that have been given new life as nails. “I wanted to express this year’s theme through something small that we could all recognize — a shared experience,” Lee explains. “This story doesn’t carry some grand narrative. Instead, it takes a second look at the familiar to help you rediscover that which has been quietly forgotten.” The base of the piece doubles as a wooden table and lamp. Sheets of paper serve as a lampshade, softly diffusing the light below, while the pencils hold them firmly in place. Applying her signature technique of building volume through repetition, Lee stacked roughly 5,000 thin sheets of veneer to construct the wooden base. Lee’s focus on overlooked structural elements extends to her workflow, where she credits iCloud, AirDrop, and Notes for keeping her process seamless. “I often use iPad Pro and Apple Pencil to create a sketch and jot down quick thoughts, but it’s how my devices connect to each other that makes them, and all their flexible features, truly useful,” she explains. Parafernalia Founded by Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla, Parafernalia is a design studio that spans from Monterrey to Mexico City. The duo’s creative process is driven by constant dialogue, questioning, and iteration, often powered by FaceTime. “For us, presence can take many forms,” says Matsumura. “We experience it with ourselves, with our surroundings, and with others. Our piece explores how all these expressions can coexist within a single object.” Their piece MonoAmbiente 1 considers presence as both a personal relationship with one’s surroundings and a collective act. When closed, its acid-etched stainless steel surface forms a vast landscape. Its dual state invites the observer not only to examine it but to experience it. Once expanded, it reveals stools and a table, turning a distant scene into an intimate setting where two people can converse, play chess, or share a drink.

events.title: The manosphere stars who helped Trump win are losing their shine
events.summary: The manosphere stars who helped mobilize young men for Donald Trump in 2024 are losing their shine with that very audience. Why it matters: Trump and Republicans rode a wave of cultural cachet to reach young male voters. Now, the president and some of his most influential online allies are showing signs of losing their grip on that audience ahead of the 2026 midterms . Driving the news: New polling from the Democratic project Speaking With American Men suggests some of the most prominent influencers during Trump's 2024 campaign have lost their luster with young male voters, per Puck News , Joe Rogan's favorable rating among young men dropped from 11 points, while Elon Musk's popularity dropped 14 points and Tucker Carlson lost 12 points. Andrew Tate, who was arrested on sex trafficking and rape charges, had "a -30 net approval rating," per Puck. Between the lines: Economic pressures and the Iran war have become major concerns for young men heading into the midterms, Puck reported. Those issues have caused tension between Trump and the influential voices who bolstered his last campaign. State of play: Young men are turning on politicians, podcasters and influencers, many of whom may have influenced recent political outcomes. They're becoming more skeptical and turning their backs on politicians, especially Trump. The 2026 Young American Men Survey from Cygnal similarly found that among 18- to 30-year-old American men, Trump, Vance and the Republican Party all were viewed unfavorably. Trump's numbers among young voters dropped precipitously. Marquette Law School national polling shows that Trump's approval dropped from 40% in January 2025 to 19% in April 2026, before rebounding to 28% in June. The law school hasn't polled on the question since then. Yes, but: Young men aren't especially enthusiastic about Democrats, either. Former President Barack Obama, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani were the only Democrats showing upticks in favorability ratings, per Puck. Context: Several prominent manosphere personalities have been critical of Trump in his second term, particularly on the Iran war and the Epstein files release. Rogan , like many MAGA influencers, has criticized the war and the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files. Tucker Carlson has chastised Trump over many issues, including his partnership with Israel in going to war. Vice President Vance has even admitted the White House "screwed up" on its communications about the Epstein files. Reality check: Researchers question how influential podcasters and personalities actually were in 2024. A September working paper from the NYU Center for Social Media, AI and Politics found that podcast exposure did not necessarily cause Trump's gains among young men. Researchers, who reviewed 36,659 podcast episodes from 2024 alongside two survey datasets, found podcasts explained only a small portion of the widening youth gender gap. The other side: Influencers still have enormous reach among young voters. A survey from Morning Consult published on Oct. 16 found that nearly two-thirds of Gen Z adults say they get news from creators, while 62% trust creator recommendations. Business Insider reports that one in four U.S. adults feel influencer content has affected their voting decisions. Separate Marquette polling found that 54% of adults who consumed podcasts for political news approved of Trump's job performance in June, compared with 38% of adults overall. The bottom line: The manosphere's biggest personalities still have sway, but the direction of the country isn't helping them — or Trump — with young men.

events.title: BBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels to be shut down next year
events.summary: Corporation announces broadcast closures and job losses in effort to find savings of £500m Television channels BBC Three and BBC Scotland are to close and the Radio 4 Extra radio station will be scrapped, as part of the corporation’s drive to cut £500m in costs. Both TV channels are to move online as executives try to plug a funding crisis and adapt the broadcaster’s output for audiences that increasingly watch content on demand. All three outlets will close in the spring. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, said the corporation needed to “make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world”. He added: “We all know that means tough choices.” A further 100 jobs will also be cut at BBC News to save £5.5m. However, the department’s new director, Rachel Jupp, warned staff that its £51m cuts target could yet increase as a result of the broadcaster’s funding crisis. Even with the channel closures, which come on top of other cuts already announced, BBC insiders said the corporation was not even half way to meeting its £500m target. Only about £200m has been cut so far, suggesting even more controversial cuts will have to be made over the next year to plug the funding gap. It marks the second time that BBC Three’s linear TV channel has been closed, having been moved online in 2016 but brought back in 2022. The Guardian revealed this month that the channels were likely to be axed. BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences, launched shows including Gavin and Stacey, Fleabag and Killing Eve. However, it was an obvious candidate to move online and have more of its content placed on YouTube, where younger audiences have migrated. Typically, about 4% of the UK population watch the channel live in a week. The BBC promised there would be increased investment in content for younger audiences. It has already cancelled the high-profile BBC Three show RuPaul’s Drag Race UK . BBC Scotland’s viewership was seen as too low to justify the cost of keeping it on air, with its digital audience increasing via the BBC’s iPlayer. Its content will also be available on BBC One and BBC Two in Scotland . The decision to close Radio 4 Extra came after it was decided much of its content could be accessed digitally, via the BBC Sounds app. The station reached an audience of 1.4 million a week, according to the most recent Rajar data. There has already been severe internal criticism from BBC staff over where the cuts are being made. BBC executives have said they planned to safeguard content that fulfilled its duty to produce programming for everyone. However, many staff now fear that the BBC is targeting public service content that commercial rivals would never replicate. There has been increasing disquiet over the decision to axe BBC Radio 4’s The World Tonight after more than 50 years. Consumer affairs show You and Yours is one of a number of fellow Radio 4 shows going, to be replaced by a new format. Some of the BBC’s freelance foreign correspondents have also been cut, while the number of local correspondents across Britain is being reduced, with those still in post asked to become general reporters rather than specialists . Meanwhile, the BBC’s local radio output is being made more regional. The BBC has also faced a backlash from politicians, as well as from the staff and crew of its flagship radio drama The Archers, after a decision not to build a planned radio drama studio for the show in its new Birmingham headquarters. The vast majority of staff accept that the corporation is under financial strain and needs to modernise in an age of streaming and digital platforms consumed over a smartphone. However, morale has been hit by the time it has taken to drip out the cuts, while others believe the cuts will result in the BBC replicating too much content similar to that on commercial networks. In a note to staff, Brittin said: “We would all prefer immediate certainty. However, it unfortunately takes time to develop proposals that ensure we focus scarcer resources on the shows, stories and services that can have the biggest impact.” Further major changes to BBC News are still to come, but have been delayed to allow Jupp to draw up her strategy for the newsroom. She has been tasked with boosting BBC News on digital platforms such as YouTube and TikTok, as well as the BBC’s own apps and iPlayer. Philippa Childs, the head of the Bectu union, said the latest cuts and channel closures were “in danger of causing irreparable damage to the BBC and will do yet more harm to the morale of its employees”. “The continued drip-feed of planned job and output cuts is putting increasing pressure on an already bruised workforce at the BBC,” she said. The BBC is having to make the cuts as a result of its serious financial challenges, with its cash revenues falling at an alarming rate over the last year.

events.title: Union attacks NatWest plans to get workers back to the office
events.summary: The Unite union has hit out at a plan by NatWest to reduce the rights of 30,000 of its employees to work from home. NatWest says it is moving to a hybrid approach where workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week, from February. The bank says this is still very competitive with the rest of the finance industry, and exceptions will be made for colleagues who require additional flexibility. But Unite said NatWest's decision was "out of touch with the realities facing its workforce", with many facing higher travel and childcare costs. Firms have been gradually drawing people back into the office since working from home became the norm for some office workers during the Covid pandemic. In January last year, Amazon required staff to return to the office five days a week after they had been working two days at home. Other firms such as Boots and JP Morgan have brought in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day. But Barclays faced a backlash from staff last month over plans to require workers to go to the office three days a week. It brought in a longer transition period in response to staff and union complaints. Unite said NatWest was abolishing its "remote first" employment category, which allows 13,497 workers to attend the office around twice a month, and requiring 17,272 hybrid workers to increase their office attendance. The union says that many of the affected workers are lower-paid grades, and the new requirements will increase cost-of-living pressures, while disrupting the arrangements of disabled workers and carers. In a statement, Unite general secretary Sharon Graham called NatWest's move a "kick in the teeth" for its workers. "Thousands of workers face higher travel and childcare costs and disruption to caring responsibilities," she said "For NatWest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce." Graham called on NatWest to "ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers". A NatWest spokesman said: "Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we've also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers - helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another. "That's why we're introducing a more consistent approach across the bank, with colleagues expected to spend at least two days a week in the office, depending on the needs of their role and business area. "We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we're giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition." events.title: How the energy crisis could become a food security crisis
events.summary: The Iran war and the Ukraine- Russia conflict are creating a "multidirectional squeeze on world agriculture" that could spiral into a crisis, a new report finds. Why it matters: Wars and extreme weather are colliding to threaten global food supplies and drive up prices, especially in vulnerable economies. The report explores how the El Niño phenomenon could compound the problems of restricted supplies of key fertilizer ingredients, higher fuel costs on the farm and more. The S&P Global Institute report is an unusually holistic look at the topic. Driving the news: The analysis comes alongside new warnings about food from the International Monetary Fund. Its World Economic Outlook last week sees an overall 10% increase in fertilizer prices this year and food costs rising by 5% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, though it depends on the region. "Higher energy and food prices could have severe effects on poverty and food security" and threaten political stability in vulnerable economies, the IMF warned. State of play: Food producers need steady supplies of natural gas and sulfur for fertilizer, diesel for farm machinery and food transport, and open sea lanes for trade, S&P notes. "Conflict is now testing all of them at once, just as El Niño tests the harvest," states the report from the research and consulting firm. "The risk is increasing, especially for low-income countries, where food costs amount to about half of household spending," it states. Zoom out: The disruptions could affect agricultural production worldwide, from soybeans and corn in Brazil to wheat in Australia, S&P finds. The intrigue: The S&P report also warns of something that has received somewhat less attention. The diesel supply crunch doesn't just raise costs for farmers. It also works alongside pro-biofuels policies to make biodiesel production more attractive. "The knock-on effect is that, in some regions, crops for fuel become more valuable than crops for food." Zoom in: A few stats via S&P illustrate the overlapping threats. Middle Eastern prices for exported sulfur, a fertilizer ingredient, reached a record $1,000 per metric ton in July, after starting the year at a historically high $500 per metric ton. 47% of the global sulfur trade normally goes through the Strait of Hormuz. In Indonesia, industrial use of palm oil, largely for biodiesel, is expected to be roughly five times its 2015-16 level. The bottom line: A global food crisis is by no means certain. But if wars keep disrupting energy and fertilizer supplies, and weather cuts harvests in key regions, "the elements of such a crisis will be falling into place," S&P warns.

events.title: UAE and France deepen defence ties with Rafale F5 fighter-jet deal
events.summary: Defence co-operation is among the areas covered by a series of agreements signed by the UAE and France as the two countries look to bolster ties amid geopolitical uncertainty triggered by the Iran war. They signed an intergovernmental agreement for co-operation on the Dassault Rafale F5 standard within the French and Emirati Rafale programmes during the visit of French President Emmanuel Macron to Abu Dhabi. The agreements also cover technical and financial specifications for industrial co-operation between the two countries on the future of combat aviation, as France and the UAE strengthen defence ties. Another agreement focuses on strategic autonomy in defence and reducing dependence on third countries as part of a strategic defence partnership between the two nations. The latest agreements come as the UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, focuses on localising defence manufacturing through Edge Group , a defence conglomerate with more than 35 companies under its umbrella. The group has played a key role in countering Iranian drones directed at the UAE during the war. Mr Macron visited an Edge Group industrial site during his visit. Edge , set up in 2019, specialises in developing advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare. The group maintains several industrial partnerships with French companies and recently signed a co-operation agreement with the French Defence Procurement Agency. Mr Macron's visit “reflects a shared commitment to strengthening industrial and technological co-operation and developing joint projects”, the Elysee Palace said in a statement. The French Defence Ministry also signed an agreement with the UAE to enhance interoperability between the two armed forces, strengthen industrial resilience and advance co-operation in future-orientated technology, including artificial intelligence and space. The latest agreements come as Abu Dhabi is preparing to host the International Defence Exhibition and Conference (Idex) in January, an event expected to attract hundreds of defence companies from across the globe to showcase their latest high-tech weapons. Mr Macron then headed to Bahrain, where French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif Al Zayani, agreed to bolster co-operation on the “peaceful uses of nuclear energy”, the French government said. France and Bahrain signed a defence co-operation agreement in February during a visit to Paris by Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa. The UAE and Bahrain were among the Gulf countries France helped protect with air defence and anti-drone assets during Iranian attacks this year. France has also co-operated closely with Bahrain at the UN Security Council to find a diplomatic solution to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz . Energy, AI and advanced technology The UAE and France signed new deals in energy, AI and advanced technology as the two countries seek to strengthen investment and economic ties. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in Abu Dhabi. In AI and advanced technology, three agreements were signed with France's AI start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several key sectors, according to the Abu Dhabi Media Office. The deals involve Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), Abu Dhabi's G42 and computing company Analog. MBZUAI will focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models. Analog's deal with AMI Labs focuses on exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications, creating new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors. The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technologies and identify opportunities to enhance operational efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems. Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts covering a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project. In his opening remarks at the UAE-France Business Dialogue at Qasr Al Watan in Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled underscored the importance of bilateral co-operation in ensuring reliable energy supplies and building resilient supply chains amid changes in the global economy. The UAE and France have strong economic ties, with more than 600 French businesses currently operating in the UAE and $4 billion worth of goods exported annually from France to the UAE, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website. UAE investments are also growing in France. In 2021, UAE-based Gulf Islamic Investments made a $301 million investment in Altais Towers, while Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Investment Company signed an initial agreement with Bpifrance, committing to invest €1 billion ($1.12 billion) in the LAC1 Fund, a €10 billion fund managed by Bpifrance.

events.title: No cancellation of planned FDI in UAE this year despite Iran war, Ministry of Investment says
events.summary: No planned foreign direct investment in the UAE has been cancelled this year, despite the uncertainties created by the US-Iran war, a senior government official has said. The overall stock of FDI in the UAE this year might be fractionally lower than the record levels achieved in 2025, as global investors assess the impact of conflict in the region. However, the Emirates remains firmly on course to achieve its 2031 FDI targets, Mohammad Abdulrahman Alhawi, Undersecretary of the UAE Ministry of Investment, told The National in an interview on Tuesday. “Everyone we've spoken to has said: 'We haven't cancelled our plans. We are just either waiting, or we're delaying a little bit, or we're decreasing the quantum a little bit but the country is capable of making up,'” Mr Alhawi said on the sidelines of the 10th HSBC Future Forum in Dubai. “Very understandable [that] people will wait and see how the conflict is resolved.” The good thing, Mr Alhawi said, is that even though the conflict been going on since late February, it has helped investors better understand the resilience of the UAE and the capabilities of its government in dealing with a crisis. “I think that's the message that our investors have received over time and I think, maybe not immediately but in the next few years, that will definitely be a positive thing, as more investment is coming,” he said. FDI into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development ( Unctad ) data. The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July. The UAE has maintained consistent FDI inflow momentum over the past few years and was expected to continue on the growth trajectory this year before the war-driven disruption to economy and trade. Like its peers in the six-member economic bloc of the Gulf Co-operation Council and its Arab neighbours, the UAE has faced waves of missile and drone attacks, but Mr Alhawi said it remains “100 per cent” on target to achieve the $65 billion annual FDI targets by 2031. “You'll have some years when it'll grow slightly less or slightly more,” he said. “But now that we've reached the $40 billion [plus] range, we expect to keep that for a couple more years before jumping to the next level, which is the $65 billion range, which is where we want to be.” While various governments at the emirate level are incentivising investors to boost FDI inflows, the UAE federal government is focused on investing in its own economy. Special attention is being paid to developing ports and related infrastructure on the East Coast, as well as improving and expanding rail connectivity, and oil and gas pipeline infrastructure. “Now, that investment does two things: one, it shows our confidence in our economy, and two, it shows that we're building different routes and paths for our main value proposition, which is being a logistical hub,” Mr Alhawi said. “We're investing in the right places, which means the investors that are already here can see the impact this will have and they will see it over the next year or so.” Partnerships with investors The UAE is more than capable of executing those projects on its own but it is seeking participation of foreign investors in these schemes to make them a part of the UAE growth story. Mr Alhawi said the Ministry of Investment is bringing capital together and is in talks with investors over joint ventures. Options for global investors to team up with the UAE sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices, are also open, he said. “We're super open,” Mr Alhawi said. “I mean, we can build infrastructure ourselves if we want to, but building it with partners makes it more efficient, makes it better, makes it more long term. “We'd love to have partners wherever we can and we've seen actually quite an influx of people saying, ‘Oh, you're building infrastructure, so let's work with you’, which is great. A very positive sign.” Infrastructure pipeline Investment in infrastructure is among the central planks of the UAE’s economic diversification agenda and Mr Alhawi said the scale of investment required for East Coast projects is significant. HSBC estimates the UAE project finance pipeline is in excess of $190 billion in funding requirements to build the planned infrastructure projects. The UAE accounts for about 22 per cent of the broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region infrastructure project pipeline of $872 billion, data from HSBC's New Networks of Capital: Menat Infrastructure report indicates. “Ultimately, these large-scale projects, such as Al Maktoum [International] Airport, the Dubai sewage system and developments in Fujairah, have strong government backing,” Mohamed Al Marzooqi, chief executive of HSBC UAE, told The National . “So, these are the paymasters and I don't think we have even touched the surface, to be honest, when it comes to tapping into those financing solutions.” The easiest solution, he said, would be to tap the loan market and financial institutions in the country. They are all “hungry for quality assets 100 per cent here in the UAE”. HSBC, Mr Al Marzooqi said, is not only willing to leverage its own balance sheet, it can also help structure deals in many other ways for project owners and investors. Opportunity knocks The sheer size of the MENAT pipeline underpins the scale of the region’s medium and long-term investment potential despite geopolitical headwinds, HSBC said in the report released on Tuesday. Even with a “complex global and regional operating environment”, international businesses and institutional investors expect the region to remain and infrastructure investment destination and flows of capital will continue over the rest of the decade, the lender said. The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data has identified the $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion planned and unawarded infrastructure pipeline. The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion,” data shows “Infrastructure planning activity has continued this year, with the pipeline increasing a further 15 per cent to $1.4tn between January and October 2026,” the HSBC report said.

events.title: Orlando Bravo on AI’s 'giant sucking sound'
events.summary: The death of software has been greatly exaggerated, said Orlando Bravo, who has more riding on its comeback than perhaps anybody in the world. The firm he runs, Thoma Bravo, oversees $170 billion in investments, nearly all of it invested in corporate software under threat from cheaper replacements spun up by AI coding bots. “Right now it’s a really, really hard time to buy and sell a company,” Bravo said on an episode of Semafor’s . “There have been four times the software industry has been doubted, and this is one of them. Every other time, it’s boomed after it’s been doubted. People got it wrong. It’ll be the same thing this time.” The sharp decline earlier this year in software stocks ground dealmaking in the sector to a halt, as CEOs were reluctant to sell at the bottom and private-equity firms struggled to raise the debt . That freeze is starting to thaw, with deals like Schneider’s $23 billion acquisition of PTC and the $6 billion takeover last week of AI cybersecurity company Varonis by a Thoma-backed competitor. The only questions that matter, he said, are “what is your level of domain expertise and how difficult it is to replicate it.” Dayforce, an HR-software provider Thoma Bravo bought in 2025, “is not selling you code. [It] is selling the following: ‘I will pay your employees on time, their deductions will be right, and their amount on their paycheck will be right. And if they’re not, I take the liability for it.’” “Yeah, somebody could try to recreate their code,” Bravo said. “Great. The business is not about that.” He also said the coming IPOs of “monster companies” like Anthropic and OpenAI will crowd others out of the capital markets — bad news for the private equity industry, which is sitting on an estimated $3.8 trillion backlog of unsold companies . “Who’s gonna pay attention with this stuff when they have to make big decisions on this enormous capital?” he said. — Liz Hoffman and Rohan Goswami

The SEC–FSA Dialogue builds upon longstanding efforts between the two authorities to increase cooperation and strengthen collaboration on key cross-border issues and developments. SEC Commissioner Mark T. Uyeda led the Dialogue for the SEC and Mr. MIYOSHI Toshiyuki, Vice Minister for International Affairs at the FSA, led the Dialogue for the FSA. At the Autumn Dialogue, participants discussed recent market developments, as well as the strategic priorities of both authorities. They also exchanged views on various regulatory and supervisory matters, including developments in private and public markets, asset management, and innovation priorities. The next SEC-FSA Dialogue is scheduled to be convened in Washington, D.C., in the spring of 2027. events.title: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
events.summary: Billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai and Elon Musk, pictured here at President Donald Trump's 2025 inauguration, have seen their wealth soar thanks to the stock market boom and beneficial tax changes. Chip Somodevilla/Pool Photo via AP The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability , but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment. A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this. This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs. I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality. Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%. Inequality by the numbers Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow . The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999. These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data. But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026. Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories. Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall . The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom. How taxes play a role Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive , often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats. The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth. Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940 . While many voters cite affordability as a top concern, concerns over inequality have increasingly been part of this debate. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from. Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership , allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash , usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares. By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%. The new drivers of inequality Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed. One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs. The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil. Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%. This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “ A Brief History of Equality ,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.” Markus Schneide

events.title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
events.summary: Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned. Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free. Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own. The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman. However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait. The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK. Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases. Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases. Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills. Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says Published 12 February Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions Published 29 January Retired civil servants left in pension limbo Published 23 January According to the latest figures up to 30 September , external , 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old. Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days. The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved. The Cabinet Office said that while the number of individuals approaching the two-year threshold was currently fewer than 10, "we are treating every case with urgency". If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance. The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate. Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty". His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability. Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim". He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month". He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear." Writing in response to Sir Geoffrey's letter, Minister Sally Jameson said neither the Cabinet Office nor the pension scheme administrator had the power under tax law to alter or waive these tax charges. However, she said where delays lead to an avoidable tax charge people "will not be left out of pocket" and the pension scheme "will ensure compensation is processed swiftly". She added that the Cabinet Office was working with Capita to ensure the oldest outstanding cases were prioritised. Money Box Live: Capita, What Went Wrong? Money Box Live looks at what is going on with Capita, which administers millions of people's pensions Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death. On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed. Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on. "It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said. "It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult." Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings. However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive. Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".
