events.title: Arada enters Saudi Arabia with $3.8bn Riyadh project
events.summary: UAE developer Arada is launching a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh and plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years as it expands in the kingdom, its chief executive has said. The company will also launch projects in Jeddah and Makkah as the Saudi market opens for foreign investment. “We have a good pipeline coming, and we will probably announce another project by the end of the year,” Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said. “As a group we plan to have 200,000 homes in the next three to five years, with half of that coming in Saudi Arabia.” Arada is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group. Following the Saudi announcement, Arada’s pipeline is valued at Dh185 billion across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the UK, Australia and Syria, comprising more than 70,000 homes. It has completed 17,000 homes so far. Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s largest economy, has overhauled its property sector, allowing foreigners to buy in designated zones in Riyadh and Jeddah, while introducing “special requirements” for home ownership in Makkah and Madinah from January. It also introduced land tax rules last year to help free up undeveloped land and spur building activity. Riyadh debut Arada’s debut project will be built in the Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a plot covering 2.5 million square metres. Apart from 3,500 villas and town houses, it will also have a school, retail outlets and a community centre, as well as sporting facilities and green areas. The project is inspired by Arada's Masaar, a Dh8 billion woodland community development in Sharjah. Units will be sold for between 1,000 and 1,400 Saudi riyals ($267 and $373) per square foot, with construction starting in mid-2027 and completing in five years time, Mr Alkhoshaibi said. Arada KSA, set up in partnership with Saudi property investor Xtopia, will spearhead its expansion in the kingdom, with Mohammed AlDhabaan, chairman of Xtopia as the new chairman of Arada KSA. Arada KSA has access to a significant 10 million square metre land bank across Saudi Arabia with a collective value of Dh49 billion, spanning key strategic locations including Riyadh, Jeddah and Makkah, it said in a separate announcement. Meeting domestic demand Demand for housing in Saudi Arabia is strong as the government pushes to increase home ownership among Saudis. Demand from expatriates following the opening of the sector to foreign buyers is also supporting the market, he said. “The real demand is by the Saudis who need a home, and this is driven further by the government, [which is] pushing for higher home ownership for the Saudis.” “The government's initiative, which we're trying to support, is that they want to provide 300,000 homes delivered in the next three years.” Saudi Arabia has set a target of raising home ownership rates among locals to 70 per cent by 2030 under the Sakani programme – a joint initiative between the Ministry of Housing and the Real Estate Development Fund. By the end of last year, Saudi citizens owning homes exceeded 66 per cent, with one million beneficiaries of government housing support programmes, the Saudi Press Agency reported in January, citing Minister of Municipalities and Housing Majed Al Hogail. Saudi Arabia’s property market was mixed in the second quarter, with nationwide residential transaction values contracting by 26.9 per cent year-on-year to 37.67 billion riyals and the total deal count falling 14.2 per cent, according to the latest CBRE report. The National Residential Price Index, however, grew 2.6 per cent on an annual basis, supported by a 1.1 per cent rise in apartment prices during the quarter. The Al Rimal project will be funded through a Capital Market Authority-regulated investment structure managed by Al Rajhi Capital, an asset-management firm in the kingdom. “We have partnered with Al Rajhi, who will provide the fund management and will also provide the funding. So there is obviously certain equity we put in, but [the] majority is through the fund and the bank,” Mr Alkhoshaibi said. The company is also entering Syria with plans to build a $7 billion “UAE-style” mixed-use real estate project in Damascus in phases over 10 years. The company's property sales are ranging between Dh400 million and Dh700 million a month despite uncertainty over the Iran war, he added. “The external factors will have an impact, but it will be mitigated or reduced by delivering a great product in a great location at a reasonable price, and that's what we've been doing.”

events.title: UAE tax rules: What businesses can claim for employee expenses
events.summary: Giving employees the tools they need to do their jobs effectively is a timeless business requirement. Whether a company has standard lists of equipment and resources for different grades and functions, which it should to make onboarding easier, most businesses could produce such lists without much difficulty. There are, however, tax considerations, particularly corporation tax and VAT . Thankfully, Federal Tax Authority Decision No 17 of 2026 has helpfully brought together answers to many of the questions businesses might have. There are five main sections, starting with transport provided for staff. It's critical that employees are not charged for the service and that transport is provided only between their homes and workplaces. Could there be a collection point for several employees, provided it is a reasonable distance from their homes? I would imagine so. Cash payments instead of transport cannot be offered, and there should be no identifiable non-business benefit. Could one employee who fails either test affect the entire arrangement? The decision says nothing about separating qualifying and non-qualifying cases. Best not be the person who tests the rules. What about pooling transport between two neighbouring companies? If the company providing the service changes according to a weekly schedule, would that complicate matters? A strict interpretation would require whichever company provides the service to invoice its commercial neighbour. I don't see how this can be avoided. Anything more complicated might best be outsourced for simplicity. Next is the provision of food and beverages. This is permissible where employees live so remotely that returning home is impractical. What constitutes remote is not defined, although I would interpret it as being unable to reach home within a reasonable time, given an individual's circumstances. This raises the possibility that only a small proportion of the workforce might qualify. No guidance has been provided on whether a minimum number of employees must meet the conditions. The provision must be linked to an employee's role and circumstances, including their workplace or residence. Suitable facilities should not be available at their accommodation or workplace, nor should local food outlets be reasonably accessible. Again, cash payments instead of food and beverages should not be an option. Moving on to company-provided accommodation, this must be an operational necessity. Perhaps the work site is in the Empty Quarter, 100 miles (160km) from the nearest town. Difficult access could make it reasonable to accommodate employees on or near the site. Accommodation and communication Accommodation should be suitable but not luxurious. No swimming pools, expansive manicured gardens, extensive household staff or additional reception rooms. The rules for onboarding new employees are a little more relaxed. Accommodation can be provided for up to 30 days, and the expense claimed, provided it is not ostentatious. Notably, the decision does not exclude employees who have already been living in the country, regardless of how long they have been here. I recall benefiting from such an arrangement when starting a role in the late 2000s. I believe there were two reasons for it. First, treating new starters differently would have been inconvenient. Second, with international personnel flying in and out of the region, putting everyone in the same hotel helped employees become familiar with the business and encouraged social interaction. Mobile phones are another area where guidance already existed, and the new decision restates and expands on it. Devices must be required for work and used only for business purposes. Each invoice should be reviewed, with personal calls identified and excluded from VAT or corporation tax claims. A company may decide to absorb the non-deductible cost rather than introduce an internal system for recovering personal expenses. Sometimes the administrative cost can outweigh the value of recovering small amounts spent on company assets. The new requirement is for a formal standard operating policy. This must be communicated to everyone affected, reviewed periodically, updated when necessary and demonstrably enforced. For businesses without standard operating procedures, this would be a good place to start. If I could, as an accountant, give human resources departments one task, it would be to map every business process and identify the roles and individuals responsible for each. This would strengthen both control and continuity. I can think of few projects more valuable when reassessing internal efficiency, particularly in an AI-driven world where automation is the mot du jour . Lastly comes parking, which is subject to the same requirements as mobile phones.

events.title: Witkoff heads to Oslo, plans Russia trip for peace talks
events.summary: White House envoy Steve Witkoff is traveling to Oslo for talks Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders, a U.S. official said. The big picture: The talks will bring together Ukraine, European allies and the U.S. as they seek to develop a peace proposal to present to Russia . The Oslo talks are expected to include Zelensky , Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Driving the news: The U.S. official said that following Oslo, Witkoff is also planning to travel to Russia, where he hopes to meet with President Vladimir Putin and present ideas developed in close consultation with Ukraine and European partners. Trump adviser Jared Kushner has the flu and will not attend the Oslo meeting in person, but will participate virtually, the U.S. official said. The planned meetings in Oslo build on the discussions held at Witkoff's Miami-area Shell Bay club , where Zelensky committed to reviewing and advancing a series of proposals aimed at creating a pathway toward a comprehensive and durable peace agreement, the U.S. official added. Zoom in: The U.S. official said American, Ukrainian and European representatives worked together over the past week to develop the proposals. "Steve and Jared also spoke with President Zelensky on Sunday to review progress and discuss next steps," the U.S. official said. The trip is also expected to include efforts to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher whom the U.S. says has been wrongfully detained in Russia. What's next: The U.S. official said the discussions are focused on two parallel tracks: Securing Ukraine's future: Establishing a sovereign, secure, and prosperous future for Ukraine, including credible security guarantees, European integration, and a comprehensive postwar economic framework that addresses Ukraine's financial needs and creates opportunities for long-term growth and investment. Creating the conditions for a durable peace: Developing a comprehensive proposal to Russia that addresses the issues necessary to end the war, establishes a new and enduring security architecture between Russia and Europe, and explores opportunities for postwar economic cooperation. "President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia," the U.S. official said. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump's objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."

events.title: El-Sayed pushes back at Republicans who judge him because he ‘might pray differently’
events.summary: The News MARQUETTE, Mich. — Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Thursday night accused President Donald Trump and Republican rival Mike Rogers of using his Muslim faith as a political cudgel. “Judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who’s ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution,” El-Sayed said in response to a question from Semafor. Republicans have recently amplified claims that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Trump posted a video Thursday night that directly called El-Sayed a member of the group, which was founded in Egypt; his administration has designated chapters as terrorist organizations. El-Sayed, an American of Egyptian descent who would be the first Muslim senator if elected, has rankled at the GOP accusations, including in a recent TV interview . His comments on Thursday are as close as he has come on the campaign trail to alleging Islamophobia by his opponents. “They don’t want to talk about any of the other issues that people are actually experiencing in their lives. They want to talk about me or point to my mom or my sister,” El-Sayed said. “My mom and my sister are not running for office. I’m running for office.” El-Sayed called it “an insane thing to assume” that members of his family were part of the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he didn’t “know what my mother was doing in Egypt in the 1970s.” Republicans have cited social media posts from his half-sister that appear to refer to his mother’s engagement with the group. “My parents got divorced when I was very young — 3,” El-Sayed said. “I didn’t see my mom for years after I was raised by my dad and my stepmom, and when I was asked, [to] the best of my knowledge, nobody in my family’s been a member of this organization.” Know More El-Sayed said insinuating he might not be loyal to the Constitution because of his faith was “the same thing that was done to JFK when they tried to say that, ‘Oh, well, he’s going to answer to the Pope because he’s Catholic.’ Same thing they tried to do to President Obama.” John F. Kennedy, the first Roman Catholic president, faced some false accusations of “dual loyalties” because of his faith. And the hard right pushed conspiracy theories about the religious practices of Obama, who is a Christian and was the first Black president. El-Sayed was campaigning in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula this week as part of a swing with progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. El-Sayed and Democrats are hoping they can grow the electorate in what has traditionally been redder territory in the state. Notable A Washington Post analysis found that rhetoric about El-Sayed from right-wing social media users has increasingly focused on his faith since his Michigan primary win this summer.

events.title: Musk to gift SpaceX shares to American children
events.summary: The News SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he would distribute to every American child a share in the AI-and-space-exploration company, a gift that, if realized, would dwarf a similar $6.25 billion gift from Michael Dell. The gift could be worth roughly $10.8 billion, based on SpaceX’s current share price and the U.S. Census’ estimate of under-18s living in the US. It would work out to roughly 1% of Musk’s current SpaceX holdings. Musk and the Trump administration originally discussed the share donations this summer when Trump accounts were first launched, Semafor scooped . Musk made the announcement Monday in response to a social media post from Anthropic , which said it would commit 5% of its listed equities to a “public benefit fund.” President Donald Trump later tweeted a thank you to Musk: “This is exactly what was envisioned when we created Trump Accounts.” Musk and a Treasury spokesperson did not return a request for comment. Rohan’s view The pledge raises some questions about what kind of voting rights the shares would have; SpaceX is a dual-class stock and Musk enjoys supermajority control of the company. Recent regulatory changes allow individual equities to be held in Trump Accounts, the childhood savings program that has been a flagship initiative of this administration. Musk has also not been a big philanthropist, relative to his wealth, and has argued before that the best way he can do good for humanity is by building great companies. Look at this through a strategic, rather than a philanthropic lens, however, and it makes a lot more sense. Musk’s planned donation could generate goodwill from a skeptical public around him, his companies and his goals — space exploration, self-driving cars and AI, among others. If other businesses chose to do something similar, they could also benefit from a public-relations boost, or possibly amass a friendly shareholder block that helps protect against others that might disagree with their strategic direction.

events.title: The affordability question Republicans can't escape
events.summary: One issue is breaking through even among the most loyal Republican supporters: gas prices . Why it matters: Republicans promised to slash gas prices. But the Iran war sent them soaring, up 37% since President Trump took office . Republicans call it temporary. But there are limits to what voters will accept. On recent campaign trips with House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), gas prices were the most frequent concern raised at events attended by Axios. These weren't rooms full of undecided voters. They were GOP donors, activists and supporters who had turned out to help Republicans win in November. Zoom in: The first question Scalise fielded at a campaign event for Republican Marty O'Donnell in Nevada was about high gas prices. "Everyone's always worried about gas prices," the attendee said, asking whether Republicans could do more to promote Trump's efforts to expand domestic energy production. Another attendee pointed to the gas-price difference between California and Oregon on a recent trip, and asked whether Congress could intervene to ease state restrictions. Scalise acknowledged the impact of the Iran war on gas prices — and said they'd fall once it's resolved — but blamed Democratic energy policies for making the U.S. more vulnerable to rising costs. Zoom out: Emmer faced similar concerns during a recent campaign trip through North Carolina and Virginia. "Four-dollar gas, five-dollar diesel, six-dollar diesel, totally unacceptable," Emmer told supporters at a North Carolina fundraiser. "But it ain't enough to make me vote for communists." "[Democrats] are talking about affordability. That's the problem. We need to be sensitive to the fact that gas and diesel are way up. Just sensitive to it because people are struggling," he told Axios in an interview. The big picture: Republican candidates are feeling the pressure too. Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed the Iran war and gas prices for his campaign struggles, according to audio obtained by Axios. "It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," Paxton told donors at a closed-door fundraiser last month, calling affordability "by far our biggest problem." The bottom line: "I don't think gaslighting works," House GOP conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) told Axios in an interview last month. "I think if you meet voters where they're at and you have an honest conversation with them ... that's pretty refreshing to them."

events.title: Inside the GOP's fight to avoid a House wipeout
events.summary: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise won't talk about defeat, even as his outside GOP allies are pulling money anyway. Why it matters: Republicans face brutal political headwinds, but Scalise (R-La.) stands out from his fellow leaders for refusing to even contemplate losing the House . Zoom in: At an event for Republican Marty O'Donnell, who's challenging Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), Scalise argued that his presence in the district was evidence Republicans are still on offense. "If it's some horrible cycle for Republicans, then why am I here?" Scalise told supporters at a Las Vegas country club Thursday. "This is a winnable race," he said. But MAGA Inc., a super PAC allied with President Trump, pulled nearly $1 million in advertising from the race last week. The big picture: House Democrats lead the generic ballot by eight points in new Washington Post-ABC polling . Trump's approval is at a record low of 31% ( Reuters/Ipsos ) and 72% say the country is on the wrong track (Post/ABC). He's making 56 campaign stops between August and Election Day as part of what he's dubbed the "Save America Tour," complete with T-shirts featuring a map of his travels. "This is like better than a rock band," Scalise told Axios during an in-flight interview while campaigning in Arizona and Nevada last week. Scalise identified 35 competitive districts , including 15 Democratic-held seats Republicans believe they have a chance to flip. He pointed to Reps. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), Juan Ciscomani (R-Ariz.), Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) and Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pa.) as races he'll watch closely as bellwethers for how the night could unfold. The pro-Scalise super PAC Save American Freedom is also launching a $3.5 million get-out-the-vote and digital advertising blitz to help 52 House Republicans, Axios' Alex Isenstadt reports. Among the Republicans benefiting are Reps. Brad Finstad (R-Minn.), Mike Carey (R-Ohio) and Rob Wittman (R-Va.), along with GOP candidates Ralph Alvarado (KY-6), Alex Mealer (TX-9) and Jenny Costa Honeycutt (S.C.-1). The intrigue: The GOP's pullback in some districts has fueled speculation that Republicans are giving up on the House to save the Senate. But Scalise argued it will still benefit his members. He pointed to Iowa, where the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC allied with House Republicans, pulled financial support from Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' district. Senate Republicans subsequently bought the airtime for Ashley Hinson. "You actually get a three for one, " Scalise said, arguing that shifting the ad time to Hinson will benefit Miller-Meeks, Rep. Zach Nunn and the Republican running to succeed Hinson in her House district. "You're going to probably see that in some other areas too," Scalise said. He pointed to Senate races in North Carolina and Texas, where he acknowledged "challenges" at the top of the ticket. The bottom line: Scalise isn't ready to look beyond Election Day, even as Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) publicly weighed in on that very scenario last week. Johnson said he intends to remain the top House Republican even if Democrats win the majority. The race for the top job could become a three-way fight among Johnson, Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio). Scalise repeatedly declined to say whether he would endorse Johnson for minority leader or consider running himself. "Anybody who's thinking about planning for us losing is in the wrong business," Scalise told Axios.

events.title: Waymo plans to quintuple its fleet

The company has also rebranded versions of a vehicle made by Zeekr, a unit of CCP-linked company Geely Holding Group. Know More Waymo recently raised debt for the first time, and it came without guarantees from Alphabet, its parent company. It borrowed the $5 billion from private credit lenders, and the deal allows the company to use its fleet in the future to borrow more by securitizing leases.

events.title: Zelensky lobbies senators to press White House on alleged intel and weapons curbs
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he claimed are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies. Why it matters: Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has quietly imposed these limits without admitting it publicly in an attempt to press Zelensky to accept a deal to end the war that includes more concessions to Russia. Trump and White House officials have denied for days that they've imposed any restrictions on Ukraine. Driving the news: The crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia during a round of negotiations between his envoys and Ukrainian officials in Miami. The Ukrainians claimed that Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened that Trump could cut off Ukraine from U.S. intelligence and stop selling weapons if it continued to ignore requests not to target Russian oil refineries . U.S. officials denied such a threat. They said Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, Witkoff and Kushner said.​ Behind the scenes: During a virtual meeting with a bipartisan group of senators led by Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Zelensky laid out the various problems Ukraine has been experiencing since the Miami meeting. Axios obtained a transcript from Ukrainian officials. Elon Musk's Starlink and the U.S. military's Starshield satellite systems remain partially restricted — despite claims by the White House to the contrary. "We still have no explanation for this. Just different strange stories we're hearing, unfortunately," Zelensky told the senators. It's hampering Ukraine's ability to shoot down Russian attack drones, he added. On three occasions the past week, including on Sunday, Ukraine didn't receive early warnings from the U.S. about Russian ballistic missile attacks, Zelensky said, suggesting it was a sign that intelligence sharing has been curbed. "We have received no clear explanation from Washington – why this is happening," he added. Zelensky said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is not signing off on the delivery of Patriot interceptors and AIM-9x missiles for the NASAMS air-defense system, even though NATO countries have already paid for them. "We have almost no Patriot interceptors left from the U.S. partners," he said. "All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us," Zelensky said. ​"We want to understand what is happening, why it's happening, and where all of this is heading." What they're saying : Tillis said after the meeting that Congress "remains committed to standing with Ukraine and our European allies to end Russia's brutal aggression and secure lasting peace." Blumenthal said afterwards that "bipartisan support for Ukraine was clear and unequivocal, which we'll be expressing in upcoming action." "Appeasement won't work with Putin, a thug who understands only strength and force," he added. The other side: President Trump told reporters on Monday that the U.S. is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine and said he didn't know who ordered the throttling of the Starlink satellite system. "But I am gonna find out," he said. "Frankly Zelensky is not helping matters much. He doesn't want to stop the war. Zelensky doesn't know what he is talking about," the president said. "Maybe it's time for Zelensky to let somebody else negotiate on behalf of Ukraine. … We have given a lot to Ukraine. They have given nothing to us." State of play: Zelensky spoke with Witkoff and Kushner on Sunday. They asked Ukraine again to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian officials said. Zelensky told the senators that he proposed to the U.S. envoys that Ukraine halt strikes on refineries for 30 days. In return, the U.S. would supply Ukraine with Patriot interceptors so it could defend itself from Russian ballistic missiles during that 30-day period. Zelensky told the senators that Witkoff and Kushner haven't shown any openness to the idea. What to watch: Zelensky told the senators that he'll be in Oslo, Norway next week and could meet with Witkoff and Kushner on Tuesday or Wednesday. Kushner and Witkoff could then continue on from Oslo to Moscow to meet with Putin, a source familiar with the matter said.

events.title: Citing ProPublica, Lawmakers Introduce Bill to Help U.S. Citizens Sue ICE for Wrongful Detentions
events.summary: Photo illustration by ProPublica. Source images: Congress and videos obtained by ProPublica. What Happened: A New Mexico Democrat in the House introduced a bill last week that would make it easier for U.S. citizens to sue immigration agents and the federal government over wrongful detentions and arrests. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández credited ProPublica’s reporting as the catalyst for the bill, the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act. Earlier this month, we revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been detained in warrantless arrests during the second Trump administration. Leger Fernández said the legislation would roll back the protections from lawsuits that agents and the federal government currently have. It would also establish a minimum level of compensation for people who win their suits, and extend the statute of limitations for such cases. The legislation would also take back any unspent Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding from President Donald Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Leger Fernández’s bill was introduced with co-sponsor Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, a New Jersey Democrat. Why It Matters: It can be difficult to sue federal officers for wrongful arrests or excessive force, or for local prosecutors to bring charges . Federal agents can claim immunity in response to civil lawsuits or to state charges and can move their cases to federal court. People who accuse immigration agents of wrongdoing can currently only sue in a narrow set of circumstances, and p revious Democratic bills aiming to change that have not passed. Some local prosecutors have announced investigations into the wrongful arrests of U.S. citizens or prosecuted federal agents accused of wrongdoing during immigration enforcement actions. What They Said: In an interview with ProPublica, Leger Fernández emphasized that accountability could not only address past wrongs, it may also help head them off in the future. “We know that when there are consequences, bad actors start behaving better because they don’t want to face those consequences,” she said. Without legislation, Leger Fernández said, agents “will continue to violate the law, to violate their own policy, and to violate the Constitution without any consequences.” Asked about the legislation, the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, repeated claims that it is not arresting U.S. citizens and defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.” Background: The federal government denies that there is any pattern of immigration agents detaining U.S. citizens, but according to ProPublica’s count, more than 100 citizens were held after agents questioned their citizenship. At least 70 children and teens were also detained. Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens after our earlier investigation found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents . events.title: US sanction waivers are Russian economic boon
events.summary: The Trump administration is delivering a string of victories — for the Russian economy. Within weeks of waiving sanctions on Russian diesel, President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia’s trading partners , prompting a fresh wave of GOP pushback that is building by the hour. “I want to see those used,” Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., said earlier Monday . Neither waiver is projected to have much long-term effect on US prices. But one expert estimated the diesel waiver alone could help Russian exporters net $30 to $40 more per ton, in turn padding Moscow’s tax revenue. The UK last year estimated that global sanctions had previously deprived Russia of $450 billion in war funds , including $154 billion in lost oil revenue and $285 billion in frozen central bank reserves. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Semafor both waivers were necessary to “see this brutal war [in Ukraine] come to an end,” echoing an argument Trump made on Truth Social . “Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia,” Rogers said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, has argued that the latest waiver did not provide Russia with sanctions relief because “no sanctions were lifted.” “There is a 60-day period so we can examine what’s going on,” he told NBC News . — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Trump open to summit with Xi and Putin — to discuss denuclearization
events.summary: President Trump wants to hold a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China next month to discuss "denuclearization" — but not necessarily Ukraine. Why it matters: Such a summit between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia would be unprecedented. Trump has been talking for two years about his aspiration to reach a deal with Russia and China to reduce the number of nuclear weapons. But so far, Putin and Xi haven't shown much openness to the idea. Driving the news: Trump is expected to travel to China in mid-November to participate in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in the city of Shenzhen. The Kremlin has been floating the idea of holding such a meeting since July. Putin raised the issue in two phone calls with Trump, including one last week. The Chinese government hasn't expressed a willingness to hold such a summit. What he's saying: When asked Monday whether such a summit could discuss ending the war in Ukraine, Trump said he wants to hold such a trilateral meeting, but in order to discuss other issues. "I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, we would have it to talk about denuclearization," he said.

events.title: Nvidia CEO urges German manufacturers to adopt AI, saying digital tech won't replace heavy industry
events.summary: Nvidia's Jensen Huang is urging German manufacturing companies to combine their expertise in physical machines with artificial intelligence to, as he put it, “re-engineer” the economy FRANKFURT, Germany -- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urged Germany's makers of cars and industrial machines to quickly adopt artificial intelligence to “re-engineer” the country's struggling business model by tapping its wealth of manufacturing data and expertise. Huang, whose company designs the powerful computer chips and software used by companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to develop AI applications, said that digital technology would never replace manufacturing and the engineering world of cars and robots where Germany has vast experience. Or, as he put it, “electrons will never replace atoms.” But he said industry would benefit by leaning into technology. “The next wave of AI is physical. This is where AI interacts with the physical world: robotics, manufacturing, cars, heavy industry,” Huang said Monday during a discussion with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at an investment conference in Berlin. "And so AI can only augment your capability. It will not replace your capability. So take advantage of the technology." Huang said Germany's data and expertise on manufacturing “is your natural resource, it belongs to the nation" but it needs to take better advantage of AI. "This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful. You don't have another chance,” he said. European leaders like Merz are looking to AI as a potential source of growth but are also concerned about the extent of European dependence on U.S. tech companies in the field. Europe's wealth of high quality public-sector and machine-readable manufacturing data could serve as grist for AI, an opportunity cited by former European Central Bank head Mario Draghi as an area where Europe could compete with the U.S. and China in the AI field. Tennessee Titans winless no more with chance to work on their offensive issues Cuba says US-based suspects confessed in armed incursion and face terrorism charges Japan launches spacecraft to mysterious moons of Mars in a bold mission to bring home soil samples Huang and Merz said AI was an opportunity for Germany's so-called “mittelstand,” the hundreds of small- and medium-sized companies in highly specialized industrial sectors. Merz is struggling to revive growth in Germany after years of near-stagnation after the pandemic. Among the economy's headwinds are high energy prices after losing cheap Russian natural gas due to the invasion of Ukraine , competition from China in sectors like autos where Germany once dominated, and excessive red tape and permissions that hold up projects for years. All that has put a damper on an economy heavily oriented toward building complicated machines for export, including cars, trains, aircraft and factory equipment. Europe lags the U.S. in building out the data centers that offer the massive computing capacity to train artificial intelligence applications, and faces concerns over the security of European companies' sensitive data against subpoenas and criminal warrants on servers owned by U.S. companies and thus exposed to the U.S. legal system even if they're in Europe. Huang appeared to address such concerns by urging Germany to import AI technology but adding that “you should not export your culture, export your values, export your knowledge." Huang said Germany should “take advantage of artificial intelligence. Let them codify, let them program, let them teach this artificial intelligence and keep it here in Germany, and let's re-engineer, the chancellor's words, Germany. This is your chance to do it.” EU leaders push back on a major budget proposal, putting a deal by 2027 in doubt 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: OpenAI Engineer Accused of Spying on Executives Ordered to Remain in Custody
events.summary: The former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a company conference room must stay in custody while he awaits trial, a federal judge ruled on Monday after expressing concerns about his ties to Saudi Arabia. US prosecutors alleged Abdulrahman Alfozan is a flight risk because the Saudi Arabian government has offered to support him with no strings attached. They cited, for example, the Saudi consulate’s offer to work with a bail bonds firm to help fund Alfozan’s release. Federal magistrate judge Alex Tse questioned whether Alfozan is an “asset” for the kingdom and how a bond backed by the government could keep him in the country. “I find that problematic,” Tse said. “It seems like a blank check. ‘We’re going to pay whatever the court wants to get him out.’ I’m more interested in people from his family wanting to put up assets.” William Pernik, an attorney for Alfozan, dismissed the flight risk worries as baseless. But he failed to convince the judge that Alfozan was committed to his life in the US. “There is a real threat here that once he leaves the case is over,” Tse said. Aflozan appeared in an orange prison uniform and a medical face mask pulled down over his neck on Monday in Tse’s San Francisco courtroom, which was filled to capacity with journalists, students on a field trip, and about 20 people supporting Alfozan. Employee attempts to steal confidential company information are common in Silicon Valley. But Alfozan’s case has drawn international attention for the alleged amateur spycraft and geopolitical tensions at the center of it. Authorities haven’t offered a potential motive but have noted Alfozan has worked for a Saudi venture capital firm, offered consulting services to Saudi companies, and is supposedly friendly with people high up in the Saudi government. Pernik said there is no evidence of Alfozan spying for Saudi Arabia or engaging in something covert. “It’s not as if he sneaked in under the covers of darkness,” he said of the OpenAI conference room. “This was an open room where anybody could work in.” The Saudi embassy didn’t respond to a request for comment. After the hour-long hearing, Pernik told reporters he was disappointed with the custody ruling and would continue to try to fight it. While Alfozan is a US permanent resident who had been on the path to obtaining citizenship, his ties to his native Saudi Arabia have come under scrutiny. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan was “in frequent communications via WhatsApp” with a member of the Saudi royal family throughout 2025 and 2026. The Saudi royal, who is not identified, was allegedly recruiting Alfozan to return to the country for a job working on a forthcoming AI initiative, according to a court filing. “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!” the individual wrote to Alfozan this past May, per the filing. Alfozan allegedly “responded ‘100,’ indicating he agreed.” US authorities also allege that the Saudi government bought Alfozan's wife and infant son a ticket to return to the country a few days after his arrest. She ended up leaving sooner on another flight booked by her sister’s husband, who works for the Saudi navy, according to attorneys for both sides. Alfozan's wife has not been accused of wrongdoing, and the FBI last week declined to comment on whether she would face any charges. Alfozan was at OpenAI for just over a year when the AI lab discovered a covert audio recording device hidden in a wad of toilet paper behind a TV in an executive conference room used for confidential business meetings. OpenAI found the device in late September, connected it to Alfozan, and then fired him earlier this month just before the FBI arrested him. Alfozan faces five years in prison on a single count of using a device to intercept communications, but prosecutors say additional charges are possible. Included among the government’s evidence are alleged conversations between Alfozan and an AI chatbot in which he asked for help setting up listening devices. Prosecutors also produced a photo taken of Alfozan looking behind the TV after OpenAI had removed the recorder. It’s unclear what, if anything, was recorded, because the device’s data was encrypted, according to authorities. Authorities say they also found components for recording devices at Alfozan’s home and photos of other OpenAI monitors and another OpenAI conference room on his phone. OpenAI previously said it recovered a second listening device in a bag Alfozan brought to the office and left unattended. Pernik claimed the electronics at Alfozan’s home were for home monitoring projects, including trying to improve a smart litter box for their cat. “This is a gentleman who spent 15 years of life immersed at this intersection of technology and personal life,” Pernik told the judge. Authorities said ahead of the hearing that they believed Alfozan had the means to flee.

events.title: PSA: Patch your Plex media server before someone hacks it
events.summary: Recently fixed vulnerabilities in the Plex Media Server are under active exploitation in attacks that, when successful, install malware, including cryptominers and residential proxy apps, a researcher said. Plex fixed four vulnerabilities at the start of last month. Three weeks later, published CVE designations revealed five vulnerabilities, with one of them carrying a severity rating of 8.6 out of 10. A researcher last week revealed an exploit that chained four of them together to achieve remote code execution of the device running a vulnerable Plex version. The researcher named the chain "Plex2Shell." Complex exploit chain The new details allowed a separate researcher to create a honeypot that could track attempts in the wild to exploit the vulnerability chain. Within a day, the researcher began seeing active scanning of the simulated Plex server and eventually successful attempts to infect devices. So far, successful attacks are installing two payloads. One is a cryptominer, which uses the device to mine cryptocurrency and deposit it into a wallet controlled by the attacker. The other payload is residential proxy software, which allows people to anonymize their Internet activity (much of it illegal) by connecting to the infected box and then using it to send the user’s traffic to a final destination. events.title: Germany Wants to Lead the World in Industrial AI: How NVIDIA Will Help
events.summary: In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI. Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing. The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies. Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA. The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI. Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.” Germany’s Ambition to Integrate AI With Industry Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition. “We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.” Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience. “The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.” Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it. “That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.” Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included. “If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.” Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution. “This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.” Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI. “I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.” Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe. NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs . Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare. Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care. Mirelo , a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen. Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years. Siemens and NVIDIA Advance Autonomous Manufacturing; Record-Breaking Quantum Simulation Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory , advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER, Europe’s largest supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a record-breaking simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The 104-qubit simulation is the largest and most detailed of its kind to date. events.title: I recently wrote about why we need to treat models as insider risks, with security controls sitting outside the model itself. [Read more]
events.summary: I recently wrote about why we need to treat models as insider risks, with security controls sitting outside the model itself. Today, were putting that principle into practice by expanding Project Perception with new capabilities to help continuously assess agent risk, adapt permissions, and contain threats. The emergence of powerful cyber models has driven organizations to focus on attackers leveraging AI to run their campaigns. We must also address the agents already deployed inside our walls: the AI Insider. Agents are now running across the enterprise at scale. They often have more privileges than they need. They aren't malicious. But they're trained to get results, not to follow an organizations norms or judgment. Securing the AI insider requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. In July, we announced Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue, and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI-driven attacks from the outside of the enterprise. Today, we are extending that cyber stack to help defenders secure AI Insiders by implementing deterministic controls on non-deterministic intelligence. Agentic security provides speed. Practitioners provide judgment. Learn how Perception can help defenders operate at the same speed as the systems they are protecting against. There shouldn't be a choice between innovation and safety. https://lnkd.in/geZZSXhd We really like the direction here. One of our concerns with AI agents has been how easily permissions can outlive the tasks they were originally granted for. Being able to continuously reassess access based on what an agent is actually doing could make a significant difference. "with security controls sitting outside of the model itself", I'd argue outside of the lab as well. Powerful framing - treating models as insider risks changes everything. Security outside the model is the real trust layer. Framing agents as insiders clicks for me. Does adapting permissions happen automatically, or does a person still sign off on each change? A crucial step towards responsible AI adoption Satya Nadella . Agents need more than safeguards built into the model itself; they need continuous monitoring, clear permission boundaries, and controls that can respond as risks change. Trustworthy AI isn’t just about what an agent can do, but how we govern what it’s allowed to do. The model diversity point from your essay matters most for the Guardian Agents. If they run on the same model family as the agents they supervise, a shared blind spot or injected instruction could get past both The Product challenge for Microsoft is making these security controls practical inside real enterprise workflows. Agents need enough autonomy to be useful, but clear boundaries for sensitive actions, exceptions, and human approval. Hayete Gallot raises an important issue here: security needs to adapt as agent responsibilities change, without making every workflow harder to complete. "Agentic insiders" frames well. We've been treating agents like software when they act more like new hires with admin access. With the “AEGIS operating model”.. said for a while that agent security should be as standard as antivirus on a laptop, so this is good to see. One thing I'd add: in regulated sectors, especially where people-money-trust play in, someone has to own agent-flow outcomes. Live monitoring tells you what an agent did. Based on risk, a named owner can align those outcomes to who answers for it. The real security problem isn’t what an agent can do. It’s how long yesterday’s permission remains valid today. Spot on, Satya Nadella and Hayete Gallot! Framing autonomous AI models as potential 'insider risks' is a critical shift toward mature enterprise governance. In industrial automation and complex asset operations, non-deterministic intelligence must always operate within strict, deterministic boundaries. Granting autonomous agents operational scope without layered permission controls, continuous monitoring, and external security constraints introduces systemic fragility. Bridging high-speed automated execution with authoritative human judgment ensures operational resilience without compromising innovation. From an executive technology governance perspective, what framework do you find most effective for defining the threshold where an autonomous agent's authority must automatically trigger deterministic human oversight? events.title: Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties
events.summary: The U.S. House of Representatives votes on the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022. AP Photo/Patrick Semansky A massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote in the U.S. House or the Senate . But the billions of dollars it authorized benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it. Enacted in 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act squeaked through the Senate only through a tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris . It authorized spending US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions , primarily through subsidies such as a tax credit of up to $7,500 for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making commercial buildings more energy efficient , rather than by imposing new fees or taxes. Before the 2024 election, over $204 billion had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives. While Republicans opposed the legislation, 79% of the law’s investment went to Republican congressional districts. Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor investing in clean energy technology at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects. Benefits of federal investment Elected officials are sometimes accused of “ pork barrel politics ,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth. Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, 18 Republican House members urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.” That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even more Republican House members called for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them. A Toyota battery-manufacturing plant in Liberty, N.C., received billions in support through the Inflation Reduction Act. Logan Cyrus/AFP via Getty Images The bill’s funding affected the 2024 election Our analysis finds that Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members of both parties in the 2024 election. During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “ economic development opportunities ,” while Democrats directly mentioned the act itself. Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in North Carolina and Georgia to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for corporate tax breaks from the law and hoped to benefit from increased consumer demand because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles. In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022. We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022. When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using statistical methods to isolate the effects of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result. Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have. These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding. While previous federal spending projects helped incumbent House members in elections , we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that incumbents claiming credit for the investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas. President Donald Trump signs a major tax cut and spending cut bill on July 4, 2025. Samuel Corum/Getty Images Dismantling the subsidies and tax breaks Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions . A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements and electric vehicle purchases. The Trump administration has also moved to expand fossil fuel production on federal lands. This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that some climate-related tax credits remained even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership. events.title: ReactOS reaches major milestone with NTFS install support
events.summary: Open source Windows alternative ReactOS has reached a major milestone: The operating system can now be installed directly onto an NTFS drive partition. As reported by Phoronix , the move to NTFS clears a long-standing hurdle for the project and brings it one step closer to finally reaching beta. Prior to this latest announcement, ReactOS required users to keep a FAT32 partition for installations. A proprietary Microsoft-developed filesystem, NTFS can trace its roots back through the Windows NT family lineage starting in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1. The variant introduced with Windows XP in 2001 remains the standard used by most Windows systems today. With ReactOS's stated goal of reaching binary compatibility with Windows Server 2003, being confined to FAT32 partitions was a practical barrier to clear on the way to reproducing the Windows environment. However, users looking to hop off the Windows train shouldn't be grabbing their bags just yet. ReactOS wrote that the new driver still "lacks caching (which causes inferior performance), journaling and security support." So while the new driver is here, even the most intrepid of OS tinkerers should tread carefully. The ReactOS team warned in its announcement on X that there are still "potentially undiscovered bugs." events.title: Anthropic commits 5% stake to 'public benefit fund' amid growing AI backlash
events.summary: Claude developer Anthropic has announced it is committing 5 per cent of its shares to a “public benefit fund” amid growing backlash over artificial intelligence. And Tesla boss Elon Musk has promised to give a share in his SpaceX company to “every kid in America” next year. AI start-up Anthropic said in a blog post the fund would be a wholly owned liability company and that it would receive an additional 2 per cent of Anthropic shares at the board's discretion for every 50 per cent increase in the company's value above a to-be-announced baseline. It said establishing the fund, which would be subject to shareholder approval, will give it more flexibility and scale to make donations “to traditional non-profit or direct distributions to specific populations”. “Because of the way the fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” it said on Sunday. The company is planning one of the biggest IPOs in history as a public benefit corporation, possibly as soon as November. The company said in June it had submitted a confidential filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission for its proposed IPO. Abu Dhabi technology investment firm MGX took part in Anthropic's recent $65 billion funding round. طحنون بن زايد يترأس الاجتماع الثالث لمجلس إدارة شركة "إم جي إكس" لعام 2026، الذي استعرض الأنشطة الاستثمارية للشركة، ومشاركتها في جولة التمويل من الفئة H لـ"أنثروبيك" بقيمة 65 مليار دولار، وجولة التمويل الاستراتيجية لـ"داتابريكس" بقيمة خمسة مليارات دولار، والاستثمار في "سبيس إكس". pic.twitter.com/YTfHQDYArP — مكتب أبوظبي الإعلامي (@ADMediaOffice) October 19, 2026 Anthropic gave the labour market as one area of focus for the fund, with a $200 million commitment to study the issue. Research from the International Monetary Fund estimates about 60 per cent of jobs in advanced economies are exposed to AI. Separate research from Goldman Sachs said recent anecdotes and data suggest AI displacement in the US could be strong among entry-level workers. Mr Musk responded to Anthropic's announcement on X saying, “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." He pledged one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year in a separate post on Monday, without providing further details. “This will be the first of many,” Mr Musk wrote. Later on Monday, President Donald Trump hailed Mr Musk's suggestion, which he implied would be applied to the Trump Accounts programme. "This is exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS — Bringing together the GREAT PRIVATE SECTOR, Elon and so many more, to invest in our children, by far our greatest and most important asset, and give every American Child a piece of the American Dream," Mr Trump wrote on social media. The programme allows donors to make contributions without paying a capital gains tax, in some circumstances. The Treasury Department said in a September notice that it was seeking to automatically enrol up to 60 million children in the programme. With about 73 million people under 18 years of age in the US, the pledge would be valued at about $10.7 billion at the company's Friday close at $146.03 a share. SpaceX was trading 0.78 per cent higher at $147.33 a share as of 2:30pm ET (8pm GST) on Monday. The pledges from Anthropic and Mr Musk come as Americans grow more concerned about AI. A recent AP-Norc poll found 64 per cent of US adults believe the technology is developing “too fast”, compared to 27 per cent saying development has been “about right” and 8 per cent saying it is moving “too slow”. Building the massive data centres housing the technology is also leading to rising energy costs. A recent poll from Quinnipiac University said about 73 per cent of US voters oppose the building of data centres in their communities. AI executives and President Donald Trump have recently adopted a defensive stance amid this growing backlash, with the US leader calling AI anxieties a "hoax". In September, he hosted chief executives from Nvidia, Meta and other Big Tech firms at the White House, where they signed what was billed as a morally binding agreement to help police AI. The document encourages companies to "implement robust internal controls" to monitor models during training, empower an internal team to ensure controls are operating as intended, link up with an independent external auditor, and designate an independent committee to oversee and receive reports from the team operating the controls. Mr Trump has also opposed AI regulations, saying such orders would put the US at a disadvantage against China in the AI race.

events.title: IEEE Report Highlights How Members Are Engineering for Public Good
events.summary: Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered. Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles: Shaping trustworthy digital experiences for children online. An IEEE collaboration with Indonesian policymakers led to a new regulation to protect children, a first of its kind in the region. The advanced frameworks used for the design of Internet platforms and systems are based on the IEEE 2089-2021 and 2089.1-2024 standards. The IEEE 2089-2021 Standard for an Age-Appropriate Digital Services Framework Based on the 5Rights Principles for Children provides practical steps to qualify online products and services. The follow-up, the IEEE 2089.1-2024 Standard for Online Age Verification, provides a framework for designing, specifying, evaluating, and deploying age-verification systems. You can learn more about the two standards in “ IEEE Makes Strides to Improve Online Safety for Kids .” Catalyzing humanitarian outreach. Last year IEEE launched its Mobile Outreach Vehicle (MOVE) program in India. The vehicle brings educational resources to communities and can provide communication and technology support to relief workers and survivors during emergencies. In 2024, for example, MOVE helped survivors of Hurricanes Helene and Milton in the Southeastern United States. When the vehicles are not deployed, IEEE MOVE remains engaged in outreach efforts, participating in 25 STEM educational events such as one in San Diego in 2023 . Preserving Tech History. The IEEE Global Museum , developed by the IEEE History Center , presents traveling exhibits to educate the public about the history of technology and its impact on society. In “ IEEE’s Global Museum Brings Engineering History to You ,” you can learn about current exhibits “Unseen Signals: E. Howard Armstrong’s Radio Revolution” and “Microchips That Shook the World.” EPICS in IEEE. This program provides nonprofit organizations with technology solutions while broadening undergraduate students’ hands-on experiences. Last year US $290,000 was awarded to a record-breaking number of service projects around the world . Among the 48 projects was one in which a student team in Macedonia created IoT-driven sensing and display devices to help measure and promote awareness of pollution and air-quality issues in the capital city of Skopje. IEEE TryEngineering. This initiative inspires preuniversity students to pursue technology and engineering careers. It awarded US $70,379 in grants to 58 programs around the world. One is its TryEngineering Summer Institute , a nine-day summer sleepaway camp for students ages 13 to 17. More than 310 students participated last year, learning about aerospace and artificial intelligence . IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu. IEEE-HKN has more than 260 collegiate chapters worldwide and more than 200,000 members. The honor society encourages and recognizes excellence in education, professional practice, and meritorious work within IEEE’s designated fields of interest. IEEE-HKN members last year contributed 110,442 volunteer hours to universities and communities, and they held 827 service and outreach events and 137 STEM outreach activities. Last year IEEE and HKN celebrated the 15th anniversary of their merger . IEEE Connecting the Unconnected Challenge. This annual global competition solicits innovative solutions from startups, grassroots organizations, universities, and others working to bridge the digital divide. The Institute wrote about last year’s winners . They included a solar-powered community broadband network in Tanzania, a low-cost method for accessing the Internet that uses FM radio and a short message service, and a strategy for utilizing India’s rural broadband infrastructure to deliver medical services to people living in isolated, tribal, and other underserved regions. Supporting Sustainable Climate Efforts. IEEE helps foster the exchange of technical knowledge and information to develop technologies for a sustainable climate. “ IEEE Plays a Pivotal Role in Climate Mitigation Talks ” reported how the organization enhanced its standing as a trusted, neutral authority on the role of technology in climate change mitigation and adaptation. Leaders, including 2023 IEEE President Saifur Rahman , showcased tech solutions at COP30 and the International Symposium on Achieving a Sustainable Climate . Also, “ IEEE Young Professionals Talked Sustainability Tech at Climate Week NYC ” reported on the group’s activities during the 2024 Climate Week NY , the largest annual climate event, featuring more than 600 activities throughout New York City. Engineering: A force for good “The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report . “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.” Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report. “Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact. “IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”

events.summary: Global financial institutions managing more than $5 trillion in assets have announced plans to establish a presence in Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM amid rapid expansion of the emirate’s economy. Overall, 14 financial firms have plans to set up base at the international financial centre, state news agency Wam reported on Monday, quoting ADGM chairman Ahmed Al Zaabi. “In 2025, Abu Dhabi's economy grew by 7 per cent and our non-oil economy grew by 8 per cent, contributing more than half of total gross domestic product,” Mr Al Zaabi told the third Abu Dhabi Investment Forum in London. Established in 2015, the ADGM operates under the direct application of English Common Law, with independent courts and a regulatory framework supporting it. A base in Abu Dhabi provides global investors and money managers with opportunities to expand regional operations and work closely with some of the world's biggest sovereign wealth funds, as well as large family offices and institutional partners. ADGM has been attracting a number of high-profile companies in recent months, including global private markets firm Pantheon , private credit lender Blue Owl Capital, tech-focused US company Vista Equity Partners, the world’s largest listed hedge fund Man Group, Barings, Bain Capital, Cantor and Swiss derivative investment company Adapt Investment Managers. Eurazeo, a European asset manager with €40 billion ($45.2 billion) in assets under management, as well as global private markets firm Pantheon, have also recently opened offices in the ADGM. Last month, Capital Group, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, secured a licence from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of the ADGM to operate as a regulated investment manager. Collectively, asset managers which had already established operations in the ADGM in the first half of the year oversee more than $2.1 trillion in global assets under management, the ADGM said last month. Abu Dhabi is developing industries across artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, energy and life sciences that will shape future markets, Mr Al Zaabi said, as reported by Wam on Monday. “Our businesses are extending their international reach, establishing partnerships and entering new markets. Abu Dhabi has long-term capital competitive energy, world-class infrastructure and access to some of the world's fastest-growing markets,” he said.
