events.title: Bob Woodward reveals "dream source" in memoir, "Secrets," out next month
events.summary: Bob Woodward — in an eye-opening excerpt from his forthcoming memoir, "Secrets," that's previewed in the new issue of The New Yorker — reveals that one of his best friends, the late Richard Darman, was also one of his best sources during the Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush administrations. "Darman was willing, even eager at times, to talk about the most sensitive intelligence matters, including N.S.A. intercepts and covert C.I.A. operations," Woodward writes in his book , out Nov. 15. "He was always careful not to talk about matters that would harm national security, I believed, but he would go right up to the edge — a reporter's dream source." Why it matters: Woodward, 83 — who followed the blockbuster Watergate reporting of his youth with a shelf of revelatory books about American presidents — gives a searingly honest account of the collapse of his friendship with Darman after a Post series that was damaging to Bush. Woodward details a disappointment in his Washington Post career and, in the case of a story where he was the responsible editor, a "moral failing." The New Yorker calls the Darman excerpt "A Dangerous Friendship," revealing the danger of "getting too close to a source." Woodward and Darman never reconciled, although "Secrets" describes their deathbed encounter. Woodward writes in his New Yorker debut that he and Darman, who controlled the paper flow to Reagan as staff secretary and was budget director for Bush 41, "had countless long lunches together — Saturday or Sunday — at the Madison Hotel, across the street from the Post , discussing government, journalism, and ourselves": "I felt like I was getting a master class in how government really operated. Plus, many scoops. In later years, Darman would drive out on weekends to our country house near Annapolis, Maryland, to spend large parts of the day with me and my wife, the journalist Elsa Walsh, who was particularly fond of him. Some people found him arrogant, but I loved his comfortable confidence as a friend and a source. It was part of what made him so extraordinary and valuable. He knew how to turn on the charm, and he did for both Elsa and me." Behind the scenes: "From critical national-security information to the colorful office tales he shared, Darman provided me with a gold mine of information," Woodward recalls. "I interviewed him in at least fifty-eight meetings or phone conversations. I have boxes filled with hundreds of pages of notes on our discussions. After our most important conversations, as is my practice, I typed a memo of one to six pages, laying out in detail what he'd said." Detailing Darman's " hatchet man " role, Woodward reveals that the "hardest of Darman's targets to dislodge was the First Lady, Nancy Reagan. While Darman poured scorn on her in private, describing her to me as a 'mean bitch,' he could not find a way to drive a stake into her heart." After a hard-won legislative victory, Darman told Woodward, Reagan said: "Whew! Ever feel like you shit a pineapple?" Keep reading ... Get "Secrets."

events.title: The Story of Billy Evans and ‘Theranos 2.0’
events.summary: Warning: Light movie spoilers below. Read at your own risk. Even before becoming the stars of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s much-buzzed-about new documentary, Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans were a special kind of couple. Holmes “may have ultimately failed to change the world in the way she set out,” Evans wrote in a letter at the time of Holmes’ sentencing in 2022, “but she has undeniably changed mine.” The Theranos founder, in the hardest years of her life, taught her husband “a patience” that he “would have previously dismissed as unnecessary and soft.” She brought out his inner light, another sentencing letter from a friend of the couple reports: When they returned from a “monthslong camping trip,” Evans “displayed a new level of compassion in his demeanor, a strong sense of intention with his actions, and a heightened desire to listen to and look at others with purpose.” Whatever others might think, Evans was saying, Holmes wasn’t the only one of the pair that had been given a second chance. And they might get a second second chance with Haemanthus, a company that Evans is keen to reassure social media followers is absolutely—most definitely— “ not Theranos 2.0 .” A person familiar with the business told The Wall Street Journal that Holmes is not involved. 🔗 Nathan Fielder Tells Us Everything 🔗 The New Fan’s Guide to the Unreal World of Nathan Fielder 🔗 How Elizabeth Holmes Tricked WIRED—and Everyone Else 🔗 From the Archive: This Woman Invented a Way to Run 30 Lab Tests on Only One Drop of Blood But viewers of You Can See Everything will watch Evans agreeing to the characterization that he and Holmes are making Theranos 2.0. They discuss the trajectory to make a working prototype of something on camera; they talk about collaborating on product ideas from prison. “To meet her, to spend time with her, that was the intention of the film,” the Austin, Texas-based Evans told David Friedberg, a cohost of the podcast All-In . “I haven’t seen it yet. I might think this is the dumbest thing that I have done.” So who is Evans? And what is he building? Long before fathering two children—son William and daughter Invicta—with Holmes, Evans grew up in San Diego in one of the city’s more prominent families, heir to midcentury pioneers in the Southern California tourism industry. His grandparents, William and Anne Evans were “two young hoteliers [who] saw the future,” according to the family’s company website, and opened up what would become a popular resort hotel on a mudflat in Mission Bay in 1953. They added a second nearby, and today own a third in La Jolla. This brought generational wealth. The business passed in part to Billy’s father, also named William. Billy went to the Francis Parker School, one of the most prestigious private schools in the city. “The Evans family is very well respected in San Diego,” said a contemporary of Evans’ who worked for the family as a teenager, but Billy “always a source of drama, would try to fight to start fights.” He had “affluenza” and was “just your classic spoiled rich kid” in a way that was not true of all his relatives. The inner light would come around later. (Evans did not want to be interviewed for the story and did not answer specific questions.) After graduating from MIT with a bachelor of science in economics, Evans reportedly tried to launch a startup offering medical concierge services. This failed. He then took jobs in a handful of tech companies, including LinkedIn and Luminar Technologies, a self-driving car company. In 2017, at a “Fleet Week charity event” in the Bay Area, the then 25-year-old met Holmes and was “captivated,” he later wrote the judge at her sentencing, “by her childish wonder and authenticity.” There was some reporting in the early years that the Evans family was not entirely enthused by this courtship, but doubts seemed to have dissipated by the time of the Holmes trial. Billy’s father, William Evans, showed up to the courtroom incognito , under the alias “Hanson,” identifying himself as a kind of mechanic. (He owns an enormous classic car collection.) To journalists, he defended Holmes’ honor. In court, he turned heads by unwrapping a “large Rice Krispies Treat” whose crinkling foil drowned out the judge on the first day of jury selection, NPR reported. While in the film Evans and Holmes are both shown on fundraising calls, her name doesn’t appear in any of the incorporation documents of Haemanthus, the company Evans founded in 2022. There is little publicly available information on the company; to date, it has released no products and barely has a LinkedIn page , let alone a website. Yet its name can’t help but conjure up Theranos, and, indeed, its stated goal is to bring blood, urine, and saliva testing to American homes in the form of a countertop-size machine, which was more or less the goal of Theranos. But the technology of Haemanthus seems to be a bit different than that of Theranos.

events.title: He Tried to Set Limits on His State’s School Vouchers. Billionaires Helped Bankroll a Campaign to Unseat Him.
events.summary: PACs targeted former West Virginia Delegate Vernon Criss following his proposal to rein in state spending on school vouchers.  Will Price/West Virginia Legislature On a cold February morning at West Virginia’s Capitol, children in winter jackets, holding signs and their homework, clogged the hallways outside the House Finance Committee room. Delegate Vernon Criss, the committee’s chairperson, popped outside his office, then promptly walked back in.  Five days earlier, the Republican lawmaker had proposed to limit payouts from a voucher program that diverts public tax dollars to private education. Since then, families had shown up each morning, and with them lobbyists and organizers posting inflammatory assertions that the proposal would kill the program. Criss didn’t want that. Five years earlier, he voted to create the Hope Scholarship program, the nation’s first educational savings account program to have no income requirements. Since then, 11 other states have passed similar legislation.  In the first year of the Hope program in West Virginia, it cost the state $9 million. Now, as 2026 was beginning, it was set to expand, with estimates that it could cost $200 million or more a year. And Criss was concerned that unchecked growth of the program, coupled with a spree of tax cuts, could put the state budget into a tailspin. The state and its lawmakers needed “to face the music,” as Criss would later say. On that February day in Charleston, a staffer unlocked the committee door. Parents and media filed in, taking seats along the narrow benches lining the committee room’s walls. Kids lay on the floor. A delegate asked if the Hope Scholarship bill would be discussed. When Criss said no, the parents and their kids stood up and filed out.  Within the next few days, lawmakers would stop the effort to curtail spending on vouchers. And Criss would soon be fighting for his political life. Criss greets constituents supporting the Hope Scholarship. Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislature The money and organizing behind the demise of the bill, as well as the targeting of Criss, can be traced to “school choice” advocates at the local and national levels and their ability to spend huge sums to have their way. When Republicans assumed control of the West Virginia Legislature in 2015, school choice — their preferred terminology for voucher-style programs — became a rallying point for an array of political nonprofits. Through lobbying and supporting sympathetic lawmakers, they helped establish the Hope Scholarship six years later.  The first year, a little more than 2,300 students enrolled in the program , which was designed to permit more students over time. Today, 26,000 students are taking part , more than the enrollment in the state’s largest public school district. West Virginia has been part of a nationwide push, partially funded by billionaire-backed political groups , to use taxpayer dollars to fund private schools. Among the proponents of these programs are the influential Koch family network and Pennsylvania billionaire Jeffrey Yass, who has spent more than $350 million since 2015 on political campaigns, including a push for public funding for private education. In West Virginia, Arkansas and Texas , proponents have been eager to challenge anyone who got in the way, including fellow Republicans who voiced concerns. events.title: Rubio is in Uzbekistan to promote US ties and trade with Central Asia
events.summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is in Uzbekistan promoting trade and ties with Central Asia U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in Uzbekistan on Monday to promote trade and ties with Central Asia, during a trip that came amid rumblings that America’s top diplomat is ignoring pressing matters in favor of politically safer visits and meetings. The trip, which involves a stop in India later this week, seeks to promote U.S. economic and security ties with Central and South Asia . But it has only tangential links to the Trump administration’s current main foreign policy dilemmas in the Middle East and with the Russia-Ukraine war . Rubio has brushed aside suggestions he is eschewing the most difficult issues in favor of taking on lower-hanging diplomatic fruit with less risk of failure and political damage, and the State Department pushed back on the criticism of his schedule. In Samarkand, Rubio was meeting with his counterparts from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan under the C5+1 diplomatic forum, which brings together the five Central Asian countries and the United States to discuss security, trade and other shared concerns. Speaking to reporters ahead of the meeting, Rubio said “the United States wants to be a strong partner in Central Asia.” “Central Asia has just not gotten the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves. But that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now,” he said. Despite repeated assurances from multiple administrations that the U.S. would become more actively involved in Central Asia, the region has often languished as a foreign policy priority in Washington. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the newly independent Central Asian nations saw a brief surge in U.S. interest, but that waned until after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States, which turned America’s attention once again toward Afghanistan and its neighbors. The U.S. established a military presence in several countries mainly as transit points for equipment, materiel and provisions needed by U.S. and allied forces fighting the Taliban and al-Qaida in Afghanistan. As the U.S. wound down its 20-year operation in Afghanistan, the Trump administration, in both its first and second terms, has sought to elevate its ties with Central Asia due to its location between Russia and China, but also as an underdeveloped area ripe for U.S. business opportunities. Rubio’s trip, which has been heavily promoted by the U.S. ambassador to India and special presidential envoy for Central Asia, Sergio Gor, is perhaps the most ambitious U.S. attempt in decades to boost economic and commercial ties with the region. Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Rubio described “an incredible delegation” with representatives of almost 300 American businesses joining. North Korea threatens to restart propaganda broadcasts, deploy more weapons at border Corruption is top worry for Brazilian voters ahead of runoff between Bolsonaro, Lula Massachusetts Republican Shawn Oliver suspends campaign after arrest “Historically, Central Asia has been the crossroads for trade between the West and the East. And today, as part of a broader renaissance and global engagement, it stands once again to play that vital role in transnational commerce," he told officials at the meeting. The region is "a new location for investment, and it serves as a new location for export, a central terminal out of which materials that are vital for the future of all nations are being delivered,” he added. President Donald Trump hosted their leaders at a White House summit last November, and announced more than $130 billion in commercial deals, including agreements for regional airlines to purchase Boeing aircraft. The administration has also been keen to get the Muslim majority countries to join the Abraham Accords, which expanded the number of Arab states with diplomatic ties with Israel. Kazakhstan, which had already recognized Israel, is the only one of the five to sign the accords . Associated Press writer Matthew Lee in Washington contributed to this report. events.title: Musk pledges 1 SpaceX share for every child in America
events.summary: Elon Musk said Monday he'd give one of his shares in SpaceX to every "kid" in America next year. Why it matters: It'd be a roughly $11 billion giveaway at current stock prices, nearly double Michael Dell's record-breaking Trump accounts gift. What they're saying: " Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post to X just before 4 a.m. ET Monday. He did not specify if "kid" meant all minors under 18 or some other status, nor did he elaborate on what "first of many" meant. He also did not reply to X accounts asking if he meant all kids present in the U.S., or just citizens. By the numbers: Per the Census Bureau, there are just over 72 million people under 18 in the U.S. If each got one SpaceX share, at Friday's closing price of $146.03, that'd be a market value of a little over $10.5 billion. Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares, so the giveaway would make only a small dent in his holdings. Zoom in: Musk's pledge isn't the first from SpaceX. In July the company's COO Gwynne Shotwell said she'd gift a share of the stock to each of 2 million Trump accounts, a gift now worth nearly $300 million. Zoom out: Musk's announcement comes one day after Anthropic said it was setting up a new public benefit fund with 5% of the company's equity, an entity potentially worth $100 billion or more. Musk responded to Anthropic's news by saying "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," later adding "This is what I will be doing." events.title: How AI giants will reshape global philanthropy
events.summary: The AI boom is about to rewrite the rules of global philanthropy, shifting its center of gravity to Silicon Valley, where the IPOs of AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI will create the world's largest charitable organizations. Why it matters: Rather than massive donations earmarked for renaming hospital wings or university graduate programs, expect the new wave of giving to mirror startup culture: flexible capital, ambitious bets and a search for measurable impact. Driving the news: Anthropic announced Sunday that it plans to launch a massive benefit fund with 5% of its shares. Zoom in: The company's pledge — which would amount to $100 billion if it reaches a value of $2 trillion in its IPO — will go to a public benefit fund and is set to grow as its valuation rises. Anthropic says the fund will be a wholly owned LLC, giving it flexibility to make large donations to nonprofits or distribute money directly to specific populations. The commitment builds on the pledges of co-founders to give away 80% of their equity. A program available to early Anthropic hires and used by a large number of company staffers matched donations at a 3:1 ratio. The company says roughly half its employees participate in donation matching. The company says the fund's shares will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or abroad. The big picture: Anthropic is joining OpenAI, which is controlled by a nonprofit foundation that holds a 26% equity stake in the company, worth about $130 billion based on the company's current valuation. The foundation has the power to appoint OpenAI's board. What they're saying: Anthropic says much of its public-benefit work — including AI safety and interpretability research, applied biomedical research and discounts for nonprofits and scientific institutions — will continue inside the company. The new fund is intended to make other kinds of giving possible at greater scale, the company says. Anthropic cited AI's effects on the labor market as one potential use and said it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing that issue, but that "bolder approaches may be needed." Anthropic has not specified what those approaches would be, or whether the fund would make direct payments to workers affected by AI. Between the lines: Anthropic's founders and some employees have close ties to effective altruism, a movement ostensibly dedicated to directing resources toward causes where they may do the most good. Effective altruism has come under sharp criticism from the Trump White House, which has emphasized aspects of the movement that are far from the philanthropic mainstream. Those include an acute interest in animal welfare, as well as seemingly abstract ponderings about the value of life, including comparing that of an infant to an adult, or future people to present people. In an X post , Taylor Budowich, a former White House official, highlighted one such comment from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2010, when he said in a blog post that an adult death is "perhaps 2 or 3 times worse than an infant's death." Budowich also shared a few other "insane beliefs of those who make up Anthropic and how they think about prioritizing charitable giving." The bottom line: Anthropic's fund — and the charitable giving of a massive new cadre of millionaires and deca-millionaires — could become one of the largest vehicles for new giving. The bigger change may come with a new generation of Silicon Valley donors aiming to reset the agenda of modern philanthropy.

events.title: The AI attack-ad nightmare is coming true
events.summary: AI is producing reality-bending midterm ads about defaced Bibles, upscale dinners and a board game with a "Death to America" playing card. Why it matters: The warnings about deepfakes are coming true. Election laws haven't kept pace with a world where campaigns can put words in opponents' mouths and create realistic-looking scenes that didn't happen. The Wesleyan Media Project found $137 million had been spent on 220 AI-generated ads through Oct. 11, mostly from Republicans. Four states have laws prohibiting certain uses of AI-generated deepfakes in political ads, while 27 more require some form of disclosure about their use. No federal law specifically regulates AI-generated political ads. The big picture: An Axios analysis found numerous political ads partly or fully made by generative AI, sometimes undisclosed. Georgia Senate: Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans, has run a series of AI-generated deepfake ads depicting Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff getting beauty treatments. The ads mock Ossoff's reported campaign spending on hair and makeup , saying he "talks pretty" but has "an ugly record" and "a lot to cover up." Ossoff said in a C-SPAN interview : "It is deeply troubling to see ... deepfake videos used to fabricate political advertising. And it's a s lippery slope toward the destruction of truth in political debate, and the ad should come down immediately." The ads don't disclose AI use, which Georgia law doesn't require. Michigan Senate: A super PAC called Front Line Action used AI in an ad depicting Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo with podcaster Hasan Piker and four women wearing niqabs. Another AI-generated scene has El-Sayed playing a Risk-style board game with his half-sister , Eman Abdelhadi, and Piker. It depicts cards bearing statements that include "Death to America," "Do not Celebrate Thanksgiving" and "Celebrate 9/11." The group has defended the ad, telling CNN it is "grounded in El-Sayed's own public statements and documented reporting and records concerning him and individuals associated with or supportive of his campaign." The ad features both a written and spoken disclosure that it was "created in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence." New York governor: Republican Bruce Blakeman's campaign and allied super PACs have repeatedly used generative AI in ads attacking Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, with varying degrees of disclosure. One AI-generated ad released by the Blakeman campaign depicts the Tooth Fairy struggling to come up with cash to give to children, saying she "just can't afford to be the Tooth Fairy in Kathy Hochul's New York." Another Blakesman spot says onscreen: "We asked AI what a truthful Kathy Hochul ad would look like." The ad features AI-generated scenes of Hochul attending an upscale dinner and standing outside a police precinct while a man asks her: "Want some crack?" Pennsylvania governor: A new ad from Republican candidate Stacy Garrity features an AI-generated version of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro talking about taxes, abortion and data centers. The spot puts this quote in his mouth: "This ad was created with AI, thanks to big, beautiful data centers. Fact is, I was the one who fast-tracked data centers right here in PA, right after they handed me $5 million in political contributions." Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder, in a statement to Axios, dismissed the ad as "cheap, dishonest AI bullshit." Texas Senate: Democratic candidate James Talarico has been a consistent target of AI-generated ads from both Republican Ken Paxton's campaign and outside super PACs. A Paxton campaign ad uses AI to depict Talarico defacing a Bible with crayon and saying, "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were." Talarico told NBC he "tried in the legislature to ban AI deepfake videos in political campaigns because they are misleading. They are lying about a candidate in this race." Kentucky's 6th District: No Going Back PAC, backed by President Trump's MAGA Inc., has run several ads using AI to boost Republican congressional candidate Ralph Alvarado. One ad features multiple AI-generated deepfakes of Democrat Zach Dembo, including one scene in which he stares into the camera. "I expected them to lie about my record, but I did not expect them to lie about my appearance," Dembo said in a statement to Axios, adding that "using AI to create fake or misleading images is the beginning of a very dangerous path for our democracy."

events.title: Ken Paxton’s Anti-Abortion Influence Already Extended Beyond Texas. He Could Take It Further in the Senate.
events.summary: Photo illustration by Lisa Larson-Walker/ProPublica. Source images: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images, skaman306/Getty Images, Mike Klein/Getty Images. Early in his tenure as Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton issued a statement commemorating what he believed was a national tragedy. “It’s impossible to fill the void of more than 50 million missing human beings,” he said in 2016. He was marking the 43rd anniversary of Roe v. Wade, the Supreme Court ruling that protected abortion rights — and had long stood in the way of efforts to ban terminations in early pregnancy, when most abortions occur. Paxton spent the years that followed testing Roe’s limits and ultimately prevailed where others had failed: In 2021, he defended a near-total abortion ban that Texas legislators had designed to evade conventional legal challenges. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed it to take effect while Roe remained in force. After the justices overturned Roe the following year, Paxton kept pushing, pursuing new ways to extend the reach of Texas’ restrictions. He prevailed against the Biden administration, picked fights with states that protect abortion access and pioneered strategies that his peers later adopted or expanded. While Paxton’s tenure as attorney general has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum for his personal scandals and alleged misuse of the office , detractors and allies alike agree that his signal achievement as the state’s top legal official has been advancing restrictions on abortion. A close look at his record shows a clear pattern in his successes: He relentlessly tests the limits of the law and employs novel legal strategies to advance his goals. Paxton’s national role as an anti-abortion warrior would change if he wins his U.S. Senate race. As Texas attorney general, he has been able to act largely on his own authority. If he prevails in November, he would become one of 100 senators in a chamber where most legislation needs 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. But allies who have witnessed his victories see an opening. “He’ll have the ability to use some of the laws that he’s defended in Texas as influence to draft legislation in the U.S. Senate,” said Mary Elizabeth Castle, director of government relations at Texas Values, a Christian advocacy group that supports a national abortion ban. Legal experts and advocates on both sides expect he could join colleagues who are pressuring the Food and Drug Administration to revoke its approval of the abortion drug mifepristone. Anti-abortion activists at the state and federal level are also trying to secure legal rights for fetuses, which could have implications for reproductive care like birth control and in vitro fertilization. Paxton, who has called himself a strong supporter of IVF, recently said he was open to restrictions intended to prevent the loss of fertilized eggs. His litigation has also raised questions that experts expect the Supreme Court to confront, including whether a federal law, which mandates hospitals provide stabilizing care to patients having an emergency, overrides state abortion bans; whether to treat a fetus as a separate patient that has its own emergency care rights; and how far states can go in pursuing out-of-state doctors who prescribe abortion medication to patients in states where it’s banned. During the current race, abortion has played a far smaller role than questions about Paxton’s ethics. His Democratic opponent, James Talarico, has said that he supports restoring a federal right to abortion and that his Christian faith calls for an end to “extreme” laws that Paxton has defended and that have forced women to flee the state for emergency abortion care. Lately, Paxton has said little about abortion — an issue on which he has defended restrictions more stringent than many Texans say they want . But those who have watched Paxton extend the reach of Texas law beyond its borders are paying close attention to his Senate bid. Dr. Jennifer Villavicencio, an abortion provider, said she has felt compelled to move her family twice to states with strong laws shielding doctors from out-of-state litigation, partly out of concern that Paxton is creating a blueprint for targeting providers like her. “It’s very disheartening and scary to think that it’s maybe coming to the U.S. Senate,” she said. Photo illustration by Lisa Larson-Walker/ProPublica. Source images: Drew Angerer/Getty Images, Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images. Paxton successfully defended a near-total abortion ban before Roe v. Wade was struck down. When Paxton became Texas attorney general in 2015, there was no ambiguity about where he stood on abortion. Raised by an anti-abortion activist , he married his sweetheart from a Christian college, who spoke proudly about the fact that she was adopted , saying her birth mother “ chose life .” She campaigned for Paxton, but he had his own bona fides. A law he’d co-sponsored as a state senator banned almost all abortions after 20 weeks. Similar 20-week bans had taken root across the country as decades of court rulings chipped away at Roe, but no state had managed to enforce a ban as early as six weeks. More than a dozen tried, passing laws that prohibited abortion when cardiac activity could be detected. One after another, they were blocked by judges. Then, in 2021, a Texas lawyer named Jonathan Mitchell worked with legislators to craft a law that would withstand similar challenges. Instead of having state officials enforce their “heartbeat law,” the new act, referred to as Senate Bill 8, allowed citizens to sue physicians they suspected were providing abortions. The law offered up to $10,000 if they won. When abortion providers and President Joe Biden’s administration separately challenged the law in federal court, Paxton’s office argued that state officials couldn’t be ordered to stop enforcing it because they had no power to do so in the first place. Only private citizens could. “Because the executive officials are expressly prohibited from enforcing SB 8,” his office wrote to the Supreme Court, “there is nothing for a federal court to enjoin.” The Supreme Court agreed that Paxton couldn’t be sued because “the petitioners have not identified any enforcement authority the attorney general possesses in connection with S. B. 8 that a federal court might enjoin him from exercising.” The law remained in effect, becoming the first enforceable six-week ban under Roe. Legislators in Idaho and Oklahoma subsequently passed similar laws. For Dr. Sam Dickman, who worked at a San Antonio Planned Parenthood, the implications were clear: “I was going to need to either entirely change the type of medicine I was providing or leave the state,” he said. He opted for the latter, moving to Montana, where abortion is legal until viability, or roughly 24 weeks. events.title: Building the future of finance in the age of AI
events.summary: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officerat Bloomberg's UK Policy Series. The Mills ReviewThat is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress.Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary.Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

events.title: Disney Asked Character.AI to Go Bankrupt for a Get-Out-of-Lawsuits Card
events.summary: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry , court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand —potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology , and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations. In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders. The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing. The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “ reverse acquihire ,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself. Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress. In the case of Character.AI, a motion filed by Character.AI’s legal counsel says that Disney required that the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy proceedings because of the startup’s “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.” A spokesperson for Character.AI referred WIRED to Disney for comment on whether the deal was contingent on the startup declaring bankruptcy. Disney declined to comment on this story. According to court filings, the deal involves “two interrelated and integrated” transactions—one before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, and one after. As part of the first transaction, which occurred in September, Disney paid the startup $5.5 million, along with a refundable “good faith deposit” of $2 million. Disney also hired the “majority” of Character.AI’s employees, including the CEO, and agreed that it would let some of the now-Disney employees help keep Character.AI operational for five months. Character.AI filed a petition for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12. Through the bankruptcy proceedings, court filings show that Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license for a huge range of Character.AI’s code, documentation, frameworks, tools, and “other artifacts,” including those produced for its trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure, and age-prediction technology. The list of IP included in the filings does not include users’ data (which can get additional protections in bankruptcy proceedings) or Character.AI’s website. That license will be auctioned off in the coming months. If Disney is chosen as the winning bidder by Character.AI and a committee of unsecured creditors—and courts approve the deal—it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment. If Disney is not selected, the company will be refunded the $2 million deposit and receive a breakup fee. In order to “preserve a competitive process,” Disney also agreed to permit the winning bidder to interview and potentially extend offers to up to 80 percent of “certain newly hired employees” that Disney already hired from Character.AI. Disney has the right to select which employees. However, experts worry that bouncing Character.AI employees from one company to another in the span of months is unrealistic, and that the deal Disney and Character.AI have struck cannot be easily unwound. In addition, Disney prepared a draft of a court order referred to as the “363 Free and Clear Order” in the filings, a version of which would be approved by the court at or before closing, that would clarify that this process should not be viewed as a merger of the two companies and that Character.AI would remain responsible for “any liability or other obligation” it might have, including any legal claims against it. A spokesperson for Character.AI said they were unable to speculate on the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings and referred WIRED to the docket.

Source images: Christopher Mark Juhn/Anadolu via Getty Images, Erlon Silva - TRI Digital via Getty Images, Mironov Konstantin via Getty Images. A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it. The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.  The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. “My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.” The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA. Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems.  In Trump’s second term, his administration has laid off or pushed out more than 1,000 CISA employees, shrinking the agency by about one-third. The president’s 2027 budget proposal would reduce funding for the agency by another $700 million, which could necessitate 900 additional layoffs.  In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not being used to support election security as directed by Congress. Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms. “There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.” While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them. Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration. In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections. “They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”  A spokesperson for the White House declined an interview request but defended Trump’s handling of election security in an emailed statement. “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections,” said Lauren Bis.  Bis referred specific questions about CISA’s handling of elections to DHS. DHS and CISA did not respond to interview requests or to a detailed list of questions. “There’s no fucking way [state governments are] ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.” A former federal cybersecurity official who advises state governments Current and former CISA employees and state election officials describe an agency that has become significantly less equipped to help states fight legitimate cyber threats. State leaders say they have used their own resources to shore up gaps left by CISA, such as paying for sensor technology that can detect unusual activity in election networks. But some services, like intel on foreign actors, can’t be replicated. Some people interviewed said they were worried that Trump and his allies continue to ratchet up rhetoric about voting security, particularly about threats to voting machines. Officials in one large voting jurisdiction said they have met privately with machine vendors to come up with a contingency plan if the federal government seizes their machines or declares them unusable. “I don’t pay attention to what the president says. I pay attention to what his administration does,” Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said. “And what they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own.” Defending elections from hackers wasn’t always part of DHS’s remit. Throughout the mid-1990s and 2000s, a series of cyberattacks rocked the federal government, demonstrating the emerging threat. In 2007, hackers broke into the Pentagon and stole terabytes of sensitive data. The digital heist, by an unknown foreign adversary, was so damaging that one intelligence leader later described it as an “espionage Pearl Harbor.” Under George W. Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina. The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure. The office’s work ranged from helping secure events like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity warnings to the private sector and the public. events.title: Democrats face Gaza litmus test
events.summary: The News FREDERICKSBURG, Va. — In a matter of weeks, when the midterm results are tallied and the next campaign begins, Democrats with presidential dreams know the question will be coming. Do Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute genocide? The question flew at Democrats all year. Progressives generally said “yes.” Pro-Israel Democrats said “no.” Many rejected the idea that they had to use that word or were otherwise endorsing every action taken by the Jewish state. As potential Democratic 2028 contenders fan out across the country this month, campaigning with battleground Democrats and building their win/loss scorecards, just two have said “yes” to the question: Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. Khanna has been particularly direct , using interviews and public appearances not only to insist that Israel committed genocide, but also that Democrats who won’t say so are too weak to lead the party. “Israel has committed a genocide in Gaza, and we should have the courage to say so,” Khanna said at the Democratic National Committee’s summer meeting in Texas — a historically red state where this year’s top statewide Democratic nominees, Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, have not gone as far. The question hasn’t dominated the last few weeks of campaigning, with primaries long over and stark differences on Israel between most Democrats and Republicans. Last week, when Ocasio-Cortez made three campaign stops for Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, neither Democrat — and no audience members — brought up the topic of Gaza. But the question still looms over the party’s first wide-open primaries in eight years. They’ll be the first since small armies of activists pressed Democrats to take more progressive positions on immigration , the environment , and criminal justice reform . In retrospect, many Democrats now think that the candidates in 2020 were too willing to bow to pressure with cameras rolling. There is no sign that anyone but Khanna or Ocasio-Cortez is moving towards a new Gaza answer that activists might prefer. “I think we have to acknowledge the seriousness of the issue, the seriousness of what’s happening in Gaza, the seriousness of what’s happening in the West Bank,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told Semafor earlier this month at a campaign stop, when asked why he thought the word “genocide” was so important to many Democrats. Moore has accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of committing war crimes, but hasn’t called the violence in Gaza a genocide. “I think it’ll be up to the voters to decide whether or not they feel that people are meeting the moment,” Moore continued. Know More When the Gaza questions do pick up again, most Democrats are likely to punt to the International Criminal Court — already a popular way to dodge them. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but hasn’t accused Israel of committing genocide. “The question of genocide is a question of whether a government has the specific intent to destroy a national or ethnic group,” Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said in his first debate against challenger Mike Collins this month. “And that is a question for the International Criminal Court.” That answer is unlikely to satisfy many Democratic primary voters, according to a poll of six early primary states conducted by YouGov on behalf of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project. In South Carolina, where Democrats opted to hold their first primary, 57% of likely primary voters said that Israel was “committing genocide against Palestinians.” In the other five early-voting states, the number was much higher: 78% in New Hampshire and Nevada, 76% in New Mexico, and 72% in Virginia. And in Michigan, where El-Sayed has said he will play an active role in the primaries if he wins his Senate race, eight in 10 likely primary voters agreed with the “genocide” term. These are more lopsided numbers than other pollsters have found, but according to an Associated Press survey this summer, half of all Democrats now agree that “genocide” was the appropriate word to describe what they saw happen in Gaza. “It’s certainly been a question that keeps coming up in debates,” said the IMEU Policy Project’s spokesman, Hamid Bendaas. “And I’d expect there will be a key 2028 moment where the candidates are asked to raise their hands with a yes or no.” Some Democrats have tried to cancel the test before they can take it. In March, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear told Politico that “genocide” was “becoming one of those new litmus tests that we said we would never do as a party again.” He wouldn’t answer the question, but assumed he’d be asked again. Democrats uncomfortable with the term have watched how even using it does not stop questions about their commitment to cutting off arms to Israel — the policy fight they expect, with a little less dread, next year. In August, two months after he defeated Rep. Dan Goldman in New York’s Democratic primary, Brad Lander joined a protest of a Hindu nationalist politician in Manhattan and was filmed being heckled as a “zionist” — even though he said that the war “meets the definition of genocide.” Last month, after Drop Site and New York magazine reported that consultants were urging Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson not to say “genocide” so much, supporters began asking him about the war again, worried that he’d gone wobbly. David’s view If Israel elects another government led by Netanyahu, just days before the US midterms, the nuanced answers that many Democrats give to the “genocide” question will grow even trickier to land. The party has already shifted leftward. Rahm Emanuel’s endorsement of conditions on aid was an early signal that the field engaged in the “invisible primary” would be less pro-Israel than Joe Biden. But most of the likely Democratic candidates simply don’t agree that a genocide happened in Gaza, and reject the question’s premise. “Having one conversation about one country means you are politicizing a term that has huge, historic, moral complications,” Emanuel told Meet the Press this month. Still, it’s possible public pressure — including demonastrations organized by interest groups — changes their stances. Eight years ago, protesters frequently drove coverage in their preferred direction by disrupting candidates (Movimiento Cosecha pushed Biden to endorse a deportation moratorium, for instance) and showing up to press them at Q&As. Kamala Harris’ defeat convinced some Democratic strategists, like the big-tenters at Third Way and the Searchlight Institute, that Democratic candidates were too easily moved by activists, and that voters held this against them. It in turn fostered a reluctance to let activists shape their next primary. This is the topic that will stir those emotions next. events.title: The national intelligence chief steering AI
events.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has received mostly positive marks so far in Washington as chair of the Trump administration’s AI task force , which is focusing on using current law to get AI companies to behave responsibly. A number of people familiar with Clayton’s work tell Semafor his experience at the Securities and Exchange Commission and Office of the Director of National Intelligence aligns well with the two areas threatened the most by advanced AI: finance and national security. “He is hyper-competent and a problem-solver with good instincts, and that’s why he’s so valued,” one former White House official told Semafor. “He’s just a guy who doesn’t f*ck up and delivers results that they need and want, and so they just keep promoting him, because there aren’t a lot of those.” Paul Lekas, executive vice president for policy at the Software & Information Industry Association, said Clayton’s role atop the task force “signals that the White House is focused on the national security dimension of super intelligence.” Three industry sources told Semafor that the task force is now focused on staffing up to carry out its work. As far as Clayton’s future goes, one tech lobbyist told Semafor to watch what happens on day 121 (the task force’s work is supposed to be completed in 120 days). “If [Clayton] can get agencies approaching AI from very different directions to keep sharing information, coordinating decisions and agreeing on responsibilities … his influence will last well beyond any one appointment,” the lobbyist said. Others are skeptical the task force can accomplish much in such a short time period, arguing that eventually sweeping new legislation will be needed to regulate AI.

events.title: White House allies play midterms blame game
events.summary: Trump administration officials and allies are starting to debate who will shoulder the blame if Republicans perform poorly in November. The White House has witnessed an uptick in drama driven by the midterms, from maneuvering to replace chief of staff Susie Wiles to finger-pointing at James Blair, President Donald Trump’s outside adviser whose recent work trip to Republika Srpska frustrated the president because of its proximity to the November elections. Wiles seems safe; Trump has issued multiple emphatic endorsements of his chief of staff. Some suggest Blair will get blamed, though his tension with Trump has subsided for now. Others predict Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could draw ire due to the unpopular Iran war. It all depends on how Republicans measure up to the dire predictions — sources close to the White House say Republicans holding onto the Senate is likely to satisfy Trump at this point. The White House dismissed the talk as “armchair” speculation. “These armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation to Semafor have no idea what they’re talking about and are focused on themselves, not helping the President,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said. “President Trump is laser-focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress this November, which is why he is traveling across the country highlighting the historic victories his Administration has delivered for the American people.” — Shelby Talcott

events.title: UAE amends e-invoicing regulations as implementation deadline draws closer
events.summary: The UAE's Ministry of Finance has made amendments to its e-invoicing system that will apply to value-added tax filing in the country from next year. Authorities are introducing a temporary exclusion for business transactions between entities that are members of the same tax group for two years, starting from January 1, 2027, the Ministry of Finance said on Monday. Such transactions will be treated as "excluded transactions" throughout the 24-month period, "giving businesses greater flexibility and more time to adapt to the system", the ministry said. David Daly, a partner at Gulf Tax Accounting Group, said the move was "welcome", but more clarity would be needed to understand specific details. For instance, in a scenario where each entity also issues invoices to non-tax group members, it still needs to be known whether these must be managed through the e-invoicing system, he said. The ministry's latest decision also amends article 11 on the storage of electronic invoice and electronic credit note data. Under the amended provision, entities must retain all electronic invoices, electronic credit notes and any associated data for the period prescribed under the Tax Procedures Law, and ensure that such records can be provided to the Federal Tax Authority on request, the ministry said. The decision "removes the previous requirement that such data be stored within the UAE, thereby shifting the focus from the location of storage to the retention and accessibility of records for tax compliance purposes", it added. The amendments also remove the requirement for companies to notify the FTA of a system failure within two business days of it happening. The ministry said the amendments are aimed at improving the ease of doing business in the UAE "by reducing operational burdens on businesses, providing greater flexibility during the implementation of the electronic invoicing system, and ensuring that regulatory requirements support an efficient and business-friendly environment". The latest decision comes as the first major compliance requirement in the phased transition to e-invoicing approaches on October 30. The ministry extended the deadline for appointing an accredited service provider (ASP) for businesses in the UAE with annual revenue of Dh50 million ($13.6 million) or more to October 30, from July 1, under the first phase of the programme. Under the UAE's unified e-invoicing model, all qualifying transactions must be validated and sent through an ASP.

events.title: Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Physical AI is the deployment of machines with autonomy, acting within the real world. It is not a single product, but a philosophy built on modular architectures. These systems can only be developed with a full systems approach, integrating sensors, actuators, and distributed compute systems, in a multi-physics methodology. Real-time constraints become much more important than in the past, and at the same time much more complex. Physical AI is changing how chips are designed and used, integrating sensing, AI inference, and real-time control into machines that can safely and predictably interact with the physical world. The challenges extend well beyond just performance. Engineers need to account for corner cases stemming from unpredictable environments, ensure these systems are safe and reliable, and they need to future-proof these systems by ensuring they are serviceable and upgradable. This will require new tools and methodologies, as well as some new design approaches. “AI is leaving the screen,” says Anthony Matarazzo, head of physical AI, digital twins, simulation-driven AI, and accelerated computing at Synopsys . “It is no longer about generating text or code. It is entering the physical world. It needs to understand, interact, sense, make decisions in a physical environment. We are moving from generative AI to agentic workflow orchestration to physical AI (see figure 1.) That is literally making intelligence actionable. But the consequences of being wrong fundamentally change. Life or death, plus or minus 1%.” Fig. 1: Three Eras of AI. Source: Synopsys Physical AI must see and interact with the real world. “It is challenging to make artificial intelligence see the world correctly,” says Chun-Ting “Tim” Wang-Lee, signal integrity application scientist at Keysight EDA . “Real-world information comes from the sensors, and the data has to be moved somewhere and processed so that the AI can decide and then act. There are decisions that need to be made.” This changes the design priorities. “Physical AI usually gets framed as a compute story,” says Justin Endo, director for marketing and sales at Mixel , A Silvaco Company. “But from our perspective it has really been an imaging story. Every robot, drone, and autonomous system comes down to cameras feeding an inference engine.” Physical AI builds on some of the connectivity and sensing technologies developed for the Internet of Things. “IoT was largely about connecting and monitoring things,” says Brad Rex, head of physical AI, UX at Renesas Electronics. “Physical AI is about giving machines the ability to perceive and act autonomously in unstructured environments. This is a completely orthogonal engineering problem, and it requires a step-change in system-level content — more sensing, more real-time compute, more sophisticated power management, and more safety considerations per device.” Within physical AI, there are two distinct classes of devices: “Those that can rely on a cloud connection and those that must operate fully locally without relying on connectivity,” says Ashley Stevens, director of product management and marketing at Arteris . “For example, vehicles cannot rely on continuous connectivity, as there are many locations where cellular coverage is inadequate. In contrast, an industrial robotic arm moves but is constrained to a particular location within a factory setting, and therefore can be connected to the cloud.” Others agree. “Unlike traditional AI applications that primarily generate information, physical AI systems influence real-world outcomes through continuous interaction with their environment,” says William Chen, product marketing group director for design IP at Cadence . “Traditional IoT often focused on collecting and transmitting data. Physical AI adds real-time interpretation and action. The result is a shift from connected devices to intelligent systems operating within sensing and control loops.” This requires new architectures and new methodologies. “The entire architecture is very different,” says Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at Vinci . “Time-to-market is going to be much slower because people are still learning. Physical AI is the next step that they want, but the switch to it is not going to be easy. The easiest entry point will be a repetitive action, but people are not willing to pay much for that. They want it to do a lot more. That’s why it is going to take a more complex architecture to build, make reliable, and make it work for at least a day on a single charge.” It also requires significant processing power. “Robotics and drones require powerful, efficient compute capable of multimodal processing and accurate, real-time responsiveness in dynamic settings,” says Sameer Sharma, associate vice president for MediaTek’s IoT business. “Because of latency and bandwidth constraints, these devices require silicon capable of handling AI workloads at the edge, including AI acceleration for machine vision and object classification.” As systems get larger or more capable, additional challenges emerge. “You need longer reach through moving joints, aggregation of many cameras into few ports, and the functional safety expectations coming over from automotive,” says Mixel’s Endo. “But the standard is already moving in that direction. The mobile camera interface is becoming the robot’s optic nerve, and that mobile-proven maturity is hard for any alternative to match.” How quickly physical AI is adopted by different markets will vary, but the overall projections are noteworthy. At a high level, PwC estimates the global physical AI market will reach ~€430 billion by 2030, with “significant upside potential as systems scale and mature.” Deloitte, meanwhile, found that 58% of companies report at least limited use of physical AI today, with that number projected to rise to 80% within two years. Not all sectors will adopt this technology at the same time. “Physical AI is not just AI at the edge,” says Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategic programs for system solutions at Synopsys. “It is broader than just robotics, but it will be uneven. The question is how quickly each industry will adopt physical AI. It requires you to go beyond the chip to the full physics. The growth inflection comes when you have this full loop of sensing, reasoning, physical action, and then autonomy. events.title: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
events.summary: U.S. consumers are uneasy about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting prices U.S. consumers aren't just frustrated with high prices . They're angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don’t understand and personal data they may not realize they’re sharing has touched a nerve. “There are major tensions happening right now between who’s really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper,” said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney. Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren’t used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. “We price the product, not the person,” Furner wrote. But companies aren't always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it's used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers’ faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said. Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny. What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand . An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber's practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing. Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers’ assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager. What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags. Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology. The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don’t necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found “virtually no surge pricing” after the labels were introduced. “Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today,” Farquhar said. Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony 'United in grief': 4 dead, 39 injured in explosion at Canadian military training base Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term “surveillance pricing" for the same practice. Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices.

events.title: Four years of Semafor
events.summary: We have been asked a lot lately: When we launched Semafor four years ago, is this what we were expecting? Did we think it would get this much traction, this fast? What has surprised us? The truth is that we would have been pleased four years ago to know the current state of Semafor — a respected brand, a brilliant newsroom, a strong, profitable business. But surprised? The honest answer is no. It took a lot of optimism to launch a new media company in 2022. This was informed optimism, however: We share a deep belief in how much the talented people we hoped we could hire could accomplish through incredibly hard work. And we were always thinking big. What’s so exciting right now is that Semafor is starting to emerge clearly as the thing that we hoped it would become — shaped and driven by our growing team in ways we couldn’t have imagined. We launched with the insight that a leadership audience — CEOs and political leaders alike — was, paradoxically, the most desperate for efficient, fair, and sophisticated news. Then, no CEO or head of state had heard of us; now, we have 1.2 million subscriptions to our briefings, and more than 16,000 people have attended our convenings around the world. We launched with global ambitions — but footprints only in the US and Africa, a start in the world’s most developed media market and one in its fastest-growing. Now we have journalists in 11 countries, scoops and email briefings and events with deep audiences in Africa and the Gulf, and we’re sprinting toward a launch in Asia next year. Our thesis at launch was that “events” was a journalism business that could help power the business of journalism. Our biggest upside surprise is how fast that’s happened, and the extent to which we quickly outgrew the category of “media events” and moved into another one: signature convenings that set the global agenda and serve both as festivals of news and crucial spaces for conversation and connection. Perhaps most important, we launched with a deep sense that audiences — buffeted by the hyper-polarizing, hyper-toxic environment in which social media had become the tail wagging the dog of journalism — wanted a new approach. And we’re so proud to have defined a style and brand of journalism that separates facts and opinion, has an eye on its own blind spots, and leaves space for reasonable disagreement, on stage, on the page, and in the other places our journalism appears. This moment feels to us the way it did in 2022 — the bullet train has just left the platform, and everyone here at Semafor is finding their feet again. We anticipate closing this year substantially bigger than the last by tangible and intangible metrics — revenue and profitability and reach, impact, and brand. And, as everyone here can feel, we’re pressing for a defining fifth year, in which we start to feel the promise of a true global journalism brand that convenes the most important conversations in the world, starting this November in Silicon Valley. We launched this project in 2022 with some ideas about what could be done. But as our colleagues have heard us both say: This is a business of people and execution. The ideas on paper are worth little. And none of it matters much without you, our community. Thank you for joining us here and please keep all of it — the ideas, tips, criticism, and feedback — coming.
