events.title: How CBS News’ Middle East war spread to the Upper Midwest
events.summary: The News Control of the US Senate for the next two years could come down to how much the news media chooses to focus in the final weeks of the midterms on a tweet sent years ago by the younger half-sister of Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate. In 2012, Abdul El-Sayed’s half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, described “an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early ’70s.” Republicans and members of the media have since pressed El-Sayed, an American of Egyptian descent, to answer whether he has ties to the Islamist movement, which was founded in Egypt and whose offshoots include US-designated terrorist groups. The subject is of particular interest at CBS News, where Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss has repeatedly encouraged the network’s journalists to dedicate serious resources to finding a potential link. In recent weeks, Weiss has personally advocated for CBS News journalists to pursue numerous story angles related to El-Sayed’s supposed sympathy towards the Muslim Brotherhood, and was directly involved in a controversial story about his previous posts comparing the COVID-19 death toll to 9/11. She has discussed the topic on editorial calls, and tasked CBS News’ investigative unit with combing through El-Sayed’s background for a potential link to the organization. The network’s investigative team is set to publish a story in the coming days on the subject, though two people familiar with the reporting said that as of Sunday afternoon, it was unclear whether the story will include new revelations . A year into a new regime at CBS News, some of the daily controversies over Weiss’ management style and relations with the White House that defined the first few months have eased. But the politics of the Middle East and the conflict in Israel and Gaza — and its echoes in American domestic politics — remain red-hot inside the company, as a network leader with strong views on the region’s dynamics has attempted to shape its coverage of stories touching its spiraling conflicts. Rank-and-file staff have clashed with editors installed by Weiss over Gaza, leaking embarrassing internal network discussions about coverage — such as last week, when the media-focused news startup Status and Guardian media reporter Jeremy Barr reported on a clash between CBS News’ London bureau and foreign editor Shayndi Raice. Weiss has taken a particularly hands-on approach to the Michigan Senate race, where campaign rhetoric has revolved around El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, and whether he can win over Jewish voters in the state. The Hollywood Reporter reported last month that Weiss faced criticism internally for “overseeing an article that critics say falsely insinuated Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed had ties to the September 11 attacks.” Some CBS News staff have privately grumbled that Weiss is particularly focused on pursuing theories about high-profile progressive candidates that bubble up on X or in right-leaning news outlets. Weiss also tasked staff with pursuing the theory that Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico was in a mental health facility after he disappeared from the campaign trail for over a week in October. He was at home with the flu, journalists from The New York Times confirmed, citing images from Talarico’s home security cameras. (CBS News never gave public credence to the theories and matched the Times’ reporting .) Two CBS News staffers complained that the network has focused on pursuing thin theories about progressive candidates but hasn’t treated conservatives the same way. “Bari’s ideas routinely come from social media influencers or from opposition research that’s been placed in conservative outlets, and those stories usually leave out important context and facts,” one CBS News staffer in New York told Semafor. “She seems more suited to editing at publications like City Journal, The Free Press, or The [Washington] Free Beacon, which take a clear side on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and match her views.” It’s unclear whether the network’s pursuit of the Muslim Brotherhood story will impact its ability to engage with El-Sayed. The candidate, whose relishing of combative interviews and debates verges occasionally on smugness, was slated to potentially appear on before the November election, people familiar with the planning said. Know More The purported relationship between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood has been the subject of political interest since his unsuccessful bid for Michigan governor in 2018. He has disavowed and strenuously denied any ties to the group, and his campaign and its allies say the attacks are thinly veiled Islamophobia; El-Sayed has grown visibly irritated in public when pressed on it. “Judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who’s ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution,” El-Sayed said in response to a question about it from Semafor . He said it was “insane” to extrapolate a connection and said he didn’t “know what my mother was doing in Egypt in the 1970s.” “My parents got divorced when I was very young — 3,” El-Sayed said. “I didn’t see my mom for years after I was raised by my dad and my stepmom, and when I asked, [to] the best of my knowledge, nobody in my family’s been a member of this organization.” Max’s view When Weiss took over CBS News, her history as The New York Times’ anti-woke columnist, combined with owner David Ellison’s overt suggestions to President Donald Trump that he would change the network if federal regulators approved his corporate deals, stoked fear that the network would be refashioned in an aggressively pro-Trump direction. The network has not become a mouthpiece for Trump. Without apparent incident, CBS News has regularly published information critical of the Trump administration and its policies. Major reports about its immigration actions and pay-for-play operations have gotten significant airtime on the network and praise from Weiss. The network does appear to have a more friendly relationship with the White House than it did, and has occasionally used that for access. But Vice President JD Vance faced his most challenging media appearance in months during a CBS News town hall last week where he was asked about the shaky US economy, the war in Iran, and self-dealing and corruption within the Trump administration. Still, if the new CBS is managing to hold the center in Washington, there’s been a far more dramatic shift in coverage of Israel and Gaza. Weiss has personally been involved in stories about Israeli settler violence. Claire Day, CBS News’ London bureau chief, was reportedly forced out over friction with Weiss regarding Middle East coverage. events.title: Rivals pile on Beshear over his resistance to Latinos' push for Texas funds
events.summary: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is in open war with prominent Latino lawmakers, and his potential 2028 rivals for president are taking advantage. Beshear, as head of the Democratic Governors Association (DGA), has resisted pressure from Latino leaders to invest heavily in Gina Hinojosa 's campaign for Texas governor, opting to focus on races in other states. In response, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker , California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore have given money to Hinojosa's bid to unseat Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) — and earned praise from Latino lawmakers. Why it matters: The back-and-forth amounts to one of the first fights of the 2028 Democratic primary, against the backdrop of the party's desperation to reverse the GOP's recent gains among Latino voters . Latino leaders are trying to flex their political muscle, fueled in part by Democrats' new primary schedule, which has Nevada and New Mexico — and their large Latino populations — the second and fourth states to vote in the nominating contest. Driving the news: In recent weeks Latino leaders have gone public in their pressure campaign to push Beshear to invest $10 million in Texas, as polls have shown Hinojosa ahead or within the polls' margin of error. Beshear, mindful of how expensive it is to campaign statewide in Texas and the DGA's limited resources, resisted and instead focused the committee's resources on governor's races in critical states like Nevada, Georgia, Arizona, Wisconsin and Ohio. Pritzker, a potential 2028 rival to Beshear who already had donated $200,000 to Hinojosa's campaign, then publicly announced he was donating an additional $1 million to Hinojosa. That won the Illinois governor, a billionaire who has strategically spread some of his personal wealth across the party, some fans. "When Latino leaders asked for the cavalry, JB Pritzker sent it, putting $1.2 million behind Gina Hinojosa because he knows the race is winnable," Cristóbal Alex, board chair of the Latino Victory Fund, told Axios. Alex noted that Pritzker, who hosted a fundraiser for the Latino Victory Fund, has "put his resources and his time into Hispanic candidates and voters around the country." Newsom, meanwhile, sent a fundraising email that brought in $75,000 for Hinojosa. Moore privately told the DGA to reallocate $100,000 from his reelection campaign to Texas, two Democratic officials told Axios. Beshear, who personally donated $25,000 to Hinojosa's campaign, ultimately announced the DGA would give her team $1 million — 10% of the original ask and a small commitment for a big state like Texas. The money arrived this past week, according to a source familiar with the situation. The intrigue: Several Latino leaders and lawmakers were furious that Beshear didn't attend a Zoom call with them and the DGA on Oct. 7 to discuss the Texas race. "It just baffles me that someone who was even thinking of 2028 would disrespect us and not meet," Rep. Silvia Garcia (D-Texas) told Axios, noting that seven Latino members of Congress were on the call. "Just freaking five minutes on a Zoom … and excuse yourself." "I really felt like he disrespected the group, and that he is going to have a serious Latino problem if he doesn't know how to do the outreach and the communication that's going to need to get us to the White House." Beshear's critics note he had time this fall for a book tour when, they argue, he could have been raising more money for the DGA. The other side: Several Democrats told Axios that they believe the DGA made the right strategic decision to send money to other states. Some of the Latino leaders pressuring Beshear also were consultants who stood to make money if he invested heavily in Texas. Many Latino leaders claim they speak for Latino voters, but have been proved wrong in recent elections, as Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) and others have pointed out. Nevada, Georgia, Wisconsin, and Arizona are swing states likely to be more critical than Texas for a Democrat to get 270 Electoral College votes in 2028. What they're saying: DGA communications director Sam Newton told Axios: "Unfortunately for the D.C. staffers who are personally obsessed with 2028 and manufacturing Democratic infighting, the DGA and our chair Gov. Beshear, along with all of our Democratic governors, remain solely focused on beating Trump and Republicans to win as many of our high-stakes 36 races for governor as possible." A person familiar with conversation within the DGA conversations told CNN that their internal polls had Hinojosa trailing Abbott by 5 points, but Hinojosa's campaign this week released an internal poll showing her up by 2. The DGA didn't respond to questions about the discrepancy and pointed Axios to its promotion of the poll showing Hinojosa up by 2. The bottom line: Even some Democrats who think the DGA made the right financial decision not to invest heavily in Texas think Beshear mishandled the politics of the situation. If he can't handle the politics of being DGA chair, they argue, how could he handle a presidential campaign, and potentially the White House?

events.title: Zelensky speaks to Witkoff and Kushner amid U.S.-Ukraine crisis
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke Sunday with President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the crisis between the countries and U.S. efforts to resume peace talks with Russia. Why it matters: It was the first call between Zelensky and senior U.S. officials since tensions spiked between their countries after Trump cut a diesel deal with Russia 10 days ago. During the call that lasted around 40 minutes, Zelensky discussed with Trump's envoy the possibility of holding an in-person meeting in the coming days. The latest: Trump defended his decision to grant a waiver related to sanctions pushed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), saying he didn't want to jeopardize negotiations with Russia. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump also accused Zelensky of targeting Russian diesel refineries and not wanting to end the war. Driving the news: The call took place amid assertions by Zelensky that the Trump administration was behind restrictions imposed on the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems used by the Ukrainian military. "Who made this decision? I don't know. I think that this is really both [a White House and SpaceX] decision. If President Trump will decide tomorrow, or better today, if he will personally decide to lift this decision, it will immediately work as it was before," Zelensky said on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday. He added, "The message came from [the U.S.] government. I don't know from whom. It's the opinion of our generals, of our government, and of course also my opinion, that it was a message from the American government to limit the speed. And technically, SpaceX did it." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the U.S. government was not involved in the Starlink restrictions and said it has been restored. Ukrainian officials dispute that. Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from President Trump.

events.title: 95% of MAGA Republicans approve of Trump. For non-MAGA Republicans, it's 47%.
events.summary: Three national polls show President Trump's approval rating hitting new lows as Democrats lead Republicans by 8 to 10 points ahead of the midterms. Why it matters: Republicans need Trump's loyalists to turn out, but embracing an unpopular president risks alienating independents they need to win competitive races . Driving the news: New polls from the Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos , NBC News and Fox News put Trump's approval at 33%, 34% and 36%, respectively — record or second-term lows in each survey. Democrats lead Republicans by eight points in the Post poll, nine points in Fox's and 10 points in NBC's among registered voters. Once a strength, the economy is now Trump's main vulnerability. Just 21% approve of his handling of the cost of living in the Post poll, 27% in NBC's and 22% approve of his handling of inflation in Fox's. Even Republicans are souring: Fox and NBC both find Trump's approval among Republicans at 76%, while the Post puts it at 79%. Zoom in: Republicans face a growing divide within their party. Fox reports 95% approval of Trump among self-described MAGA Republicans, versus 47% among non-MAGA Republicans. The Post finds 75% of MAGA Republicans say they're certain to vote or have already voted, compared with 57% of non-MAGA Republicans. The Post poll also says 37% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents want GOP leaders to take the party in a different direction from Trump, an all-time high. The big picture: A Reuters review published earlier this month found that Republican candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races either broke with Trump on policy or downplayed their ties to him. At least a dozen of those candidates removed Trump's name, image or endorsement from their campaign websites, according to Reuters. Even some Trump voters see the problem: A Politico poll found 26% of people who voted for Trump in 2024 believe Republican candidates would be better off breaking with him. What they're saying: " Distancing yourself in general, that isn't anything new," Principles First executive director and Republican political strategist Brittany Martinez told Axios. "But Republicans, many Republicans, all over the country … intentionally, strategically" moving away from him "speaks volumes." She noted some Republicans have criticized his policies without directly blaming him, pointing to an ad from Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) that warned Trump he should be careful about what his advisers were telling him about immigration policy. Kentucky Senate nominee Andy Barr , Florida gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds and Georgia gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson are are among the candidates who removed references to Trump from their websites. What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress." Donalds' campaign comms director Gates McGavick said the congressman is "proud to have President Trump's endorsement." A White House official told Axios there's no distance between Trump and candidates. Several candidates still sport their Trump ties front and center. Between the lines: Republicans still appear with him, even if they don't always agree with his policies. Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton has privately lamented the impact of the Iran war and gas prices on his campaign. But he also appeared onstage with Trump at a campaign rally. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who is also locked in a tight Senate race, called for an end to the war in Iran, citing high fuel prices for Iowans. Days later, she appeared in the Oval Office alongside Trump and fellow lawmakers. The bottom line: Republican candidates are trying to hold onto Trump's devoted base without letting his growing unpopularity define their campaigns.

events.title: Wright calls Trump's diesel deal a peace incentive. Rubio says Russia would sell anyway.
events.summary: President Trump's top aides offered sharply different explanations this weekend of his Russian diesel deal amid a barrage of bipartisan criticism calling the move a gift to Russia. Why it matters: Oil , gas and petroleum products help finance Russia's war on Ukraine, and Trump's moves are bringing rifts within the GOP just ahead of midterm elections. Catch up quick: Late Friday, Trump waived new sanctions against Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act he signed last month. That came just days after the administration waived certain sanctions as part of a deal aimed at enabling higher exports of Russian diesel after high prices have become a political millstone for Republicans. Driving the news: Energy Secretary Chris Wright argued Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" that Russia could only benefit from the diesel deal if it scales back its war on Ukraine enough to increase exports. "This is a carrot to try to end a war. It's not an economic lifeline for Russia," he said. Yet Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a different explanation Saturday, saying Russia would have sold the diesel regardless of Trump's intervention. "That diesel was going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, per a State Department transcript. The diesel deal "is an incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC's "This Week." Context: Ukranian drone strikes against Russian refineries have dramatically hindered Russia's diesel exports. Ukraine resumed those strikes after Russia continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, despite Trump's claim that the two sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire. The combination of the Iran war — which has throttled supply and damaged Middle East refineries — and Russia's export decline have pushed up diesel costs. Zoom out: The Sunday shows and Rubio's remarks provided the Trump team's most detailed comments on Friday night's executive order , which declines to use new powers under the law named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The move avoids putting fresh pressure on China and India, both major buyers of Russian oil. Rubio said Trump wants time to "analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy." Wright pointed to ongoing negotiations with China on trade and the war in Ukraine, stressing to CNN that Trump retains the power to impose the penalties later. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on NBC's "Meet the Press," defended the recent decisions by pointing to sanctions the administration imposed on Russian oil and gas giants Rosneft and Lukoil in 2025. "No one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump," he said. The other side: A number of Republicans have criticized the White House. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) called the sanctions waiver "beyond irresponsible," while Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said the late Lindsey Graham "would be appalled." Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) called the waiver a "mistake," and Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) said the U.S. should be increasing pressure on Russia and requested a classified briefing on the decision. What we're watching: As the midterms hit their final frenzied weeks, Republicans have shown an increasing willingness to put distance between themselves and Trump.

events.title: Trump tells Axios why he endorsed Netanyahu's reelection
events.summary: President Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, just nine days before Israel's Oct. 27 elections. Why it matters: Trump's decision to weigh in nine days ahead of the election could give Netanyahu a boost at a critical moment in the Israeli leader's fight for political survival, with most polls showing his coalition falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government. This is the first time in the history of the U.S.–Israel relations that a U.S. president explicitly and publicly endorsed a candidate in the Israeli elections . What he is saying: In a Sunday post on Truth Social , Trump called Netanyahu "a Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a "great partner" in the war against Iran. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work [in Iran] ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote. Trump called Netanyahu "the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel" and gave him his "Complete and Total Endorsement." Behind the scenes: Trump began planning his endorsement earlier this week. "I was always going to do that. I just didn't want to do it too soon," Trump told Axios in a short phone interview on Sunday. Trump said he endorsed Netanyahu because they have a "good relationship" and would "continue to do well" together if Netanyahu is reelected. "It is important that Israel has a person they can count on," Trump said. Asked if he could work with another Israeli leader, Trump said: "Maybe I will, maybe I won't. Who wants to take the chance?" The other side: Netanyahu thanked Trump for his endorsement in an X post. "Together we will complete the mission," Netanyahu wrote . Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, told Israel's Channel 12 that he respects the U.S. president and appreciates what he has done for Israel. "But the elections are a domestic Israeli issue. The only ones who will decide are the citizens of Israel, and I will stand firm on this," Eisenkot said. The big picture: Trump had repeatedly declined to endorse Netanyahu in recent months amid growing tensions between the two leaders over Iran and Gaza. ⁠Some of Netanyahu's rivals urged Trump to remain neutral, Axios previously reported . Some of Trump's closest advisers believed his Middle East agenda would fare better if Netanyahu lost and a different government formed. Trump himself has been very frustrated with Netanyahu, including in recent weeks. In private conversations, Trump blamed Netanyahu for Israel's failures to prevent the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks. Trump called the prime minister "his own worst enemy" and questioned whether Netanyahu was damaging Israel's international reputation, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president. However, Trump decided to stick with Netanyahu. Driving the news: Netanyahu and Trump discussed two weeks ago the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, Axios reported . Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward accepting Netanyahu's proposal and resuming attacks, but he grew more hesitant and decided to wait until after the elections. In his endorsement, Trump seemed to suggest he would let Netanyahu strike Iran after the midterm elections, saying "we will soon finish the job." This is a breaking news story. events.title: Trump once questioned Obama's citizenship. Now Obama is speaking out for Ilhan Omar.
events.summary: Former President Barack Obama issued a forceful denunciation of the Trump administration's legal pursuit of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar over suspicions she fraudulently obtained U.S. citizenship decades ago, an allegation the Minnesota lawmaker has called "disgusting lies." Why it matters: Obama — who faced false claims for years from Donald Trump that he wasn't an American citizen — is selective about when he weighs in on political issues or the president. His decision to speak out reflects his view that the DOJ raid on Omar's home last week was a betrayal of American values. What he's saying: " The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar's political views," Obama wrote on X . "Because if this becomes the new normal, there's no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same." Driving the news: Federal agents raided Omar's Washington home Monday, seizing her phone as part of an investigation into whether she or her late father provided false information on immigration paperwork 26 years ago. The Wall Street Journal reported the administration aims to build "a case to strip her of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her." Omar arrived in the U.S. from Somalia in 1995 as a child. She became a citizen through her father's naturalization in 2000 when records indicate she was 17. But investigators are seeking evidence that she was a year older and therefore not automatically eligible for citizenship. Flashback: The first Trump administration reviewed similar allegations in 2019, including questions about her birth date and her father's immigration, but found insufficient evidence to pursue a full investigation, the Washington Post reported . The allegation gained attention through a viral claim on social media, according to the Post . The other side: Omar has denounced the investigation as a witch hunt meant to intimidate one of Trump's fiercest critics in Congress. Democrats have called it an abuse of power — especially just weeks before an election. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro also said her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures, despite a congressional watchdog's recommendation last month to dismiss allegations of misconduct related to the filings. Zoom in: Obama's more than 400-word statement was a full-throated denunciation of the Trump administration. "Think about that. The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president. And it's not the first time this has happened," he wrote. He added, "In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case. But not before Congresswoman Omar's life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she's been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota."
